Claude Architect Workshop

One story, Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. Each lesson is a claim you test by running the agent: watch it fail, fix it, then prove the fix.

How each lesson runs

  • I do: Watch the failure and its fix.
  • We do: Change one setting at a time and predict.
  • You do: Fix the starting code, then test yourself.
  • Check: exam-style questions, each with why every option is right or wrong.
  • Play: one short drill on a mistake the quiz does not cover.
  • References: the primary sources, each with a line on why to read it.

Foundations, lesson 1

The agent loop

An agent is a loop that ends on stop_reason

Your support agent needs four tool calls to refund one order. Its loop stops when the reply says done, or after three turns. So the refund never runs, and nothing reports that work was left. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch the loop fail, then fix it so the API decides when the work is over.

I doWatch the failure and its fix.

One loop, four tools, one refund

The loop is the code around Claude. It sends the system prompt and the history, runs the tools Claude asks for, and sends the results back. Claude decides, the loop runs, and only code can guarantee anything. The history holds three kinds of turn: user, assistant and tool_result.

A refund needs four tools in a fixed order: get_customer takes the email, lookup_order takes the customer id, check_return_window takes the order, and process_refund pays. The next tool depends on the last result, so the plan adapts as results arrive.

Four calls in a row end in a refund

Each card is one tool call; open it to read it field by field. Every reply carries a stop_reason, the field that says why Claude stopped. Here it is tool_use, which means Claude wants a tool run, and the tool_use block carries an id, a name and an input. The loop answers with a tool_result block that repeats that id.

The loop stopped only when Claude stopped asking. Nothing counted turns and nothing read the words.

Ended on end_turn after 4 tool calls. 1 refund paid.

The stop rule is a few lines

This loop decides from the words in the reply. If Claude writes "done", it stops, and it never runs more than three turns. Text is not a signal: a customer can ask for it, and Claude can write it early.

Every turn also resends the whole history, so each request is longer than the last. A five-turn refund sends 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 messages.

starter/loop.py
1"""The agent loop for the Lumen Supply support agent.2`box.ask(messages)` sends the conversation to Claude and returns its reply.3`box.answer(call)` runs one tool call and returns its `tool_result` block.4"""56from app.agent import Box7from kit.api import Json89MAX_TURNS = 3101112def reply_text(response: Json) -> str:13 """The words Claude wrote in one reply."""14 blocks = [b for b in response["content"] if b["type"] == "text"]1516 return " ".join(str(b["text"]) for b in blocks)171819def next_step(response: Json) -> str:20 """Say whether the loop goes on: "continue" or "stop"."""21 # TODO(workshop): decide from response["stop_reason"], not from the text.22 if "done" in reply_text(response).lower():23 return "stop"2425 return "continue"262728def run(ticket: str, box: Box) -> None:29 """Work one ticket until Claude has finished."""30 messages = [{"role": "user", "content": ticket}]3132 for _ in range(MAX_TURNS):33 response = box.ask(messages)34 if next_step(response) == "stop":35 return3637 calls = [b for b in response["content"] if b["type"] == "tool_use"]38 if not calls:39 return4041 messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response["content"]})42 messages.append(43 {"role": "user", "content": [box.answer(c) for c in calls]}44 )

What if Claude writes the word done early?

A customer asks the agent to write the word done after each step, so they can follow along.

Predict: Will this loop reach the refund tool on that ticket?

  1. AYes. The loop runs until the tool calls stop.
  2. BNo. The first done in the text ends the loop early.
Show the answer

B. The loop reads reply text, and Claude wrote the word beside a tool request. The loop stopped with the tool still waiting to run.

Stopped after 3 tool calls. The work is unfinished.

The loop reads stop_reason

Every reply carries a stop_reason. It is tool_use when Claude wants a tool and end_turn when it is finished. With these four client tools, the fixed loop continues on tool_use and stops on anything else, including max_tokens and stop_sequence. A server tool can also return pause_turn, which the loop must send back to continue.

The turn cap stays as a backstop, now 10. Every tool_use id gets a tool_result in the next user turn. A result with no matching tool_use returns a 400, and so does dropping a block from an assistant turn.

loop.pygreen lines are what the fix adds

We doChange one setting at a time and predict.

The same ticket now finishes

Switch between the two loops on the narrated ticket. On the second button, the card marked "This is where the runs split" is the first call the text loop never reached.

The fix did not make Claude smarter. It made the loop follow what the API reports.

The same idea applies to a code review. A 14-file change needs one pass on each file and then one pass on how the files connect, because a single read misses bugs that span files.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch agent-loop.

Try it: stop rules

Change one setting at a time. Pick the narrated ticket: the text loop stops after two calls, even with room for 10 turns. Pick the refund ticket with the fixed loop capped at 3: it stops too. A cap alone is a backstop, not the stop rule.

Pick the cut-off ticket: both loops end on max_tokens, and both leave half an answer. Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch agent-loop.

The Agent SDK runs the loop for you

The Claude Agent SDK is your loop with the hand-written part removed. query calls Claude, runs each tool and stops on its own. max_turns is the backstop. The refund ticket takes five turns: four tool calls and a final reply. Claude picks each next tool from the last result. This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run.

Claude picks each step from the last result, so the plan adapts. It maps the task, works by priority and adds steps as findings turn up.

A chain is the other shape: the same fixed steps in order, which suits a monthly review. Each step gives its output a check, and a final pass catches what spans steps. A chain loses any lead it has no step for, so an open investigation needs the adaptive plan.

You doFix the starting code, then test yourself.

You do: fix the loop

Copy the starting code and open work/agent-loop/loop.py. It has two planted defects. next_step() stops when a reply says "done" instead of reading stop_reason, and a turn cap of three ends a four-call refund early.

Terminal
./workshop start agent-loop
./workshop check agent-loop
./workshop watch agent-loop

The checks run each ticket on scripted replies. They expect the loop to continue only on tool_use, answer every tool call with a result, stop on max_tokens, and still bound a runaway model.

Check your understanding

Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.

1. A support loop handles 200 tickets. On 41 of them Claude returns stop_reason tool_use after the customer lookup and the refund call is still to come. Which rule decides whether the loop goes round again?

  1. AA sentence in the system prompt telling Claude to say when it is finished.
  2. BContinue while stop_reason is tool_use, and stop on any other value.
  3. CCount the turns and stop once the count reaches the cap.
  4. DStop as soon as the reply text reads like a finished answer.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A A prompt sentence changes what Claude writes, not what the loop does. The loop still needs its own rule.
  • B Correct. stop_reason is the field the API sets to say Claude is waiting for tool results.
  • C A cap is a backstop for runaway loops. As the main rule it cuts tickets that still have work left.
  • D Reading the text lets the wording of a reply decide the flow, which is how narrated turns end early.

2. The loop caps a ticket at 3 turns. A refund ticket needs get_customer, lookup_order, check_return_window and process_refund, which is 4 calls. On 41 of 200 tickets the run ends with no reply. What is the fix?

  1. ARaise the cap to 4, which covers exactly the tickets seen so far.
  2. BStop on the first reply that contains text, so the cap is never reached.
  3. CKeep stop_reason as the rule, with a cap far above any normal ticket.
  4. DRemove the cap, because stop_reason already ends every run.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A A cap set to the longest ticket seen fails on the next ticket that is one call longer.
  • B Text is often written beside a tool request, so this ends runs with the refund still unpaid.
  • C Correct. The rule ends normal runs, and the cap only catches a run that never ends.
  • D A run that keeps asking for tools would loop until the bill stops it. The backstop is cheap insurance.

3. To save tokens a developer skips the tool_result for a lookup whose output was empty. The next request returns a 400. Why?

  1. AEvery tool_use id must be answered by a tool_result in the next user message.
  2. BEmpty results are dropped by the API, so the request is missing a field.
  3. CTool results belong in the assistant turn, next to the tool_use block.
  4. DThe request hit a rate limit, and sending it again will succeed.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. The history is checked on every call, and an unanswered tool_use makes it invalid.
  • B Nothing is dropped. An empty result is still a block the loop must send, for example with text saying no rows.
  • C Results go in a user message that follows the assistant turn. Claude never writes them.
  • D A 400 means the request is malformed. Sending the same history again returns the same error.

4. Select two statements about stop_reason that a loop should rely on.

  1. Aend_turn means Claude has finished and the loop can return the reply.
  2. Bmax_tokens means Claude finished its answer within the limit.
  3. Cmax_tokens means the reply was cut off, so the loop must not treat it as complete.
  4. Dtool_use means the loop must wait for the customer to approve the tool.
Show the answer

Answer: A, C

  • A Correct. end_turn is the normal finish with nothing left to run.
  • B max_tokens is the opposite of finished. The reply stopped at the limit, possibly in mid sentence.
  • C Correct. A cut reply is partial, so the loop raises the limit or reports it.
  • D The loop runs the tool itself and sends the result back. The customer is not asked.

5. A 14-file change is reviewed in one pass. The review misses a bug where file 3 sends a field that file 11 no longer reads. What review design catches it?

  1. AKeep the single pass, because one careful read sees the whole change.
  2. BAsk for a shorter change, since large diffs are where bugs live.
  3. CRun the same single pass three times and merge the comments.
  4. DReview each file alone, then run a pass on how the files connect.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A Attention thins across 14 files. A single read misses what sits far apart.
  • B Smaller changes help, but the review design still has to handle the change in front of it.
  • C Repeating the same pass repeats the same blind spot. The design has to change.
  • D Correct. Per-file passes find local bugs, and the link pass finds cross-file ones.

6. An open investigation uses a fixed 5-step chain. At step 2 the agent finds a lead the chain has no step for, and it is lost. What should change?

  1. AAdd more steps to the chain so it covers the lead next time.
  2. BLet Claude adapt the plan as findings arrive, inside the loop.
  3. CHave the code pick the next tool from a list of rules.
  4. DRun all five steps at once so none waits on another.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A A longer chain still cannot cover a lead nobody predicted.
  • B Correct. When the next step depends on what was found, the plan has to be chosen by Claude as it goes.
  • C Code rules are a fixed chain in a different form. They miss the same unforeseen lead.
  • D The steps depend on each other, so running them at once breaks the order.

7. A monthly review has the same 4 steps every time, and the output feeds an audit. Which pattern fits?

  1. AAn adaptive plan, because it copes with any input.
  2. BOne prompt that does all four steps in a single pass.
  3. CPrompt chaining with a final pass that checks the results together.
  4. DAn open loop, because it is more reliable than fixed steps.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A Adaptive plans suit unknown work. Fixed work gains nothing from them and gets less predictable.
  • B One pass is where steps get skipped or blurred, and there is no place to check each one.
  • C Correct. Fixed steps are predictable and each output can be checked. The last pass joins them.
  • D An open loop varies from run to run, which is a cost when an audit needs the same steps.

8. Select two facts about an adaptive investigation plan.

  1. AAll subtasks are listed before any file is read and stay unchanged.
  2. BIt maps the structure first and plans the work by priority.
  3. CCode chooses the next tool from a table of rules.
  4. DNew subtasks are added as findings turn up.
Show the answer

Answer: B, D

  • A A list fixed up front is a chain. The point of adapting is that the list grows.
  • B Correct. A map shows where the risk is, so the highest priority work goes first.
  • C Choosing the tool is left to Claude each turn. A rule table removes the adaptation.
  • D Correct. A finding can open a subtask nobody listed, and the plan takes it in.

Play: predict the output

This loop checks the stop reason, but it checks for the wrong one.

python
def next_step(response: Json) -> str:
    if response["stop_reason"] == "end_turn":
        return "stop"
    return "continue"

Predict: Claude declines a request, and the reply comes back with stop_reason "refusal". What does the loop do?

  1. AIt stops, because the reply holds no tool call.
  2. BIt sends the refused turn back and asks again until the turn cap.
Show the answer

B. Only end_turn stops this loop, so refusal, max_tokens and pause_turn all count as continue. Continue only on tool_use and stop on everything else.

  • Tool use overview: the request and response shapes the loop passes back and forth.
  • The Agent SDK loop: the same loop run for you, with its turn limit.
  • Building effective agents: when a loop is the right shape and when a fixed workflow is better.

Conclusions

  • The loop follows stop_reason: tool_use means run the tools and ask again, and end_turn means finished.
  • Every tool_use gets a tool_result in the next request, or the request fails.
  • A turn cap is a backstop against a runaway loop, never the stop rule.

You can now write an agent loop that ends when Claude does.

stop_reason

The field on every reply that says why Claude stopped

tool_use

A stop_reason meaning Claude wants a tool run before it can go on

tool_result

The block that returns a tool's output for one tool_use id

Turn cap

A limit on loop turns that guards against a runaway loop

Foundations, lesson 2

Tool descriptions

The description decides which tool Claude picks

Your agent has four tools, and three of them say "Gets order info". A customer asks about an old order, and Claude picks the tool that only knows recent ones. The lookup finds nothing. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch the wrong tool answer, then fix it with four better descriptions.

I doWatch the failure and its fix.

Claude sees only a name and a description

The Lumen Supply agent has four tools. One looks up recent orders, one finds older orders, one lists orders by email, and one tracks a shipment. Claude never sees the code behind them.

Claude sees each tool's name, its description and its input schema, and nothing else. The input schema lists the fields a tool takes.

The harness is the code around Claude that runs each tool. Claude picks the tool, the harness runs it, and no code checks the pick. The description is the only place to say what a tool is for.

A clear description gets the right tool

A customer asks about order 1042. Claude stops with stop_reason set to tool_use, and the reply holds one tool_use block: an id, the name Look up order and the input it chose. Open the card to see that input and what the tool sent back.

  1. CustomerWhat is the status of order 1042? I placed it on 12 September.
    Show the result
    What is the status of order 1042? I placed it on 12 September.
  2. Claudepicks Look up order: 1042
    Show the result
    {
  "input": {
    "query": "1042"
  },
  "output": {
    "order_id": "1042",
    "email": "dana@example.com",
    "item": "USB keyboard",
    "amount": 89.0,
    "days_ago": 18
  }
}
  3. Result{'order_id': '1042', 'email': 'dana@example.com', 'item': 'USB keyboard', 'amount': 89.0…

Claude picked Look up order, the right tool.

Three tools that say the same thing

Three of the four descriptions read "Gets order info". Nothing says which orders each tool covers or what to pass in. A description that reads like a label gives Claude nothing to choose with.

Every tool is sent on every request, so each one costs input tokens and adds a choice. A long list of tools lowers accuracy. The fix here keeps four tools and makes them distinct.

The same idea holds for bigger agents. One agent with 18 tools, where each role needs about 4, picks wrong more often, so give each role only the tools it needs. A subagent is a second agent started for one job. If it inherits every tool, it can call process_refund, and a prompt line against it is only a request.

Descriptions say what goes in and when to use them

Each precise description gives the input, what comes back, when to use the tool and which tool to use instead. The boundary is a number: 90 days.

A catch-all tool is better split into narrow ones with clear contracts. Rename a tool only after its description is fixed, because the description is what Claude reads.

Descriptions steer the choice. The tool_choice setting forces it. auto is the default and lets Claude answer with no tool. any forces some call, and none forbids calls. A named tool, such as get_customer, forces that one, which a step that must run first needs. This lab sends any.

Try it: descriptions

Change one setting at a time. Pick the status ticket with vague descriptions. Claude picks the right tool but sends "order 1042" as the query, and the lookup finds nothing. Nothing said what to pass in.

On the precise set, a prompt that leans on Look up order moves nothing. On the vague set, that prompt sends even the email and parcel tickets there. Every run is recorded, so this works with no internet.

The Agent SDK reads the same descriptions

The lab above sent the tool list itself, so you could see what Claude reads. The Claude Agent SDK serves the same four tools from an in-process MCP server, a tool host inside your program. Each name gains an mcp__ prefix. The same wording drives the same choice.

This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run through the SDK. With the vague descriptions, the same ticket asks the wrong tool first.

app/sdk_agent.pyfile: 113 lines
1"""The same four tools served by an in-process MCP server on the Agent SDK.23The SDK shows each tool's description to Claude exactly as written, so the4descriptions in `tools.py` decide the pick here too.5"""67import json8from types import ModuleType910from claude_agent_sdk import (11 McpSdkServerConfig,12 SdkMcpTool,13 create_sdk_mcp_server,14 tool,15)1617from kit import sdk18from kit.api import Json19from .prompt import SYSTEM20from .tickets import Ticket21from .tools import run_tool2223SERVER = "support"24PREFIX = f"mcp__{SERVER}__"25MAX_TURNS = 3···5 lines not shown31 def make(spec: Json) -> SdkMcpTool[Json]:32 @tool(spec["name"], spec["description"], spec["input_schema"])33 async def handler(args: Json) -> Json:34 output = run_tool(spec["name"], args)3536 return {37 "content": [{"type": "text", "text": json.dumps(output)}],38 "is_error": "error" in output,39 }4041 return handler4243 return create_sdk_mcp_server(SERVER, tools=[make(s) for s in tools.TOOLS])444546def request_for(ticket: Ticket, tools: ModuleType, tag: str) -> Json:47 """The plain request a recording is keyed by."""48 return sdk.build_request(49 ticket.text,50 SYSTEM,51 tools=[PREFIX + spec["name"] for spec in tools.TOOLS],52 max_turns=MAX_TURNS,53 tag=tag,54 )55···58 lines not shown

You do: rewrite the descriptions

Copy the starting code and open work/tool-descriptions/tools.py. All four tools say "Gets order info" or close to it, so Claude guesses. Rewrite each description: what goes in, what comes back, when to use it and which neighbour to use instead.

Terminal
./workshop start tool-descriptions
./workshop check tool-descriptions
./workshop watch tool-descriptions

The checks want four different descriptions, the 90-day boundary on both order tools, an email on search and a "use when" line on each. Then every recorded ticket must pick the right first tool.

Check your understanding

Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.

1. Two order tools both say "Gets order info". On 31 of 100 tickets about orders older than 90 days the agent asks the recent-orders tool and answers "not found". What fixes it?

  1. ARaise max_tokens so the model has room to think about which tool to call.
  2. BCut each description to two words so the model has less text to compare.
  3. CSay in each what goes in, which orders it covers and the tool to use instead.
  4. DRetry every "not found" with the other order tool, and keep the descriptions.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A The pick is one short block of output. The limit was not the cause of the wrong tool.
  • B Shorter text gives the model less to choose with. Two tools with the same two words are still a coin flip.
  • C Correct. The model reads only the description, so the boundary of 90 days has to be written there.
  • D A retry hides the miss and doubles the calls. The next ticket still starts with the wrong tool.

2. After a rename from lookup_order and find_order to get_order and fetch_order, the same 31 of 100 tickets still go to the wrong tool. The one-line descriptions did not change. What is the cause?

  1. AThe descriptions still say nothing about which orders each tool covers.
  2. BThe new names are still not clear enough, so a third rename with better words should fix it.
  3. CTwo tools are too few, so a third order tool should be added to split the traffic between them.
  4. DThe sampling settings are too loose, so the model picks a different tool on each ticket.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. The fix is in the description. Rename after the boundary is written, not instead of it.
  • B Names help a little, but two names with no coverage still leave the choice open. Renaming again repeats the miss.
  • C A third tool with the same kind of description adds one more choice and no more information.
  • D Settings change how varied the pick is, not what the descriptions say.

3. A system prompt says "call lookup_order for any question about an order". The descriptions still all say "Gets order info". Every order ticket now goes to lookup_order, and 38 of 100 are old orders that fail. What is the right fix?

  1. AAdd a routing line for each ticket type that has failed so far, one by one.
  2. BAdd a prompt line that names find_order for old orders, so the descriptions can stay vague.
  3. CSwitch to a larger model, which reads the system prompt more carefully.
  4. DWrite the coverage and the neighbour into each description, and drop the routing line.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A A list of ticket types grows with every miss, and the next new ticket type fails again.
  • B This ties the tool boundary to one prompt. Any other prompt or subagent that uses these tools gets no routing and misses again.
  • C A larger model still cannot read coverage that nobody wrote into the descriptions.
  • D Correct. A lean in the prompt only matters because the descriptions do not separate the tools. Fix them first.

4. Select two things a good tool description states.

  1. AThe code that the tool runs, so the model can read how it works.
  2. BWhat the tool takes as input and what it returns.
  3. CThe pass rate the tool had in last month's evaluation.
  4. DWhen to use the tool, and which neighbouring tool to use instead.
Show the answer

Answer: B, D

  • A The model never sees the code. It sees the name, the description and the input schema.
  • B Correct. Inputs and outputs tell the model what to send and what to expect back.
  • C A pass rate is for the team that runs the evaluation. It does not help the model pick a tool.
  • D Correct. The boundary with the neighbour is what keeps two similar tools apart.

5. One agent holds 18 tools and picks the wrong one on 1 in 5 tickets. Each role uses about 4 of them. What is the fix?

  1. AAdd six more tools, so every ticket type has a tool made for it.
  2. BGive each agent only the few tools its role needs.
  3. CKeep one list for everyone, because one list is simpler to maintain.
  4. DPut a paragraph in the prompt that says which tool suits which ticket.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A More tools mean more choices and more tokens on every request, and accuracy falls as the list grows.
  • B Correct. A short list per role leaves few tools to confuse, and each tool reads as distinct.
  • C Maintenance is easier, but the miss rate is the cost, and it lands on customers.
  • D A paragraph of routing is a patch for a list that is too long. It also costs tokens on every call.

6. A research subagent called process_refund twice in 50 runs. The tool was in its list because every subagent gets the parent's tools. What should change?

  1. AKeep the shared list, because two calls in 50 runs is a rate the team can accept.
  2. BMove the subagent to a larger model that follows the prompt better.
  3. CGive the subagent only the read tools its research needs.
  4. DAdd a line to its prompt that says never to call process_refund.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A Two refunds moved by a research agent is not an acceptable rate. Removing the tool makes it zero.
  • B A larger model may miss less often, but the tool is still there to be called.
  • C Correct. A tool the subagent cannot see cannot be misused.
  • D A prompt rule is a request. It lowers the rate, and two misses in 50 runs are still money moved.

7. A step in the agent must run get_customer first on every ticket. Which tool_choice setting does that?

  1. A{"type": "auto"}, because the model always calls a lookup first.
  2. B{"type": "tool", "name": "get_customer"}, which forces that tool.
  3. C{"type": "any"}, which forces the model to call get_customer.
  4. DA prompt line that says to call get_customer first, with auto left on.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A With auto the model may answer without a tool, and it may pick a different one.
  • B Correct. A named tool forces that tool on this request.
  • C any forces some tool call, but the model chooses which. It may call another tool first.
  • D A prompt line makes the call likely, not certain. A step that must run needs the setting.

8. Select two valid values for the type of tool_choice.

  1. Aauto, where the model chooses on its own whether a tool is needed.
  2. Ball, where the model calls every tool once.
  3. Csequential, where the tools run in the order they are listed.
  4. Dany, where the model must call some tool.
Show the answer

Answer: A, D

  • A Correct. auto is the default, and the model may answer without a tool.
  • B There is no such setting. The model calls the tools it needs, not every tool.
  • C There is no such setting. Order comes from the model's turns, not from the list.
  • D Correct. any forces a call, and the model picks which tool.

This search tool says what it does, but not what goes in.

tool("search_orders", "List the orders for a customer.", "query")

Predict: A ticket reads "Hi, it's Dana Reyes. Where are my orders?" What does Claude send as the query?

Conclusions

  • The description is how Claude chooses a tool. It is the interface, not a comment.
  • A good description gives the input, the output, when to use it and which neighbour to use instead.
  • Tool choice is testable: run tickets, count the right picks, fix the words.

You can now write tool descriptions that keep similar tools apart.

Tool description

The text Claude reads to decide when to call a tool

Boundary sentence

A line that says which tool to use instead

Tool choice

The setting that says whether Claude may, must or cannot call a tool

Misrouting

Claude calls a tool that cannot answer the ticket

Foundations, lesson 3

Tool preconditions

Refunds need a check the model cannot skip

Your support agent has a refund tool. Your prompt says to verify the customer first, and nothing in the code holds the agent to it. Nothing sets a limit either, so one ticket gets a $640 refund no human approved. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch it fail, then fix it with code the model cannot skip.

I doWatch the failure and its fix.

The agent has one tool that moves money

The Lumen Supply agent looks up customers, looks up orders, and refunds orders. It can also hand a ticket to a human. Only the refund tool moves money.

You will put a precondition check in front of that tool. A precondition check is code that runs before a tool call and can refuse it. The model never sees the code. It sees a clear refusal it can act on.

A verified refund takes three calls

A customer writes in with an email and an order number. The agent looks up the customer, then the order, then pays the refund. Open any card to see the data the tool received and returned.

This run works because the customer gave an email and the model chose to check it. Nothing forced that choice.

A rule in the prompt is a request

One sentence in the system prompt asks for verification. A rule in the prompt is a request, and models follow requests most of the time. A tool that moves money needs a rule that holds every time.

A precondition check runs before the tool

The check sits between Claude and the tools, so every tool call passes through it first. For the refund tool it asks two questions: is the customer verified, and is the amount within the limit?

When the answer is no, the check returns a refusal with a category, a retry hint and a plain message. The model reads the refusal and recovers.

policy.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""Solution: verification, the limit and escalation are code, not prompt."""23from app.state import State, Ticket4from kit.api import Json56REFUND_LIMIT = 500.0789def _deny(category: str, message: str, retryable: bool) -> Json:10 """Build a refusal the model can read and act on."""11 return {12 "error": {13 "category": category,14 "retryable": retryable,15 "message": message,16 }17 }181920def precondition(tool: str, args: Json, state: State) -> Json | None:21 """Refuse a tool call before it runs, or return None to allow it.22 The model never sees this code. A refusal must say what to do next

The check can refuse in two ways. A bare no says only that the refund is denied. A structured refusal adds a category, a retry hint and a message that names the missing step.

Switch between them. After the bare no, the agent still hands the ticket to a human. It can only say the refund was declined with no reason, and the handoff says the same. After the structured refusal, it tells the customer that refunds over $500 need a human, and the handoff names the limit.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch refund-guard.

We doChange one setting at a time and predict.

The same ticket now ends safely

Use the switch to run the same ticket without the check, then with it. The card marked "This is where the runs split" is the refusal.

The check did not make the model smarter. It made the outcome independent of what the model decided.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch refund-guard.

Try it: precondition checks

Change one setting at a time. Turn the check off and pick the big ticket: a $640 refund goes through with no limit. Turn the check on and set the limit to $50: the $89 ticket now goes to a human at intake.

Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch refund-guard.

The same check runs in the Agent SDK

The Claude Agent SDK runs the same loop for you. The four tools are served in-process, and the same policy.py is registered as a PreToolUse hook. The hook returns a deny decision with a reason, and the model reads that reason as the tool result.

This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run through the SDK. Without the hook, the same ticket pays all $640.

You do: fix the refund check

Copy the starting code and open work/refund-guard/policy.py. It has two planted defects. precondition() allows every call, and route() escalates angry tickets instead of large or explicit ones.

Terminal
./workshop start refund-guard
./workshop check refund-guard
./workshop watch refund-guard

The checks expect a structured refusal for an unverified refund and for a verified one over the limit. They also expect routing on amount or an explicit request, never on tone. When they pass, watch runs your code on the $640 ticket.

Check your understanding

Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.

1. A support agent must never refund before verifying the customer. Logs show it skipped verification in 2 of 50 tickets even though the system prompt says to verify first. What is the most reliable fix?

  1. AMove the verification sentence to the top of the prompt and write it in capital letters.
  2. BDeny process_refund in the dispatcher until get_customer has succeeded.
  3. CAdd three worked examples of correct verification steps to the system prompt.
  4. DLower the temperature to zero so the model follows every instruction more closely.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A Emphasis raises the odds but is still a request. A 4% miss on a refund tool is still money moved without a check.
  • B Correct. A rule that must hold belongs in code that runs before the tool, and a structured denial lets the model recover.
  • C Examples help style and format. They do not guarantee a step happens on every ticket.
  • D Temperature changes variety, not obedience. The model can skip a step at any setting.

2. A team enforces a $500 refund limit with a paragraph in the system prompt. A reviewer says this is a weakness. Which statement explains why?

  1. ALong prompts are truncated by the API, so the paragraph may not be read at all.
  2. BThe model cannot reliably understand numeric limits written in plain sentences.
  3. CA prompt is guidance, so nothing stops an over-limit call.
  4. DPrompts cost tokens on every single request, which makes the rule expensive to keep.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A Truncation is not the risk here. The paragraph is read and can still lose to a persuasive customer message.
  • B Models handle numbers well. Understanding is not the problem, enforcement is.
  • C Correct. A prompt shapes behaviour. A programmatic check refuses the call whatever the model decides.
  • D Cost is real but is not why a prompt-only limit fails a compliance review.

3. Which two rules should be enforced in code instead of the prompt? Select two.

  1. ANo refund before the customer is verified.
  2. BKeep every reply under 120 words for readability.
  3. CA refund above $500 needs a human.
  4. DPrefer plain language over technical jargon.
Show the answer

Answer: A, C

  • A Correct. Skipping it has a financial and legal cost, so it must hold every time.
  • B Style rules fail softly. A long reply is a nuisance, not a breach.
  • C Correct. A money limit is a hard rule, so code refuses the call whatever the model decides.
  • D Tone guidance is a prompt job. There is nothing to enforce in code.

4. The dispatcher denies process_refund because the customer is unverified. What should the denial return so the agent recovers on its own?

  1. AThe single word Error, which is short and clear.
  2. BAn empty result, so the model tries another approach on its own.
  3. CThe full stack trace from the failed check for debugging.
  4. DAn error with category, retryable flag and the step to take.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A A bare string gives the model nothing to act on, so it guesses or gives up.
  • B An empty result looks like success with no data. The model may report the refund as done.
  • C A stack trace leaks internals and does not say what to do next.
  • D Correct. Category, retryable and an action in the message let the model fix the cause and continue.

5. A PreToolUse hook receives a process_refund call for $640, and the limit is $500. How does the hook stop the call?

  1. AIt edits the system prompt so the next turn avoids the call.
  2. BIt logs a warning and lets the call through for later review.
  3. CIt asks the model whether it is sure about the refund amount.
  4. DIt exits with a blocking status and a stderr message.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A The call is already made. A later prompt edit does not undo it.
  • B A warning after the fact means the money has moved.
  • C Asking the model to confirm puts the decision back in the model, which is the weakness the hook removes.
  • D Correct. A blocking exit stops the tool, and the message goes back to the model as the reason.

6. Where should a hook that checks refund limits run?

  1. ABefore the tool executes.
  2. BAfter the tool returns, on the result.
  3. CAt the end of the session, over the whole transcript.
  4. DOnly when the user asks for a review.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. A pre-tool hook can refuse the call, so the money never moves.
  • B A post-tool hook can annotate a result but cannot undo the refund.
  • C An end-of-session check finds problems after they are done.
  • D A gate that depends on a request is not a gate.

7. Intake routing already sends every ticket over $500 to a human. Why keep the refund limit in a hook too?

  1. AHooks make the model respond faster on every turn.
  2. BRouting is optional in production, so the hook is only a duplicate.
  3. CThe hook sees every call, so it catches limits crossed after intake.
  4. DRouting cannot read amounts.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A Hooks add a check. They do not speed up the model.
  • B Routing is not optional here. The point is a second layer for cases it cannot see.
  • C Correct. Intake sees the ticket once. The hook sees every tool call, so it catches limits crossed later.
  • D Routing can read amounts. The gap is what changes after intake.

8. A refund hook denies a call because the customer is unverified. The next model turn calls process_refund again with the same arguments. What is the best design response?

  1. AGive the model unlimited attempts until it finally complies.
  2. BName the missing step in the denial and mark it retryable.
  3. CDisable the hook after two denials so the ticket can be finished.
  4. DEscalate every ticket that triggers any denial to a human.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A Repeated blind retries waste turns. The model needs to learn what to change.
  • B Correct. A clear, actionable denial lets the model call get_customer and then retry the refund.
  • C Turning the gate off after two denials defeats it.
  • D Escalating every denial floods humans with tickets the agent could finish.

9. A team escalates any ticket where the customer sounds angry. Resolution rate is low and humans are overloaded. What is the flaw?

  1. ATone says nothing about whether the agent can solve it.
  2. BAnger detection is too slow to run during a live chat.
  3. CHumans cannot be expected to read angry messages all day.
  4. DThe model refuses to reply to customers who sound angry.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. A furious customer with a simple refund is well within the agent's ability. Sentiment is not complexity.
  • B Speed is not the issue. The signal is the wrong one.
  • C Humans handle angry messages every day. That is not the flaw.
  • D Models answer angry customers without trouble.

10. Which two escalation triggers follow good practice? Select two.

  1. AA negative sentiment score above 0.7 on the last message.
  2. BAn over-limit refund or a policy exception.
  3. CThe customer writes in capital letters or uses several exclamation marks.
  4. DAn explicit request to speak to a person.
Show the answer

Answer: B, D

  • A A sentiment threshold measures mood, not difficulty.
  • B Correct. Each trigger is explicit, testable and tied to a real limit of the agent.
  • C Typography says nothing about whether the agent can solve the ticket.
  • D Correct. A request for a person is honoured whatever the amount or the tone.

11. A customer writes 'I want to speak to a real person.' The order is a simple $20 refund. What should the agent do?

  1. AComplete the refund first, then mention the option of talking to a person.
  2. BHand the ticket to a human, as the customer asked.
  3. CAsk the customer to explain why they want to talk to a person.
  4. DReply that the agent can handle it fully and carry on with the ticket.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A This overrides the request. The customer asked for a person, and honouring it is a rule.
  • B Correct. An explicit request for a human is a clear trigger, whatever the amount or tone.
  • C Interrogating the customer adds friction and delays the handoff.
  • D Insisting on continuing ignores an explicit request.

12. You want to check that your escalation rule is not driven by tone. Which test best does that?

  1. ARun twenty calm tickets and confirm that none of them escalate.
  2. BCheck that the word angry appears in none of the code files.
  3. CAsk three teammates whether the rule feels fair to customers.
  4. DRun same-facts tickets in two tones and assert equal routing.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A Calm tickets alone do not show what happens when the tone changes.
  • B Words can hide in data or in a model call. Absence in code proves little.
  • C Opinions are not a test. The rule needs an assertion that can fail.
  • D Correct. Holding the facts fixed and changing only the tone isolates the variable the rule must ignore.

Play: spot the bug

A teammate wrote this check. It passes their one test, and a stranger still gets paid.

python
def precondition(tool: str, args: Json, state: State) -> Json | None:
    if tool != "process_refund":
        return None
    if args.get("customer_verified"):
        return None
    return refusal("unverified", "Look up the customer first.")

Predict: Why can an injected ticket still move money?

  1. AIt trusts the customer_verified flag, a value the model writes into the call.
  2. BIt refuses without a retry hint, so the model retries until it wins.
Show the answer

A. The model fills in every tool argument, so an injected ticket can set the flag. A check must read state your code wrote, like state.verified_customer, never a claim inside the call.

References

  • Agent SDK hooks: how to register this check as a PreToolUse hook in your own agent.
  • Claude Code hooks: the same deny decision guarding tools in Claude Code itself.
  • Tool use overview: where a tool call and its result sit in the loop.
  • Handle tool calls: how to return a tool error the model can read and act on.
  • OWASP prompt injection: why ticket text is untrusted input, with more attack shapes.

Conclusions

  • A rule in the prompt is a request. Code that runs before the tool is a guarantee.
  • A precondition check refuses with a category, a retry hint and a message, so the model can recover.
  • Escalate on amount, policy or an explicit request, never on tone.

You can now put a precondition check in front of any tool that moves money.

Precondition check

Code that runs before a tool call and can refuse it. The Agent SDK calls it a PreToolUse hook

Structured refusal

A denial with a category, a retry hint and a message

Prompt-only rule

A rule that exists only as text in the prompt

Explicit criteria

The rules for escalating: amount, policy or a request, never tone

Foundations, lesson 4

Escalation and handoff

Rules decide who takes over, and the handoff carries the case

Your support agent escalates when a customer sounds angry, and keeps going when a customer asks for a person. The people who do get a ticket receive one line and start from zero. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch it fail, then fix it with three small rules.

I doWatch the failure and its fix.

Rules run first, then Claude finishes the rest

Three parties split the work. Code routes the ticket first. Claude resolves what the agent can solve. A person takes the rest.

Two triggers send a ticket to a person. The customer asks for one, or the shop has no policy for the request.

A solvable ticket stays with the agent

The customer wants a refund the shop allows. No rule sends it to a person, so Claude calls get_customer. The tool call carries the email it read from the ticket. The result carries the customer and the orders.

Claude reads that result and writes the reply. The code never wrote the reply and Claude never chose the route.

Three rules as written

route in the starting code escalates on tone: two exclamation marks or the word "ridiculous". Tone is not difficulty. An angry customer with a simple refund is easy, and a calm customer who wants a policy the shop lacks is hard.

Sentiment does not measure difficulty, and neither does the model rating its own confidence. A rule needs a signal that names the ticket, such as a request for a person.

A prompt line that says not to invent policies only lowers the rate. When the shop has no policy, route to a person in code before the agent answers.

Three rules replace tone with criteria

Escalate on an explicit request for a person, or on a policy the shop does not have. Ask when two customers match. The text matches in route stand in for a real classifier.

When the model must judge the gray cases, write two to four worked examples, each a sample ticket with the right call and its reason. A reason teaches the boundary, which a bare label cannot. "Be conservative" is not a criterion, because it names no case.

Split a message that holds several asks into items, and decide each one. The routing is plain code, so the same ticket goes the same way every time.

handoff.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""Three rules: who decides, who the customer is, and what a person gets."""23from kit.api import Json45ASK_FOR_PERSON = ("speak to a person", "talk to a human", "real person")6POLICY_GAPS = ("price match", "match the price", "match their price")789def route(text: str) -> str:10 """Escalate on a request for a person or a missing policy."""11 lowered = text.lower()12 if any(p in lowered for p in (*ASK_FOR_PERSON, *POLICY_GAPS)):13 return "human"1415 return "agent"161718def match(query: str, customers: list[Json]) -> Json:19 """Find one customer, or ask for one more identifier."""20 found = [21 c22 for c in customers23 if query.lower() in f"{c['name']} {c['email']}".lower()24 ]25 if len(found) > 1:26 return {27 "ask": "More than one customer has that name. Ask for the email."28 }2930 return {"customer": found[0]} if found else {"error": "No customer."}313233def handoff(case: Json) -> Json:34 """Everything a person needs, so nobody asks the customer again."""35 return {36 "customer": case["customer"],37 "order": case["order"],38 "issue": case["issue"],39 "tried": case["tried"],40 "ask": case["ask"],41 }

The handoff carries the case

The shop has no price match policy, so a person must decide. With the starting rules the handoff is one line. Press the second button: the handoff holds five fields, which are customer, order, issue, what was tried, and the ask.

A handoff is a data structure, not a sentence. The person who opens it should not have to ask the customer again.

The same care applies to alert flags that tell staff a ticket needs a look. If one flag category fires on 40 percent of tickets, staff stop reading every flag. Switch that category off until its criteria are fixed, and keep the others on.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch escalation-handoff.

Try the angry ticket too. The starting rules escalate it with a one line summary. The fixed rules leave it with the agent, which can solve it.

Examples earn their place on the ambiguous tickets, so do not fill the prompt with easy ones. Vary the ticket layouts in them, so the model learns the rule and not one channel's format.

The same lookup runs in the Agent SDK

The Claude Agent SDK serves tools from an in-process MCP server. The route rule still runs in code first. A ticket for a person gets the tool hand_to_person. Its result is the handoff, and Claude reads that result to write a short reply.

You do: fix the three rules

Copy the starting code and open work/escalation-handoff/handoff.py. It has three planted defects. route() escalates on tone, match() answers about the first of two customers with one name, and handoff() sends a one-line summary.

Terminal
./workshop start escalation-handoff
./workshop check escalation-handoff
./workshop watch escalation-handoff

The checks send a request for a person and a price match to a human, and keep a solvable angry ticket with the agent. They expect a question when two customers match, and five fields in every handoff.

Check your understanding

Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.

1. A team escalates every ticket with an angry tone. Of 100 escalations last week, 34 were simple refunds the agent could have finished. What is the right change?

  1. AEscalate on named criteria, such as a request for a person or a policy the shop lacks.
  2. BHire more people for the escalation queue, so the extra 34 are handled quickly.
  3. CAdd more angry words to the rule, so the tone check is more exact.
  4. DKeep the tone rule and add a sentiment score, escalating only when the score is very low.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. A criterion says something about the ticket, such as what is asked or whether a policy exists.
  • B More staff clears the queue and leaves the rule unchanged. The 34 simple refunds still reach a person.
  • C A longer word list misses calm hard tickets and still catches angry easy ones.
  • D A sentiment score is still tone. A calm ticket can be hard, and an angry one can be a simple refund.

2. Select two valid triggers for sending a ticket to a person.

  1. AThe customer asks for a person.
  2. BThe sentiment score of the message is below a threshold.
  3. CThe shop has no policy for what the customer asks.
  4. DThe model rates its own confidence under 0.8.
Show the answer

Answer: A, C

  • A Correct. An explicit request is honoured at once.
  • B Sentiment measures tone, not difficulty. A calm ticket can need a person and an angry one may not.
  • C Correct. When the policy is silent the agent would have to invent one, so a person decides.
  • D A model's rating of itself does not track whether it is right, so it cannot route tickets.

3. A lookup for Sam Lee returns two customers, and the agent answers about the first one. In 50 such tickets, 19 were about the wrong person. What should the lookup do?

  1. AReturn the first match, because the first record is right more often than not.
  2. BReturn the account with the newest order, since it is more likely to be active.
  3. CReturn a question asking for one more identifier, such as the email.
  4. DSend every name collision to a person, so nobody has to choose.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A The first record is an arbitrary pick. In the tickets above it was wrong 19 times in 50.
  • B Recency is a guess. The customer who wrote in may be the one with the older account.
  • C Correct. One more identifier settles it, and the agent never has to guess.
  • D A collision can be settled by one question. Sending it to a person spends a person on a simple case.

4. A routing rule sends a ticket to a person when the model rates its own confidence under 0.7. The model rated 0.9 on an answer that was wrong. What does this show?

  1. AThe threshold is too low, so raising it to 0.95 will catch this kind of miss.
  2. BThe model should rate its confidence a second time, and the second rating is the one to use.
  3. CAveraging three ratings will give a number that follows whether the answer is right.
  4. DSelf-rated confidence does not measure difficulty, so route on explicit criteria.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A A higher threshold still relies on a number that can be 0.9 on a wrong answer.
  • B A second rating comes from the same source and has the same flaw.
  • C An average of numbers that do not track correctness does not track it either.
  • D Correct. Name the triggers, and check accuracy against labelled tickets instead of trusting a score.

5. A customer writes "I want a person" after three replies from the agent. The agent writes a fourth answer. What should happen instead?

  1. AThe agent tries one more answer first, since it might solve the ticket.
  2. BThe ticket goes to a person at once.
  3. CThe agent asks the customer to confirm that they really want a person.
  4. DThe agent waits to see whether the next message sounds angry.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A The customer has already asked. A fourth attempt repeats what they are tired of.
  • B Correct. An explicit request is a rule with no judgement in it, so it is honoured at once.
  • C A confirmation turns a clear request into one more step the customer did not ask for.
  • D Tone is not the trigger. The customer has already said what they want.

6. A customer asks for a price match, which the shop has never offered. The agent quotes a price match policy it made up, in 12 of 40 such tickets. What is the right fix?

  1. AAdd a line to the prompt that says not to invent policies.
  2. BLet the agent offer the nearest policy it has, such as a return window.
  3. CLower the temperature so the agent stays closer to the facts it has.
  4. DEscalate to a person in code whenever the policy is silent.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A A prompt line lowers the rate but is still a request, and 12 in 40 shows how often it slips.
  • B A different policy is still not the one asked for, and the customer is misled.
  • C Temperature changes variety, not whether the agent knows a policy exists.
  • D Correct. A named criterion sends the ticket to a person, and no policy gets invented.

7. The prompt says "be conservative about escalating". On 60 borderline tickets, 18 go the wrong way. What should change?

  1. AMake it stronger, for example "be very conservative about escalating".
  2. BHave the model rate its confidence and escalate below a threshold.
  3. CName the categories, what to escalate in each and what to handle.
  4. DEscalate every borderline ticket, so none are handled wrongly.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A A stronger word is still not a criterion. The model still has to guess what conservative means.
  • B A confidence rating does not track whether the ticket is hard.
  • C Correct. Named categories with a clear action each leave the model nothing to guess.
  • D This fixes the 18 by sending all 60 to people, which is the cost the agent was built to avoid.

8. One flag category is raised on 40 percent of tickets, and staff have stopped reading any flags. What is the best response?

  1. ASwitch that category off until its criteria are fixed.
  2. BAsk staff to read every flag, since the noisy category may hide real ones.
  3. CReword the flag so it sounds less urgent, so staff take it less seriously.
  4. DRemove all flagging, so nobody has to sift through them.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. Trust is restored by removing the noise, and the category comes back once its criteria are sound.
  • B Staff already stopped. A flag nobody trusts costs time and protects no one.
  • C A quieter flag on 40 percent of tickets is still noise.
  • D This drops the useful flags along with the noisy one.

9. An escalation note reads "customer unhappy". The person who takes the ticket has to ask the customer everything again, and handling time is 11 minutes longer. What is the fix?

  1. AWrite a longer free-text summary of the conversation.
  2. BAttach the full transcript and let the person find what matters in it.
  3. CHand over a structured case: customer, order, issue, tried, ask.
  4. DAdd a mood score, so the person knows how careful to be.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A A longer summary can still leave out the order or the ask, and a person has to read it all.
  • B A transcript holds the answer but buries it, so the person still starts from zero.
  • C Correct. Each field answers a question the person would otherwise put to the customer.
  • D A mood score says how the customer feels and not what to do.

10. Select two fields a handoff needs when a person takes over a refund case.

  1. AThe model's confidence score for its last answer.
  2. BWhat the agent already tried.
  3. CA label for the customer's mood.
  4. DWhat the person is asked to do.
Show the answer

Answer: B, D

  • A The score does not say what happened or what to do, and it is not reliable.
  • B Correct. It stops the person from repeating a step the agent already took.
  • C A mood label does not help the person act on the case.
  • D Correct. The ask is the reason the ticket reached a person.

11. One message asks for a refund and an address change. The agent answers the refund and ignores the address in 14 of 30 such messages. What should change?

  1. ATell customers to send one request per message.
  2. BAnswer the longer request first, since it is likely the main one.
  3. CTreat the second request as out of scope, so the agent only takes the first.
  4. DSplit the message into separate items and handle each one.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A This moves the work to the customer, and many will not read it.
  • B Length does not show which request matters, and the other is still dropped.
  • C The address change is in scope. Dropping it means a second ticket and a second wait.
  • D Correct. A list of items makes each request visible, so none is dropped.

12. An escalation must carry the case history. The model writes a free summary, and 9 of 30 leave out the order number. How should the handoff be fixed?

  1. AAdd a sentence to the prompt that says to include the order number.
  2. BFix the fields in a schema, so a handoff with no order fails.
  3. CLet the person who takes the ticket ask the model for what is missing.
  4. DAsk for a summary of exactly 60 words, so the length is always the same.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A A prompt line lowers the misses but does not stop them, and nothing flags a missing field.
  • B Correct. A schema makes a missing field an error the harness can see and reject.
  • C The person now has to spot what is missing, which is the work the handoff should save.
  • D A word count says nothing about which facts are in the summary.

13. On borderline tickets the same input is escalated on one run and handled on the next, in 15 of 60 repeats. What is the most reliable change?

  1. AAdd two to four borderline examples, each with action and reason.
  2. BWrite a longer list of rules that covers every case in words.
  3. CAdd a stricter instruction, since examples only change the style of the reply.
  4. DRaise the temperature so the model explores more before it settles.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. Examples with reasons settle the cases the words leave open, the same way every time.
  • B A long list still leaves the boundary cases to judgement, and the prompt grows.
  • C Examples show the model where a line falls, which is more than style.
  • D More variety makes the runs differ more, not less.

14. Select two things a few-shot example for a borderline ticket should show.

  1. AThe ticket as it arrives.
  2. BThe action chosen and the reason for it.
  3. CThe probability the model gave to each action.
  4. DWho wrote the example and when.
Show the answer

Answer: A, B

  • A Correct. The model matches new tickets against the inputs it has seen.
  • B Correct. The reason tells the model what to weigh, so it can apply it to a new ticket.
  • C Probabilities are not part of the pattern the model learns from.
  • D Authorship does not help the model decide anything.

15. The prompt holds four examples, and all four are easy tickets. The agent fails on 7 of 20 hard tickets. What is the fix?

  1. AAdd more easy examples, since more examples help.
  2. BReplace them with ambiguous cases, each with a reason.
  3. CMove to a larger model that copes better with the hard tickets.
  4. DRemove the examples and rely on the written rules alone.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A More easy cases teach the model the part it already gets right.
  • B Correct. Examples earn their place on the tickets where the wording alone is not enough.
  • C A larger model can still have no example of where the line falls.
  • D This throws away the one part of the prompt that shows the boundary.

16. All the prompt's examples use one ticket layout. A new layout from another channel breaks the routing on 11 of 40 tickets. What is the fix?

  1. AAdd more examples in the same layout, so the pattern is stronger.
  2. BReplace the examples with a pattern match on the new channel's header.
  3. CAdd a special rule that handles only the new layout.
  4. DVary the layouts, so the model learns the rule and not the format.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A More of one layout repeats the format and teaches the model nothing new.
  • B A header match is a rule for one channel, and the routing still breaks on the next.
  • C The next channel needs another special rule, and the list grows with every layout.
  • D Correct. Different layouts with the same outcome show what stays fixed and what changes.

def route(text: str) -> str:
    return "human" if "person" in text.lower() else "agent"


route("Please update the personal address on my account.")

Predict: Where does this ticket go?

  1. ATo a person, because "personal" holds the word person.
  2. BTo the agent, because nobody asked for a person.
Show the answer

A. A single word matches inside other words and other meanings. Match whole requests such as "speak to a person", and test the rule on tickets that use the word without asking.

References

  • Use examples effectively: why two to four examples, each with a reason, teach a rule.
  • Be clear and direct: how to state escalation criteria the model can apply.
  • Tool use overview: how a handoff tool returns its result to the model.
  • Agent SDK custom tools: the handoff tool served in-process by the SDK.

Conclusions

  • Escalate on explicit criteria: a request for a person, or a policy the shop does not have.
  • Ask for one more identifier when a lookup matches more than one customer.
  • Give the model two to four examples with reasons for the gray cases.
  • A handoff carries customer, order, issue, what was tried and the ask.

You can now write escalation rules that send the right tickets to a person, with the whole case.

Escalation criteria

Rules that name when a person takes over, such as a request or a policy gap

Handoff

The case a person receives: customer, order, issue, tried and ask

Ambiguous match

A lookup that finds more than one customer, so Claude asks

Policy gap

A request for something the shop has no rule for

Foundations, lesson 5

Structured tool errors

A tool error should say what to do next

Your refund tool fails with the single word Error. The agent cannot tell a timeout from a refusal, so it retries a refusal and then guesses at a reason for the customer. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch it fail, then fix it with two small functions.

I doWatch the failure and its fix.

Every failure has a category and a flag

Three parties share the work. The tool reports the failure. The harness, the code around Claude that runs each tool, decides whether to retry. Claude explains the result to the customer.

A refund can fail four ways: transient, validation, permission or business. A timeout is transient and a wrong order id is validation. Another customer's order is permission, and a closed refund window is business.

Each failure needs two answers. What kind is it, and can a retry help? The tool reports both, so the harness never guesses from a sentence.

A refusal is explained, not retried

The order is 239 days old. The harness stops after one attempt, and Claude tells the customer why.

Open the error card. The tool result carries isError, which marks it as a failure. MCP, the standard protocol that connects tools to Claude, spells it isError, and the API and the Python SDK spell the same flag is_error. Inside are the errorCategory (business), isRetryable (false) and a message the customer can read.

    "error": {

Tried once, then explained the result.

Two functions as written

fail builds every error the tool returns. The starting code returns the word Error and nothing else. should_retry decides whether the harness tries again, and the starting code always says yes.

A retry of a refusal is not free. Three attempts are three tool calls for one answer that never changes.

starter/errors.py

A category of "empty" is not a failure: return the empty13 # list with the message and no error.14 return {"error": {"message": "Error"}}151617def should_retry(error: Json) -> bool:18 """Whether the harness should try the same call again."""19 # TODO(workshop): retry a transient failure and nothing else.20 return True

Tried 3 times. A retry could not have helped.

A category and a flag replace the word Error

fail now sets isError and carries errorCategory, isRetryable and the message. Only a transient failure is retryable. should_retry reads the flag, so a timeout is retried and a refusal is not.

The harness bounds the retries and waits a short random time between them. Any transient fault gets the same bounded retry.

errors.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""A failure names its category, says if a retry can help, and explains."""23from kit.api import Json45RETRYABLE = {"transient"}678def fail(category: str, message: str) -> Json:9 """The result a tool returns when it fails.10 Nothing found is a valid answer, so "empty" carries no error.11 """12 if category == "empty":13 return {"orders": [], "message": message}1415 return {16 "isError": True,17 "error": {18 "errorCategory": category,19 "isRetryable": category in RETRYABLE,20 "message": message,21 },22 }232425def should_retry(error: Json) -> bool:26 """Retry only a failure that says a retry can help."""27 return bool(error.get("isRetryable"))

Nothing found is not a failure

A customer with no orders asks for a list. The lookup finds nothing, and that is a valid answer. With structured errors the result has no error flag, and Claude says there are no orders.

The starting code reports the empty list as a failure and retries it. Tell an access failure from a valid empty result: only the first carries an error.

The same tool runs in the Agent SDK

The Claude Agent SDK serves the refund and the lookup from an in-process MCP server. The Python SDK spells the failure flag is_error, as the API does.

Here Claude decides whether to retry, so the error shape is all it has. That is why the prompt asks for one retry, a line the harness above never needs. This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run. With the starting code the reply blames a system error, and with structured errors it explains the refund window.

A subagent is a second agent that a coordinator starts for one job. It should retry a transient fault locally and pass up only what it cannot fix, with the partial results. Two mistakes to avoid: returning an empty result as if it worked, and aborting all four subagents because one failed. This is the report a coordinator receives:

text
failed:  lookup for order 1050, timed out twice
tried:   retried once, locally
partial: orders 1042 and 1043 found, 1050 not checked
next:    the customer can wait for a call back or ask again
