./workshop watch structured-errors

The checks want an error flag, a category, a retry hint and the message on every failure. Only a transient failure is retried, and an empty result is an empty list with no error.

Check your understanding

Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.

1. A refund tool returns the text "Error" for every failure. The agent retries an order that is past the refund window and then guesses at a reason. What is the best fix?

  1. AAdd a long prompt paragraph that lists every reason a refund can fail and what to say for each.
  2. BRaise the retry limit so the agent has more chances to find the cause.
  3. CReturn an error with a category, a retryable flag and a message the agent can read.
  4. DLog the failure on the server and return an empty result so the agent moves on.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A A prompt cannot know which reason applied to this call. The tool knows.
  • B More retries repeat a refusal that no retry can change.
  • C Correct. The category and the flag tell the harness whether a retry can help, and the message tells Claude what to say.
  • D An empty result hides the failure, and the agent has nothing to explain.

2. Which failure should the harness retry without asking Claude?

  1. AA refund request for an order that is 239 days old.
  2. BA refund request for an order id written with a letter in it.
  3. CA refund request for an order that belongs to another customer.
  4. DA payment service that timed out once.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A This is a business refusal. Trying again gives the same answer.
  • B This is a validation error. The input has to change first.
  • C This is a permission error. A retry does not change the owner.
  • D Correct. A timeout is transient, so the same call may succeed a moment later.

3. Which fields make a tool error useful to both the harness and Claude? Select two.

  1. AA stack trace from the server that raised it.
  2. BAn error category such as transient, validation, permission or business.
  3. CThe HTTP status code alone, such as 500, used as the whole category.
  4. DA retryable flag the harness can read without parsing text.
Show the answer

Answer: B, D

  • A A stack trace is operator detail. A customer never needs it.
  • B Correct. The category says what kind of failure it is, so each kind gets the right response.
  • C A status code says where a call failed, not what to do next. A 500 can be a timeout or a bug.
  • D Correct. The harness decides on the flag, not on a guess from a sentence.

4. A tool fails because the customer gave an order id that matches no order. Which category fits, and what follows?

  1. ATransient, so the harness retries the same call again.
  2. BValidation, so Claude asks for a corrected id.
  3. CPermission, so Claude asks the customer for a manager.
  4. DBusiness, so Claude explains the refund window to them.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A The same id fails again. Only a transient failure earns a retry.
  • B Correct. The input is wrong, so the next step is a corrected input.
  • C Nothing was denied. The order was not found.
  • D The refund window is not the problem. The id never matched an order.

5. A lookup returns an empty list for a customer with no orders. The agent calls it three times and then says the lookup failed. What is the right handling?

  1. AReturn the empty list, no error flag, and say nothing was found.
  2. BRaise the retry limit to five, in case the orders load on a later try.
  3. CReturn an error flag on an empty list, so the agent stops asking.
  4. DDrop the result and ask the customer to try again later.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. Nothing found is a valid answer. An access failure is different, and it carries an error.
  • B The list is empty because the customer has no orders, so five tries return the same list.
  • C An error flag says the call failed. This one worked and found nothing.
  • D The customer learns nothing, and the real answer is lost.

6. Where should retries of a transient failure live?

  1. AIn the system prompt, as a rule for Claude to follow.
  2. BIn a background job that replays every failed call until one succeeds.
  3. CIn code around the tool call, bounded by the retryable flag.
  4. DIn the tool description, as a sentence that tells Claude to try the call twice.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A A prompt rule depends on Claude counting attempts. Code counts exactly.
  • B Replays with no bound hammer a tool that refuses. A retry needs a limit and a flag.
  • C Correct. Code can bound the attempts and stop on a refusal.
  • D A description says what a tool does. It cannot enforce a limit.

7. A refund fails with a permission error because the order belongs to another customer. Which reply is best?

  1. AApologise, say something went wrong, and ask them to try again later.
  2. BSay the refund cannot be done on that order, and offer to look up their own orders.
  3. CSay who owns the order, so they can contact that person and sort it out between them.
  4. DClose the ticket at once, because the first failed call ends the conversation.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A This hides the reason, and a later try gets the same refusal.
  • B Correct. It refuses plainly and offers a next step that stays within their account.
  • C Naming the owner leaks another customer's data.
  • D One refusal does not end the ticket. The customer still needs a reason and a next step.

8. A coordinator runs four subagents and one fails. Select two mistakes in how the failure is handled.

  1. AThe subagent swallows a timeout and returns an empty result as if it had worked.
  2. BThe reply names what failed, what was tried, and what the customer can do next.
  3. CThe subagent retries a timeout once, and passes up only what it could not fix.
  4. DThe coordinator aborts the whole run because one of four subagents failed.
Show the answer

Answer: A, D

  • A Correct. The coordinator now trusts a result that is not real.
  • B This is what a good failure report contains.
  • C A local retry of a transient fault is good practice. Only what it cannot fix goes up.
  • D Correct. Three good results are lost, and the failed one could have been reported as partial.

Play: spot the bug

The retry rule is right, but the harness hands it the wrong thing.

python
def should_retry(error: Json) -> bool:
    return bool(error.get("isRetryable"))


result = lookup_order("1042")  # times out
if result.get("isError") and should_retry(result):
    result = lookup_order("1042")

Predict: The lookup times out, and its error says isRetryable is true. Is it retried?

  1. AYes. The error says a retry can help.
  2. BNo. The flag sits inside result["error"], so the rule reads nothing and says no.
Show the answer

B. The rule reads isRetryable from the top of what it gets, and the flag is one level down. Pass result["error"], and test the harness with a real failure, not only the rule alone.

References

  • Handle tool calls: how to return is_error so the model knows a call failed.
  • MCP tools specification: the isError field an MCP server returns on a failed tool.
  • Tool use overview: where a tool result sits in the conversation.
  • Agent SDK custom tools: how an SDK tool reports an error to the model.

Conclusions

  • A tool failure carries a category, a retryable flag and a readable message.
  • Only a transient failure is retried, in code, with a bound.
  • An empty result is a valid answer, not an error.
  • Claude explains a refusal in plain words and leaves out operator detail.

You can now build tool errors that tell the harness whether to retry and tell Claude what to say.

Error category

The kind of failure: transient, validation, permission or business

Retryable flag

A field that says whether the same call may succeed later

Transient error

A temporary fault, such as a timeout, that a retry can clear

Empty result

Nothing found, reported with no error flag

Business error

A refusal by a rule, such as a closed refund window

Foundations, lesson 6

Long conversations

A summary drops the facts unless code keeps them

After 30 turns your agent summarises the case, and the refund amount and the approval date fall out of the summary. Full order and shipment results fill the rest of the window. The customer asks how much was refunded and the agent has no answer. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch it lose the facts, then fix it with two small functions.

I doWatch the failure and its fix.

Facts sit outside the summary

Three parts share the work. Code keeps the facts. Code also trims each tool result before Claude reads it. Claude answers the question.

The case is Dana's refund: 30 turns over two days. A long case reaches Claude as a summary of the story, a few recent messages, and a facts block of values that must not be lost.

The facts block answers the question

Dana asks for the refund amount and the approval date on turn 31. The facts block holds both, so Claude answers in one sentence.

Open the harness card. The recorded request is 460 input tokens, and the facts block sits first, under a heading. Without the trim and the facts it is 2,138 tokens, and the answer is missing.

  1. CustomerRemind me of my refund amount and the date it was approved.
    Show the result
    Remind me of my refund amount and the date it was approved.
  2. HarnessClaude is given 1147 characters (460 tokens), with case facts: order_id 1042, customer Dana Cho, amount 89.0, refund_approved_on 2026-02-14
    Show the result
    {
  "order_id": "1042",
  "customer": "Dana Cho",
  "amount": 89.0,
  "refund_approved_on": "2026-02-14"
}
  3. ClaudeDana's refund for order 1042 is $89.00, and it was approved on February 14, 2026. I don't have any other details about…
    Show the result
    Dana's refund for order 1042 is $89.00, and it was approved on February 14, 2026. I don't have any other details about the refund's processing or when the money will reach her account.

1147 characters, 460 tokens given: the reply holds what was asked.

Two functions as written

update returns the facts after one more turn. The starting code returns them unchanged, so no fact is ever kept. trim cuts a tool result to the fields that matter. The starting code returns the whole result.

Each request carries a rolling window: a summary plus the last eight turns. A shipment result of 1,776 characters is paid for on every request while it stays in that window, and the case holds four of them.

starter/facts.py

What happens when the facts are not kept?

B. The amount sat in a tool result on turn 3. The summary kept the story and dropped the number.

The agent has no amount to give

This is the same question with the starting code. The context is over four thousand characters, most of it full shipment results, and none of it holds the amount or the date. The result card is red.

This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run, recorded once and replayed here. Claude was told to say when a detail is missing, so it says so and asks Dana again.

Facts are kept in code, output is trimmed

update copies the customer, order, amount and approval date from the order lookup into the facts. Later turns do not erase them. trim keeps only the fields each tool is used for, and the tests need the result under a quarter of its size.

Put the key facts at the start or the end of the context, under a heading. The middle of a long input is where detail is missed. None of this needs a model.

facts.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""Case facts live outside the summary, and tool output is cut to size."""23from kit.api import Json45NEEDED = {6 "lookup_order": ["order_id", "customer", "amount", "refund_approved_on"],7 "track_shipment": ["order_id", "status", "eta"],8}9FACTS = ("customer", "order_id", "amount", "refund_approved_on")101112def trim(tool: str, result: Json) -> Json:13 """Return only the fields the next step needs from a tool result."""14 return {k: result[k] for k in NEEDED.get(tool, []) if k in result}151617def update(facts: Json, turn: Json) -> Json:18 """Return the case facts after one more turn."""19 if turn["tool"] != "lookup_order":20 return facts2122 kept = trim(turn["tool"], turn["result"])2324 return {**facts, **{k: v for k, v in kept.items() if k in FACTS}}

The same rules run in the Agent SDK

In the Claude Agent SDK, trim runs as a PostToolUse hook, code the SDK runs right after a tool returns. In this real Claude Haiku 5.5 run, the shipment result reaches Claude at 74 of 1,776 characters. With the starting code, Claude cannot give the amount or the date.

Because a hook is plain code, it is deterministic. A rule that must hold before every refund goes in a PreToolUse hook on the refund tool, for example HookMatcher(matcher=REFUND, hooks=[check]).

A session is one saved conversation, and session_extras picks how the next one starts: {"resume": id} replays the saved history, adding "fork_session": True copies it first, and {} starts fresh. Resume suits a session whose context is still true. Start fresh with a summary and the facts when it is stale, and tell a resumed agent which files changed.

Copy the starting code and open work/long-conversations/facts.py. update() keeps no case facts, and trim() passes every tool result through whole. By the last turn the amount and date are buried, and the agent asks again.

The checks keep the customer, order, amount and approval date as facts across later turns, and cut a shipment result to a quarter of its size. Then the recorded long ticket must answer from the facts block.

Check your understanding

Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.

1. A 30-turn refund case is summarised three times. On turn 31 the customer asks for the refund amount and the agent asks them again. What is the best fix?

  1. AKeep the amount and date in a facts block that code rebuilds and puts first.
  2. BSwitch to a model with a larger context window so the whole history fits.
  3. CWrite a longer summary prompt and ask the model to keep every number.
  4. DAsk the customer to repeat the amount at the start of each session.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. Code keeps the facts exactly, so no summary can rewrite them.
  • B A larger window holds more text but does not stop a summary from dropping the amount.
  • C A longer prompt still asks a summary to rewrite itself, and each rewrite blurs numbers again.
  • D This moves the work to the customer and leaves the agent unchanged.

2. Each order lookup returns 40 fields and the agent uses 5. After four lookups, 85 percent of the context is tool output. What should change?

  1. ARaise the output token limit so the model can read the longer results.
  2. BTell the model in the prompt to ignore the extra fields.
  3. CSummarise the tool results once the window is nearly full.
  4. DCut each result to the five fields needed before the model reads it.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A The output limit controls the reply, and the results still fill the input.
  • B The ignored fields still cost tokens on every request.
  • C A late summary can blur the values the answer needs.
  • D Correct. Trimming keeps the needed fields and drops the rest, so every later turn is cheaper.

3. A 60,000 token input holds two key findings in the middle. The model misses both and finds a third one at the top. What is the best change?

  1. APut the key findings first, under a clear heading.
  2. BShorten the sentences around the findings.
  3. CLeave them in the middle, because the model reads the whole input evenly.
  4. DRepeat the question twice at the end of the prompt.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. The start and the end of a long input are read most reliably, and a heading names what matters.
  • B Shorter sentences do not change where the findings sit.
  • C Attention is uneven across a long input, and the middle is where detail is most easily missed.
  • D The question is not the problem. The findings are hard to find.

4. Select two effects of a history that grows to 30 turns of full tool output.

  1. AOld detail is buried, so a value from turn 3 is easy to miss.
  2. BThe model reads the old lines more carefully than the new ones.
  3. CEvery request carries the whole history, so cost rises each turn.
  4. DThe model reads the history once, so later turns cost nothing extra.
Show the answer

Answer: A, C

  • A Correct. The value is still there, but the model has more to search.
  • B Attention does not favour the old lines. Detail in the middle is easily missed.
  • C Correct. Each turn resends the history, so it is paid for again.
  • D Every request sends the history again, so the cost recurs on each turn.

5. An investigation was left for two weeks, and most of the files it read have changed since. The agent resumes the named session and quotes the old results. What is the best handling?

  1. AResume and raise the turn limit so the agent has time to notice.
  2. BStart fresh with a summary and the facts, because the old context is stale.
  3. CResume again and trust the old results, since the session remembers the work.
  4. DFork the session so the stale results are copied into a safe branch.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A More turns do not tell the agent that the files changed.
  • B Correct. A fresh start with the facts drops the stale output.
  • C A resumed session carries the old results, which are now wrong.
  • D A fork copies the same stale history into the branch.

6. A team wants to compare a refactor and a rewrite, both starting from the same 40-turn investigation. Which approach fits?

  1. AResume the same session twice and run both approaches in it.
  2. BStart two fresh sessions and paste a summary into each.
  3. CRun the refactor first, then the rewrite, in one session.
  4. DFork once per approach, so each branch starts from the same history.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A Both approaches would write into one history and mix their results.
  • B A fresh summary loses detail that the forks would keep.
  • C The rewrite would start from the refactor's results, not the original state.
  • D Correct. A fork copies the history into a new session, so each branch starts equal.

7. A named session continues after two files changed. The agent still quotes the old file contents. What do you add when you resume?

  1. AA longer system prompt that says to trust the session.
  2. BNothing, because a resumed session refreshes its own files.
  3. CA line that tells the agent which files changed, so it reads them again.
  4. DA second fork of the same session.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A Trusting the session is what keeps the old results in use.
  • B A session holds what was read then. It does not watch files.
  • C Correct. The agent cannot see the change unless it is told, and it can read the two files again.
  • D A fork copies the same old results.

8. Select two valid uses of resuming a named session.

  1. AContinue work after a large refactor changed most of the files.
  2. BContinue a task in the same session, where the context is current.
  3. CStart a follow-up on the same task the next morning, when no files changed.
  4. DBranch into two experiments from one saved point.
Show the answer

Answer: B, C

  • A After a large change the old results are stale, and a fresh start with a summary is safer.
  • B Correct. The context is still true, so resuming saves the work.
  • C Correct. Nothing changed, so the history is still accurate.
  • D Branching is a fork, which copies the history into a new session.

9. A shipment tool returns dates in three formats. Downstream code parses 1 in 6 of them wrongly. What is the most reliable fix?

  1. ANormalise the dates in a PostToolUse hook, before the model reads the result.
  2. BTell the customer which format to expect.
  3. CRetry the tool until it returns a format the parser knows.
  4. DAsk the model in the prompt to rewrite each date before it uses it.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. A hook runs every time and reshapes the result before the model sees it.
  • B The customer did not choose the format.
  • C A retry returns the same mixed formats.
  • D A prompt is probable, not certain, and 1 in 6 misses would persist.

10. A business rule must hold before any refund, with no exception. Which control fits?

  1. AA longer tool description that explains the rule.
  2. BA hook that checks the rule in code before the refund tool runs.
  3. CA sentence in the system prompt that states the rule.
  4. DA reviewer who reads the transcripts each week.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A A description guides the choice of tool and does not block a call.
  • B Correct. A hook is deterministic, so the rule holds on every call.
  • C A prompt rule is followed most of the time, and this rule needs every time.
  • D A weekly review finds a breach after the refund is paid.

11. A prompt asks the model to trim its own tool output. In a test of 12 replies, 1 skips the trim. What is the best change?

  1. AReword the prompt to say trim in capital letters.
  2. BMove the trim into a PostToolUse hook that runs on each result.
  3. CAdd two examples of a trimmed result to the prompt.
  4. DLower the temperature and run the test again.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A Emphasis improves the odds but leaves a chance of a miss.
  • B Correct. A hook runs in code, so the trim does not depend on the model.
  • C Examples help, and the model can still skip the step.
  • D A lower temperature reduces variety and does not make a step certain.

12. Select two things a PostToolUse hook can do.

  1. AChange what the model decided before it called the tool.
  2. BLog each result for later review.
  3. CReshape a tool result before the model reads it.
  4. DUndo a tool call that already finished.
Show the answer

Answer: B, C

  • A The call was already made. A PreToolUse hook acts before it.
  • B Correct. The hook sees the result, so it can record it.
  • C Correct. The hook can replace the output the model reads.
  • D The tool already ran. A hook cannot take that back.

Play: predict the output

This version keeps facts, but it takes them from every tool.

python
def update(facts: Json, turn: Json) -> Json:
    kept = trim(turn["tool"], turn["result"])
    return {**facts, **kept}

  1. A1042, the order the case is about.
  2. B1077, from the shipment lookup.
Show the answer

B. Every result merges into the facts, so a later lookup overwrites a case fact. Take each fact from the tool that owns it, and keep only the keys you named.

References

  • Context windows: how every turn and tool result counts against the window.
  • Context editing: the API feature that clears old tool results for you.
  • Effective context engineering: why a small, curated context beats a full one.
  • Agent SDK sessions: resume, fork or start fresh, and what each one keeps.

Conclusions

  • Case facts are kept in code, outside the summary, and placed first.
  • Each tool result is cut to the fields the next step needs.
  • Resume, fork or start fresh depends on whether the history is still worth its size.

You can now keep the facts of a long case exact and keep the window small.

Facts block

Values kept in code and placed first, so a summary cannot drop them

Summary

A rewrite of the story that loses specific values

Trim

Cutting a tool result to the fields the next step needs

Fork

A new session that starts from a copy of an old one

Foundations, lesson 7

The CLAUDE.md hierarchy

Team rules live in the project and load only where they apply

A new hire opens the shop repository and asks Claude to edit the cart. Claude does not know that money is stored in cents, because that rule sits in one colleague's personal file. The test naming rule loads for every file, even when nobody is writing a test. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch Claude miss the money rule, then fix it with two small files.

I doWatch the failure and its fix.

Claude loads what the project gives it

Claude Code reads memory files before it answers. A file in the project travels with the repository. A file in a person's home folder stays on that person's machine.

A rules file can also name the paths it covers. It then loads only when Claude works with a file that matches.

Memory stacks: the user file loads first, then the project file, then a file in the directory being worked on. The /memory command lists the files that loaded, which is the first check when a rule goes missing.

The right rules reach the right file

Claude is asked about the test file. It names the money rule from project memory and the test naming rule from the path rule. Both loaded, and nothing else came along.

The recording keeps four fields: result is the reply text, is_error is false, num_turns counts the turns and stop_reason is end_turn. Open the reply card to read result in full.

  1. New hireRead src/cart.test.ts. Then list, one short line each, the team conventions that apply…
    Show the result
    Read src/cart.test.ts. Then list, one short line each, the team conventions that apply when editing it. Do not edit anything.
  2. Claude namesthe money rule and the test naming rule
  3. Claude- Money in cents: store amounts as integer cents, never floats (CLAUDE.md). - Display format: show money as integer cents…
    Show the result
    - Money in cents: store amounts as integer cents, never floats (CLAUDE.md).
- Display format: show money as integer cents with two decimals (docs/style.md, pulled in by CLAUDE.md).
- Test names: start each test name with "should" (.claude/rules/tests.md). The current test, "adds the prices", doesn't follow this.
- One assertion per test: each test gets exactly one expect (.claude/rules/tests.md).
- Run tests before finishing: run the test suite before wrapping up any change (CLAUDE.md).

Claude named the rules that apply, no more.

Two files as written

Project memory is CLAUDE.md at the root of the repository. The starting file is an empty stub, so no team rule reaches a new hire. The rules folder, .claude/rules/ in a real project, holds tests.md, and the starting copy has no paths line, so it loads for every file.

That costs real tokens. Say the test rule is 300 tokens and Claude edits 200 source files. The rule rides along on each one, which is at least 60,000 tokens those requests never use.

starter/CLAUDE.md
1# Lumen shop23TODO(workshop): add the team rules and import the style guide.

What does Claude know about a source file?

Take the question "What conventions apply when editing src/cart.ts?" The money rule lives only in a colleague's personal file. The test naming rule sits in a rules file with no paths line.

Predict: What does Claude list for the source file?

  1. AThe money rule, because the team agreed on it.
  2. BThe test naming rule, and no money rule.
Show the answer

B. The personal file never reaches this repository. The test rule has no path limit, so it loads for the source file too.

Claude gets the wrong rules

This is the same question with the starting files. The reply names the test naming rule for a file that has no tests, and it does not name the money rule. The result card is red.

- docs/style.md: money is stored as integer cents and shown with two decimals. total() doesn't state its unit, so keep prices in cents.
- CLAUDE.md: the team rules section is still a TODO(workshop) placeholder, so there are no team rules yet.
- .claude/rules/tests.md: test names start with "should" and each test has one assertion. This governs src/cart.test.ts, not cart.ts itself.

The test naming rule loaded for a file it does not fit.

Move the rule in, and scope the other

The team rules go into project memory, and the style guide comes in with one @docs/style.md line. The guide stays in one file. The test rule gets a paths list in its frontmatter, the settings block between two --- lines at the top of the file. The list matches **/*.test.*.

Both files are plain text, and a colleague gets them with a clone. One glob covers tests in any number of folders, where a CLAUDE.md in each folder would need one file per folder. A long file is better split by topic into the rules folder.

CLAUDE.mdgreen lines are what the fix adds
1# Lumen shop23Team rules for every file in this repository.45Money is stored in cents, never as a float.67@docs/style.md89Run the tests before you finish a change.
We doChange one setting at a time and predict.

The same question now has the right answer

Use the switch to run the question with the rule in a colleague's user file, then in project memory. The card marked "This is where the runs split" shows which rules Claude named.

With the rule in project memory, the source file reply names the money rule and the reminder to run the tests, and the test naming rule stays out.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch claude-md-hierarchy.

Commands and skills follow the same folders

The switch below is the memory switch again: a colleague's user folder never reaches the new hire, and the project does. A command is one markdown file run by its name, such as /review, and where it lives decides who gets it.

Folder Who gets it
.claude/commands/ in the repository everyone who clones it
~/.claude/commands/ in a home folder only that person

A command file and a skill take the same frontmatter. A skill is a SKILL.md with its own directory, so it can also carry files, and Claude can pick it by its description.

The setting context: fork gives the skill its own fresh context, and only its summary comes back to the main conversation. The list allowed-tools pre-approves tools, and argument-hint shows what to type after the name.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch claude-md-hierarchy.

Try it: memory and path rules

Change one setting at a time. Pick the source file or the test file, then move the money rule and the test rule. A rule in a colleague's user file never reaches the new hire, and a test rule with no paths line leaks into the source file.

Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet. Eight recordings cover every cell.

The same files run in Claude Code

The harness copies your CLAUDE.md and rules folder into a sandbox project and runs claude -p --output-format json there. Replay needs nothing installed. A live run needs the claude command-line tool, signed in.

Only project files load, so a rule in a colleague's user file never reaches the run. The reply for the source file names the money rule and leaves the test rule out. A CLAUDE.md inside a subfolder loads too, when Claude works on a file there. This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run.

You do: write the memory files

Copy the starting files and open work/claude-md-hierarchy/CLAUDE.md. It holds a TODO in place of the team rules. Add the rules, import the style guide and say how to run the tests. Then give rules/tests.md a paths block.

The checks want no TODO, an @docs/style.md import and a test command in project memory. The test rule must load only for test files and stay out of CLAUDE.md.

Check your understanding

Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.

On the exam, "new team member", "consistently" and "only for test files" point to project memory and path rules. "Put it in the user config" is the wrong answer for a team rule.

1. A new hire's Claude writes prices as 12.99 floats. The team stores money in cents, and that rule sits in a colleague's personal Claude file. Two earlier hires hit the same problem. What is the best fix?

  1. ALeave it in the personal file, because user memory is shared with anyone who opens the same repository.
  2. BMove the rule into the project CLAUDE.md so it is committed and loaded for every clone.
  3. CAsk each hire to start their first prompt with a reminder that money is stored in cents.
  4. DHave the colleague sit with each new hire during the first week and correct their sessions.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A User memory lives in one person's home folder. It never travels with the repository, so nobody else loads it.
  • B Correct. A file committed at the project root goes wherever the repository goes, so every teammate loads the same rule.
  • C This treats the symptom on one session at a time. The next hire has to be told again.
  • D A person correcting sessions does not change what Claude loads, and it does not scale to the next hire.

2. A 900-line CLAUDE.md mixes API, test and deploy rules. Engineers cannot tell which rule applies to which work, and every session loads all 900 lines. What is the best fix?

  1. AKeep one file so every rule is in one place, and add a table of contents at the top.
  2. BMove each topic into the user memory of the engineer who owns that topic.
  3. CDelete the oldest rules until the file is 300 lines, whatever they cover.
  4. DSplit it by topic into separate files in the project's rules folder.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A A table of contents helps a reader, but Claude still loads all 900 lines and the topics stay mixed.
  • B Owners' personal files never reach the team, so their rules disappear for everyone else.
  • C Age says nothing about whether a rule still matters, so this deletes rules that may be needed.
  • D Correct. One file per topic makes each rule easy to find, and the files live in the repository.

3. A monorepo has a payments package with a 40-line money guide and a docs package with a 10-line writing guide. Both guides are pasted into every CLAUDE.md, so each session carries 50 lines. What is the best fix?

  1. AKeep each guide in one file and import only the one each package needs with an @ line.
  2. BMerge both guides into one 50-line guide at the root and delete the two originals.
  3. CPut the payments guide in the user memory of the people on the payments team.
  4. DWrite a hook that removes the other package's guide at the start of each session.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. An import pulls the file in where it is named, so each package loads its own guide and there is one copy to edit.
  • B A merged guide puts all 50 lines in front of every session, which is the cost you started with.
  • C User memory does not travel with the repository, so a teammate outside that team misses the guide.
  • D A hook adds a moving part to undo what the files already decide. Importing only what is needed costs nothing.

4. Which two statements about memory files are true? Select two.

  1. AAn import line copies the guide's text into the file once, so later edits to the guide do not reach it.
  2. BA user-level file in a home folder stays on that machine and never travels with the repository.
  3. CA user-level file is shared with teammates through the repository, like a project file.
  4. DUser, project and folder memory files layer, and all the ones that apply load together.
Show the answer

Answer: B, D

  • A An import is read when memory loads, so the guide is pulled in fresh and stays one copy.
  • B Correct. Only files inside the project are committed, so a home folder file is personal.
  • C A home folder file is not in the repository, so a clone does not carry it.
  • D Correct. The layers add up, and the closest file covers the work Claude is doing.

5. A test naming rule of 300 tokens sits in project memory. It loads for each of the 200 source files Claude edits, about 60,000 tokens of text those edits never use. What is the best fix?

  1. AShorten the rule to 150 tokens and keep it in project memory.
  2. BMove the rule into each author's user memory so source edits skip it.
  3. CPut the rule in a rules file with a paths list that matches only test files.
  4. DAdd a hook that removes the rule whenever Claude opens a source file.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A A shorter rule still loads for every file, and it may be too short to help.
  • B A personal file hides the rule from the rest of the team, including the people who write tests.
  • C Correct. A paths glob loads the rule only when Claude works with a matching file.
  • D Path matching is built in. A hook adds code to do what one line of frontmatter does.

6. Tests sit in 14 folders, and one naming rule covers all of them. A teammate proposes a CLAUDE.md in each folder. What is the better fix?

  1. AOne rules file whose paths list holds a glob such as **/*.test.*.
  2. BFourteen folder files, each holding a copy of the rule.
  3. COne folder file in the first test folder, which covers the other 13 folders.
  4. DOne rules file plus a hook that loads it when a test file is opened.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. One glob matches test files in every folder, so there is a single file to keep current.
  • B Fourteen copies drift apart the first time someone edits one and forgets the rest.
  • C A file in a directory loads for work in that directory and below. It does not reach sibling directories.
  • D The glob already does the matching, so the hook is an extra step with nothing to add.

7. A terraform rule of 3,000 tokens loads on every request, but only 5 in 100 requests touch a .tf file. What is the best fix?

  1. ATurn it into a skill that Claude must call before each edit to any file.
  2. BCut it to the 10 most important lines and keep it in project memory.
  3. CMove it to the user memory of the platform team so other requests skip it.
  4. DScope the rule with a paths glob that matches .tf files, so it loads only for them.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A A skill Claude must call before each edit adds a step to all 100 requests instead of removing the cost.
  • B A shorter rule still loads on every request, and cutting it may drop rules that matter for terraform.
  • C A personal file leaves other teammates without the rule when they edit terraform.
  • D Correct. The rule now loads for the 5 requests that need it and costs nothing on the other 95.

8. Which two effects follow from adding a paths list to a rule file? Select two.

  1. AThe rule loads only when Claude works with a file that matches the glob.
  2. BThe rule becomes personal and is left out of the repository.
  3. CRequests that touch other files skip the rule's tokens.
  4. DA hook must also be added before the match takes effect.
Show the answer

Answer: A, C

  • A Correct. The match on a file's path is what switches the rule on.
  • B The file stays in the project's rules folder and travels with the repository.
  • C Correct. A rule that does not load costs no tokens, so work on other files is cheaper.
  • D The match is built into how rules load, and no hook is involved.

9. A team pastes the same 12-line review prompt by hand each week, and five teammates now hold five versions. Where should the shared prompt live?

  1. AOn a wiki page that each teammate copies from before a review.
  2. BIn a file in the project's commands folder, committed to the repository.
  3. CIn each teammate's user commands folder, kept in step through a chat message.
  4. DIn the project CLAUDE.md as a paragraph that loads on every session.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A Claude cannot run a wiki page, and each copy drifts as soon as someone edits their own.
  • B Correct. A committed command is one file that everyone who clones the repository can run by name.
  • C Home folders are not shared, so the versions drift again and new hires have none.
  • D A paragraph in memory loads on every session, even when nobody is reviewing anything.

10. A developer keeps a personal review shortcut that calls their own scripts. It should not reach the other 30 people on the team. Where should it live?

  1. AIn the project's commands folder, with a note asking the team not to call it.
  2. BIn the project CLAUDE.md, written as a paragraph only they are expected to use.
  3. CIn the commands folder of their own home directory.
  4. DIn a project skill, because skills are the personal version of commands.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A The file would still be cloned by all 30 people, and a note does not stop it from showing up.
  • B Everything in project memory loads for every teammate.
  • C Correct. A user-level command stays on that machine and is never committed.
  • D A skill is also shared when it sits in the project. Where the skill lives decides who gets it, not the file type.

11. A review skill prints a 4,000-line diff summary into the main session, about 48,000 tokens. What keeps that work out of the main session?

  1. ASetting context to fork in the skill's frontmatter, so the skill runs apart.
  2. BWriting a longer description so Claude picks the skill more carefully.
  3. CSetting allowed-tools to Read so the skill can open fewer files.
  4. DSaving it as a command instead, since commands run apart from the session.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. A forked skill runs in its own context and returns only a summary to the main session.
  • B The description helps Claude choose the skill. It does not change where the work is done.
  • C A tool limit decides what the skill may use. What it reads still lands in the session.
  • D A command runs in the main session too. Only a fork moves the work apart.

12. Which two settings can a skill's frontmatter hold? Select two.

  1. AA share key that publishes the skill to every teammate.
  2. BAn allowed-tools list that pre-approves tools while the skill runs.
  3. CA memory key that rewrites CLAUDE.md each time the skill runs.
  4. DAn argument-hint that shows a person what to type after the name.
Show the answer

Answer: B, D

  • A There is no share key. The location of the skill decides who gets it.
  • B Correct. The listed tools run without a permission prompt while the skill is active.
  • C There is no memory key, and a skill does not rewrite memory files by itself.
  • D Correct. The hint labels the argument, for example a path to a diff, for the person typing.

Play: predict the output

A teammate wrapped the import in backticks so it reads like a path.

markdown
# Lumen shop

Money is stored in cents, never as a float.

Follow the style guide in `@docs/style.md`.

Predict: Does the style guide load into the session?

  1. AYes. The import line is still in project memory.
  2. BNo. Imports inside a code span are skipped, so the path stays plain text.
Show the answer

B. Claude Code reads an @ import only outside code spans and code blocks. Write @docs/style.md on its own line with no backticks, and keep backticks for a path you only mention.

References

  • Claude Code memory: where each memory file lives, and how imports and rules load.
  • Best practices: what belongs in CLAUDE.md and what to leave out.
  • Settings: the user, project and local scopes that sit beside memory.
  • Slash commands and skills: when a rule should be a skill that loads on demand.

Conclusions

  • Rules the whole team needs belong in project memory, so they travel with the repository.
  • A paths list loads a rule only for the files it fits.
  • A shared command belongs in the project, and a personal one stays in the home folder.

You can now place a rule where the right people and the right files will load it.

Project memory

CLAUDE.md in the repository, loaded for everyone who clones it

User memory

A file in a person's home folder that only that person loads

Import

An @ line that pulls another file into memory

Path rule

A rules file with paths that loads only for matching files

Foundations, lesson 8

Commands and skills

A repeated prompt becomes a skill with limits

The team pastes the same review prompt into Claude every day. When someone saves it as a skill, the skill reads the whole diff inside their session. A long diff fills the session before the real work starts. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch a plain skill flood a session, then fix it with three lines of frontmatter.

I doWatch the failure and its fix.

A skill is a prompt the project keeps

A skill is a SKILL.md file. The file holds a name, a description that tells Claude when to use it, and the prompt itself.

It lives in the project, so a clone brings it to the whole team. A personal skill lives in the home folder and follows one person.

A skill suits work a person starts by name, such as a review. A rule every edit must follow belongs in project memory, and a rule for some files belongs in a path rule. Those two load by themselves, so nobody has to remember to call them, and a missed call would drop the rule.

The review runs and the session stays small

A colleague types /review with a 1,000-line diff file. The skill reads it and finds the rounding bug. Your session made no model calls of its own.

The skill ran in a fork, a separate context that returns only its result. The fork read the diff with tokens of its own, about as many as the starting skill spends in your session, and only its review came back.

Open the reply card to read the whole review.

  1. Colleague/review diffs/big.diff
    Show the result
    /review diffs/big.diff
  2. Your session0 turns; the fork used 27,552
    Show the result
    Your session took 0 tokens in 0 model turns. Tokens used by a fork, outside your session: 27,552.
  3. Claude- average calls reduce without an initial value, so average([]) throws a TypeError. - average returns a float in cents…
    Show the result
    - average calls reduce without an initial value, so average([]) throws a TypeError.
- average returns a float in cents (the trailing comment flags this as a rounding bug) and is not rounded or converted to an integer like the PRICE_* constants.
- The hunk header @@ -1,3 +1,1000 @@ says three original lines were replaced, but the hunk has no - lines, so the diff is malformed or drops the original three lines.
- The constants jump from PRICE_0999 to the average function with no PRICE_1000, so the numbering is capped at 999 and any later price entry would need a different scheme.

Your session made 0 model calls. The fork used 27,552 tokens of its own, and only its review came back.

The skill file as written

The description tells Claude when the skill applies. The body is the prompt, and it reads the diff named in $ARGUMENTS. The starting file has nothing else, so it runs in your session and pre-approves no tools.

starter/SKILL.md
1---2name: review3description: Review a diff file for bugs.4---56TODO(workshop): this skill runs in your main session and pre-approves no tools.7Give it a hint for its argument, fork it and pre-approve only Read.89Read the diff file named in $ARGUMENTS and list the bugs you find, one short10line each. Do not edit anything.

Where does the diff get read?

Take a review of a 1,000-line diff with the starting skill. The skill has no context line and no allowed-tools line.

Predict: Where does Claude read the diff?

  1. AIn your own session, so the diff sits there with everything else.
  2. BIn a separate context, so your session stays small.
Show the answer

A. Without context: fork, a skill is a prompt added to your session. Every read it makes lands there too.

The starting skill fills the session

This is the same review with the starting skill. The review is fine, but your session pays for every token of the reading, and the whole diff stays in your context. The result card is red.

The session card shows the count. The small diff costs about a quarter as much.

This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run through claude -p, recorded once and replayed here.

  1. Colleague/review diffs/big.diff
    Show the result

  2. Your sessiontook 29,570 tokens in 2 turns
    Show the result
    Your session took 29,570 tokens in 2 model turns. Tokens used by a fork, outside your session: 0.
  3. Claude- src/prices.ts:1004: average calls reduce with no initial value, so an empty array throws a TypeError instead of returning…
    Show the result
    - src/prices.ts:1004: average calls reduce with no initial value, so an empty array throws a TypeError instead of returning a value.
- src/prices.ts:1004: the comment says "rounding bug: float cents", but the function never rounds. Integer-cent inputs can return fractional cents.
- src/prices.ts:1: the hunk header says the old file has 3 lines (-1,3), but the diff has no - lines, so the patch can't apply cleanly to a file that has those 3 lines.

I read the diff only and didn't edit anything. The repo isn't a git repository, so I couldn't check these against the source tree.

The review ran in your session, which took 29,570 tokens in all.

Fork it, limit it, hint its argument

With context: fork, the skill runs apart and returns only its result. With allowed-tools: Read, the fork reads without asking. argument-hint tells a person what to type after the name. The solution file also pins the model to Claude Haiku 5.5 and ends the description with the trigger phrase "Use when asked to review a diff."

The line only names what the skill may use without asking. A tool that settings deny stays denied.

SKILL.mdgreen lines are what the fix adds
1---2name: review3description: Review a diff file for bugs. Use when asked to review a diff.4argument-hint: <diff file>5context: fork6allowed-tools: Read7model: claude-haiku-5-58---910Read the diff file named in $ARGUMENTS and list the bugs you find, one short11line each. Do not edit anything.
We doChange one setting at a time and predict.

The same diff ends differently

Run the big diff with the starting skill, then with the forked skill. The card marked "This is where the runs split" shows what your session took: tens of thousands of tokens against no model calls at all. The fork spent about as many of its own, outside your session.

The review itself is as good in both. The difference is where the reading happened.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch commands-skills.

Commands and skills side by side

A command is one markdown file named for what it runs. A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md, optional frontmatter and support files. A file in .claude/commands/ and a skill both give you /name.

Where it lives Who gets it
.claude/skills/ in the repository everyone who clones it
~/.claude/skills/ in a home folder only that person

A personal variant of a team skill gets a different name. The argument arrives as $ARGUMENTS, or as $0 and $1 by position, counting from zero.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch commands-skills.

Try it: skill and diff

Change one setting at a time. Pick the small diff or the big one, then switch between the starting skill and the fix.

Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet. The small diff hides the problem, because a session of several thousand tokens looks like any other review.

The same skill runs in Claude Code

The harness copies your SKILL.md into a sandbox project and runs claude -p "/review diffs/small.diff". It reads the skill's settings back and reads two numbers from the CLI's usage report: the tokens your session used and the tokens the fork used. Replay needs nothing installed. A live run (LIVE=1) needs the claude command-line tool installed and signed in.

This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run.

- total now divides the cent sum by 100, so it returns dollars as a float while its signature and name still say cents. Any caller expecting integer cents will get wrong amounts.
- The result is a non-integer float (e.g. 0.07), so further money arithmetic or equality checks on it can pick up floating-point error.
- The function's return type is still number, so TypeScript won't flag callers that treat the value as cents.

Check your understanding

Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.

1. A team pastes the same review prompt into each session, and five teammates now hold five different versions. What is the best fix?

  1. AKeep the prompt on a wiki page and ask each teammate to copy the latest version.
  2. BSave it as a project skill that is committed, so every clone runs the same review.
  3. CSave it as a skill in one teammate's home folder, which the others pick up automatically.
  4. DPaste the prompt into the project memory so that it loads on all 200 requests a day.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A Each copy drifts the first time someone edits it, which is how you got five versions.
  • B Correct. A committed skill is one file that travels with the repository.
  • C A home folder skill follows one person. A teammate's clone does not include it.
  • D Memory loads on every request. A skill loads only when the review runs.

2. A review skill reads a 4,000-line diff, about 48,000 tokens, and fills the main session. Which frontmatter line keeps that reading out of the session?

  1. Aallowed-tools set to Read, which stops the reading from landing in the session.
  2. Bargument-hint set to a diff path, which makes the skill check its input first.
  3. Ccontext set to fork, so the skill runs apart and returns a summary.
  4. DA longer description, so Claude reads the diff more carefully.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A The list names what may run without asking. Reads by Read still land in the session.
  • B A hint labels the argument for the person typing. Nothing checks it.
  • C Correct. A fork gives the skill its own context, and only its summary comes back.
  • D The description helps Claude choose the skill. It does not move where the work is done.

3. A review skill edited two files while it was reviewing, and a review must only read. What is the best fix?

  1. ATreat allowed-tools as a note for readers and rely on a sentence in the body instead.
  2. BTurn the skill into a command, because commands cannot edit files.
  3. CFork the skill, because a fork hides its edits from the main session.
  4. DList only Read in allowed-tools, so no write tool is pre-approved for the skill.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A The list is a real setting. A sentence in the body is the weaker control.
  • B A command file is a skill without extras. It has the same tools available.
  • C A fork moves where the work runs. It does not change what the skill may use.
  • D Correct. With only Read listed, an edit is not pre-approved and has to ask first.

4. Which two statements about skill frontmatter are true? Select two.

  1. AAn argument-hint is checked, and a call with the wrong argument is refused.
  2. Bcontext set to fork runs the skill apart and returns a summary.
  3. CA skill's full body loads in every session, so a long one costs tokens on each of 200 requests.
  4. DAn allowed-tools list names the tools the skill may use without asking.
Show the answer

Answer: B, D

  • A The hint is a label shown while typing. No check refuses a call.
  • B Correct. The fork gives the skill its own context.
  • C The description is what loads up front. The body loads when the skill runs.
  • D Correct. The list pre-approves those tools for the skill.

5. A colleague runs the review but forgets the diff path on 3 of 10 runs. What is the best fix?

  1. ASet argument-hint to show that a diff file goes after the name.
  2. BLoad the skill in every session so Claude remembers the path.
  3. CWrite the path into the skill body, so the skill reviews one diff only.
  4. DFork the skill so the missing path is filled in from the summary.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. The hint shows the expected argument while they type the name.
  • B Loading more does not tell the person what to type.
  • C A fixed path stops the skill from reviewing any other diff.
  • D A fork changes where the work runs, and it does not supply a missing argument.

6. A developer keeps a personal review shortcut that calls their own scripts. It should not reach the other 30 people on the team. Where should it live?

  1. AIn the project's skills folder, since a skill there stays personal.
  2. BIn the project's commands folder, since commands stay personal.
  3. CIn the skills folder of their own home directory.
  4. DIn a forked project skill, because a fork hides it from the team.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A Everything in the project's skills folder is cloned by all 30 people.
  • B A command in the project is cloned too. Where the file lives decides who gets it.
  • C Correct. A user-level skill stays on that machine.
  • D A fork decides where the work runs, not who can see the file.

7. A teammate wants a personal variant of the team's review skill with 2 extra checks, and keeps the team one too. What is the best way?

  1. AEdit the team's file in place, since a user skill is shared anyway.
  2. BAdd the 2 checks to the description of the team skill.
  3. CSave the variant under the same name in the project, since commands and skills merge.
  4. DSave the variant in the home skills folder under a different name.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A An edit in the project changes the review for all 30 people.
  • B The description says when to use the skill. The checks belong in the body.
  • C A project file is shared, and two files with one name compete for the same command.
  • D Correct. A different name at user level keeps both skills available.

8. Which two statements compare a command file with a skill folder? Select two.

  1. AA skill folder can hold support files next to its SKILL.md.
  2. BA command and a skill are different features that cannot share a name.
  3. CA skill can set frontmatter such as a fork and a tool list.
  4. DA skill loads its full body into every session, and a command does not.
Show the answer

Answer: A, C

  • A Correct. A skill is a directory, so it can carry extra files.
  • B A command file and a skill both create the same slash name and work alike.
  • C Correct. Frontmatter is where a skill sets its fork and its tools.
  • D Only the description loads up front. The body loads when the skill runs.

9. A terraform convention must apply every time Claude edits a .tf file, with nobody typing a command. Which choice fits?

  1. AA skill that each developer runs by name before editing a .tf file.
  2. BA rule file with a paths glob that matches .tf files, so it loads by itself.
  3. CA shorter version of the rule, kept in project memory for every request.
  4. DA skill that Claude loads into every session whether or not a .tf file is open.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A A skill waits to be called, so a developer who forgets drops the rule.
  • B Correct. A path rule loads by itself when Claude works with a matching file, and costs nothing otherwise.
  • C A shorter rule still loads on every request, and it may lose detail terraform needs.
  • D A skill is not loaded by default into every session, and this would not limit the cost to .tf files.

10. A review reads a 1,000-line diff and should run only when a person asks for it. Which choice fits?

  1. AA skill with context fork, which a person starts by name.
  2. BA rule file whose paths glob matches diff files, so it runs on its own.
  3. CA paragraph in project memory that tells Claude to review each diff it sees.
  4. DA rule file plus a hook that starts the review when a diff file opens.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. A skill runs when called, and the fork keeps the reading out of the session.
  • B A path rule adds guidance when a file matches. It does not run a task on demand.
  • C Memory loads on every session and costs tokens whether or not a diff is open.
  • D A rule only supplies text, and a hook adds code to do what calling a skill already does.

11. Which two statements compare a skill with a path rule? Select two.

  1. AA skill must list a glob in its frontmatter, or Claude can never pick it.
  2. BA path rule loads by itself when Claude touches a file matching its glob.
  3. CA path rule runs only when a person types its name, the way a command does.
  4. DA skill runs when a person types its name, as in /review with a diff file.
Show the answer

Answer: B, D

  • A A glob is optional. A person starts a skill by name, or Claude picks it from its description.
  • B Correct. The path match switches the rule on, with no command from anyone.
  • C Nobody calls a path rule. It loads when a matching file is in play.
  • D Correct. A skill is a prompt that someone can start by name.

12. A money rule of 200 tokens must apply to all 500 files in the repository. Where should it live?

  1. AIn a skill that developers call before each edit.
  2. BIn a path rule with a glob that lists every folder, plus a hook for the rest.
  3. CIn a forked skill, so the rule stays out of the session.
  4. DIn project memory, which loads for every file with no command.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A A skill must be called each time, and a missed call drops the rule.
  • B A long glob list still misses files, and the hook adds a moving part.
  • C A fork hides the work from the session, and a rule the model must follow has to be in its context.
  • D Correct. A rule all files need loads by itself from project memory.

References

  • Skills: every front matter field, including context and allowed-tools.
  • Slash commands: how a skill becomes a command you type.
  • Settings: how permission rules decide which tools ask first.
  • Claude Code memory: why a rule you always want is memory, not a skill.
  • Agent skills: how skills load only what a task needs.

Conclusions

  • A repeated prompt becomes a skill file that the project keeps and the team shares.
  • context: fork keeps a skill's reading out of your session.
  • allowed-tools pre-approves only the tools a skill's job needs.

You can now turn a pasted prompt into a shared skill that stays small and safe.

Skill

A SKILL.md prompt that Claude loads when the task fits

Fork

Running the skill in its own context, so only its result returns

Allowed tools

The tools a skill may use without asking; settings can still deny them

Argument hint

A short label that shows what to type after the skill's name

Foundations, lesson 9

Plan mode

Plan wide changes and edit small ones directly

A team asks Claude to migrate every order module to a new call style. Claude starts editing at once, and 15 files change before anyone sees the approach. The same team's one-word typo gets an hour of planning that it never needed. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch Claude edit every module with no plan, then fix it with a short team file.

The size of the change picks the way to work

A wide change, or one with several valid designs, gets a plan first. Claude reads the code and lists every file it would change. A person approves the plan, and only then do edits begin.

A fix in one file with one clear answer is edited directly.

    This change touches 15 files, and there are two reasonable designs, so under the project's CLAUDE.md I have not edited anything. Here is the plan for your approval.

Current state

- All 14 modules in src/orders have the same shape: export function X(id, done: (total: number) => void) calling fetchOrder(id, (order) => done(order.total)).
- Nothing in src outside these files references fetchOrder. I did not search the rest of the repo.

Files I would change, in order
1. src/lib/orders.ts: make fetchOrder(id) return Promise<{ total: number }> instead of taking a callback.
2. src/orders/cart.ts
3. src/orders/checkout.ts
4. src/orders/coupons.ts
5. src/orders/fraud.ts

12. src/orders/shipping.ts
13. src/orders/tax.ts
14. src/orders/tracking.ts
15. src/orders/wishlist.ts

Each module would become export async function X(id: string, done: (total: number) => void): Promise<void> { const order = await fetchOrder(id); done(order.total); }.

Approach choices
- A (recommended): Change fetchOrder to return a Promise and make each module an async function that awaits it. Each module keeps its done callback, so its public signature stays the same and no callers break.
- B: Also drop the done callback, so each module returns Promise<number>. This is a cleaner API, but it changes every export's signature. Since no callers exist in src, the breakage is limited, but I would need to confirm there are none elsewhere in the repo.
- C: Add a new promise-returning fetchOrderAsync and keep the callback fetchOrder. This is the safest for other callers, but it leaves two code paths behind.

Should I go ahead with A? If you choose B or C, tell me which. I would also grep the whole repo for other fetchOrder callers before editing. I have not run any tests, since I haven't found a test setup yet.

How it works

- src/lib/orders.ts: fetchOrder is now async and takes only id. It returns Promise<{ total: number }> instead of calling a callback.
- Each module (tax, cart, payments, refunds, returns, wishlist, fraud, checkout, shipping, loyalty, inventory, tracking, invoices, coupons): the function is now async, takes only id, and returns Promise<number>:

ts
export async function tax(id: string): Promise<number> {
  const order = await fetchOrder(id);
  return order.total;
}


Choices I made

- I replaced the done callback with the return value. Nothing outside src/orders imports these modules, and fetchOrder has no other callers, so no call sites broke. If you want to keep the done parameter for compatibility, that's a small change.
- I didn't touch the import lines or the file layout. Each module is still one file.

Verification

- A search finds no done or callback usage left under src/.
- All 14 modules contain exactly one await fetchOrder(id).
- The repo isn't a git repository, so I didn't commit anything.

The CLAUDE.md file has no workflow guidance for changes like this, so I followed the defaults above.

Claude edited 15 files with no plan.

Say when to plan and when to edit

The fix is two bullets, and the house facts stay. A change to more than three files, or one with several valid approaches, gets a list of every file and a stop for approval. A fix in one file with one clear answer is edited directly.

Claude Code also has a plan mode, switched on with --permission-mode plan. It blocks every edit for the session. The team file sets the habit for everyone, and still lets a one-file fix through.

Planning is one way to choose a shape for the work. A fixed chain runs the same steps in order, such as 4 checks on each pull request, then a last pass on how the parts fit. An adaptive plan lets each finding pick the next step, which suits an open investigation.

CLAUDE.mdgreen lines are what the fix adds
1# Lumen shop23Choose how to work before you touch a file.45- A change to more than three files, or one with several valid approaches:6 do not edit. List every file you would change, in order, and stop for7 approval.8- A fix in one file with one clear answer: edit it directly. Do not plan.910- The order modules live in `src/orders`, one file per module.11- `src/lib/orders.ts` holds the shared order helpers.
We doChange one setting at a time and predict.

The same file, two different ends

Use the switch to run the migration with the starting file, then the fixed file. The card marked "This is where the runs split" shows what Claude did with the files.

Try the typo request too. Both files fix it in one edit, which is right. Send linked problems in one message, because one fix may solve both. Send independent problems one at a time, so each result is easy to check.

A code review has the same problem at file scale. One pass over 15 files spreads attention thin. Review each file on its own, then run a last pass on the links between files.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch plan-and-refine.

Search by content, match by name, edit by text

The tool calls card lists what each run did: the starting run used Edit, and the planning run did not. Grep searches inside files, so it finds every caller of fetchOrder. Glob matches file names, so it lists the modules. Edit replaces text that appears once.

When the text appears 6 times, Edit cannot choose. Add more surrounding text so the match is unique, or set replace_all when every copy should change. If neither works, Claude falls back to Read and Write for the whole file.

To trace a function through 3 wrapper modules, Grep the entry point, then Read each match to follow it. For noisy discovery, an Explore subagent reads the files and hands back a short summary.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch plan-and-refine.

Refine with examples and a failing test

When the first result is close but wrong, paste the failing test and a concrete input with its expected output, so Claude can check its own fix. Give 2 or 3 examples and write the failing test first. When decisions are open, let Claude interview you before it builds. For the migration:

text
Convert fetchOrder to async. Two examples:
  before: fetchOrder(id, (o) => done(o.total))
  after:  return (await fetchOrder(id)).total
  before: fetchOrder(id, cb)
  after:  cb(await fetchOrder(id))

This test fails now. Make it pass:
  test("refund awaits fetchOrder", async () => {
    expect(await refunds("A1")).toBe(40);
  });

The harness runs claude -p with --permission-mode acceptEdits and judges a run by the files it changed. Replay needs nothing installed. A live run needs the claude command-line tool, signed in. Every run on this page is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run.
