Check your understanding

Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.

1. A migration touches many modules, and the edits collide in one module because nobody agreed the approach. What is the best fix?

  1. AEdit the modules one at a time and re-run the tests after each edit.
  2. BUse plan mode first, agree the approach, then execute the edits.
  3. CPlan every change from now on, including one-line fixes.
  4. DRun the same migration again with a longer prompt.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A Testing after each edit finds collisions late. The approach is still undecided.
  • B Correct. A plan agrees the design before any module changes.
  • C Planning a one-line fix costs more than the fix. Match the effort to the change.
  • D A longer prompt still starts editing at once, with no agreed approach.

2. A stack trace points at one line in one file, and the fix is clear. A plan would take 40 minutes. What is the best way to work?

  1. APlan it in plan mode so a person approves the edit first.
  2. BSplit the fix across two sessions so each one stays short and cheap.
  3. CInterview Claude about the design before touching the file.
  4. DEdit it directly. One file with one answer needs no plan.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A A plan adds 40 minutes to an answer that is already clear.
  • B Two sessions add overhead to a one-line change.
  • C An interview is for open decisions. This one has none.
  • D Correct. A small, clear fix is edited directly.

3. A caching change has three valid options with different costs, and the team has not chosen one. Claude starts editing. What should change?

  1. AStart in plan mode to weigh the options before any edit.
  2. BEdit directly but keep the diff under 50 lines so review stays easy.
  3. CPick the cheapest option and let the tests decide.
  4. DAsk for the change one file at a time.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. An open design needs a proposal a person can choose from.
  • B A short diff can still lock in the wrong option.
  • C Tests check behavior. They do not compare three designs.
  • D Smaller steps do not settle which design to use.

4. Which two things does plan mode give you? Select two.

  1. AClaude edits files faster, because it skips reading.
  2. BPlan mode writes the plan into the source files as comments.
  3. CClaude explores the code without editing any file.
  4. DA person approves the approach before edits start.
Show the answer

Answer: C, D

  • A A plan reads more, not less, before anything is edited.
  • B A plan is a proposal. It does not change the source files.
  • C Correct. Reading and proposing change nothing.
  • D Correct. The approval is the point of the plan.

5. The request says make the parser better, and each of 4 passes drifts somewhere new. What is the best fix?

  1. AAsk Claude to score each pass out of 10 and keep the best.
  2. BSwitch to plan mode, which makes the goal clear.
  3. CGive 2 or 3 input and output examples that show the target.
  4. DAsk for a fifth pass with a longer description of quality.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A A score from the same vague goal still has no target to measure against.
  • B A plan of a vague goal is still vague. The missing piece is an example.
  • C Correct. Examples turn a wish into something Claude can match.
  • D More adjectives are still not a target, so the next pass drifts too.

6. A fix must handle 5 edge cases, and each pass breaks a different one. What is the best fix?

  1. ADescribe all 5 edge cases in one long sentence before any code runs.
  2. BFix them one by one and hope none come back.
  3. CWrite the tests for the 5 cases first, then fix what fails.
  4. DEdit the file directly so the passes are faster.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A A sentence cannot tell Claude which case broke. A failing test can.
  • B Without tests, a fix for one case can break another silently.
  • C Correct. Failing tests name what is left, and Claude can run them.
  • D Speed is not the problem. The passes have no check between them.

7. The cache and failure decisions are unclear, and Claude assumes answers for both. What is the best fix?

  1. AGive Claude a longer description and let it assume again.
  2. BLet Claude interview you about the open decisions first.
  3. CPlan every module in detail, including the ones that are already clear.
  4. DPick an answer yourself and hide the question.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A More words still leave the two decisions open, so Claude assumes again.
  • B Correct. The questions bring out the requirements before code exists.
  • C The clear modules do not need a plan. Only the open decisions do.
  • D A hidden choice is still an assumption, and the team cannot review it.

8. Which two rules apply when you send fixes to Claude? Select two.

  1. ASend linked problems together, because one fix may solve several.
  2. BSend every issue in one message, whether linked or not.
  3. CSend independent problems one at a time.
  4. DSend one problem only when it touches one file.
Show the answer

Answer: A, C

  • A Correct. Linked problems share a cause, so they belong in one request.
  • B Independent issues in one message blur which change fixed which problem.
  • C Correct. One request per independent issue keeps each result easy to check.
  • D The link between problems decides this, and not the file count.

9. A search must find every caller of fetchOrder across the modules. Which tool fits?

  1. AGrep, because it searches the contents of files.
  2. BEdit, because it can find a string.
  3. CGlob, because the callers share a file name.
  4. DGlob, because it searches the text inside files.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. Grep searches contents, so it finds each caller.
  • B Edit replaces text. It does not report where text appears.
  • C Callers sit in many differently named files, so names do not help.
  • D Glob matches file names. It does not look inside files.

10. Edit fails because the text it must replace appears 6 times in the file, and only the copy in the refund function should change. What is the best fix?

  1. ASet replace_all, so all 6 copies change in one call.
  2. BInclude more surrounding text, so the match is unique.
  3. CSwitch to Glob, which can pick one match inside a file.
  4. DUse Grep to rewrite only the line inside the refund function.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A replace_all is for changing every copy. Here 5 of the 6 must stay.
  • B Correct. With enough context the text appears once, and Edit can choose it.
  • C Glob matches file names, so it cannot choose between matches in a file.
  • D Grep finds text. It does not change any file.

11. A function is called through 3 wrapper modules, and you need the real one. What is the best way to trace it?

  1. AGlob every file whose name contains the function's name, then edit those.
  2. BRead every module before searching.
  3. CGrep the entry point, then Read each match to follow it.
  4. DEdit each wrapper to print its name.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A File names do not show who calls whom.
  • B Reading everything first spends context on files that do not matter.
  • C Correct. Grep finds the next hop and Read confirms it.
  • D Editing the code to learn what it does changes files for no reason.

12. Which two facts about the built-in tools are true? Select two.

  1. AGrep matches file names only.
  2. BEdit replaces text that appears once.
  3. CGlob searches the text inside each file.
  4. DRead and Write handle whole files.
Show the answer

Answer: B, D

  • A Grep searches contents. Glob is for names.
  • B Correct. The text must be unique, or Edit cannot choose.
  • C Glob matches names. Grep is the tool for contents.
  • D Correct. They read or write a whole file.

13. A review of 14 files in one pass misses bugs because attention is spread thin. What is the best fix?

  1. AReview each file on its own, then the links between files.
  2. BReview all 14 files again in the same pass, more carefully this time.
  3. CReview only the 3 largest files.
  4. DAsk for a longer review of everything.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. One pass per file keeps attention local, and a last pass checks the links.
  • B A second identical pass has the same spread of attention.
  • C Bugs in the 11 other files stay unread.
  • D More length does not focus the attention.

14. An open investigation of an unknown codebase has steps nobody can list in advance. Which plan fits?

  1. AA fixed chain of 5 steps written up front and followed in order.
  2. BAn adaptive plan that changes with what turns up.
  3. COne step that reads everything at once.
  4. DNo plan, only direct edits.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A A fixed list cannot follow what the code turns up.
  • B Correct. Each finding picks the next step.
  • C One read of everything fills the context with files that may not matter.
  • D Edits come after the code is understood.

15. The same 4 checks run on every pull request, in the same order. Which plan fits?

  1. AAn adaptive plan built afresh each time.
  2. BAn interview before each check.
  3. CA plan mode session for each pull request.
  4. DA fixed chain of the 4 checks.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A A predictable task does not need a new plan on each run.
  • B The questions are known, so there is nothing to interview.
  • C A reviewed plan for a routine check adds an approval that changes nothing.
  • D Correct. Steps that repeat make a fixed chain.

16. Which two facts describe task decomposition with a chain? Select two.

  1. AThe steps run in order, each using the one before.
  2. BA last pass checks how the parts fit together.
  3. CThe steps run at once, with no order.
  4. DEach step repeats the whole task.
Show the answer

Answer: A, B

  • A Correct. A chain is sequential.
  • B Correct. The integration pass catches what single steps miss.
  • C A chain has an order. Steps that run at once are a different shape.
  • D Each step does a part of the task, not the whole of it.

Play: predict the output

The team wants a plan approved before any wide change, so they wrote it into project memory.

markdown
# Lumen shop

Before a change to more than three files, plan first.
Do not edit anything until I approve the plan.

Predict: What stops Claude from editing before you approve?

  1. AOnly the instruction. Memory is context, so nothing blocks an edit.
  2. BClaude Code reads the rule and blocks Edit until you approve.
Show the answer

A. Memory steers what Claude does but enforces nothing. When an edit must wait, start in plan mode, which explores and proposes without editing until you approve.

References

  • Common workflows: how to plan a change in plan mode, then make the edits.
  • Claude Code memory: where the team file loads and what it should hold.
  • Permission modes: plan mode, which reads and proposes before any edit.
  • Best practices: explore, plan, code and commit, and when to skip the plan.

Conclusions

  • A wide change, or one with several valid designs, gets a plan before any edit.
  • A one-file fix with one clear answer is edited directly.
  • Refinement works best with examples of input and output and a failing test.

You can now pick the way to work by the size of the change, and refine a result with evidence.

Plan mode

Claude reads and proposes, and edits wait for approval

Direct edit

Claude changes the file at once, for a small clear fix

Refinement

Improving a result with examples and tests, not a vague request

Interview

Claude asks questions first, so the requirements come out

Foundations, lesson 10

Coordinator and subagents

One coordinator spawns focused researchers together

A team asks Claude for a recall report on a faulty power bank. The coordinator plans only the cause and the scope, so customers and the regulator are never researched. It also starts one researcher per turn, so the report is slow and incomplete. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch one coordinator miss angles and wait, then fix it with a plan and a brief.

I doWatch the failure and its fix.

A coordinator plans the angles and researchers cover them

The coordinator does not research. It splits the topic into angles that together cover the whole report, briefs one researcher for each, and merges what comes back. The plan lists the angles, the model spawns and merges, and the Agent SDK runs the subagents.

This design fails in three ways. The split is too narrow, the researchers run one per turn, and the subagents get steps instead of goals. You will see the first two fail, then fix them.

The coordinator runs the same agent loop as in An agent is a loop that ends on stop_reason. Claude picks the next tool, each result joins the history, and the loop continues on tool_use and stops on end_turn. A turn cap is only a safety net, never the stop rule.

Every angle is covered and the researchers run together

The coordinator spawns a researcher for the cause, the scope, the customers and the regulator. All four Agent calls arrive in one response, so the researchers run at the same time.

Open the coordinator card to read the four angles. The report holds one finding for each. The tool that spawns a researcher is the Agent tool. Older releases and the exam guide call it Task.

  1. ColleagueWrite the recall report for the power bank.
  2. Researcher toolseach researcher may call 1 tool(s)
  3. Coordinatorresponse 1: 4 researcher(s)
    Show the result
    Power bank recall: cause of fault
Power bank recall: affected units scope
Power bank recall: customers with units
Power bank recall: regulator to notify
  4. ClaudePower bank recall report - Cause of fault: Cells swell because one separator batch was faulty (one note, found…
    Show the result
    Power bank recall report

- Cause of fault: Cells swell because one separator batch was faulty (one note, found in two searches; no further detail).
- Scope of affected units: Units made in March, lots seven to nine. No models, serial ranges, exact batch dates, or total unit count in the notes.
- Customers with a power bank: Customer instruction in the notes: "Stop using it and quote swap code PB7." No count of affected customers and no method for identifying them.
- Regulator to tell: Notes say "Tell the consumer safety agency within ten days." The agency's name, jurisdiction, required form, and what starts the ten-day clock are not in the notes. The ten-day deadline can't be dated until the trigger is confirmed.

Gaps to close before filing: the affected model and serial ranges, the number of units and customers, how customers are contacted, and the regulator's identity and filing requirements. I haven't sent any notice to a regulator.

4 of 4 angles covered, all spawned in one response.

The plan and the brief as written

plan chooses the angles and brief writes the coordinator's instructions. The starting plan lists two angles and the starting brief says to research one at a time.

The wait adds up. If each researcher takes 6 seconds, four in a row take 24 seconds. Four at once take 6.

Research each angle below one at a "21 "time: spawn a researcher, wait for its findings, then spawn the "22 "next.\n"23 f"{lines}\n"24 "Then write the report."25 )

What does the report hold when the plan has two angles?

Take the recall request. The plan lists the cause and the scope. The brief says to spawn a researcher, wait for its findings, then spawn the next.

Predict: What does the report say about customers and the regulator?

  1. ANothing researched, because no researcher was asked.
  2. BA finding for each, because researchers are thorough.
Show the answer

A. The coordinator follows its plan. An angle nobody owns is never researched, so the report has gaps or fills them with guesses.

The report has gaps and takes two turns

This is the same request with the starting plan and brief. Two researchers appear, one per response, and the report has no finding on the regulator. The outcome line is red.

This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run through the Agent SDK, recorded once and replayed here.

  1. ColleagueWrite the recall report for the power bank.
  2. Researcher toolseach researcher may call 1 tool(s)
  3. Coordinatorresponse 1: 1 researcher(s)
    Show the result
    Research power bank fault cause
  4. Coordinatorresponse 2: 1 researcher(s)
    Show the result
    Research power bank affected scope
  5. ClaudeRecall Report: Power Bank Status: Draft. The notes support a cause and a partial scope, but several required…
    Show the result
    Recall Report: Power Bank

Status: Draft. The notes support a cause and a partial scope, but several required fields are missing.

1. Defect and cause
- Failure mode: Battery cells swell.
- Root cause (as recorded in the notes): One separator batch was faulty.
- Evidence: The notes contain one statement of the cause. It has no source ID, test data, or description of how the swelling was observed.
- Open questions: The notes don't say whether the faulty separator batch is the only cause, whether swelling is linked to overheating, or how the defect was confirmed.

2. Affected units (scope)
- Confirmed from the notes: Units made in March, lots 7 through 9.
- Not yet established: Model numbers, serial ranges, year of manufacture, total unit count, markets, and customers or distributors.
- Caution: The March / lots 7–9 entry is the only scope note found. Follow-up searches found nothing else. It can't be treated as the complete scope until it's confirmed against manufacturing or lot records.

3. Customer action
- The notes give the interim instruction: "Stop using it and quote swap code PB7." It doesn't say which units this covers, so it should be confirmed against the scope above before it's published.

4. Gaps before this can be finalized
1. Confirm the separator-batch root cause with engineering or supplier records, and get the source reference.
2. Obtain the affected model numbers, serial or lot ranges, and manufacturing dates from production records.
3. Establish the unit count and the markets and channels where the units were sold.
4. Confirm the PB7 swap code and customer instructions against the confirmed scope.
5. Check whether a regulator notice is required. I did not send one, since the scope is not yet confirmed.

3 of 4 angles covered, spawned across 2 responses.

Cover the whole topic, then spawn together

The fix has two parts. plan lists an angle for each concern the report must answer. brief tells the coordinator to spawn every researcher in the same response. It also tells the coordinator to name any angle with no findings.

The brief also gives each researcher a goal, not a script of steps. A subagent starts fresh: it sees none of the coordinator's turns, so the goal and the fact it must return are all it learns about the task. Independent angles have no reason to wait.

Angles must not overlap. If two researchers repeat the same queries, divide the topic so each owns one question. Ask each subagent a specific question, and keep the coordination in the main agent. When the merged findings hold an empty section, have the coordinator send a new task for that angle.

coordinator.pygreen lines are what the fix adds

Do not wait between spawns. Each researcher starts "21 "fresh and sees none of your turns, so give it its goal: the one "22 "fact the report needs from that angle. "23 f"Angles: {listed}. "24 "Then write a report with one line per angle, keeping each "25 "researcher's facts. Name any angle that has no findings."26 )
We doChange one setting at a time and predict.

The same request, two different ends

Use the switch to run the request with the starting coordinator, then the fixed one. The card marked "This is where the runs split" is the first difference between the two runs.

Try the smart plug too. The fix holds on a different recall.

The shape of the work picks the plan. A fixed chain runs the same steps in order, which suits a weekly report. An adaptive plan lets each finding pick the next step, which suits an unknown incident. A review that reads files one at a time misses links between them, so add a last pass on how they connect.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch coordinator-subagents.

Each role gets only its tools

Every researcher here needs one tool, the notes search. Switch to the run where it may also call the notice sender and the web search. The report is the same, but a researcher that could send a notice to a regulator could have done it.

An agent with 18 tools picks the wrong one more often than one with 4 or 5, so give each role its own tools. When one step must come first, set tool_choice, the setting that names the tool Claude must call, to it. The value any only forces some call.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch coordinator-subagents.

Try it: coordinator and recall

Change one setting at a time. Pick the power bank or the smart plug, the plan and the spawn. A broad plan alone still costs four responses, and spawning together alone still leaves two angles with no findings.

Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch coordinator-subagents.

Researchers in the Agent SDK

A researcher is a subagent defined by a description, a prompt and a tool list. The coordinator starts it with the Agent tool, so that tool must be allowed. The notice sender and the web search go in disallowed_tools, so not even the coordinator can call them.

The harness runs the request through the SDK's query() and counts the researchers spawned in each response. This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run.

In a long investigation the early findings scroll far back. A scratchpad is a plain file the agent writes findings to and rereads on resume. fork_session branches a resumed session to try another approach. Keep noisy discovery in a subagent, and after a crash resume from saved state.

- Cause: The relay sticks closed when it overheats. This is the only cause in the notes. Why it overheats, and whether a fix or recall exists, are not recorded.
- Scope: Partial. The only note says "Units sold from June to August," with no year. No models, serial or lot ranges, quantities, or regions are recorded.
- Customers: No findings for customers. The only related note is "Unplug it and quote credit code SP3." It names no customers, counts, contact details, or units.
- Regulator: The electrical safety board must be told "within a week." The notes don't give its proper name, jurisdiction, reporting form, or the date the week starts.

I did not send a notice to the regulator. The notes don't include the agency's name or reporting form, and the notice tool was not needed to write this report.

Terminal
./workshop start coordinator-subagents

The checks want the cause, scope, customers and regulator in the plan, and every angle in the brief. They expect all researchers spawned in one response, and a named gap for an angle with no findings.

Check your understanding

Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.

1. A recall report for a power bank has sections on the cause and the scope but nothing on the regulator. The coordinator's plan listed two angles, and each got a researcher. What is the root fix?

  1. AAdd a line saying the regulator is out of scope, since both researchers finished.
  2. BChange the plan so its angles cover the whole topic, including customers and the regulator.
  3. CTell the writer to sound more confident in the regulator section.
  4. DGive each researcher 10 more search turns.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A Both researchers finishing shows only that the two angles were covered. The report still lacks what it must answer.
  • B Correct. An angle nobody owns is never researched, so the gap starts in the plan.
  • C Confident wording cannot add a finding that no researcher produced.
  • D More turns deepen the two angles. They do not create a third or a fourth.

2. Two researchers repeat the same search: 40 percent of their queries overlap. Their angles are both worded as 'the power bank' plus a verb. What fixes the overlap?

  1. ARun them one at a time so the second can skip what the first found.
  2. BRaise the search limit so both researchers can finish every query they start without being cut off.
  3. CUse one researcher for all four angles so nothing repeats.
  4. DDivide the topic into angles that do not overlap, each with its own question.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A A researcher starts fresh and never sees what the first one found, so it cannot skip anything. The wait only adds seconds.
  • B A higher limit lets both repeat more. The overlap is in the split.
  • C One researcher loses the parallel speed and still needs the angles defined.
  • D Correct. Distinct angles give each researcher different work, so the repeated queries disappear.

3. The coordinator reads the merged findings and sees that the customer section is empty. The plan listed only cause and scope. What should happen next?

  1. ASend a new task out for the missing angle, then merge again.
  2. BPublish the report and note that customers were out of scope.
  3. CAsk the scope researcher to guess what customers must do.
  4. DRestart the run with a longer brief for the cause researcher.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. A coordinator judges the synthesis and sends work back out when an angle has no findings.
  • B The plan was narrow by mistake. Calling it out of scope hides a gap the report must fill.
  • C A guess is not a finding, and that researcher has no notes on customers.
  • D A longer brief changes one angle. The missing angle still has no owner.

4. Select two duties the coordinator owns in a hub-and-spoke design.

  1. ARouting work to subagents and merging what they return.
  2. BRunning every search itself so the subagents stay idle.
  3. CPassing every message between subagents, so they never talk to each other directly.
  4. DLetting each subagent read the whole history so it can decide alone.
Show the answer

Answer: A, C

  • A Correct. Splitting, briefing and merging are the coordinator's job.
  • B Then there is nothing to coordinate and no parallel speed.
  • C Correct. All traffic goes through the hub, which is what keeps the run observable.
  • D A subagent has its own context, and deciding alone breaks the single point of control.

5. Four researchers are spawned one per turn. Each takes 6 seconds, so the report takes 24 seconds for work that could take 6. What change removes the wait?

  1. ARun them one at a time to be safe, and check each answer.
  2. BLower each researcher's turn limit to 1.
  3. CTell the coordinator to spawn all four in the same response.
  4. DGive one researcher all four angles in one long brief.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A Independent researchers do not affect each other, so serial runs buy no safety.
  • B A turn limit does not change when a researcher starts.
  • C Correct. Independent angles have no reason to wait, so the time becomes the slowest researcher.
  • D That one researcher still works through them in turn, so the 24 seconds stay.

6. A recall report needs the cause, the regulator and the customers, plus a supplier audit that depends on which part the cause researcher names. Which researchers should the coordinator spawn in its first response?

  1. AAll four in one response, since spawning together always beats waiting for any result.
  2. BThe cause, regulator and customer researchers now, and the audit once the cause returns.
  3. COne researcher per response, since a single dependency makes the whole plan run in series.
  4. DThe cause researcher alone, then the other three together once its finding is in.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A The audit needs the failed part, so spawning it now gives it nothing to audit.
  • B Correct. Independent angles go out together, and only the dependent one waits.
  • C Only the audit depends on another angle. The other three have no reason to wait.
  • D The regulator and customer angles do not need the cause, so holding them back adds a turn.

7. An AgentDefinition exists for a researcher, yet no subagent is spawned in 12 turns. The coordinator's tool list holds only the search tool. What is missing?

  1. AA higher turn limit, since 12 turns is too few to start a subagent.
  2. BA model setting on the definition so it runs on a larger model.
  3. CA second AgentDefinition so the coordinator has a choice.
  4. DThe Agent tool (Task in older releases) in the allowed tools.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A Starting one takes a single call. The tool is missing, not the turns.
  • B The model of a subagent matters after it starts.
  • C A second definition cannot be spawned either without the tool.
  • D Correct. Without it the coordinator has no way to start a subagent.

8. Select two facts about four researchers spawned by Agent calls in one coordinator response.

  1. AThey share one context, so each can read the findings of the others.
  2. BThey run at the same time instead of one after another.
  3. CThe wait becomes the slowest researcher, not the sum of all four.
  4. DThe coordinator must still read each result before the next can start.
Show the answer

Answer: B, C

  • A Each subagent starts fresh with its own context. Findings come back only to the coordinator.
  • B Correct. Several Agent calls in one response start together.
  • C Correct. Four 6-second researchers finish in about 6 seconds, not 24.
  • D That is the one-per-turn pattern this replaces. Calls in one response do not wait on each other.

9. An outage of unknown origin needs investigating, and nobody knows which service is involved. Which plan fits?

  1. AA fixed chain of ten steps written before the first query.
  2. BAn adaptive plan that maps the system, then picks each next step from what the last one found.
  3. COne long prompt that lists every likely cause and tells the researcher to check each one in order.
  4. DNo plan: let each researcher run until it feels done.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A A script cannot react to what the first query shows.
  • B Correct. When the steps are not known, each finding decides the next step.
  • C A checklist spends turns on causes the findings already rule out.
  • D With no plan, angles overlap and gaps stay.

10. A weekly report runs the same 5 steps every Monday and its format never changes. Which design fits?

  1. AAn adaptive plan that rediscovers the steps each week.
  2. BA coordinator that spawns 5 researchers with open goals.
  3. CA fixed chain, because the steps repeat.
  4. DOne prompt with no steps.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A Rediscovery costs tokens each week for a result that never changes.
  • B Open goals suit unknown work. Here the work is known.
  • C Correct. Known, repeated steps are cheapest and most predictable as a fixed pipeline.
  • D Without steps a repeated job drifts from week to week.

11. A code review reads 14 files one at a time and misses that a function in one file is called wrongly from another. What fixes the miss?

  1. AAdd an integration pass that reads across files after the per-file passes.
  2. BRead each file twice with a stricter prompt.
  3. CFit all 14 files into one pass with a larger window.
  4. DDrop the per-file passes and review only a summary.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. Links between files only show when files are read together.
  • B Each read is still one file, so the link stays invisible.
  • C A larger window does not fix how attention spreads across 14 files.
  • D A summary drops the detail where the bug lives.

12. Select two true facts about fixed pipelines and adaptive plans.

  1. AA fixed pipeline suits work that repeats with known steps.
  2. BAn adaptive plan is cheaper because it needs no planning calls.
  3. CA fixed pipeline handles a surprise by rewriting its own steps.
  4. DAn adaptive plan suits discovery, where each step depends on the last finding.
Show the answer

Answer: A, D

  • A Correct. Predictable work gets predictable cost.
  • B Adaptive plans spend calls on planning as they go.
  • C A fixed pipeline cannot change its steps.
  • D Correct. Unknown problems need the next step chosen from evidence.

13. One agent holds 18 tools and picks the wrong one in 3 of 10 calls. What should you change?

  1. AWrite a longer description for each of the 18 tools.
  2. BGive every agent every tool so the model can choose freely.
  3. CSet tool_choice to any so it must call something.
  4. DGive it the 4 to 5 tools that fit its role.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A Longer text adds more to compare across 18 choices.
  • B More choices make selection worse for every agent.
  • C That forces a call. It does not make the call the right one.
  • D Correct. Fewer tools raise selection accuracy, and other roles get their own tools.

14. A search researcher was given an email tool just in case. In 2 of 20 runs it emailed a draft to a customer. What is the fix?

  1. AKeep the email tool and add a prompt line that asks the researcher not to send email to customers.
  2. BRemove the email tool, because it sits outside the researcher's role.
  3. CGive the email tool to every other agent too, for consistency.
  4. DLower the temperature so it stops using tools it does not need.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A A prompt line is a request, and 2 in 20 shows requests slip.
  • B Correct. A tool outside the role invites misuse. Removing it removes the failure.
  • C That spreads the risk to every agent.
  • D Temperature changes variety, not which tools are offered.

15. The first step of a run must be a lookup, but 4 runs in 20 skip it and search first. How do you fix the order?

  1. ASet tool_choice to any so the model picks the best first tool.
  2. BPut the lookup last in the tool list so it is read last.
  3. CForce one named tool on the first turn with tool_choice.
  4. DAdd a bold line to the prompt asking for the lookup first.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A Any means a tool must be called, and the model still picks which.
  • B List order does not set call order.
  • C Correct. A named tool fixes which call comes first.
  • D Emphasis raises the odds and still leaves 1 run in 20 to chance.

16. Select two values that tool_choice accepts.

  1. Abest, where the model picks the most accurate tool.
  2. Bany, where the model must call some tool but picks which.
  3. CA single named tool, which forces that call.
  4. Dsequence, which runs the tools in the listed order.
Show the answer

Answer: B, C

  • A There is no best value. The model chooses among tools only under auto or any.
  • B Correct. It guarantees a call and leaves the choice to the model.
  • C Correct. It fixes the exact tool, and auto lets the model decide whether to call.
  • D tool_choice does not schedule tools.

17. A 3-hour investigation starts quoting generic patterns instead of its 12 early findings, which have scrolled far back in the context. What helps?

  1. AWrite findings to a scratchpad file and re-read it when the work resumes.
  2. BRepeat the original goal every 10 turns.
  3. CRaise the turn limit so the agent has more room.
  4. DAsk for a one-line summary of everything each turn.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. A file keeps exact findings outside the context that scrolls.
  • B The goal is not the findings that were lost.
  • C More turns add more context to scroll past.
  • D A summary drops the specifics and sources.

18. Noisy discovery adds 60,000 tokens of search output to the main context, and later answers get worse. What is the better design?

  1. AKeep the raw output and tell the model to ignore the noise.
  2. BHave a subagent do the search and return a short answer.
  3. CCut the search output to its first 500 tokens.
  4. DRun the searches on a larger model.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A Tokens in context still draw attention whether or not they are ignored.
  • B Correct. The noise stays in the subagent's context and only the answer comes back.
  • C The answer may sit after the cut.
  • D A larger model does not shrink the context.

19. A run crashed at phase 3 of 5 after 40 minutes. How should it resume?

  1. AStart again from phase 1 with the same prompt.
  2. BAsk the model to recall what phase 3 held and to redo only the parts it remembers.
  3. CResume from the last chat message alone.
  4. DLoad the saved structured state and continue from phase 3.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A That repeats 40 minutes of finished work.
  • B A new session has no memory of the old one.
  • C Chat text is not structured state.
  • D Correct. Saved state lets a run resume without repeating finished phases.

20. Select two coordination rules for a multi-step investigation.

  1. AAsk subagents specific questions rather than open topics.
  2. BLet each subagent decide the next phase and start it.
  3. CKeep the coordination in the main agent.
  4. DPass each subagent the full history so it can coordinate.
Show the answer

Answer: A, C

  • A Correct. A specific question returns a finding the coordinator can merge.
  • B Subagents deciding for themselves lose the single point of control.
  • C Correct. One place decides the next step, so the run stays understandable.
  • D A subagent does not see the history, and it should not need to.

21. A loop stops when the reply text contains the word done. In 6 of 30 runs the model writes done while a tool call is still pending. Which stop rule is right?

  1. AStop when the reply text names no tool.
  2. BStop once the reply is longer than 200 words.
  3. CStop on the end_turn stop reason and continue on tool_use.
  4. DStop after a fixed 3 turns.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A Text parsing misreads a reply that mentions a tool by name.
  • B Length says nothing about pending calls.
  • C Correct. The stop reason is the model's own signal that it has no more calls.
  • D A fixed count cuts off long jobs and pads short ones.

22. Tool results are not added to the history, and the model repeats the same call 5 times. What is missing?

  1. ARaise the turn limit so it finds the answer eventually.
  2. BAppend every tool result to the history before the next request.
  3. CLower the temperature so it stops repeating.
  4. DSet tool_choice to any so it always picks a tool.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A More turns give more repeats.
  • B Correct. The model reads the history, so a result it never sees is a call it repeats.
  • C Temperature does not show the model a result.
  • D It picks a tool again, blind to the last result.

23. A loop ends after 5 turns because the cap is 5, even when the work is unfinished. How should the cap be treated?

  1. AAs a safety net, with the model's end_turn as the stop rule.
  2. BAs the main stop rule, tuned for each job.
  3. CAs a way to set the answer length.
  4. DAs the retry count for failed tool calls.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. The cap guards against a runaway loop and should rarely be reached.
  • B A tuned number still cuts off jobs that need more turns.
  • C A turn cap does not shape length.
  • D Retries are a separate, bounded policy.

24. Select two facts about what drives an agentic loop.

  1. AThe code picks the next tool from a fixed list.
  2. BThe model picks the next tool from the history.
  3. CThe history is cleared after every tool call.
  4. DEach tool result joins the history before the next model call.
Show the answer

Answer: B, D

  • A A fixed list is a script, not a loop.
  • B Correct. Choosing the next step is the model's part of the loop.
  • C A cleared history would lose every result.
  • D Correct. That is how the model sees what its call did.

A. When tools is left out, the subagent inherits every tool it can be given. List the tools it needs, such as WebSearch and WebFetch, so a researcher cannot write files.

References

  • Agent SDK subagents: how a coordinator defines its researchers and spawns them.
  • Agent SDK sessions: what each session keeps, and how to resume or fork one.
  • Define tools: how a tool and its input are described to the model.
  • How we built our multi-agent research system: how a lead agent splits research across parallel subagents, and what it costs.

Conclusions

  • A coordinator plans angles that cover the whole topic, then checks for a gap.
  • Independent researchers are spawned in the same response, so they run together.
  • A researcher knows only its brief, so the brief names its goal and the reply shape.

You can now split a research task into angles, spawn researchers together, and give each role only its tools.

Coordinator

The agent that plans the angles and joins the findings

Subagent

A helper with its own context, prompt and tool list

Angle

One question a researcher answers for the whole report

Coverage gap

An angle with no findings, named in the report

Foundations, lesson 11

Passing context

A subagent knows only what its prompt holds

A coordinator collects findings from researchers, then starts a writer subagent to draft the recall report. The writer is handed the task and nothing else. It cannot name a source for any claim, and nobody can check a figure. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch the writer work with no findings, then fix the handoff so every claim keeps its source and date.

I doWatch the failure and its fix.

The brief is the writer's whole world

A subagent starts fresh, with its own prompt and tools. It does not see the coordinator's turns, the researchers' notes or the tool results the coordinator read. Whatever the writer must use has to be in the prompt the coordinator writes. That prompt is the brief.

This design fails in three ways. The findings never reach the writer, a summary drops each source, and two figures that differ only by date look like a conflict. You will see the first fail, then fix it, then see the third.

Do not solve this by sending the whole history. Every request carries it, so each call costs more as it grows, and early facts get buried in the middle of a long input. Send the findings the writer needs and nothing more.

A brief with findings gives a sourced report

The brief holds the task and every finding. Each one has its claim, its evidence, its source and its date. The coordinator starts the writer with the Agent tool, called Task in older releases, and gives the brief as the prompt.

Open the prompt card to read what the writer got. Every line of the report ends with the source and date it came from.

  1. ColleagueWrite the recall report for the power bank.
  2. Writer prompt6 of 6 findings in the brief
    Show the result
    Task: Write the recall report for the power bank.

Findings from the researchers
- Claim: The cells swell when a separator is thin. Evidence: A teardown found separators under spec. Source: Lab teardown Date: 3 Mar
- Claim: The thin separators came from one batch. Evidence: The batch code matches every failed unit. Source: Supplier audit Date: 5 Mar
- Claim: Units made in March are affected. Evidence: Failures cluster in lots seven to nine. Source: Batch log Date: 6 Mar
- Claim: Forty units swelled in the field. Evidence: Reports came from six countries. Source: Field report Date: 9 Mar
- Claim: No unit has caused an injury. Evidence: No claim was filed. Source: Claims desk Date: 11 Mar
- Claim: Customers can swap a unit for free. Evidence: The offer needs the lot code on the base. Source: Returns desk Date: 12 Mar

How to write
Write one line per finding. Cite each line: end it with its source and date in brackets. If two findings give different figures for the same thing, keep both figures with their dates and do not pick one.
  3. WriterPOWER BANK RECALL REPORT (built only from the researcher findings supplied; the sources give day and month but no…
    Show the result
    POWER BANK RECALL REPORT (built only from the researcher findings supplied; the sources give day and month but no year)

Findings, one line each:

1. Cells swell when the separator is thin. A lab teardown found the separators under spec. [Lab teardown, 3 Mar]
2. The thin separators came from one batch. The batch code matches every failed unit. [Supplier audit, 5 Mar]
3. Failures cluster in lots seven to nine. [Batch log, 6 Mar]
4. Units made in March are affected. [Batch log, 6 Mar]
5. Forty units swelled in the field. Reports came from six countries. [Field report, 9 Mar]
6. No unit has caused an injury. The supporting evidence is that no claim was filed. [Claims desk, 11 Mar]
7. Customers can swap a unit for free. The offer requires the lot code on the base of the unit. [Returns desk, 12 Mar]

Conflicting figures (both kept, not resolved):
- Scope of the batch: Finding 2 says the thin separators came from one batch [Supplier audit, 5 Mar]. Finding 3 says failures cluster across lots seven to nine [Batch log, 6 Mar]. Whether the affected population is one batch or three lots is not settled by the findings.

Caveats for the reader:
- Finding 4 (March) is not shown directly in its evidence. The cited evidence refers to lots seven to nine, and the link from those lots to March production is not stated in the findings.
- Finding 6 is weak support for its claim. No claim being filed does not establish that no injury occurred. The wording should be treated as unverified.
- Finding 7 is conditional. The free swap depends on the lot code being on the base, so the offer does not cover every unit without qualification.
- The findings do not name the product model, the total number of units affected, or the total units sold. These are needed for a complete recall scope.

6 sources and 6 dates kept of 6.

The brief as written

brief turns the task and the findings into the writer's prompt. The starting version passes the task and ignores the findings, so the writer has nothing to cite.

Findings cost little to pass. Each one is about 40 tokens, so twelve are about 480 tokens. Passing none costs 0 and loses every citation.

Two habits keep the brief lean. Ask each researcher to return only the few fields the writer needs, with the source and date kept on each claim. Tell a subagent what is already covered, so it does not repeat a search the coordinator finished.

starter/handoff.py
1"""The handoff: what the report writer is told, since it knows nothing else."""234def brief(task: str, findings: list[dict[str, str]]) -> str:5 """The writer's whole prompt.6 TODO(workshop): the writer starts fresh and cannot see the findings.7 Pass each one with its claim, evidence, source and date.8 """9 return f"{task}\n\nWrite one line per finding."

What does the writer see of the coordinator's work?

Take the request for the recall report. The coordinator holds six sourced findings. It calls brief with the task and the findings, and the starting version returns only the task.

  2. BAll six, because they share the session.
Show the answer

A. A subagent does not inherit the coordinator's context. Pass the findings in the prompt, or they do not exist for the writer.

Pass the claim, evidence, source and date

The fix writes each finding into the brief as one block with separate fields: the claim, the evidence, the source and the date. It then asks for one line per finding, each ending with its source and date.

Keeping the four fields apart is what lets a source survive the writing. Data and its metadata travel together.

The same findings, two different ends

Use the switch to run the request with the starting handoff, then the fixed one. The card marked "This is where the runs split" shows how many findings the writer was given.

Try the shorter set of six too. The starting handoff keeps none of the findings in either set, and the fix keeps all of them in both.

This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch passing-context.

Conflicts keep both sources

The twelve findings hold two figures for one thing: 40 swollen units on 9 March and 65 on 18 March. The fixed brief tells the writer to keep both with their dates. Switch to a brief that keeps only the newer figure. The report lists only the 65 and moves the 9 March count to a superseded note.

A date often explains a gap between two figures, so show both. Match the format to the content: a table for finance figures, prose for news and a list for technical facts. Put key findings first under clear headings, because a long input is read least in the middle.

Passing findings to a subagent in the Agent SDK

The writer is defined with AgentDefinition: a description, a prompt, an empty tool list and a model. The coordinator starts it with the Agent tool, so that tool must be in the allowed tools. The harness runs the request through the SDK's query() and reads the prompt the writer was given from the recording.

The run starts in an empty folder, and the writer has an empty tool list, so any tool it tries is refused. A session resumed with fork_session branches into a new session, to try an alternative from one history. This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run.

Check your understanding

Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.

1. A writer subagent returns a fluent recall report with no sources. The coordinator read six sourced findings earlier in its session and then asked the writer to write the report. What is the root fix?

  1. AAsk the writer to be more careful about sources, since it has the same session as the coordinator.
  2. BPaste the six findings, each with its source and date, into the writer's prompt.
  3. CRaise the writer's turn limit from 4 to 12 so it can search for the sources itself.
  4. DAsk a second writer to edit the report and add the missing citations afterwards.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A The writer does not share the session. Care cannot cite what it has never seen.
  • B Correct. A subagent knows only its prompt, so whatever the writer must cite has to be in it.
  • C More turns let it guess longer. The sources are in the coordinator, and a limit does not move them.
  • D A second writer starts just as fresh, with no findings. It can only invent a citation.

2. A subagent repeats a search the coordinator finished an hour ago, and 9 of its 12 queries match earlier ones. The coordinator's history holds the results. What fixes the repeat?

  1. AGive the subagent read access to the coordinator's conversation so it can look for itself.
  2. BTell the coordinator to run every search twice so one copy is always in the subagent's cache.
  3. CAsk the subagent to write shorter queries, since long queries are likely to match older ones.
  4. DPass the earlier findings in the subagent's prompt and tell it what is already covered.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A A subagent starts with a fresh context and does not see the coordinator's turns.
  • B A cache is not a context. The duplicate work doubles and the subagent still does not know the results.
  • C Query length is not the cause. The subagent does not know what was already searched.
  • D Correct. The subagent has no history, so the prompt is the only place the earlier work can reach it.

3. A coordinator pastes 12 findings into the writer's prompt as one paragraph of prose. The report cites 4 sources and gets the dates wrong for 7 claims. What change keeps the metadata?

  1. AKeep each claim, its evidence, its source and its date as separate fields in the brief.
  2. BAsk the coordinator to write a shorter paragraph so the writer can hold all 12 facts at once.
  3. CTell the writer to add the dates from memory when a claim has none, to keep every line uniform.
  4. DMove the source names to the start of the paragraph, before the first claim.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. Separate fields let the source and date travel with the claim, so nothing has to be guessed from prose.
  • B Shorter prose drops more detail. The loss comes from blending fields, not from length.
  • C Memory is how an invented date gets into a report. The date has to be in the brief.
  • D Moving the names does not tie each one to its claim. The link is lost either way.

4. Select two statements that are true of a subagent started by a coordinator.

  1. AIt starts fresh, with none of the coordinator's turns.
  2. BIt sees the findings the coordinator read, because both work on one request.
  3. CIt learns about the task only from the prompt it was given.
  4. DIt reads the coordinator's earlier tool results when it needs a source to cite.
Show the answer

Answer: A, C

  • A Correct. The coordinator's turns and tool results are not copied into it.
  • B They work on one request but hold separate contexts.
  • C Correct. Anything the coordinator read and did not write into the brief is missing for the subagent.
  • D Tool results stay in the coordinator's context. The subagent only sees what the brief repeats.

5. A coordinator merges 12 findings into one summary paragraph for the writer. The report reads well but a reviewer cannot trace 9 of its claims to a source. What should the coordinator keep?

  1. AA longer summary, so the 9 untraceable claims each get a full sentence of their own.
  2. BOnly the claims that more than one researcher found, since those need no source.
  3. CThe mapping from each claim to its source, passed along with the claim.
  4. DA note at the top of the report saying the claims come from trusted researchers.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A A longer summary still has no source attached. The mapping is what is missing.
  • B Agreement between researchers is not a citation. A reviewer still has nothing to check.
  • C Correct. A claim with its source can be checked. A summary without the mapping cannot.
  • D A general note names no source. Each claim needs its own.

6. A lab report says 12 percent of units failed, while a retailer call says 15 percent. A reviewer asks the writer which figure is right. What should the report do?

  1. AShow both figures, each with its source, and say which numbers conflict.
  2. BReport the 15 percent, since the higher figure is the safer one for a recall.
  3. CAverage the two and report 13.5 percent with no sources, to keep the line short.
  4. DDrop both figures and write that failures were reported, to avoid taking a side.
Show the answer

Answer: A

  • A Correct. The reader can judge the gap only when both figures and their sources are visible.
  • B Choosing by size hides the other source. The reader cannot see the conflict.
  • C An average belongs to neither source and cannot be checked.
  • D Dropping both loses the evidence. The report should show the conflict.

7. A report holds two figures for swollen units: 40 from a 9 March field report and 65 from an 18 March field update. A reviewer calls it a contradiction. What explains it?

  1. AOne of the two sources is wrong, so the writer should keep the newer one and drop the other.
  2. BThe dates differ, so the later figure may count units that swelled after the first report.
  3. CThe writer rounded one of them, so the figures should be averaged to 52.5.
  4. DThe researchers used different search tools, so the figures cannot be compared at all.
Show the answer

Answer: B

  • A Nothing says either is wrong. Dropping one throws away the trend.
  • B Correct. A date often explains a gap. Keeping both dates lets the reader see that.
  • C An average hides both the dates and the two sources.
  • D Different tools do not make two dated counts incomparable. The dates are the difference.

8. A report holds quarterly financial figures from 4 sources. Select two rules for presenting them.

  1. AWrite them as flowing prose, since one format suits every kind of content.
  2. BUse a table, since numbers are easier to compare across rows and columns.
  3. CPut the sources in a single list at the bottom, since rows read more cleanly without them.
  4. DKeep the source with each row, so every figure can be traced.
Show the answer

Answer: B, D

  • A A table suits figures, prose suits narrative. One format does not suit both.
  • B Correct. Finance figures are compared by row and column, which is what a table is for.
  • C A list at the end breaks the link between a figure and its source.
  • D Correct. Without a source beside the row, the reader cannot check a number.

9. A coordinator passes a 60,000 token input to the writer. The 2 findings that matter most sit in the middle and the report misses both. What helps most?

  1. ALeave them in the middle and ask the writer to read the whole input twice.
  2. BMove to a model with a larger window, so 60,000 tokens no longer counts as long.
  3. CAdd a sentence at the end saying the middle of the input is important.
  4. DPut the key findings at the start under clear headings and trim the rest.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A Asking twice does not change where the model attends. The position is the problem.
  • B A larger window holds more, but key facts in the middle are still missed.
  • C A sentence at the end does not bring the middle findings forward.
  • D Correct. Models read the edges of a long input most reliably, so headings and position help.

10. A researcher returns 40 fields per finding and the writer uses 5 of them. The report still loses dates. What should the researcher return?

  1. AAll 40 fields, since the writer can decide which to use for its report.
  2. BOnly the claims, since the source and date are kept in the coordinator's notes.
  3. CThe few fields the writer needs, including the source and the date with each finding.
  4. DA one-line summary per finding, to cut the result from 40 fields to 1.
Show the answer

Answer: C

  • A Extra fields bury the few that matter and fill the context.
  • B The writer does not see the coordinator's notes. The metadata must travel with the claim.
  • C Correct. A smaller result keeps the context lean, and the date and source still travel with the claim.
  • D A summary drops the source and date that the report needs.

11. A report passes through 3 rounds of summary. A finding of 12.5 percent comes out as about 12 percent, and the source is gone. What prevents it?

  1. AAsk each round to summarize more carefully, since the wording is the source of the loss.
  2. BAdd a fourth round that compares the summary with the first to catch any drift.
  3. CRaise the context window so all 3 rounds fit without any trimming.
  4. DKeep the facts in a block outside the summary and pass them unchanged.
Show the answer

Answer: D

  • A Careful wording still rounds and drops. The fix is to stop re-summarizing the facts.
  • B The first summary has already lost the detail. A comparison cannot restore it.
  • C Fit is not the issue. Each round still blurs the figure.
  • D Correct. Each summary rounds and drops detail, so the exact figures and sources stay in a block of their own.

12. A coordinator keeps a long history of 80 turns and sends every turn to each new subagent. Select two effects of a long history.

  1. AEvery request carries it, so each call costs more as the history grows.
  2. BOlder turns are read better than new ones, since the model reads from the start.
  3. CA bigger window removes the cost, since nothing has to be trimmed any more.
  4. DOld detail is buried, so early facts are easier to miss in the middle.
Show the answer

Answer: A, D

  • A Correct. The whole history is sent with each request, so cost and delay grow with it.
  • B Attention to the middle falls off. Age alone does not make a turn clearer.
  • C A bigger window holds more, but the cost of carrying it stays.
  • D Correct. Facts placed early in a long input compete with everything after them.

Play: predict the output

This handoff keeps each finding whole but trims the list to save tokens.

python
def brief(task: str, findings: list[dict[str, str]]) -> str:
    lines = "\n".join(
        f"- {f['claim']} ({f['source']}, {f['date']})" for f in findings[:5]
    )
    return f"{task}\n\n{lines}\n\nCite the source and date of each line."

Predict: Seven findings come back, and the regulator's notice is the seventh. What does the report say about the regulator?

  1. ANothing. The writer never saw the seventh finding.
  2. BIt mentions the notice, since the researchers found it.
Show the answer

A. A writer can cite only what its prompt holds. To save tokens, cut the fields a finding carries, never the findings themselves.

References

  • Agent SDK subagents: a subagent starts fresh, so its prompt is all it knows.
  • Citations: how the API ties each claim to the passage that supports it.
  • How we built our multi-agent research system: how a lead agent briefs each subagent with a task, a format and sources.
  • Effective context engineering: why a brief should hold only what the next agent needs.

Conclusions

  • A subagent does not inherit context, so its prompt must carry everything it needs.
  • Each finding travels as claim, evidence, source and date, kept together.
  • A summary hides conflicts and sources, so pass the findings themselves.

You can now write a brief that keeps provenance alive from the researchers to the final report.

Brief

The prompt a coordinator writes for a subagent

Provenance

Where a claim came from, and when

Finding

One claim with its evidence, source and date

Fresh context

What a subagent starts with: its own prompt and tools, none of the coordinator's turns

Foundations, lesson 12

Surfacing failures

A failed search must reach the report

A coordinator starts three researchers to search the recall notes, then a writer drafts the report. The regulator search times out and the merge drops it, so the report reads as complete and a whole section is missing. A reader trusts it. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch a failure vanish, then fix the record and the merge so the report names what was not covered.

I doWatch the failure and its fix.

A failure is a result the writer must see

Researchers search and report back. A search can fail in two ways: it times out, or it half works. Two sources that disagree are not a failure, but both figures must stay in the report. The researcher classifies the failure, the coordinator decides what to do and the writer says what is solid and what is not.

This design goes wrong in three ways. A timeout is swallowed, one failure aborts every angle, and a merge picks one of two conflicting figures. You will see the first fail, then fix it, then see the third.

A failure that travels gives an honest report

The coordinator starts three researchers with the Agent tool, called Task in older releases, one for each group of searches. The regulator search fails, and its result comes back with an error flag and a category. The harness reads that result as the researcher got it, and your failure and merge turn it into a line the writer reads.

Open the writer prompt card to read the failure record field by field: the kind, the query, the attempt and the partial results. The report names the regulator as a gap.

The failure record and the merge as written
failure builds the record of a failed search and merge turns every result into the writer's prompt. The starting failure returns nothing and the starting merge skips any result with no text, which is every failed search.


Aborting on one failed search would lose the other angles. Here 4 of the 5 searches worked, so about 80 percent of the work would go. A record that travels keeps all of it.

Keep the kind, the query and what came back
The fix gives a failure a record with four fields: the kind, the query, the attempt and the partial results. The merge writes a line for each failed search and tells the writer not to call the report complete. A transient failure is retried once where it happens, and only the rest is passed up.


An empty result is different. A search that ran and found nothing is a valid answer. Only a search that could not be done is a failure.


A gap can also start in the plan. An angle nobody owns is never searched, so the report has an empty section and no failure to show for it. Broaden the split so every topic has a researcher, instead of retrying the same narrow plan.


report.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""Failure handling: what a failed search says, and how results are merged."""23from typing import Any456def failure(7    kind: str, query: str, partial: list[str], attempt: int = 18) -> dict[str, Any]:9    """The record of a failed search: what failed, on what, what was got."""10    return {11        "kind": kind,12        "query": query,13        "partial": partial,14        "attempt": attempt,15    }161718def merge(results: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> str:19    """One line per result. A failure and a conflict stay visible."""20    lines = []21    for r in results:22        error = r["error"]23        if error:24            got = ", ".join(error["partial"]) or "nothing"25            lines.append(26                f"GAP: the {r['angle']} search failed ({error['kind']}) "27                f"on '{error['query']}' after {error['attempt']} attempts. "28                f"Partial results: {got}. Say this area is not covered."29            )30        else:31            lines.append(f"- {r['angle']} ({r['source']}): {r['text']}")3233    angles = [r["angle"] for r in results if not r["error"]]34    if len(angles) != len(set(angles)):35        lines.append("Some sources disagree. Report every figure and source.")3637    if any(r["error"] for r in results):38        lines.append("Some searches failed. Do not call the report complete.")3940    return "\n".join(lines)

The same trouble, two different reports
Use the switch to run the request with the starting handling, then the fixed one. The card marked "This is where the runs split" is the first difference between the two runs.


Try the half-working search and the two conflicting figures too. The fix holds on all three.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch failures-surface.
Errors need a category
A tool that fails with only "Operation failed" gives the researcher nothing to report. In the bare run the regulator researcher passes on just those two words. Switch to the run where the error carries a category, a retry flag, a message, the attempt and the partial results. There the researcher reports a timeout that cannot be retried.


An MCP tool, one served through the Model Context Protocol, sets isError on its result and puts the errorCategory in the content. A business rule that rejects a request is not retryable, and the error should say why, so the agent stops instead of retrying.


The writer should also mark how well the merged report is supported. Mark the claims that their sources support well, apart from the ones sources dispute, and show the sources of each dispute. Mark every gap where a search failed or no source was found, and never hide one inside the conclusion.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch failures-surface.
Try it: trouble and failure handling
Change one setting at a time. Pick a timeout, a half-working search or two conflicting figures, then switch between the starting handling and the fix. Swallowing a failure and aborting on it are both wrong.


Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch failures-surface.
Passing failures back in the Agent SDK
A failed search is an MCP tool result with its error flag set and an errorCategory in its text. The flag has two spellings: is_error in Python and isError in MCP.


Researchers are defined with AgentDefinition and started with the Agent tool, so that tool must be allowed. The harness runs both phases through query(). This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run.


A coordinator could also send a new task out for a gap. These recordings never loop back: the gap goes to the writer, and the report names it.
