The checks want the kind, query, attempt and partial results in a failure record. The merge must name the failed search and warn the writer not to call the report complete. It keeps both conflicting sources, and an empty result is not a failure.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A regulator search times out. The merge drops that angle, and the writer produces a report that reads as complete. 1 of 4 angles is missing. What is the root fix?
  1. AAsk the writer to sound less certain in the conclusion, since one of the four angles may be thin.
  2. BPass the failure to the writer with its kind and its query, so the report can name the gap.
  3. CAdd a second search for the regulator each time, so that a timeout becomes unlikely on the next run.
  4. DDrop the regulator angle from the plan for good, since its search is not reliable enough to keep.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Hedged wording does not tell the reader which angle is missing or why.
  • B Correct. A failure that never reaches the writer cannot appear in the report, so it must travel as a result.
  • C A retry may help once, but a search that fails again is still dropped without a word.
  • D Removing an angle hides the gap instead of reporting it.
2. A researcher times out on one of 4 searches. The coordinator aborts the whole run, so the 3 good results, about 75 percent of the work, are lost. What should happen instead?
  1. ARetry the whole run from the very start until all 4 searches pass in the same attempt.
  2. BKeep the abort, but add a clearer error message for the person who reads the log later.
  3. CSkip the failed search quietly and report the 3 results as if they were the whole answer.
  4. DReturn the failure together with the 3 good results, and let the report name the gap.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A repeat of a failing search may time out again, and every pass throws away the good work.
  • B A better message does not save the 3 results that were lost.
  • C Skipping quietly hides the gap, which is the opposite mistake.
  • D Correct. Partial results still have value. The report can use them and say what is not covered.
3. A subagent returns the string 'search unavailable'. The coordinator cannot tell whether to retry, try another source or stop. What should the subagent return?
  1. AThe kind of failure, what was tried, what came back before it failed and what to try next.
  2. BThe same string unchanged, since the coordinator can read it and judge for itself what it meant.
  3. CAn empty list, since no results were found and that is the honest answer to give here.
  4. DA longer sentence that says the search was unavailable for some unknown reason.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A coordinator can decide only when it knows the kind, the query and the partial results.
  • B A bare message carries no kind and no query, so the coordinator is left guessing.
  • C An empty list looks like a valid search with no hits. A failure must not look like that.
  • D More words without a kind or a query still give the coordinator nothing to act on.
4. Select two wrong ways to handle a failed search in a research run.
  1. APass the failure up with its kind, query and partial results.
  2. BDrop the failed angle from the merge and call the report complete.
  3. CRetry once where the failure is transient, then pass up what remains.
  4. DAbort every researcher because one of them failed.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A This is the right way, because the failure can reach the report.
  • B Correct. The reader is told nothing, so a missing section looks finished.
  • C A bounded retry is sound. Only an unbounded loop would be wrong.
  • D Correct. The good results are lost, and the coordinator learns nothing about what worked.
5. Two sources give different failure rates for the same batch: 12 percent from a lab report and 15 percent from a claims desk. The merge keeps 15 percent. What is wrong?
  1. ANothing, since the higher figure is the safer one to report for a recall.
  2. BThe report should have averaged them to 13.5 percent, which is closer to the truth.
  3. CThe other figure and its source are gone, so the reader cannot see the conflict.
  4. DThe report is fine as long as it mentions that some sources were consulted.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Safer is a judgement the reader should make with both figures in front of them.
  • B An average belongs to neither source and cannot be checked.
  • C Correct. Two figures from two sources are a finding. Keep both and say where each came from.
  • D A general note names no source, so the reader still cannot check anything.
6. A report lists 40 swollen units from a 9 March field report and 65 from an 18 March claims update. A reviewer calls it a contradiction. What explains it?
  1. AThe dates differ, so the later count may include units that swelled after the first.
  2. BOne source is wrong, so the writer should keep the newer figure and delete the other.
  3. CBoth figures are noise, so the writer should report only that some units swelled.
  4. DThe claims desk counted the same units twice, so its figure should be halved.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A date often explains a gap, and only a report that shows both dates lets the reader see it.
  • B Nothing says either count is wrong. Deleting one throws away the trend.
  • C Dropping both loses the evidence the reader needs.
  • D That is a guess with no source. The report should show the figures, not invent a fix.
7. A synthesis of 14 findings mixes 11 settled claims with 3 that sources dispute. The reader cannot tell which is which. What should the writer do?
  1. AWrite all 14 in one list with the same wording, so the report reads evenly.
  2. BLeave out the 3 disputed claims, since a report should hold only what is certain.
  3. CPut the disputed claims first, since the reader should see the risks before anything else.
  4. DMark the settled claims and the disputed ones apart, and show the sources of each dispute.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A An even tone hides which claims are solid.
  • B Leaving them out hides the dispute, and a reader may need it.
  • C Order alone does not mark them as disputed or show the sources.
  • D Correct. A reader can weigh a disputed claim only when it is marked and its sources are shown.
8. A report merges findings from 5 researchers. Select two rules for marking the quality of the synthesis.
  1. AMark the findings that are well supported by their sources.
  2. BHide the gaps inside the conclusion, so the report reads as one piece.
  3. CMark the gaps where a search failed or no source was found.
  4. DGive every claim the same confidence, so the report stays consistent.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. A reader needs to know which claims are solid.
  • B A gap that cannot be found cannot be acted on.
  • C Correct. A marked gap tells the reader what the report does not cover.
  • D A uniform tone hides which claims are weak.
9. A coordinator never heard that one of its 3 researchers failed. The researcher wrote the failure to its own notes. What does the design need?
  1. ALet researchers message each other directly, so a failure reaches whoever needs it without delay.
  2. BAll messages pass through the coordinator, so a failure is a message to it.
  3. CHave the writer read every researcher's notes before it starts, including any that failed.
  4. DGive the researcher a much longer timeout so that it rarely fails at all in practice.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Side channels skip the coordinator, which is where the gap needs to be handled.
  • B Correct. The coordinator is the one place that routes results and errors, so nothing can be lost on the side.
  • C The writer would read what was written, not what failed. The coordinator still would not know.
  • D A longer timeout reduces some failures. It cannot make the coordinator hear of the rest.
10. The synthesis shows that 1 of 4 angles has no findings. The coordinator can still start a researcher. What should it do next?
  1. AFinish the report and leave the gap for a reader to spot.
  2. BRestart the whole run with all 4 angles, since partial work is not trusted.
  3. CSend a new task back out for the uncovered angle, then merge what it returns.
  4. DAsk the writer to fill the missing angle from its own general knowledge.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A gap the coordinator can close should not be shipped as it is.
  • B The 3 good results are thrown away to redo work that was fine.
  • C Correct. A coordinator can loop back out for a gap instead of reporting it as it is.
  • D The writer has no source for it, so the section would be unsourced.
11. A plan split a recall into 2 angles, and 2 topics have no owner. The report has two empty sections. What is the fix?
  1. ABroaden the split so every topic the report needs has an angle and a researcher.
  2. BGive each of the 2 researchers a longer brief, so they cover the extra topics.
  3. CAdd a line to the report that says the empty sections are out of scope.
  4. DRetry the 2 researchers until the empty sections fill in.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. An angle nobody owns is never searched, so the gap starts in the plan.
  • B A longer brief does not change which angles exist.
  • C Declaring it out of scope hides a gap the plan created.
  • D A retry repeats the same narrow plan and gets the same result.
12. A coordinator sits between 4 subagents. Select two things it owns.
  1. ALetting every subagent write to the report directly.
  2. BRouting every message between the subagents and the writer.
  3. CHandling the errors that the subagents report.
  4. DHiding failed searches from the writer so the report reads cleanly.
Show the answer
Answer: B, C
  • A Direct writes bypass the merge, where gaps and conflicts are marked.
  • B Correct. All traffic passes through it, so it is the one place that can route.
  • C Correct. Retrying, passing up or recording a failure is a decision for the coordinator.
  • D Hiding a failure is how a report ends up claiming to be complete.
13. A tool returns the text 'operation failed' for 6 different faults. The agent cannot decide whether to retry. What should the tool return?
  1. AThe same text, since the agent can read it and judge which fault it was.
  2. BAn empty result, so the agent treats it as a search with no hits.
  3. CA stack trace from the server, since it holds the most detail about the fault.
  4. DAn error flag with a category, whether it is retryable, and a readable message.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A The text is the same for all 6 faults, so there is nothing to judge.
  • B An empty result hides a failure behind a valid answer.
  • C A trace is for the operator. It is not a category the agent can act on.
  • D Correct. With a category and a retry flag, the agent can choose to retry, ask or stop.
14. A refund tool rejects a request under a business rule: the order is 90 days old and the limit is 30. The agent retries 5 times. What was missed?
  1. AThe limit should be raised to 90 days so the retry succeeds.
  2. BThe error should say it is not retryable and explain the rule, so the agent stops.
  3. CThe agent should retry more times, since some retries succeed after a delay.
  4. DThe tool should return an empty result, so the agent gives up on its own.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A The rule exists for a reason. The fault is that the agent was never told it is final.
  • B Correct. A business rule is not a transient fault. A retry cannot change the answer.
  • C A delay does not change a business rule.
  • D An empty result looks like a valid search. The agent needs the reason.
15. A customer search returns 0 rows for an email that is not in the system. The agent treats it as an error and retries 3 times. What is the right reading?
  1. AIt is an access failure, so the tool should raise an error for each empty result.
  2. BIt is a timeout, so the agent should wait and run the same search again.
  3. CIt is a valid empty result, not a failure, so the agent reports that nobody was found.
  4. DIt is a sign the search tool is broken, so the agent should stop all work.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A An error for every miss drowns the real failures in noise.
  • B Nothing timed out. The same search will return the same empty list.
  • C Correct. The search worked and found nothing. A failure is when the search could not be done.
  • D One empty answer says nothing about the tool, and stopping loses the rest of the work.
16. An MCP tool call fails. Select two things its result can carry.
  1. AAn isError flag that marks the result as a failure.
  2. BA promise that the next call will succeed.
  3. CNothing, because an error is shown only in the server log.
  4. DA category such as timeout, with a message the agent can read.
Show the answer
Answer: A, D
  • A Correct. The flag tells the agent the call failed, and the content says why.
  • B A tool cannot know that, and the agent should not expect it.
  • C The result reaches the agent, which is why it must carry the kind of failure.
  • D Correct. A category lets the agent choose between retrying, asking for help and stopping.

Failure record
The kind, query, attempt and partial results of a failed search
Partial result
What a search returned before it failed
Coverage gap
An angle the report could not research, named in the report
Transient failure
A fault worth one retry where it happens, such as a timeout
Foundations, lesson 13
Built-in search tools
Search with Grep and Glob, not with a shell
A new developer at Lumen Supply asks where the tax amount is rounded. The agent has a shell, so it runs command after command and reads far more files than the answer needs. The answer sits in one of them. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch a shell search, then give the agent search tools and a brief that says to read only what matches.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
Built-in tools find files and text
Claude Code and the Agent SDK ship tools for exploring a repository. Grep finds lines by content. Glob finds files by name. Read and Write handle a whole file, and Edit replaces text that appears once, unless it is told to replace every copy with its replace_all option.


The model picks the tool. The harness runs it and returns the result. A shell returns whatever a command prints, so the agent can pull far more into its context than the question needs.


On macOS and Linux, a current Claude Code session searches through its shell unless Glob and Grep are named in the tool list. The fix in this lesson names them, and that is what puts them in the agent's hands.

Offer search tools and say to search first
The fix takes away the shell and lists Glob, Grep and Read. An agent that only explores needs no tool that changes a file. The brief says to search first, read the one file that matches, and name the file in the answer.


A question like this one never edits, but the tools you list for a task that does matter. Edit needs text that appears once.


A longer piece of the surrounding text can make it unique, and replace_all changes every copy. When a file holds the same line six times and only two should change, neither helps. The agent reads the whole file and writes it back with the change.

Long investigations: subagent, scratchpad, compact
A real investigation runs for hours, so the context fills and answers drift toward generic ones. The run below is the coupon question with search tools: two searches and one file opened, where the shell printed every file. Three habits keep a long session small.


    

  • An Explore subagent does the noisy discovery in its own context and returns a short answer.
    • 

  • A scratchpad file keeps the findings outside the window, so a reset does not lose them.
    • 

  • /compact replaces a long history with a summary. The session goes on.
    • 



Write a short summary before the next phase. A run that stops partway needs state saved on disk, such as a manifest of finished steps, because a new session starts empty.


Resume a named investigation when its files are unchanged. Fork it to try two approaches from one point. Start fresh with a summary when files changed, since old results are stale. Use plan mode, which never edits, for open designs, and edit directly when one file and one answer are clear.

The checks want Grep and Glob in place of the shell. The brief must keep the question, say to search before reading, and ask for the file name in the answer.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A teammate must find every caller of applyDiscount across 60 source files. Which built-in tool answers it in one call?
  1. AGlob with the pattern **/*applyDiscount*.
  2. BGrep for applyDiscount across the source directory.
  3. CRead every file under src and scan the text.
  4. DRun ls -R in a shell and look for the name.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Glob matches file names. A caller sits inside a file, so no name holds it.
  • B Correct. Grep searches file contents, so each caller comes back with its file and line.
  • C Sixty reads put the whole repository in the context to find a few lines.
  • D A listing shows file names only, never the lines inside them.
2. An agent must list the 40 files whose names end in .test.ts. Which call does it in one step?
  1. AGlob with the pattern **/*.test.ts.
  2. BGrep for .test.ts across the repository.
  3. CRead each directory and note the test files by eye.
  4. DGrep for the word describe and keep the matching files.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. Glob matches file names and returns the paths without opening any file.
  • B Grep looks inside files. It would only find files that mention that text.
  • C That reads far more than the 40 paths needed, one directory at a time.
  • D A file can hold describe and not be a test file. The name is the signal here.
3. Edit refuses to change TIMEOUT = 30 because that text appears 6 times in one file. Only 2 of the 6 lines should change, and no nearby text tells them apart. What gets the change made?
  1. ARetry the same Edit call, since a later try picks the first match.
  2. BTurn on replace_all, so Edit changes all 6 copies.
  3. CUse Glob to narrow the file list until the match is unique.
  4. DRead the file, then Write the whole file back with the 2 lines changed.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Edit needs text that appears once. Repeating the call gives the same refusal.
  • B replace_all would change all 6 lines, and 4 of them must stay as they are.
  • C Glob works on file names. The 6 matches are inside one file.
  • D Correct. Read and Write handle whole files, so they do not need unique text.
4. Which two statements about Read, Write and Edit are true? Select two.
  1. ARead and Write handle a whole file at a time.
  2. BBy default, Edit changes every matching line in one call, however many match.
  3. CEdit replaces a piece of text that appears once in the file.
  4. DWrite patches only the lines it is given and keeps the rest.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. Read returns the file and Write replaces it.
  • B Edit needs text that appears once unless replace_all is set. By default a repeated string is refused.
  • C Correct. The text must be unique so the tool knows which spot to change.
  • D Write replaces the whole file with what it is given.
5. A 3-hour investigation starts giving generic answers. The first findings are about 90,000 tokens back. What fixes the drift?
  1. AAsk for shorter answers from here on.
  2. BStart a new session and repeat the work from the top.
  3. CWrite each finding to a scratchpad file and re-read it when answers drift.
  4. DAdd a line to the prompt that says to stay specific.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Short answers do not bring the early findings back in reach.
  • B That throws away 3 hours of findings and pays for them again.
  • C Correct. The file keeps the findings outside the window, so they stay within reach.
  • D A prompt cannot return text that has left the window.
6. Noisy discovery pours 60,000 tokens of search output into the main context before any real work starts. What keeps it out?
  1. AHand the discovery to a subagent that returns a short answer.
  2. BAsk the agent to print less of each result.
  3. CSwitch the main agent to a larger model.
  4. DClear the context after discovery and ask the question again.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The subagent holds the noise in its own context and returns a few lines.
  • B Tool results enter the context whatever the agent prints.
  • C A larger model still carries the same 60,000 tokens.
  • D A clear drops the findings along with the noise.
7. A long run stops partway through its steps. Which thing lets a fresh session continue from the next one?
  1. AThe old chat transcript, which reloads itself in the new session.
  2. BThe model's memory of the run.
  3. CA longer timeout on the next run.
  4. DA saved manifest of the 40 finished steps.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A new session starts empty unless something is loaded into it.
  • B The model keeps nothing between sessions.
  • C A timeout limits a run. It stores no progress.
  • D Correct. Structured state on disk tells the new session where to start.
8. A long task is about to start its next phase. Which two steps carry the work across? Select two.
  1. ARun /compact to delete the session and begin with nothing.
  2. BWrite the findings so far as a short summary.
  3. CPaste in every file that was read, so nothing is lost.
  4. DRun /compact so the session shrinks and keeps a summary.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A Compaction replaces the history with a summary. The session goes on.
  • B Correct. A summary gives the next phase its starting facts in a few lines.
  • C Pasting 40 files refills the window the phase needs free.
  • D Correct. Compaction trades the long history for a summary and frees the window.
9. Yesterday's 2-hour investigation of a flaky test is saved as checkout-flake, and no file has changed since. What is the best start today?
  1. AStart fresh and paste a summary.
  2. BResume the named session.
  3. CFork the session so the original is kept.
  4. DCompact the old session and delete it.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A That rebuilds context that is still current and loses the detail.
  • B Correct. The context is current, so resuming keeps every finding.
  • C A fork is for trying a second path. It is not needed to continue one.
  • D Compaction shrinks a session and deleting it would lose the work.
10. Two fixes could work, and you want to try each from the same point without either disturbing the other. What do you do?
  1. AResume the session and try them one after the other.
  2. BStart two new sessions and read the code again in each.
  3. CFork the session at that point, one fork per fix.
  4. DResume the same session in two terminals at once.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A The second try would start from the first one's changes.
  • B That repeats the reading twice and loses the shared context.
  • C Correct. Each fork starts from the same history and then goes its own way.
  • D Both terminals would write into one history and mix the two tries.
11. Two files read yesterday changed overnight after a pull of 14 commits, so old tool results are stale. What is the best start?
  1. AStart a new session that opens with a summary of the findings.
  2. BResume the old session and carry on.
  3. CFork the old session and keep going in the fork.
  4. DRun /compact and continue in the same session.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The summary keeps the conclusions and drops the stale file contents.
  • B Resume would trust tool results that no longer match the files.
  • C A fork copies the same stale results.
  • D Compaction summarizes old results. It does not re-read the changed files.
12. Which two things make resuming a session go well? Select two.
  1. AA session name or id to find it again.
  2. BA fresh summary, since resume discards the old history.
  3. CNo check of the repo, since resume reads changed files on its own.
  4. DA note of which files changed since the session ended.
Show the answer
Answer: A, D
  • A Correct. Without a name there is no session to resume.
  • B Resume keeps the history. A summary is for starting fresh.
  • C Resume does not refresh old tool results, so changed files go unnoticed.
  • D Correct. The note tells the agent which old results to distrust.
13. A caching change has three valid designs with different costs, and the team has not picked one. How should the work start?
  1. AEdit directly and benchmark afterward.
  2. BPick the cheapest design and let the tests decide.
  3. CAsk for the change one file at a time.
  4. DStart in plan mode and weigh the three designs first.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Edits would lock in one design before anyone compared the three.
  • B Tests check behavior, not which design is better.
  • C Small steps do not settle which design to follow.
  • D Correct. Plan mode explores and proposes, so a person chooses before any edit.
14. A stack trace names one line in one file, and the fix is clear. A plan would take 40 minutes. How should you work?
  1. APlan it in plan mode so a person approves the edit.
  2. BSend an Explore subagent to map the repository first.
  3. CEdit it directly, since one file with one answer needs no plan.
  4. DHave Claude interview you about the design.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A plan adds 40 minutes to a fix with one answer.
  • B The trace already names the file, so there is nothing to discover.
  • C Correct. A small, clear fix is faster to do than to plan.
  • D An interview is for open questions. This one has none.
15. A migration touches many modules, and finding them means reading dozens of files. What keeps that discovery out of the main context?
  1. APlan mode on its own, since it reads without editing.
  2. BAn Explore subagent that searches and returns a short list.
  3. CDirect edits, so nothing needs to be read first.
  4. DA longer system prompt with the module names.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Plan mode still reads those 45 files into the main context.
  • B Correct. The reading stays in the subagent and only the list comes back.
  • C Editing the modules unread is how the wrong edits happen.
  • D A prompt cannot list what nobody has searched for yet.
16. Which two rules help you pick between plan mode and a direct edit? Select two.
  1. AUse plan mode so Claude writes the plan into the source files.
  2. BPlan when the design is open or many files change.
  3. CEdit directly when one file and one answer are clear.
  4. DPlan every change so nothing surprises the team.
Show the answer
Answer: B, C
  • A Plan mode blocks edits. The plan is a proposal, not a change.
  • B Correct. A plan lets a person choose before a wide change lands.
  • C Correct. Planning a clear fix costs more than the fix.
  • D Planning a one-line fix wastes the time the plan was meant to save.

Foundations, lesson 14
Scoped tools
Each agent gets only the tools its job needs
A review agent must only read records, but it holds every one of the tools in the catalogue. Most of them change data. The answer comes out right, yet a wrong pick would have paid a refund or sent an email. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch an agent hold every tool. Then you fix it so each role holds only the few its job needs.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
A tool you never give cannot be called
An agent picks from the tools it can see. Every extra tool is another wrong option, and a tool that changes data turns a wrong pick into a real mistake.


The code decides the list and the model picks inside it.


Three things go wrong as the list grows. The pick gets less accurate. A read-only role holds a tool that writes. Nothing fixes the order of steps, so a required lookup can be skipped.


A scoped agent has few tools and picks right
The reviewer holds four read tools. It calls three of them, lookup_order, list_refunds and get_policy, finds the refund and the limit, and answers.


Open the agent card to see the tools it held. None of them can change data.


  1. ColleagueRefund 5501 on order 1042 was $80. Is that within the refund limit? Answer from the…
    Show the result
    Refund 5501 on order 1042 was $80. Is that within the refund limit? Answer from the records and change nothing.
  2. Agentholds 4 tools, 0 that change data unasked
    Show the result
    lookup_order
list_refunds
get_policy
get_customer
  3. Toolscalled: lookup_order, list_refunds, get_policy
    Show the result
    lookup_order
list_refunds
get_policy
  4. AgentYes, refund 5501 for $80 on order 1042 is within the limit. The refund policy sets a $500 limit, and the records show…
    Show the result
    Yes, refund 5501 for $80 on order 1042 is within the limit. The refund policy sets a $500 limit, and the records show only this one $80 refund against an $80 order. I made no changes.
4 tools held: only what the job needs.
The roles as written
tools_for returns the tools an agent in a role may call. The starting version returns the whole catalogue for every role, so a reviewer can pay a refund.


Each tool also costs context. A schema of about 150 tokens goes out with every request. The whole catalogue is thousands of tokens on each call, and four tools is a few hundred.

18 tools held: more than the job needs.
Give each role only the few tools it needs
The fix maps each role to its own short list of no more than five tools. The reviewer gets four read tools, the refunder gets the refund tool with its lookups, and an unknown role gets none. A tool several roles need, such as the policy lookup, sits in each list.


A broad tool is the same problem in one piece. Swap a general run_query for a narrow tool that reads one named table, and a wrong pick stays small.


Tools can also come from an MCP server, a program that offers tools over a standard protocol. A server can also offer a resource, a catalogue the agent can list. A team shares servers in a .mcp.json file at the repository root, and a user-level file lives on one machine.


roles.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""Which tools each role may use, and how a step must choose among them."""23ROLES = {4    "reviewer": ["lookup_order", "list_refunds", "get_policy", "get_customer"],5    "refunder": [6        "lookup_order",7        "get_customer",8        "get_policy",9        "process_refund",10    ],11    "shipper": ["lookup_order", "track_parcel", "get_customer"],12    "stock": ["check_stock", "reorder_stock", "price_history"],13    "support": ["lookup_order", "get_customer", "add_note", "escalate_ticket"],14}15FIXED = {"policy": "get_policy"}16MUST_CALL = {"read"}171819def tools_for(role: str) -> list[str]:20    """The tools an agent in `role` may call; an unknown role gets none."""21    return list(ROLES.get(role, []))222324def choice_for(role: str, step: str) -> dict[str, str]:25    """The `tool_choice` for `step`: auto, any, or one named tool."""26    held = tools_for(role)27    named = FIXED.get(step)28    if named in held:29        return {"type": "tool", "name": named}3031    if step in MUST_CALL and held:32        return {"type": "any"}3334    return {"type": "auto"}
auto, any or one named tool
A short tool list says what the agent may call. tool_choice says whether a step must call one. With auto the model may answer in words and call nothing. With any it must call some tool, and which one is still its pick. With one named tool the step is fixed.


A fourth value, none, stops every tool call. Claude Haiku 5.5, the model in these runs, accepts a forced choice. Some larger current models reject any and a named tool with a 400 error. There, keep auto and mark the tool strict, so its input still follows the schema.


choice_for(role, step) returns the choice for a step, and the tests assert it. Force a lookup first, then let the model choose for the rest. A line in the system prompt cannot set the choice, because it is a request field.

Scoped tools in the Agent SDK
The harness serves only the tools tools_for returns from an in-process MCP server. It lists the same names as the allowed tools. role_agents writes the same table as one subagent per role.


The Agent SDK does not expose tool_choice, so the three choice rows above call the Messages API directly. This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run.


Every connected server's tools are available to the agent, though Claude Code may defer loading their definitions behind tool search when there are many.


app/sdk_agent.py
1"""The scoped tools on the Agent SDK: one server, one subagent per role."""23from types import ModuleType45from claude_agent_sdk import (6    AgentDefinition,7    McpSdkServerConfig,8    create_sdk_mcp_server,9    tool,10)1112from kit.api import Json13from .tools import TOOLS1415SERVER = "lumen"16PREFIX = f"mcp__{SERVER}__"17SYSTEM = (18    "You are a support agent at Lumen Supply. Use your tools to do the "19    "job, then answer in one or two sentences."20)212223def build_server(names: list[str]) -> McpSdkServerConfig:24    """Serve exactly the named tools from the catalogue."""25    served = []26    for name in names:27        described, result = TOOLS[name]2829        @tool(name, described, {"id": str})30        async def handler(args: Json, result: str = result) -> Json:31            return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": result}]}3233        served.append(handler)3435    return create_sdk_mcp_server(SERVER, tools=served)363738def role_agents(roles: ModuleType) -> dict[str, AgentDefinition]:39    """The role table as subagents: each holds only its role's tools."""40    return {41        role: AgentDefinition(42            description=f"Does the {role} job.",43            prompt=SYSTEM,44            tools=[PREFIX + n for n in roles.tools_for(role)],45            model="haiku",46        )47        for role in ("reviewer", "refunder", "shipper")48    }

The checks want five tools or fewer per role, no tool that changes data for a reviewer, and a refund tool for the refunder. An unknown role gets nothing, the read step must call a tool, and the policy step must call get_policy.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A support agent holds 18 tools and picks the wrong one in 3 of every 10 calls. What is the most direct fix?
  1. ARewrite each of the 18 descriptions to be twice as long.
  2. BRaise the turn limit so a wrong pick can be tried again.
  3. CGive each role the 4 or 5 tools its job needs.
  4. DKeep all 18 so the agent can handle any request.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Longer text adds to the crowd the model sorts through. The list is the problem.
  • B Extra turns give more chances to pick wrong, and a wrong write is not undone.
  • C Correct. A short list leaves few wrong picks, and the tools a job needs stay in reach.
  • D Every extra tool is another wrong option, and some of the 18 change data.
2. A read-only reviewer called the refund tool even though its prompt said never to refund. What fixes it for good?
  1. ARemove the refund tool from the reviewer's tool list.
  2. BRepeat the rule three times in the system prompt.
  3. CAsk the reviewer to confirm before each call.
  4. DRename the refund tool so it is harder to spot.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A tool the role does not hold cannot be called, whatever the prompt says.
  • B A prompt is a request. The tool stays in the list and can still be picked.
  • C A confirmation still lets the call through once the model says yes.
  • D The model reads the description too. The tool is still held and callable.
3. Every review must start with the policy lookup, but in 2 of 10 runs the agent answers first. What makes the first step fixed?
  1. AAdd a line to the system prompt that says to look up the policy first.
  2. BGive the agent only the policy tool for every step.
  3. CSet tool_choice to auto so the model decides each step.
  4. DSet tool_choice to the policy tool on the first request.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A prompt line is followed most of the time. The 2 misses show it does not fix the order.
  • B That removes the other tools the later steps need.
  • C With auto the model may answer in text and skip the lookup.
  • D Correct. A named tool makes the first call that tool, and the model picks freely after.
4. Which two statements about the values of tool_choice are true? Select two.
  1. AWith auto, the model may answer in text and call nothing.
  2. BWith any, the model picks the best tool for the question.
  3. CWith a named tool, the model calls that tool first.
  4. DA system prompt line can set the value for a step.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. Auto leaves the decision to the model, and text is a valid answer.
  • B Any only requires some call. Which tool comes back is still the model's pick.
  • C Correct. The named tool is forced, so the step cannot be skipped.
  • D The value is a request field. Prompt text cannot set it.
5. An agent with one broad run_query tool can read or delete any of 12 tables, and it once deleted rows. What is the better design?
  1. AKeep run_query and add a prompt line that forbids deletes.
  2. BSwap it for a few narrow tools, such as one that reads a named table.
  3. CAdd 12 more tools so the agent has a choice for each table.
  4. DForce run_query with tool_choice so it is always used the same way.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A The tool can still run a delete. A prompt line does not narrow it.
  • B Correct. A narrow tool can only do its one job, so a wrong pick stays small.
  • C Twelve more tools add twelve more wrong picks and keep run_query in reach.
  • D Forcing the broad tool makes the risk certain. It does not narrow it.
6. One developer wants a private notes server on their own machine, and the other 5 on the team must not get it. Where does its configuration go?
  1. AThe .mcp.json file at the root of the repository.
  2. BThe system prompt of the reviewer role, as an instruction.
  3. CA note in the README telling each person to opt in.
  4. DA user-level file on that developer's machine.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A That file is checked in, so all 6 people would get the server.
  • B A prompt cannot connect a server. Servers come from configuration.
  • C A README only describes a setup. It connects nothing, for anyone.
  • D Correct. A user-level file lives on one machine, so only that developer gets the server.
7. A team of 6 wants the same MCP servers for everyone who opens the repository. Where does the configuration go?
  1. AEach person's own user-level file.
  2. BThe system prompt of each role.
  3. CA .mcp.json at the repository root.
  4. DThe README, with steps for each person to follow.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A user-level file lives on one machine. The other 5 never get it.
  • B A prompt cannot connect a server. Servers come from configuration.
  • C Correct. It is checked in, so everyone who opens the repository gets the same servers.
  • D A README is read once. Nothing connects until each person does it by hand.
8. Two MCP servers are connected, one with 5 tools and one with 7. Which two statements are true? Select two.
  1. AOnly the first server's tools load until it is disconnected.
  2. BAll 12 tools are available to the agent at once.
  3. CConnecting more servers makes the agent safer, since it has more options.
  4. DA resource can list what a server offers, so the agent sees a catalogue.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A Connected servers are available together, so all 12 tools are in reach at once.
  • B Correct. Each connected server's tools join the same list, even if their definitions load on demand.
  • C More tools are more wrong picks. Connect only what the job needs.
  • D Correct. A resource gives the agent a summary of what it can reach.
9. A connected server offers 9 tools, 3 of which change data, and the reviewer role must only read. What keeps the 3 out of its reach?
  1. AConnect the server and list only the read tools the role may call.
  2. BConnect the server and tell the reviewer in its prompt to skip 3 of them.
  3. CConnect a second server so the reviewer has a safer choice.
  4. DLeave the server unconnected and give the reviewer no tools.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The role's list names the tools it may call, so the other 3 are never offered to it.
  • B A prompt is a request, and the 3 tools stay callable.
  • C A second server adds tools and leaves the 3 in reach.
  • D That also removes the read tools the review needs.

Conclusions
    

  • An agent can only call what it holds, so give each role the few tools its job needs, never more than five.
    • 

  • A prompt that says "do not use it" is weaker than removing the tool.
    • 

  • Use tool_choice to make a step call a tool, and name the tool when the order is fixed.

You can now write a role map and a choice for each step, so an agent's tools and its mistakes stay small.


Role
The job an agent does, which decides its tools
Scoped tools
A short list held by one agent, not the full set
Write tool
A tool that changes data or sends something
Default deny
A role that is not listed holds no tools
tool_choice
A request field set to auto, any or one named tool
Foundations, lesson 15
Sharing an MCP server
Share the MCP server, keep the token in the environment
A team shares one MCP server through .mcp.json, and the file carries the access token inline. The file is committed, so the token is now in git for everyone who clones the repository, and in every copy of its history. This is the agent at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch a token travel with the file, then fix the file so it names the variable and the value stays on each machine.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
The file is shared, the value is not
An MCP server is a separate program that offers tools to an agent over a standard protocol. A project .mcp.json file lists the servers Claude Code starts, and it is committed, so every teammate gets the same ones. That is the point of it. It also means anything written in it is shared.


Claude Code reads ${NAME} in that file from the environment. The file holds the name and each machine holds the value.


A variable name in the file gives a working server
The file names the variable. Claude Code fills in the value from the environment when it starts the server. The agent calls the tool and answers.


The call list also shows Bash, Read and ToolSearch. The agent asked for Bash and Read too, but this run allows only the stock tool. Claude Code defers MCP tool definitions until they are needed, so the agent calls ToolSearch to load the stock tool's definition before it calls the tool.


Open the agent card to read the committed file. It holds no token.

Write the name of the variable, not the value
The fix writes the name in the form ${STOCK_TOKEN} and never the value. Each teammate sets the variable on their own machine.


The server still gets its token. The repository never holds it. A token that was already committed stays readable in history, so rotate it: revoke the old value and issue a new one.


A server only one person needs stays in that person's own user file. Before writing a custom server, check whether a maintained community one fits. The run shows both files active: two servers connected, and the stock tool answers.

Descriptions decide which tool is called
A shared server only helps if the model picks the right tool from it, and it picks from each tool's description. A description that says "gets data" gives the model nothing to choose by, so a question can go to the wrong tool. State the inputs, give an example of one, and say what the tool does not return.


The stock server, shown below, says that get_stock reads units for a product id from P-1 to P-30 and returns no price. Two tools with overlapping descriptions are the same fault, so give each its own inputs and limits.


Split a catch-all tool, one that takes a mode field, into narrow tools. Prompt wording pulls too: "always check the policy first" makes the policy tool run on every question, even a greeting. Word it for the case that needs it.


app/fixture/stock_server.py
1"""The Lumen Supply stock server, started by `claude` from `.mcp.json`.23It answers only when its STOCK_TOKEN variable is the demo token.4"""56import os78from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer910DEMO_TOKEN = "demo-token-1234"  # noqa: S105 - a fixture value11PRODUCTS = 3012server = MCPServer("stock")131415def allowed() -> bool:16    """Whether the caller passed the token through the environment."""17    return os.environ.get("STOCK_TOKEN") == DEMO_TOKEN181920def number(product: str) -> int | None:21    """The catalogue number in an id such as P-7, or None."""22    head, _, tail = product.partition("-")23    if head != "P" or not tail.isdigit():24        return None2526    return int(tail) if 1 <= int(tail) <= PRODUCTS else None272829@server.tool()30def get_stock(product: str) -> str:31    """Read the units in stock for one product id, from P-1 to P-30.3233    Read only. It does not return a price.34    """35    n = number(product)36    if not allowed():37        return "unauthorized"3839    return (40        "unknown product" if n is None else f"Stock: {12 + 5 * (n - 1)} units."41    )424344@server.tool()45def get_price(product: str) -> str:46    """Read the price in dollars for one product id, from P-1 to P-30.4748    Read only. It does not return a stock level.49    """50    n = number(product)51    if not allowed():52        return "unauthorized"5354    return "unknown product" if n is None else f"Price: ${19 + 3 * (n - 1)}."555657if __name__ == "__main__":58    server.run()

The same file in the Agent SDK
The Agent SDK takes the path of the same .mcp.json, so the file you committed serves both the command line and code. Built-in tools are turned off here, so the model has only the server's tools.


This server is a local process that talks over stdio. A remote server uses streamable HTTP, and SSE is deprecated. Every connected server's tools are available to the agent, though Claude Code may defer loading their definitions behind tool search. A resource is content the agent reads, such as a catalogue of what exists, while a tool acts.


app/sdk_agent.py
1"""The same committed file, handed to the Agent SDK."""23from pathlib import Path45from claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeAgentOptions67from app.runner import BUILTIN8910def options(project: Path) -> ClaudeAgentOptions:11    """Options that load the project's `.mcp.json` and nothing else."""12    return ClaudeAgentOptions(13        cwd=project,14        mcp_servers=project / ".mcp.json",15        disallowed_tools=BUILTIN,16    )

Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A committed .mcp.json holds a token in its env block, and 12 people can clone the repository. What is the right fix?
  1. ADelete the token from the file in the next commit and leave the history as it is.
  2. BWrite ${STOCK_TOKEN} in the file, set the value per person, and rotate the old token.
  3. CKeep the token in the file and mark the repository private so only the team reads it.
  4. DAdd a line to the system prompt that tells the agent never to print the token.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A The old commit still holds the token, so all 12 can still read it. Rotate it too.
  • B Correct. The file names the variable, the value stays on each machine, and the committed token is rotated.
  • C Everyone with access still reads it, and a private repository can be shared or cloned.
  • D The token is in the file, not in the agent's answer. A prompt does not remove it.
2. Six developers need the same stock server to start on every clone of a repository. Where does its configuration live?
  1. AIn each developer's own user file, since it reaches every session they open.
  2. BIn the system prompt of the agent that uses it.
  3. CIn a README that lists the command to run by hand.
  4. DIn a .mcp.json at the repository root.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A user file lives on one machine. The other five never receive it.
  • B A prompt cannot start a server. Servers start from configuration.
  • C A README is read once, and each of the six must repeat the steps.
  • D Correct. It is committed, so every clone starts the same server.
3. One developer wants to try a server that nobody else needs yet. Which choice keeps it away from the other 11?
  1. APut it in their user-level MCP file, which stays on their machine.
  2. BAdd it to the project .mcp.json and ask the others to ignore it.
  3. CWrite a custom server first, since a community one cannot be trusted.
  4. DUse the legacy SSE transport so it stays separate.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The user file is personal, and it runs beside the shared servers.
  • B Everyone who clones gets it started. Asking them to ignore it does not stop that.
  • C A maintained community server is the start. Write your own only when none fits.
  • D SSE is the older transport and it does not keep a server private.
4. Which two statements about MCP servers are true? Select two.
  1. AThe tools of every connected server are available to the agent, though definitions may load on demand.
  2. BSSE is the current transport for a remote server, and stdio is the legacy one.
  3. CA resource can act as a catalogue of what the server offers.
  4. DA resource and a tool are the same thing under two names.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. Each connected server's tools join the same list, and a definition may load on demand.
  • B Streamable HTTP is current for a remote server. Stdio suits a local one.
  • C Correct. A resource gives the agent content to read, such as a list of what exists.
  • D A tool acts. A resource is content the agent reads.
5. Two tools are described as "gets order info", and 4 of every 10 calls go to the wrong one. What fixes it?
  1. AAdd more examples of the question to the system prompt.
  2. BRename both tools to the same short name.
  3. CRewrite each description to state its input, its output and its limit.
  4. DRemove one tool and let the other handle both jobs.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A That treats the symptom. The two descriptions still look the same to the model.
  • B Two tools with one name are harder to tell apart, not easier.
  • C Correct. Distinct inputs and limits let the model tell the two tools apart.
  • D A catch-all tool with two jobs is the same problem in a single piece.
6. A single tool takes 12 modes through a mode field, and the model passes the wrong mode in 3 of 10 calls. What is the better design?
  1. ASplit it into narrow tools, one for each job.
  2. BList all 12 modes in the system prompt.
  3. CForce the tool with tool_choice so it is always called.
  4. DRaise the turn limit so a wrong mode can be retried.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A narrow tool has one input and one purpose, so there is less to get wrong.
  • B The tool still takes any mode. The prompt is a request, not a limit.
  • C Forcing the call does not choose the right mode.
  • D Each retry is another chance at the wrong mode, and some modes write data.
7. A system prompt says "always check the policy first", and now the policy tool runs on all 10 of 10 questions, even a greeting. What is the likely cause?
  1. AThe policy tool is named badly, so it is always picked.
  2. BThe model ignored the prompt and chose by chance.
  3. CTool choice is stored in a config file the prompt overrides.
  4. DThe wording "always" biased the choice toward that tool.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A name does not force a call. The prompt wording does.
  • B It followed the prompt. That is the problem.
  • C Wording in a prompt can bias the pick. No config file is involved.
  • D Correct. Prompt wording can bias tool choice, so reword it for the case that needs it.
8. Which two things belong in a good tool description? Select two.
  1. AA one-word name, since the model picks by name alone.
  2. BThe inputs the tool takes and what they look like.
  3. CThe token the tool needs, so the model can pass it along.
  4. DThe limits of the tool, such as what it does not return.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A The model reads the whole description to decide. A bare name gives it little.
  • B Correct. The form of the inputs tells the model when the tool fits.
  • C A secret in a description is shared with every reader. Keep it in the environment.
  • D Correct. A stated limit keeps a call from going to the wrong tool.

Foundations, lesson 16
Claude in CI
CI reads a fresh review as data, not as prose
The review job at Lumen Supply returns prose the pipeline cannot read, from the session that wrote the code. Nothing tells a rerun which comments the team has already closed. This is the pipeline at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch a review fail, then fix it with a schema, a fresh session and a list of what is closed.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
A pipeline needs a result it can parse
A review job runs on every pull request. The CI runner starts it, the model reviews the change, and code reads the answer and posts inline comments.


Four things can go wrong. A job run without -p waits for input nobody types and hangs. The harness always passes -p, so you will not watch that one fail.


The other three are in review.py. The answer is prose that cannot be parsed, the review resumes the author's session, and a rerun is not told which comments are closed.


A schema gives the pipeline findings it can read
The fixed job runs claude -p, which takes its prompt from the command and exits. It asks for JSON that matches a schema, so every finding has a file, a line and an issue.


Open the cards. The reviewer read the existing tests, found that the discount is subtracted instead of multiplied, and reported one finding on the line that holds it.

+}

  2. Jobclaude -p --json-schema --tools Read (fresh session)
  3. ClaudeRead src/pricing.ts
  4. ClaudeRead tests

    Show the result
    src/pricing.ts:6 applyDiscount subtracts the rate from the total (total - rate) instead of applying it as a fraction (total * (1 - rate)). Per CLAUDE.md, a rate of 0.1 means 10 percent off. applyDiscount(100, 0.1) returns 99.9 instead of 90, so the existing test at tests/pricing.test.ts:7-9 ('a rate of 0.1 takes 10 percent off') fails.
The findings parse, name the bug and repeat nothing closed.
The job and the brief as written
The starting code asks for no schema, so its answer is free text. Its brief asks about style and documentation and passes nothing that is closed. Its session resumes the author's session for the review.


A hang costs the most: a job that waits for a prompt holds a runner until the runner's timeout, which can be hours. A print run takes seconds.

src/pricing.ts, the…
    Show the result
    Bug: applyDiscount subtracts the rate instead of the discounted amount.

src/pricing.ts, the return total - rate; line. A rate is a fraction (0.1 means 10% off, per CLAUDE.md), so applyDiscount(100, 0.1) returns 99.9 instead of 90. Any caller that applies a discount gets a result that is almost the undiscounted total. The fix is return total * (1 - rate);.

No other bugs in this change. I haven't run it or checked any callers, since the repo has no git history and I only have this diff.
The pipeline cannot parse this answer.
Ask for a schema, a fresh reviewer and the closed findings
The fix has three parts. The schema asks for a findings list. The brief holds the diff, the rules to apply and the findings already closed. The session function returns no flags, so the review starts fresh and does not resume the author's session.


Team standards and test rules live in the project CLAUDE.md, which a print run loads like any other session. Memory files stack: user, project, then directory, and each adds to the last. A user-level file stays on one machine, so a rule the team needs belongs in the committed project file.


A long file splits into topic files, and each package imports the ones it needs with an @path line. Import a shared file rather than pasting a copy, because two copies drift apart.


review.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""What the CI review job asks for, how it wants the answer, its session."""23from typing import Any45FINDING = {6    "type": "object",7    "properties": {8        "file": {"type": "string"},9        "line": {"type": "integer"},10        "issue": {"type": "string"},11    },12    "required": ["file", "line", "issue"],13}141516def schema() -> dict[str, Any]:17    """A `findings` list the pipeline can read."""18    return {19        "type": "object",20        "properties": {"findings": {"type": "array", "items": FINDING}},21        "required": ["findings"],22    }232425def brief(diff: str, prior: str) -> str:26    """The prompt for a reviewer that sees only the diff and what is closed."""27    return (28        "Review this change for bugs that give wrong results. Read the "29        "existing tests for the changed file first. Skip style and "30        "missing doc comments.\n"31        f"Already reported, do not repeat: {prior}\n\n{diff}"32    )333435def session(author: str) -> list[str]:36    """Flags for the session the review runs in: none, so it starts fresh.37    The author's session holds the author's reasoning, and a review there38    starts from it instead of from the diff.39    """40    return []

The same change, two review jobs
Switch between the starting job and the fixed job. The card marked "This is where the runs split" is the parse result. One job hands the pipeline prose and the other hands it a finding.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch claude-in-ci.
Why the author's session does not review
The session that wrote a change holds the reasoning that led to it, and the Author card shows what it held. In this recording the author's own session says the change has a bug, so the resumed review finds it too. That is the lucky case.


A fresh session is the safer default: it sees only the diff and the repository, so no earlier reasoning can anchor it. A review of many files spreads attention thin, so review each file on its own and add a pass for how the files connect.


A verification pass checks each finding and attaches a confidence. Send only the high tier to a person once that confidence is calibrated against labelled outcomes. A score the model gives itself is not a measure, and neither is tone.


When CI should use a batch
A pre-merge review blocks a developer, so it runs now, as the review in the recording does. A batch costs half and takes up to 24 hours, so it fits an overnight report and not a blocking check.


Each batch request is a single Messages call, so a multi-turn tool loop cannot run inside it. Results come back in any order, and each carries the custom_id of its request. If some fail, resend only those by custom_id.

The same review on the command line
The job in this lesson is the command line itself. It passes -p, --output-format json and --json-schema. The parsed answer lands in the structured_output field of the JSON it prints.


The --tools Read flag limits the run to reading files. The --allowedTools Read flag only lets a read run without a permission prompt. The --bare flag starts faster by skipping CLAUDE.md, hooks and .mcp.json, so a job that relies on them leaves it off.


The author session is opened with --resume only in the starting job. Replay needs nothing installed. A live run (LIVE=1) needs the claude command-line tool installed and signed in.

The checks want a findings list where each finding has a file, line and issue. The brief must hold the diff and the closed findings, and the review must start a fresh session.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A CI job runs claude on each pull request. It sits idle until the runner kills it after 6 hours. What is the cause and the fix?
  1. AA permission prompt is blocking it, so add --dangerously-skip-permissions.
  2. BThe runner is too strict, so raise its timeout to 12 hours.
  3. CThe model is too slow, so switch the job to a larger one.
  4. DWith no -p, claude waits for input nobody types, so run it with -p.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A The skip flag removes a prompt but leaves the run interactive. The job still waits for input.
  • B A longer timeout only holds the runner longer. Nobody will ever type the input.
  • C A bigger model answers no faster than a session that is waiting on a keyboard.
  • D Correct. Print mode takes the prompt from the command, runs once and exits.
2. A review bot must attach each finding to a file and a line in the pull request. Today the job prints a paragraph. What changes?
  1. APrint JSON with --output-format json and pass --json-schema for a findings list.
  2. BAsk for JSON in the prompt and parse the reply with a regular expression.
  3. CSplit the paragraph on new lines and treat each line as a finding.
  4. DPost the whole paragraph as a single comment on the pull request.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The schema makes each finding carry a file, a line and an issue the bot can read.
  • B A request in the prompt is not a check. One odd reply breaks the regular expression.
  • C Lines of prose carry no file or line, so there is nothing to attach a comment to.
  • D One comment cannot sit on a line of code, which is what the bot was asked to do.
3. After a push, the review job posts 5 comments that the team already closed. What is the root fix?
  1. ARun the job on the same runner, so the model remembers the last run.
  2. BLower the temperature so the same review is not reworded.
  3. CDelete the repeated comments from the pull request after they post.
  4. DPass the closed findings into the brief and ask for only new ones.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Each run is a new session. The model has no memory of the last run, wherever it runs.
  • B A lower temperature makes the repeats more stable, not rarer.
  • C Cleaning up after the post treats the symptom, and the next push posts them again.
  • D Correct. The run can skip only what it is told was closed.
4. Select two things a claude -p run in CI can use from the repository to shape its review.
  1. AThe project CLAUDE.md, which holds the team standards.
  2. BThe author's chat history from their laptop.
  3. CThe existing tests, which it can open with a read tool.
  4. DNothing, because print mode skips CLAUDE.md.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. Print mode loads the project CLAUDE.md like any other session.
  • B A CI runner has no access to a laptop's chat history.
  • C Correct. Tests say what the code should do, and a read tool can open them.
  • D Print mode changes how the run ends. It does not change what it loads.
5. The rule that money is in dollars lives in one teammate's user-level CLAUDE.md. Three reviewers in CI miss it. What is the fix?
  1. ACopy the file into each reviewer's home directory by hand.
  2. BMove the rule into the project CLAUDE.md and commit it.
  3. CPaste the rule at the top of every review prompt.
  4. DAsk that teammate to start every review.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Hand copies drift, and a CI runner has no home directory to copy into.
  • B Correct. A project file travels with the repository, so every session loads it.
  • C A pasted rule is one more thing to keep in step, and it is easy to forget in a new job.
  • D This makes one person the gate. A user-level file still never reaches the runner.
6. One CLAUDE.md holds 9 topics and runs long. Sessions in each package load all of it. What is the fix?
  1. ADelete the topics that few packages use.
  2. BMove it to a user-level file so the repository copy is shorter.
  3. CSplit it into topic rule files and import only what each package needs.
  4. DShorten every topic to a single word.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Deleting loses the rules those packages do need.
  • B A user-level file is not shared, so the team would lose the rules.
  • C Correct. Topic files load where they apply, and each package imports only its own.
  • D A single word cannot carry a rule, so the standard stops being enforceable.
7. The payments package needs the same money rules that sit in the shared standards file. The text is being pasted into both. What is better?
  1. AImport the shared file with an @path line.
  2. BKeep the paste and add a note to update both together.
  3. CMention the shared file by name in a sentence, and trust readers to open it.
  4. DKeep both copies, because a duplicate does no harm.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. An @path import loads the shared file, so there is one source of truth.
  • B A note does not stop the copies from drifting apart.
  • C A sentence is not loaded. The session never sees the rules.
  • D Two copies disagree the first time one is edited.
8. Select two facts about how CLAUDE.md files layer.
  1. AA file in a directory replaces the project file for that directory.
  2. BUser, project and directory files stack, and each adds to the ones above it.
  3. CThe project file loads only when the prompt asks for it.
  4. DA user-level file stays on one machine and is not in the repository.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A A directory file adds to the project file. It does not replace it.
  • B Correct. The layers add up, so a session sees the user, project and directory rules together.
  • C The project file loads at the start of the session, with no request.
  • D Correct. Only files in the repository reach the team and the CI runner.
9. The review that gates a deploy has a 2-minute budget, and it is set up to use the Batches API for the price. What is wrong?
  1. ANothing, since the half price is worth a short wait.
  2. BNothing, since the deploy step can wait until the batch ends.
  3. CSplit the review into 40 smaller batches so each ends sooner.
  4. DA batch has no latency promise, so a blocking check runs sync.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A The wait is not short. A batch may take up to 24 hours.
  • B A deploy that waits on an unbounded batch is the failure. Nobody can say when it ends.
  • C Smaller batches are still batches, and none of them has a promise.
  • D Correct. The API answers now only on the sync path.
10. A weekly job tags 10,000 old reviews with a topic, and the team reads the tags on Monday. It runs sync and the bill is high. What should change?
  1. AStart the sync run at night, when the price is lower.
  2. BMove it to the Batches API, which costs half the price.
  3. CKeep it sync, since a faster answer must cost less.
  4. DKeep it sync, since 10,000 is too many for a batch.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A The sync price does not change with the hour.
  • B Correct. Nobody waits on the tags, so the half price costs nothing you notice.
  • C Sync answers sooner and costs more. The price is for the wait you give up.
  • D Size does not decide the mode. A large overnight job is the usual batch.
11. A batch of 10,000 review requests ends and 40 results are errors. How do you recover?
  1. ASubmit the full batch again and use the newer answers.
  2. BCount the error lines in the results file and resend that many requests.
  3. CFind the 40 by their custom_id and send only those again.
  4. DIgnore the 40, since the other results are enough.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A This pays for 9,960 answers you already have.
  • B Results come back in any order, so a position or a count says nothing.
  • C Correct. Each result carries the custom_id of its request.
  • D An unreviewed change is a hole in the pipeline, and the error says it needs another try.
12. Select two facts about the Message Batches API.
  1. AA batch has a 24 hour window and promises nothing faster.
  2. BResults come back in the order the requests were sent.
  3. CA batch ends within the hour, so it suits a blocking check.
  4. DA batch request cannot run a multi-turn tool loop.
Show the answer
Answer: A, D
  • A Correct. The window is a limit, not a promise.
  • B Results can come in any order. The custom_id is what ties a result to its request.
  • C No such promise exists, so a blocking check cannot depend on a batch.
  • D Correct. A batch request is one call, with no turn after a tool result.
13. The session that wrote a change reviews it and finds 0 issues. A teammate who reads the diff cold finds 3. What is the fix?
  1. ATell the author's session to be more critical of its own work.
  2. BReview in a fresh session that sees only the diff and the repository.
  3. CGive the author's session more turns to look again.
  4. DKeep the author's session, since it knows the intent best.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A The session still holds its own reasoning, and a stricter tone does not remove it.
  • B Correct. A fresh session has none of the reasoning that led to the code.
  • C More turns give it more time to agree with itself.
  • D Knowing the intent is the problem. It reads the code as it meant it, not as it is.
14. A review of 14 changed files finds the local bugs but misses one that only shows between two files. What is the root fix?
  1. AAdd a line to the prompt that says to be thorough.
  2. BMove to a model with a larger context window.
  3. CReview each file on its own, then run a pass on how the files connect.
  4. DReview a sample of the files, so attention goes further.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A plea for thoroughness does not widen attention across 14 files.
  • B A larger window holds more text, but attention still thins across it.
  • C Correct. Each file gets full attention, and a cross-file pass reads the links.
  • D A sample leaves files unreviewed, so it misses more.
15. A review job posts findings on three tiers of trust, and a human reads only the top tier. How should it route them?
  1. ATrust the model's tone, and post the findings that sound most confident first.
  2. BVerify each finding, score it on labelled outcomes, and route by that confidence.
  3. CPost every finding in one list, and let the human reader sort noise from signal.
  4. DMeasure overall accuracy once, and route the whole review by that single number.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Tone is not a measure. A wrong finding can sound sure.
  • B Correct. A second pass checks each finding, and a confidence calibrated on labelled outcomes is one the router can trust.
  • C One list sends the noise to the human along with the signal.
  • D One overall number hides which findings are wrong, so it cannot route them.
16. Select two reasons to review with a second instance of Claude.
  1. AIt remembers earlier runs, so it repeats fewer of the comments already closed.
  2. BIt never saw the code being written, so the author's reasoning does not anchor it.
  3. CIt can catch subtler issues that the author's session argued past.
  4. DIt reuses the files the author already read, so it needs no reads of its own.
Show the answer
Answer: B, C
  • A An instance carries nothing from earlier runs. Closed findings must be passed in.
  • B Correct. The second instance starts without the generation context.
  • C Correct. A fresh reader is not committed to the author's decisions.
  • D A fresh instance reads for itself. Its independence is the point.

A. Properties describe a field, and required makes it mandatory. List file, line and issue in required, so every finding the pipeline reads can be pinned to a line.

Foundations, lesson 17
Review criteria
Name what counts, then review one file at a time
A Lumen Supply release changes many files. A review told to be thorough reads them all in one request, flags files that are fine, and buries the real bugs. The team stops reading the comments. This is the review bot at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch it drown its own findings, then fix it with named criteria and one pass per file.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
Say what counts, then look at one file at a time
A review has two parts you control. The criteria say what to report and what to skip. The passes say which files go into which request. The code splits the files, and the model reviews each one.


Three things go wrong. Being thorough flags style noise and real bugs alike. One pass over many files spreads attention thin. A fault between two files has no pass that looks for it.


Criteria and passes give findings you can trust
The fixed review names what to report and what to skip, with an example of each. It gives each file its own request, then one last request that reads all of them together.


Open the cards. The result line counts the bug files that were flagged and the clean files that were flagged.


All six bug files are flagged. Three clean files, config.py, slug.py and tax.py, are still flagged. Criteria cut the noise. They do not remove it, so a human still reads what is left.

slug.py: label returns title[: n - 1].rstrip() + "…", which is n characters total, but the docstring-implied budget and short aside, nothing wrong here; no finding.
slug.py: slug lambda splits on whitespace and joins with dashes but does not strip non-alphanumerics, so titles with punctuation yield non-clean slugs (e.g. "Desk, Lamp" -> "desk,-lamp"), contradicting the module's stated purpose of turning punctuation into dashes.
cart.py: subtotal adds l.price instead of line_total(l), dropping the quantity factor, so subtotal ignores multi-unit lines and summary shows the wrong total.
tax.py: add_tax hardcodes the 1.2 (20%) multiplier and ignores the category, so reduced-rate amounts get taxed at the standard rate.
refunds.py: auto_approve uses amount < limit, but its docstring says refunds up to and including the limit are paid without a person, so a refund of exactly 50_00 is wrongly sent to review.
stock.py: can_reserve checks qty against on_hand instead of available (on_hand minus reserved), so reserve() can over-reserve stock already held for other carts.
discount.py: apply_coupon uses max(percent_for(code), CAP), which picks the larger discount, so the cap is inverted: WELCOME10 becomes 50% off instead of 10%, and VIP60 is cut to 50% instead of 60%. It should be min(...).
discount.py: bulk_percent's docstring says 5% from 10 units and 10% from 50, which the code matches, but sale_price is documented as rounding to a cent while round() on float prices can give banker's rounding, not a wrong result. No finding there.
dates.py: is_expired returns True on the expiry date itself (today >= expiry), but the docstring says a voucher can still be used that day, so the check should be today > expiry.
orders.py: shipping_for passes weight_kg to quote, but shipping.shipping_cents expects grams, so shipping is undercharged (a 2.5 kg parcel is priced as 1 step instead of 5).
discount.py: apply_coupon uses max(percent_for(code), CAP), but the docstring says "never more than CAP percent off"; this should be min, so WELCOME10 takes 50% off.
cart.py: subtotal adds l.price and ignores l.qty, so multi-unit lines are undercounted, which flows into orders.goods_total.
stock.py: can_reserve checks qty <= item["on_hand"] while its docstring says it checks unreserved stock, and reserve relies on it, so stock can be over-reserved.
refunds.py: auto_approve uses amount < limit, but its docstring says amounts up to and including the limit are paid at once, and needs_review depends on it.
dates.py: is_expired uses today >= expiry, so a voucher is expired on its expiry date, contradicting the docstring that says it can still be used that day.

The criteria and the passes as written
The starting criteria say "be thorough" and nothing else. The starting passes put every file into one request. A request of this size carries the whole release, and the reviewer spreads its attention across all of it.


The fixed review sends 15 requests: one per file, then one across all the files. Together they read about two and a half times the input tokens of the one request, and each file gets the reviewer to itself.
