    config.py: load() omits free_shipping_from, coupon_cap, low_stock, RESERVE_MINUTES, BACKOFF and DEBUG inconsistently, so only some settings can be overridden from the environment.
config.py: env_int lets int() raise ValueError on a bad value, crashing startup instead of falling back to the default.
config.py: PAGE has no lower bound, so zero or negative values pass through min() unchecked.
config.py: REFUND_LIMIT, FREE_SHIPPING_FROM, COUPON_CAP and LOW_STOCK are duplicated in refunds.py, shipping.py, discount.py and stock.py, so the copies can drift apart.
config.py: USE_NEW_TAX_TABLE is read but the tax module never uses it.
slug.py: slug is a lambda assignment (E731) and it doesn't strip punctuation, unlike clean_slug, so the two produce different slugs for the same title.
slug.py: ascii_only drops every non-Latin character, so titles in other scripts produce an empty slug from clean_slug and unique_slug returns just "-2".
slug.py: short slices without stripping or adding an ellipsis, unlike label, which is inconsistent.
notify.py: import os is unused (the TODO is noted) and import sys is unused.
notify.py: customer names are interpolated unescaped, which is an injection risk if these messages are ever rendered as HTML.
notify.py: delayed says "0 days late" or negative days without checking.
notify.py: refunded converts cents to float dollars and omits the thousands separator used elsewhere.
logs.py: record, record_error and timed write with print instead of a logger, so levels and handlers are ignored.
logs.py: record_error has a commented-out debug line left in.
logs.py: line() lets fields overwrite ts, level and msg, and json.dumps raises on non-serializable values such as datetimes.
logs.py: redact() matches only exact lowercase keys, so card_number, api_key and authorization are not redacted, and mixed-case secret_keys passed by a caller never match.
logs.py: redact() does not recurse into nested dicts.
logs.py: the timed decorator's inner does not use functools.wraps, so the wrapped function loses its name and docstring.
cart.py: subtotal() adds l.price instead of line_total(l), so every quantity beyond one is ignored; this also breaks summary().
cart.py: add() accepts zero or negative qty without validation and ignores a differing price when the SKU is already in the cart.
cart.py: for l in uses the ambiguous name l (E741).
tax.py: add_tax hardcodes a 1.2 multiplier, ignoring RATES and the category, so it will go stale.
tax.py: describe uses int(rate * 100), which truncates floating-point results such as 28.999… to 28; round should be used.
tax.py: round() uses banker's rounding on half cents, which may not match the tax rules expected.
refunds.py: auto_approve uses amount < limit, but its docstring says refunds up to and including the limit are paid automatically, so an amount equal to the limit is wrongly sent for review.
refunds.py: partial does not check that returned_units is within 0..units, so it can refund more than the order total.
refunds.py: refundable allows status "shipped", so refunds can be issued before delivery.
refunds.py: restocking_fee floors the fee with //, so the fee is rounded down on each return.
formatting.py: m() renders negative amounts as "$-5.00".
formatting.py: q() pluralizes by appending "s", which gives wrong plurals for words such as "box".
formatting.py: receipt() column widths of 6 and 10 are exceeded by longer quantity or total strings, and pad does not truncate, so the table misaligns.
stock.py: can_reserve compares qty to on_hand instead of on_hand - reserved, so units already held for carts can be sold again (overselling). The docstring says "unreserved stock".
stock.py: ship decrements on_hand without checking for it going negative.
stock.py: LOW = 5 duplicates config.LOW_STOCK.
discount.py: apply_coupon uses max(percent_for(code), CAP), which should be min; coupons are forced up to at least 50% off, and unknown codes get 50% off.
discount.py: sale_price uses round() (banker's rounding) on cents, which can misprice half-cent results.
discount.py: CAP duplicates config.COUPON_CAP.
greet.py: birthday_note never matches a February 29 birthday in non-leap years.
greet.py: greeting and welcome_back both take the full name and first name separately, so banner is inconsistent with its own helpers.
dates.py: is_expired returns today >= expiry, which marks a voucher expired on its expiry date, contradicting its docstring.
dates.py: add_working_days skips weekends but not public holidays, despite the "working days" wording.
dates.py: delivery_window and add_working_days do not reject negative n, and the loop silently returns start for it.
shipping.py: shipping_cents expects grams (per its docstring), but orders.parcel_weight_kg supplies kilograms, so a 2 kg parcel is charged as weight 2 g.
shipping.py: zone_price silently falls back to the far-zone multiplier for unknown zones.
shipping.py: express ignores the free-shipping threshold, which may be intended but is undocumented.
orders.py: parcel_weight_kg raises KeyError for a SKU missing from weights, with no fallback or message.
orders.py: shipping_for passes kilograms to quote, which expects grams, so shipping is undercharged (see shipping.py).
orders.py: order_total applies tax only to goods and not to shipping, which may be wrong for the jurisdiction.
orders.py: order_total always uses the standard rate, so the per-category rates in tax.py are never applied to order totals.
orders.py: build() recomputes goods, shipping and total separately, so the stored goods and total can diverge if these functions change.
6 of 6 bug files flagged, 8 clean files flagged. The noise hides the bugs.
Write criteria with examples, and split the passes
The criteria now say to report a wrong result and to skip style, names, notes and magic numbers. Each line starts with Report or Skip and gives a small example.


The passes return one request per file, then a last request over all the files. A category that flags too many clean files is switched off until its criteria are fixed.


The recorded criteria are short. A harder review adds more, and each addition has a job:


    

  • Define each severity level by what puts a finding there, and show one finding at the level. A bare word such as high leaves the boundary to the model, and two runs can draw it differently.
    • 

  • Show the output format in an example, with the file, the issue, the severity and the fix. A review that comes back in five shapes cannot be read by a pipeline.
    • 

  • Give two to four examples that cover the ambiguous cases, and the reason each is right or wrong. The reason lets the model carry the rule to a new case. A long pile of examples costs tokens on every call.
    • 

  • For extraction, show documents in different layouts, including one where a field is missing, so a missing field stays empty and is not invented.
    • 



review.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""What the reviewer is told, and which files it sees in each pass."""234def criteria() -> str:5    """Report wrong results, with examples of what to report and skip."""6    return (7        "Report a problem only when the code gives a wrong result, moves "8        "money the wrong way, or can crash. Skip style, names, missing "9        "docstrings, TODO notes and magic numbers. Most files have no "10        "problem; when you cannot point to the line and the wrong result "11        "it gives, report nothing.\n"12        "Report: arithmetic that drops a factor the code needs.\n"13        "Report: a check on the wrong side of a boundary.\n"14        "Report: a docstring that says one thing while the code does "15        "the opposite.\n"16        "Skip: a variable named `p`.\n"17        "Skip: a `print` call in a demo helper.\n"18        "Skip: a TODO note next to code that works."19    )202122def passes(files: list[str]) -> list[list[str]]:23    """One file per pass, then one pass over all of them for the links.24    A file on its own gets the reviewer's full attention. A fault between25    two files shows only when a pass reads both.26    """27    return [[name] for name in files] + [list(files)]
We doChange one setting at a time and predict.
The same release, two reviews
Switch between the starting review and the fixed review. The card marked "This is where the runs split" is the flags. The same files go in, and a different set of files comes out flagged.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch review-criteria-passes.
The small change shows the noise too
Both cards use the starting review: one on the hotfix, one on the release. A short change leaves the reviewer less to read, yet the hotfix reply still flags logs.py and tax.py, two files that are fine, beside the refund bug.


A smaller change does not remove the cause. The criteria are still vague, so noise arrives whenever a file looks odd.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch review-criteria-passes.
A fixed chain, or an adaptive plan
The arrows show files going in and flags coming out. A release review has known steps, so the code runs them as a fixed chain: one pass per file, then the pass across files. Nothing is decided by the model about which step comes next.


An open investigation is different. Its next step depends on what the last one found, so it uses an adaptive plan. Map the structure first, then plan the work by priority.


Measure by type before you automate
The result line of this run keeps two counts apart, the bug files flagged and the clean files flagged. One total would hide that. A job that is right 97 times in 100 may be wrong on 4 in 10 of one kind of form. Break accuracy down by type and by field.


Sample the output at random from each group. A labelled set is a batch of outputs a person has marked right or wrong. Use one to set a confidence cutoff for each field, the score below which an item goes to a person, and send unclear items there too.


A review that posts too many findings can add a verification pass. That is a second request that reads each finding again and attaches a confidence, a number for how sure it is. Route by that number only after checking it against labelled findings, because a score the model gives itself is not a measure.

The same review in the Agent SDK
The Claude Agent SDK runs each pass as a one-turn query with no tools. A second instance that reviews a file has no memory of how the file was written, so that reasoning does not anchor it.

app/sdk_agent.py
1"""The same per-file review on the Claude Agent SDK.23The SDK runs each pass as a one-turn query with no tools, so a second4instance reviews a file with no memory of how it was written.5"""67from types import ModuleType89from kit import sdk10from kit.api import Json11from .agent import SYSTEM, Handled, flagged_in12from .tickets import FILES, Ticket131415def request_for(review: ModuleType, names: list[str]) -> Json:16    """The plain request a recording is keyed by."""17    body = "\n\n".join(f"### {name}\n{FILES[name]}" for name in names)18    prompt = f"{review.criteria()}\n\nReview these files:\n\n{body}"1920    return sdk.build_request(prompt, SYSTEM, tools=[], max_turns=1)212223def text_of(messages: list[Json]) -> str:24    """The last assistant text in a message stream."""25    final = ""2627    for message in messages:28        for item in message.get("content", []):29            if item["type"] == "text" and message["type"] == "assistant":30                final = item["text"]3132    return str(final)333435async def run(36    ticket: Ticket, review: ModuleType, llm: sdk.Live | sdk.Replay37) -> Handled:38    """Review each group of files the review names, on the SDK."""39    groups = review.passes(list(ticket.files))40    replies: list[str] = []4142    for names in groups:43        replies.append(text_of(await llm(request_for(review, names))))4445    text = "\n".join(replies)4647    return Handled(ticket, len(groups), flagged_in(text, ticket.files), text)

The checks want criteria that name what to report and what to skip, with examples. Each file gets its own pass, none is left out, and a last pass reads the links between files.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A review bot posts comments on 9 of 14 files, and 6 of those files are fine. The team has started to ignore the bot. What is the root fix?
  1. ATell it to be more thorough, so it finds the bugs among the noise.
  2. BName which problems to report and which to skip in the criteria.
  3. CAsk it for a longer report, so each comment carries more detail.
  4. DLower the severity of every comment so nobody is alarmed by them.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A plea for thoroughness names no category, so style noise counts as much as a bug.
  • B Correct. Explicit criteria separate a wrong result from a matter of taste.
  • C A longer report gives the reader more to skip. It does not change what gets flagged.
  • D A softer label keeps the noise and makes the real bugs easier to miss.
2. The prompt already says to be conservative and only flag what matters. Even so, 60 percent of the flags on a release are noise. What works better?
  1. AWrite conservative in capitals, so the instruction carries more weight.
  2. BAsk the model to flag only when it is certain, and trust its answer.
  3. CSend the review to a model with a larger window, so it sees more.
  4. DName the categories that count, with a sample of each.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Volume does not define the word. The model still has no list of what matters.
  • B Stated certainty is not a measure, and a wrong flag can sound as sure as a right one.
  • C A larger window holds more text. It gives no rule for what to report.
  • D Correct. Named categories tell the reviewer where the line is, and a sample shows it.
3. One review category flags 8 false positives in every 10 comments. The team now distrusts the other categories too. What should you do?
  1. AKeep it on, because a noisy category still finds some real problems.
  2. BRaise the severity of the other categories so they stand out from it.
  3. CTurn that category off until it is fixed, and keep the rest.
  4. DTurn the whole review off until every category is accurate.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A The real problems it finds are lost among the false ones, and readers stop looking.
  • B Louder labels do not remove the noise. The reader still sifts the noisy category.
  • C Correct. One noisy category costs the trust in all of them, so switch it off until it is fixed.
  • D This throws away the categories that work, along with the one that does not.
4. Select two things that make a severity level usable in a review prompt.
  1. AA definition of when each level applies.
  2. BA single word for each level, such as high or low.
  3. CA short code example that shows each level.
  4. DA sentence that asks the reviewer to use good judgement.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. A definition says what puts a finding at that level.
  • B A bare word leaves the boundary to the model, so two runs can split it differently.
  • C Correct. An example shows a finding at the level, so the line is concrete.
  • D Judgement with no rule is the gap the criteria are meant to fill.
5. Across 10 runs, a review comes back in 5 different shapes, and the pipeline cannot read half of them. What is the fix?
  1. AShow the format in examples: file, issue, severity, fix.
  2. BRun it again each time until the shape matches what the parser wants.
  3. CWrite in the prompt that the format must be followed strictly.
  4. DAdd 12 more examples of findings, so the shape is averaged out.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. An example of the exact format is the clearest way to fix the shape.
  • B Each rerun costs a call and still may not match.
  • C A stern line names no shape. The model still has to guess one.
  • D More examples raise the cost, and a long pile can pull the output toward the wrong one.
6. A print call in a demo helper is fine, but the review flags it in every run. How do you stop that without hiding real problems?
  1. ALet it flag the print call, and have a person drop it each time.
  2. BAdd an example of the print call as acceptable, with the reason.
  3. CForbid the word print in the review comments.
  4. DRemove every example from the prompt, so there is less to copy.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A This spends a person's time on the same noise every run.
  • B Correct. An acceptable pattern with its reason settles an ambiguous case.
  • C The call is still flagged, only under different words. The judgement was never made.
  • D Without examples the model has even less to go on.
7. An extraction job invents a value for a field when the document has none. The documents come in 4 different layouts. What helps most?
  1. AMove to a model with a larger context window, so it holds more text.
  2. BName every field in the prompt and add nothing else to the instructions.
  3. CShow examples in other layouts, with one that has a missing field.
  4. DSet the temperature to 0 so the model stops inventing values for fields.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A larger window adds room, not a rule for a missing field.
  • B Names say what to extract. They do not show what to do when a field is absent.
  • C Correct. Examples across layouts show that a missing field stays empty.
  • D A lower temperature makes the model more repeatable, and it can repeat an invented value.
8. Select two rules for the examples in a review prompt.
  1. AUse as many as will fit, because each one improves the review.
  2. BUse two to four examples that cover the ambiguous cases.
  3. CShow the output each time and leave the reason out.
  4. DGive the reason each example is right or wrong.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A A long pile costs tokens on every call, and it can crowd out the instructions.
  • B Correct. A few well-chosen cases settle the ambiguity without swamping the prompt.
  • C Without the reason the model copies the surface and misses the rule.
  • D Correct. The reason is what lets the model carry the rule to a new case.
9. A single request reviews a release of 14 files. The two bugs in the middle files are missed. What is the root fix?
  1. AKeep one request, since one call is cheaper than fourteen.
  2. BUse a model with a larger window, so the whole release fits.
  3. CAdd a line that asks the model to read the middle carefully.
  4. DReview each file in its own request.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A The saving is real, but the bugs that slip through cost more.
  • B The release already fits. The problem is attention spread across many files.
  • C A request to read carefully does not widen attention across 14 files.
  • D Correct. A pass on one file gives it the reviewer's full attention.
10. Each of 14 files passes its own review, yet a parcel weight in kilograms is passed to a function that expects grams. Which step finds it?
  1. AA last pass that reads all the files together.
  2. BNothing more, since every file was reviewed.
  3. CThe same 14 passes again, to see whether they agree.
  4. DA pass over only the files that looked risky.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A fault between files shows only when a pass reads both.
  • B Each pass saw one file, so none could see that two files disagree.
  • C The same single-file passes see the same single file, and they reach the same answer.
  • D The fault sits in files that look fine on their own.
11. A review posts findings that a person must read, and there are far too many to read. How should they be routed?
  1. APost the ones that sound the most certain first, and trust the order they come in.
  2. BAdd a verification pass, calibrated on labelled findings, and route by its score.
  3. CPost every finding in one list, and let each reader sort the list by hand.
  4. DPost the average accuracy of the whole review next to the list of findings.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Tone is not a measure, and a wrong finding can sound sure. A score needs checking against labels.
  • B Correct. A second look attaches a confidence, and calibrating it on labelled findings makes it usable for routing.
  • C One list sends the noise to the person along with the signal.
  • D An average does not say which findings to read first.
12. Select two reasons to add a review pass that is separate from the pass that wrote the code.
  1. AIt has no memory of how the code was written, so nothing anchors it.
  2. BIt remembers the bugs from earlier runs and looks for them first.
  3. CIt reruns the same check, so a bug is confirmed by two identical answers.
  4. DIt can read across files, which a pass on one file cannot do.
Show the answer
Answer: A, D
  • A Correct. A fresh instance starts with none of the author's reasoning.
  • B An instance carries nothing from earlier runs.
  • C An identical rerun adds nothing. The value is in the different view.
  • D Correct. A pass that holds several files can see how they fit together.
13. A release review always takes the same steps over 14 files, in the same order. How should you build it?
  1. AAs an open plan that the model redraws after every file.
  2. BAs an adaptive plan, because adapting is always safer.
  3. CAs one step, because fewer steps always means fewer errors.
  4. DAs a fixed chain of passes that the code runs in order.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A An open plan spends calls deciding what the code already knows.
  • B Adapting helps when the steps are not known, and here they are.
  • C Fewer steps here means one pass over 14 files, which is the failure.
  • D Correct. A predictable job is a fixed chain, which is easy to test and to repeat.
14. An investigation of an unfamiliar code base keeps turning up modules nobody expected. How should the work be planned?
  1. AAs a fixed chain written before the work starts.
  2. BBy reading every file in the repository before doing anything else.
  3. CAs an adaptive plan that is revised as each finding comes in.
  4. DBy writing the full plan up front and never changing it.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A fixed chain cannot follow modules it did not know about.
  • B This is slow and it fills the context before the work has begun.
  • C Correct. When each step depends on what the last one found, the plan has to adapt.
  • D A plan that never changes cannot follow what the work turns up.
15. A chain reviews each of 14 files alone, and nobody checks how the files call each other. What should be added?
  1. AA last pass over all the files, reading the links.
  2. BNothing, because each file was checked in full.
  3. CA bigger context window on each single-file pass, so it sees more.
  4. DFold every file into one pass, so the links are visible.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The integration pass reads the calls across files that no single pass sees.
  • B Checking each file in full does not check how two files fit together.
  • C A single-file pass still holds one file, however large its window.
  • D This brings back the dilution the per-file passes removed.
16. Select two steps that start an adaptive plan for an unfamiliar project.
  1. ARead every file in full before forming any plan.
  2. BMap the structure of the project first.
  3. CPlan the work by priority, from what the map shows.
  4. DFix the order of all the steps before looking at the code.
Show the answer
Answer: B, C
  • A This fills the context with files that may not matter.
  • B Correct. A map shows where the code lives at a low cost.
  • C Correct. The map says which areas matter, so the work starts there.
  • D An order fixed in advance cannot respond to what the map shows.
17. An extraction job scores 97 percent overall, but one of its 6 form types scores 61 percent. What should you do before automating it?
  1. AAutomate it, since 97 percent is above the bar.
  2. BTest more of the form types that already pass.
  3. CRaise the pass mark to 98 percent and stop there.
  4. DBreak accuracy down by form type and field.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A The 97 percent hides a form type that fails 4 times in 10.
  • B More passing forms make the average look better and hide the weak one.
  • C A higher mark says nothing about which form type fails.
  • D Correct. An average hides a weak type, and the breakdown shows it.
18. The extractions marked high confidence are not reviewed. A check of 100 of them finds 4 wrong. How should such output be sampled?
  1. AIt needs no sampling, because high confidence means correct.
  2. BSample at random from each confidence and type group.
  3. CRead the first 100 that arrive each day.
  4. DSample only the low-confidence ones, since they are the risky ones.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Four in a hundred were wrong, so high confidence does not mean correct.
  • B Correct. A stratified random sample shows the error rate in each group.
  • C The first 100 are not random, and they may all be one type.
  • D This leaves the high-confidence group, where the wrong answers were found, unchecked.
19. The team sets the confidence cutoff for each field by feel, and the cutoffs keep drifting. What makes them stable?
  1. ACalibrate each cutoff on a set of labelled documents.
  2. BTrust the model's own score, since it knows how sure it is.
  3. CKeep the cutoffs by feel, and revisit them each week.
  4. DUse one cutoff for every field, so there is nothing to drift.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. Labelled documents show how often each score is right, so a cutoff can follow.
  • B A model's score is not calibrated to the truth until it is checked against labels.
  • C This is the drift. A cutoff should be set from data.
  • D Fields differ in how hard they are, so one cutoff is wrong for most of them.
20. Select two kinds of extraction that should go to a person.
  1. AEvery extraction, because a person must see them all.
  2. BAnything from a source the model has read before.
  3. CLow confidence on a field.
  4. DA source that is unclear or contradicts itself.
Show the answer
Answer: C, D
  • A This removes the value of automating. Reserve a person for the cases that need one.
  • B A familiar source can still be wrong, and being familiar is not a reason to skip a check.
  • C Correct. Low confidence is the signal that a person should check the value.
  • D Correct. Where the source is unclear the model cannot be checked against it.

Criteria
The rules for what a review reports and what it skips
Pass
One request that shows the reviewer only the files it names
Integration pass
A last pass that reads several files together for the links between them
Fixed chain
Steps the code runs in a set order
Foundations, lesson 18
Sync or batch
Blocking checks run sync; overnight work runs batch
The pre-merge check at Lumen Supply goes through the batch API, so developers may wait for hours with no promise of an answer. The nightly report runs sync at full price, so the bill is double for a wait nobody feels. This is the code at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch a plan send work down the wrong path, then fix it with one rule about who is waiting.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
Who is waiting decides the path
Claude answers in one of two ways. The Messages API answers in the same call. The Batches API takes a list of requests, each with a custom_id, and answers later at half the price.


The plan decides the path, and the API runs it. A plan that picks wrongly fails in three ways.


A blocking check waits on a batch. A nightly job pays full price. A failed batch is rerun whole. The first two fail in a recorded run, and the third shows in the code and the fixed run.


A blocking check answers in the same call
The merge check is a job someone waits on, so the plan runs it sync. The request goes to the Messages API and the reply comes back in the same call. Open the card to read what Claude answered.


This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 call, recorded once and replayed here. Nothing about it depends on how large the change is.

]

The merge check answered in the same call. Nobody waited.
The starting plan sends the check to a batch
mode picks the path for a job, and resubmit picks what to send again. The starting mode has the rule backwards: it sends the blocking job to a batch and runs the overnight jobs sync.


The starting resubmit returns every custom_id, so one failed result sends the whole batch again.


The price is what makes this tempting. A batch costs half as much, so a check that runs on every change looks like the place to save. But a batch trades a wait for that price, and this check cannot wait.

How long will the merge check wait?
The starting plan has sent the merge check to the Batches API. A developer has pushed a change and is watching the merge button.


Predict: How long does the developer wait for the answer?

  2. BA few seconds, because the change is small to Claude.
Show the answer
A. A batch trades a wait for half the price. It gives no latency promise, so a blocking check cannot rely on it.
The merge waits for a batch
The plan chose batch, so the check was submitted as a request with a custom_id and a batch to poll. The outcome line is the cost: the developer waits on a path with no latency promise. The last call sends the batch's one request again, because the starting resubmit returns every custom_id.


A batch may end sooner than its window, but nothing promises it. The window is up to 24 hours, and the API does not say when inside it.

The merge check went to a batch. It has no latency promise, so the developer may wait up to 24 hours.
Sync for blocking work, batch for the night
The fixed mode asks one question: is someone waiting? If so it runs sync. If not it runs batch, whatever the size of the job. The fixed resubmit reads each result's type and returns the custom_id of every result that did not succeed.


Follow the arrows. The expired result is matched to its request by custom_id, and only that request goes again. A batch whose results all succeeded sends nothing.


plan.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""The plan: which path a job takes, and which results to send again."""23from app.tickets import Job4from kit.api import Json567def mode(job: Job) -> str:8    """Blocking work runs sync; overnight work runs batch, whatever its size.9    A batch is half the price but has no latency promise, so nobody who is10    waiting can depend on it.11    """12    return "sync" if job.blocking else "batch"131415def resubmit(results: dict[str, Json]) -> list[str]:16    """The custom_ids to send again: only the results that did not succeed.17    A finished batch has none, so nothing is sent.18    """19    return [cid for cid, r in results.items() if r["type"] != "succeeded"]
We doChange one setting at a time and predict.
The same jobs, two plans
Switch between the starting plan and the fixed plan on the merge check. The card marked "This is where the runs split" is the plan's choice. One path answers now and the other answers later.


Then pick the nightly jobs. The starting plan runs them sync at full price, and the fixed plan runs them as a batch at half price.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch sync-or-batch.
Size does not decide the mode
Both nightly jobs are overnight work, 12 tickets and 10,000 orders. Both cards use the fixed plan, and the large one goes to a batch too. It is not special, because nobody is waiting on either.


Work out the window from the deadline. A batch ends within 24 hours, so it fits a report due in 30 hours and not one due in 6. Before a full run, tune the prompt on a small sample. A bad prompt on the whole job is paid for in full.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch sync-or-batch.
Try it: plans and jobs
Pick the starting plan on the merge check to see the wait, or on a nightly job to see the full price. Pick the fixed plan on the nightly tags to see one result sent again alone. The harness simulates that expired result, and only the resend is a recorded call.


Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch sync-or-batch.
The sync path in the Agent SDK
The Claude Agent SDK answers now, so it is the sync path. It has no batch. Each batch request is a single Messages call, so a multi-turn tool loop cannot run inside it.


For a CI job, claude -p is the same sync path from the command line. It runs once, prints its result, and lets the job read it. This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run.


app/sdk_agent.py
1"""The blocking path on the Claude Agent SDK.23The SDK answers now, so it is the sync path. It has no batch: a batch4request is a single Messages call, so no tool loop can continue in it.5"""67from kit import sdk8from kit.api import Json9from .agent import Run, ids_for10from .tickets import SYSTEM, Job111213def request_for(job: Job, prompt: str) -> Json:14    """The plain request a recording is keyed by."""15    return sdk.build_request(prompt, SYSTEM, tools=[], max_turns=1)161718def text_of(messages: list[Json]) -> str:19    """The last assistant text in a message stream."""20    final = ""2122    for message in messages:23        for item in message.get("content", []):24            if item["type"] == "text" and message["type"] == "assistant":25                final = item["text"]2627    return str(final)282930async def run(job: Job, llm: sdk.Live | sdk.Replay) -> Run:31    """Answer each item of the job now, on the SDK."""32    found = Run(job, "sync")3334    for cid, prompt in zip(ids_for(job), job.items, strict=True):35        messages = await llm(request_for(job, prompt))36        found.replies[cid] = text_of(messages)37        found.events.append({"kind": "sync", "ids": [cid]})3839    return found

The checks want a blocking job on sync and a nightly job on batch, whatever its size. Only results that did not succeed are sent again, by custom_id.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A pre-merge check must finish within 2 minutes or the developer stops waiting. It reviews a change of 400 files. Which way should it run?
  1. AAs a batch, because the batch price is half.
  2. BSync, so the answer comes back in the same call.
  3. CAs a batch, with the poll timeout set to 2 minutes.
  4. DAs several small batches, so each one ends sooner.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Half the price does not help a check that someone is waiting on. A batch trades a wait for the price.
  • B Correct. A sync call answers now. A check that blocks a merge needs an answer now.
  • C A poll timeout only stops your own loop. The batch still has no promise of finishing in 2 minutes.
  • D Smaller batches are still batches. None of them carries a latency promise.
2. A report over 10,000 orders runs sync each night and is read at 8 the next morning. The bill is high. What is the root fix?
  1. AKeep it sync and shorten the prompt to cut the tokens.
  2. BKeep it sync, because 10,000 requests are too many for one batch.
  3. CKeep it sync, but start it at noon when the price is lower.
  4. DSubmit it as a batch, which costs half the price and can wait.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A shorter prompt trims a little from every request. The mode still pays full price for a wait nobody feels.
  • B Size does not decide the mode. Nobody waits on the report, so it belongs in a batch at any size.
  • C The price does not change with the hour. The half price belongs to the batch path.
  • D Correct. Nobody waits on an overnight report, so the half price costs nothing you feel.
3. A nightly batch of 10,000 requests ends with 40 results that expired. How should the job recover?
  1. ASend again only the 40 requests, found by their custom_id.
  2. BSubmit all 10,000 again and keep the newer results.
  3. CFind the gaps by position in the results file and resend those lines.
  4. DDrop the 40, since 9,960 answered and the report is nearly whole.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. Each result carries the custom_id of its request, so the failed ones can be found and sent again alone.
  • B Sending everything again pays for 9,960 answers you already have.
  • C Results can come back in any order, so a position says nothing. The custom_id is the link.
  • D A silent gap in a report is a defect. The failed items still need an answer.
4. Select two facts about a Message Batches job.
  1. AIt has a 24 hour window and promises nothing faster.
  2. BIts results arrive in the order the requests were sent.
  3. CEach request is a single Messages call, so a multi-turn tool loop cannot run in it.
  4. DIt ends within the hour, which suits a check that blocks a merge.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. The window is a limit, not a promise. A batch may finish sooner, and nobody can count on it.
  • B Results can come in any order. A result is matched to its request by custom_id.
  • C Correct. A batch request is a single call. A tool loop needs a call after each tool result.
  • D There is no such promise. A merge-blocking check cannot depend on a batch.
5. A nightly code review of the whole repository is due in 30 hours. The window of a batch is 24 hours. Which path fits?
  1. ASync, because any deadline past 6 hours is too close to trust a batch.
  2. BHalf sync and half batch, so both halves end early.
  3. CBatch, submitted now, since its window ends before the deadline.
  4. DBatch, and tell the reader to expect it in 12 hours.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A 24-hour window fits inside 30 hours, so the batch is the cheaper path and still on time.
  • B Splitting by size adds cost and complexity. The deadline already fits one batch.
  • C Correct. Work out the window from the deadline. 24 hours is less than 30, so batch fits.
  • D A batch makes no promise about 12 hours. Promise the reader only what the window guarantees.
6. The first trial of a batch prompt fails on 12 of 100 items. The full run is 50,000 items. What comes next?
  1. ASubmit all 50,000 and fix the failures from the results later.
  2. BFix the prompt, then test it on about 100 items.
  3. CRun all 50,000 sync so the failures show up right away, at full price.
  4. DResubmit the 12 failed items until they pass.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Every bad answer in the full run is paid for, and the prompt fault repeats across thousands of items.
  • B Correct. A small sample shows the fault cheaply. The full run starts when the sample is clean.
  • C A sync run at this size pays full price to find a fault a small sample would show.
  • D The 12 failed because of the prompt. Sending them again fails the same way.
7. A CI job reviews a change and its result decides whether the deploy step runs. How should the job call Claude?
  1. ASubmit a batch, because the tool loop the review needs runs there.
  2. BSubmit a batch and poll it, since it usually ends within the hour.
  3. CSubmit a batch and deploy when it ends, since that halves the cost.
  4. DRun it sync with claude -p, and read the result in the job.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A batch request cannot run a multi-turn tool loop, so it is the wrong home for an agent review.
  • B A batch has no latency promise. The deploy step could wait for up to a day.
  • C The half price is real, but the deploy waits on this result. The saving is not worth the wait.
  • D Correct. A blocking job needs its result now. claude -p runs once and returns it to the job.
8. Select two rules for choosing the path of a CI job.
  1. AWork that blocks a merge or a deploy runs sync.
  2. BA job of more than 1,000 items runs batch, blocking or not.
  3. CWork that is read the next morning runs batch.
  4. DEvery job runs batch, because the half price is the point.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. Someone is waiting, and only a sync call answers when they need it.
  • B Size does not decide the mode. A large blocking check still needs an answer now.
  • C Correct. Nobody feels the wait, so the half price is free.
  • D The half price comes with a wait and no latency promise. A blocking job cannot pay that.

    return "sync" if job.size < 100 else "batch"

  1. ASync, at full price, though nobody reads the result until morning.
  2. BBatch, because it runs overnight.

A. Size says nothing about who is waiting. Send a job sync only when someone blocks on it, and batch everything that can wait, whatever its size.

Batch
A list of requests the API answers later, at half the price, with no latency promise
custom_id
The label on each batch request that matches its result back to it
Blocking job
Work someone waits on before they can go on
Resubmit

Foundations, lesson 19
Schema extraction
A nullable schema and a forced tool make extraction trustworthy
Lumen Supply reads supplier invoices into its ledger. One vendor never prints a PO number, the schema demands one, and the model writes a value nobody wrote. You will watch that happen, then fix it. This is the extractor at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. The schema is the contract, and you will change what it allows.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
The schema is the contract Claude writes to
The extractor gives Claude one tool. The tool's input schema is the shape of the record the ledger wants. Claude fills the tool in, and the ledger checks the result.


Three things go wrong in turn. The answer is free text that code cannot parse. A required field the invoice lacks gets a made-up value. A category list with no place for an odd invoice files it wrongly.


A clean invoice becomes a valid record
A supplier invoice goes in and a record comes out, with vendor, total, PO number and category. Open a card to see the data each side saw.


This works because every field is printed on the invoice. The harder cases are invoices that are silent about something.

The starting schema demands a value for everything
Every field is required, the tool choice is auto (Claude may answer in text instead of calling the tool), and the category list has no escape. Each of those is a reasonable default, and each one fails on a real invoice.


A field that is required when the source may lack it leaves Claude only one way to comply: write something.

What happens with an invoice that has no PO number?
One Lumen vendor sends freight invoices with no PO number on them. The schema says the PO number is required.


Predict: What does the record hold for the PO number?
  1. AA value the invoice does not hold, since the field must be filled.
  2. BNull, since the invoice has none.
Show the answer
A. A required field the source lacks invites a guess. The recording shows what kind of guess.
The record holds a guess, or never arrives
With tool_choice on auto, Claude called the tool and wrote an empty string for the PO number. The schema accepts an empty string, so the ledger got a valid record that is not null.


Auto also lets Claude answer in text: on the odd invoice it replied in prose and the ledger got no record at all. Try forcing the tool, and Claude has to fill the field.


Forcing the tool kept the shape and still broke the value: the PO number became the placeholder <UNKNOWN>. A forced tool guarantees a record. It does not make the values true.

The record is valid but wrong. It should hold {'vendor': 'Brightline Freight', 'total': 310.0, 'po_number': None, 'category': 'freight'}.
This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch schema-extraction.
Force the tool, allow null, keep an escape
Three changes. The tool is forced, so a record always arrives. The PO number may be null, so silence on the invoice has somewhere to go. The category list ends with other and a detail field, so an odd invoice is not misfiled.


Vendor and total stay required, because every invoice has them. Those changes fill schema() and choice(), in that order: nullable PO number and other first, then the forced tool. The third stub, examples(), is filled in the examples step below.


tool_choice takes four values: auto, any, a named tool and none. A named tool forces that tool, which suits a first step that must be an extraction. Claude Haiku 5.5 accepts a forced tool. Some larger current models reject it with a 400 error, and there a structured output format (output_config.format) returns the record.

The same invoice now ends differently
Switch between the two schemas. The card marked "This is where the runs split" is the PO number: an empty string before, null after.


The invoice did not change. The schema gave the model an honest answer to give.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch schema-extraction.
Examples settle what a schema cannot
Some invoices print the PO number as a bare number, and the ledger wants the PO- form. A schema cannot say that. Worked examples of differently laid-out invoices can, and examples() returns them.


Switch between no examples and the examples. Without them the model copies the number as printed. With them it writes the form the ledger expects.


An example can also settle a name written three ways, with a one-line reason.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch schema-extraction.
Try it: schemas and invoices
Change one setting at a time. Pick the odd invoice with the starting schema and Claude answers in prose. Pick it with the fixed schema and it is filed under other, with a detail.


Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet. A record can have the right shape and a wrong value.

The Agent SDK serves the same tool in-process, with the same schema as its input. The SDK cannot force a tool, so the system prompt asks Claude to call it once.

Copy the starting code and open work/schema-extraction/schema.py. It has three steps. The schema requires a PO number and has no "other" category, the tool choice is auto, and the prompt has no examples.


Terminal
./workshop start schema-extraction

The checks let a missing PO number be null, add "other" with a detail field and keep vendor and total required. They want the tool forced and examples from two different layouts.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. 40 of 800 weekly invoices reach the ledger with the PO number PO-0000. The vendor behind them prints no PO number at all. What is the fix at the source?
  1. AAdd a prompt line that tells the model not to invent a PO number.
  2. BLet po_number be null in the schema, so silence has a place to go.
  3. CReject every record whose PO number is PO-0000 after extraction.
  4. DKeep the field required, and add a regex that checks the PO format.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A prompt line asks politely, while the schema still demands a value. The model has to comply with one of the two.
  • B Correct. A field the source may lack is nullable, so the honest answer fits the schema.
  • C This filters one placeholder. The model will write another one, such as N/A or 0.
  • D A format check cannot tell a real PO number from a made-up one that looks right.
2. The extractor offers its tool with tool_choice set to auto. In 5 of 100 runs the reply is prose that the ledger cannot parse. What should change?
  1. AWrite a longer system prompt that insists on a tool call.
  2. BRetry any prose reply until a tool call comes back.
  3. CPull the JSON out of the prose with a regular expression.
  4. DSet tool_choice to the extraction tool, so a record always arrives.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Insisting is still a request. On auto the model may choose prose on any run.
  • B Retries hide the cause and cost a call each time. The next prose reply is only a matter of time.
  • C Prose has no stable layout, so a pattern breaks on the first reply that is worded differently.
  • D Correct. A named tool in tool_choice turns the reply into tool input that follows the schema.
3. A category list has six values. Each week 30 invoices for event hire land under freight, since nothing else fits. What is the change?
  1. AAdd an other value and a category_detail field that says what the item is.
  2. BMake category optional, so the model can leave it empty.
  3. CAdd ten more categories until every invoice seen so far fits.
  4. DTell the model in the prompt to pick the closest category.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. An escape value keeps the odd invoice out of a wrong category, and the detail keeps what it was.
  • B An empty category hides the problem from the ledger and loses the information.
  • C A longer list still has an end. The next odd invoice will not fit, and there is nowhere for it.
  • D Closest is how the misfiling happens. The record looks fine and is wrong.
4. Which two statements about extraction with a tool schema are true? Select two.
  1. AA record can match the schema and still hold a value the invoice does not contain.
  2. BA record that matches the schema holds values that match the invoice.
  3. CA forced tool means the reply is a record rather than prose.
  4. DA forced tool corrects wrong values in fields the invoice cannot fill.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. The schema checks the shape. A placeholder in a string field is valid.
  • B Shape and meaning are different checks. The schema only does the first.
  • C Correct. With a named tool the model has to reply with that tool's input.
  • D Forcing makes the model fill the field, which is when an invented value appears.
5. Totals are wrong on 12 of 100 scanned invoices. The total sits in a different place on each layout. What helps most?
  1. ALower the temperature to zero so the model reads more carefully.
  2. BAdd a regular expression that finds the word Total in the text.
  3. CShow examples of invoices with the total in different places.
  4. DShow one example of a typical invoice with the total at the bottom.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Temperature changes variety, not whether a layout is understood.
  • B A pattern tied to one word breaks on a layout that says Amount due or puts the figure in a table.
  • C Correct. Examples of differing layouts show the model where the value hides.
  • D One layout teaches one place to look. The others stay as wrong as before.
6. Across 5 invoice layouts the PO number comes out as 5530, PO5530 or PO-5530. The ledger wants PO-5530. What settles the format?
  1. AWrite a cleanup rule for each of the five layouts after extraction.
  2. BShow examples whose records write the number in the PO- form.
  3. CMake po_number required, so it is always filled in the same way.
  4. DForce the tool, so the format is fixed by the tool choice.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Five rules grow to six with the next layout, and each is code to keep.
  • B Correct. An example shows the target form once, and the model carries it across layouts.
  • C Required says the field must exist. It says nothing about how the value is written.
  • D Forcing settles the shape of the reply. The form of a string is not part of it.
7. One vendor appears as Harlow & Pike, Harlow and Pike Ltd, and H&P. The ledger wants one name. What gives the most consistent result?
  1. ATurn vendor into an enum of every name seen so far.
  2. BAdd a prompt line asking the model to be consistent.
  3. CMerge the names with a regular expression after extraction.
  4. DShow an example that maps the short form to the full name, with a one-line reason.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A new vendor has no place in a closed list, and the model misfiles it into the nearest name.
  • B Consistent with what? The model has no way to know which form the ledger prefers.
  • C A pattern merges the names someone thought of. The next variant slips through.
  • D Correct. An example that settles the ambiguity, with its reason, carries to similar names.
8. Which two effects do worked examples have on extraction? Select two.
  1. AThey let the model call tools that have no schema.
  2. BThe format of a record becomes the same from one run to the next.
  3. CEvery layout is handled, including layouts that were not shown.
  4. DInvented values are less likely on layouts close to the ones shown.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A Tools come from the request. Examples only show inputs and outputs.
  • B Correct. A shown format is the one the model copies.
  • C Examples cover the layouts they resemble. A new layout is still a risk.
  • D Correct. Seeing where values sit on a layout cuts the guessing on similar ones.
9. A pipeline has three tools, and the first call must be extract_invoice. Some runs open with a different tool. What guarantees the order?
  1. ASet tool_choice to the extract_invoice tool for the first request.
  2. BWrite the first step in capital letters in the system prompt.
  3. CSet tool_choice to any, so a tool is always called first.
  4. DCheck the first call in code and rerun the request when it is wrong.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. Naming the tool forces that tool on the first turn, and later turns can go back to auto.
  • B Capital letters are emphasis, which is still a request.
  • C Any guarantees some tool is called. It may be the wrong one.
  • D A rerun costs another call and does not stop the next wrong opening.
10. A step must call one of three tools, and which one is the model's choice. Some replies are chat instead. What setting fits?
  1. ASet tool_choice to auto, so the model calls a tool when it needs to.
  2. BName one tool, so the model always has a tool to call.
  3. CSet tool_choice to any, so a tool call is required and the model picks.
  4. DSay in the prompt that a tool call is needed on every turn.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Auto allows chat, which is the problem.
  • B Naming one tool takes the choice away from the model.
  • C Correct. Any forces a call and leaves the pick of tool to the model.
  • D A prompt line is a request, and the chat replies show it is not always followed.
11. An assistant has three tools and should answer in text when none of them applies. Which tool_choice fits?
  1. AAny, so the model is sure to use a tool.
  2. BOne named tool, so the model is never without one.
  3. CPut the choice into each tool description instead of the request.
  4. DAuto, so the model decides between a tool and plain text.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Any requires a tool call, so a text answer is no longer possible.
  • B A named tool forces that tool on every turn, even when it does not apply.
  • C Descriptions help the model understand a tool. The request decides whether one is required.
  • D Correct. Auto leaves both the tool and the text option open.
12. Which two statements about tool_choice are true? Select two.
  1. AIt takes auto, any, or the name of one tool.
  2. BWith one named tool, the reply holds that tool's input.
  3. CAuto makes the model call a tool on every turn.
  4. DIt decides which model answers the request.
Show the answer
Answer: A, B
  • A Correct. Those are the three forms of the setting.
  • B Correct. A named tool is called, so its input is the answer.
  • C Auto lets the model choose, and a text reply is one of its choices.
  • D The model is set elsewhere in the request. The tool choice only shapes the reply.
Play: predict the output
The extractor offers one tool and asks for any tool.


python
tools = [{"name": "extract_invoice", "input_schema": schema()}]
tool_choice = {"type": "any"}





Predict: Does every reply call extract_invoice?
  1. AYes. Any means some tool must be called, and there is only one.
  2. BNo. Any lets Claude answer in prose when it is unsure.

A. With one tool, any and a named tool force the same call. Name the tool anyway, so adding a second tool later cannot change which one the first call picks.

Conclusions

You can now write an extraction schema that stays honest when an invoice is silent.


Tool schema
The input schema of a tool, used as the shape of the output
Forced tool choice
Setting tool_choice to one named tool, so a record always arrives
Nullable field
A field allowed to be null when the source has no value
Escape value
An other category, paired with a detail field
Worked example
A sample input and its record, shown to the model
Foundations, lesson 20
Validate and retry
Retry with the exact error, and only when a retry can help
The invoice extractor fails a record, asks again, and asks again. One invoice has a date in the wrong form, and another has no date at all. Only one of them is worth a second call. This is the extractor at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch a blind retry lose a good record, then write a validator that decides when another call can help.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
The validator decides whether another call can help
Claude fills in an invoice record through a tool. A validator checks the record against what the ledger accepts. When the record fails, the validator has to decide what happens next.


Three things go wrong in turn. With no retry, invalid output ends the run. A blind retry that sends only "Try again" loses the record. A retry on absent data has nothing to fix.


A format error is fixed by one retry
The invoice writes its due date as "3rd of September 2026". The ledger wants a year, month and day. The validator returns the exact error, and the second call fixes the date.


Open the cards to see what the second call was sent: the document, the failed record and the error.


  1. SupplierInvoice from Brightline Freight
Total: $310.00
Due date: 3rd of September 2026

Due date: 3rd of September 2026

The record was accepted after 2 call(s).
The starting retry says try again
The starting validator retries every error, and the retry is two words. It does not say what failed, and it does not even repeat the invoice.


It also cannot tell a value that is wrong from a value that is not there.


A good retry names the field and the error, shows the failed record, and puts the invoice text in front of the model again. You will write that retry in the fix below.


starter/validate.py
1"""Check a record, decide whether to retry, and write the retry."""23from typing import Any45from app.model import raw_errors678def check(data: dict[str, Any], document: str) -> list[dict[str, str]]:9    """Every error in `data`, each with a field, a kind and a message.10    TODO(workshop) step 1 of 4:11    kind is "absent" when the field is null and the document12    never mentions it, and "format" when the value is there but wrong.13    """14    return [{**e, "kind": "format"} for e in raw_errors(data)]151617def retryable(errors: list[dict[str, str]]) -> bool:18    """Whether asking Claude again can fix these errors.19    TODO(workshop) step 2 of 4:20    retry only format errors. Absent data stays null.21    """22    return bool(errors)232425def retry_prompt(26    document: str, data: dict[str, Any] | None, error: dict[str, str]27) -> str:28    """The next request.29    TODO(workshop) step 3 of 4:30    send the document, the failed output and the error.31    """32    return "Try again."333435def more_tokens(stop_reason: str, tokens: int, calls: int) -> int | None:36    """A larger token limit for a reply that was cut off, or None.37    TODO(workshop) step 4 of 4:38    when the reply stopped at max_tokens and this was the39    first call, return a larger limit. Otherwise return None.40    """41    return None
Will a retry find a due date the invoice never had?
One invoice says only that payment terms are to be agreed. It has no due date, and the validator reports an error.


Predict: What does a second call return?
  1. AThe due date, since asking again gives the model another chance.
  2. BAnother failure, or a made-up date, since the fact is not in the document.
Show the answer
B. The fact is not in the document, so no wording of a retry can find it. The recording shows what the blind retry did instead.
Blind retries lose the record
The first call was right: the date is null, because the invoice has none. The validator called that an error, and the retry said only "Try again." The second call had no invoice to read, and it returned placeholders for every field.


A retry without the document can turn a good record into a worse one.

    "kind": "format"
  }

The run made 2 call(s) and did not end well.
Name the error, then retry only what can change
The validator now sorts each error. A date that is null and never mentioned in the document is absent. A value that is there but written wrong is a format error.


Only a format error is retried, once, and the retry carries the document, the failed record and the exact error. Absent data stays null and is flagged for a human to review.


Refining code with a model follows the same rule: give it information, not pressure. Add an input and expected output example for each shape that fails. Write tests first for requirements you can check, and iterate on their failures. When the requirement is unclear, ask the model to interview you before it writes code.


validate.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""Check a record, decide whether to retry, and write the retry."""23from typing import Any45from app.model import LABELS, raw_errors67GROWTH = 108910def check(data: dict[str, Any], document: str) -> list[dict[str, str]]:11    """Each error, as absent when the document never mentions the field."""12    found: list[dict[str, str]] = []1314    for e in raw_errors(data):15        label = LABELS[e["field"]]16        gone = data.get(e["field"]) is None and label not in document.lower()17        found.append({**e, "kind": "absent" if gone else "format"})1819    return found202122def retryable(errors: list[dict[str, str]]) -> bool:23    """Only a format error can be fixed by asking again."""24    return any(e["kind"] == "format" for e in errors)252627def retry_prompt(28    document: str, data: dict[str, Any] | None, error: dict[str, str]29) -> str:30    """The document, the failed output and the exact error."""31    return (32        f"{document}\n\nYour last record was {data}.\n"33        f"It failed on {error['field']}: {error['message']}. "34        "Record the invoice again and fix only that field."35    )363738def more_tokens(stop_reason: str, tokens: int, calls: int) -> int | None:39    """A larger limit for a reply cut off at max_tokens, once."""40    if stop_reason == "max_tokens" and calls == 1:41        return tokens * GROWTH4243    return None

The same invoice, now ending differently
Switch between the blind retry and the exact-error retry. The card marked "This is where the runs split" is the second call: a record of placeholders in one run, and no second call in the other.


The invoice did not change. The validator decided whether another call could help.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch validate-retry.
When a reply stops at max_tokens
A long invoice can use up the token limit before the record is finished. This loop starts every call with a limit of 100 tokens, small on purpose, so the long invoice shows the cut-off. The reply stops at max_tokens, and the record arrives with its last fields missing. The starting loop accepts it.


Switch to the retry with more room. The validator sees the stop reason, asks once more with a larger limit, and every field arrives. A prefill starts the reply for the model and keeps a plain-text answer in shape, though newer large models reject one. This loop forces a tool, so it raises the limit instead.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch validate-retry.
Try it: retries and invoices
Change one setting at a time. With no retry, the first invalid record ends the run. With a blind retry, the second call loses the record. With the exact error, the date is fixed, and an absent date is flagged after one call.


Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet. A schema cannot tell a missing date from a badly written one. The validator can.


A schema checks shape only. It cannot tell a true value from a wrong one of the right form, and it cannot fill a fact the document lacks. Code checks a value against its source. Force the tool so a record always arrives, and make a field nullable when the source may lack it.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch validate-retry.

You do: retry what a retry can fix
Copy the starting code and open work/validate-retry/validate.py. It has four steps. Every error counts as a format error, every error is retried, the retry says only "Try again" and a cut-off reply is never given more room.


Terminal
./workshop start validate-retry

The checks tell an absent field from a badly written one and retry only format errors. The retry carries the document, the failed output and the error, a cut-off reply is retried once, and no run makes more than two calls.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A due date written as "3rd of September 2026" fails validation on 12 of 200 invoices. The value is on the page, only in the wrong form. What is the best response?
  1. ADrop due_date from the required fields, so those records pass.
  2. BSend the same request again, since output varies between runs.
  3. CRetry once with the document, the failed record and the exact error.
  4. DRaise the retry limit to five, so the same request gets more chances.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Dropping the field hides the failure, and the ledger loses a date it could have had.
  • B An identical request has the same odds of the same mistake. Nothing tells the model what was wrong.
  • C Correct. The fact is in the document, so one retry with the exact error can fix the form.
  • D More attempts of a request that does not mention the error only repeat the error.
2. 20 invoices in a batch state no due date. The loop retries each one 5 times and then fails. What should the loop do instead?
  1. AKeep the date null and flag the invoice for a person after the first call.
  2. BRetry until a date appears, since every invoice has one somewhere.
  3. CRetry with the exact error each time, so the message eventually gets through.
  4. DRemove due_date from the record, so the validator stops complaining.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The document has no date to find, so a retry cannot help and a person has to decide.
  • B Not every invoice has a date, and a loop that waits for one will eventually get an invented one.
  • C A clear error message does not add a fact the document lacks.
  • D The ledger needs to know the date is missing. Removing the field loses that.
3. The retry message is "Try again." and the same error comes back on 9 of 10 retried records. What change fixes it?
  1. AAllow more retries per record, so one of them gets it right.
  2. BKeep the message short, since the error text only adds noise.
  3. CRaise the temperature, so the second reply differs from the first.
  4. DSend the document, the failed output and the specific error.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Each extra attempt carries the same two words, so it has the same odds.
  • B The error text is the information the model needs to change anything.
  • C More variety is not aimed at the mistake. It can turn a small error into a different one.
  • D Correct. With the document, the output and the error, the model can see what to change.
4. Which two items belong in a retry message after a format error? Select two.
  1. AA request that the model tries harder this time.
  2. BThe record that failed validation.
  3. CThe specific validation error, such as the field and what was wrong with it.
  4. DPermission to leave the field out if it is hard to fill.
Show the answer
Answer: B, C
  • A Effort is not the problem. The model needs to know what to change.
  • B Correct. The failed record shows the model exactly what it wrote.
  • C Correct. The field and the reason point the retry at the one thing to fix.
  • D Leaving the field out trades a fixable format error for missing data.
5. On 6 of 300 invoices the record matches the schema, but the total is 1,000 times too large. What catches this?
  1. ATighten the schema until it forbids the wrong number.
  2. BA check in code that compares the value with what the document says.
  3. CRetry every record once to be safe.
  4. DForce the tool, so the values are checked by the API.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A schema says what shapes are allowed. A wrong number of the right shape passes it.
  • B Correct. A value is checked against its source by code that knows what the source says.
  • C A blind retry on every record doubles the cost and may produce the same wrong number.
  • D Forcing the tool fixes the shape of the reply. It has no say over what the values mean.
6. 5 of 100 replies arrive as prose, and the ledger needs a record every time. What should change?
  1. ARetry the prose replies until one of them holds a record.
  2. BPull the fields out of the prose with a regular expression.
  3. CRun the validator on the prose, so it rejects anything that is not a record.
  4. DSet tool_choice to the extraction tool, so a record always arrives.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Each retry may answer in prose again, and each costs a call.
  • B Prose changes wording from run to run, so a pattern breaks on the first new phrasing.
  • C A validator rejects prose. It cannot turn it into a record.
  • D Correct. A named tool makes the reply the tool's input, in the shape of the schema.
7. Invented values appear in 15 of 100 records, all in a field the source often lacks. What is the fix at the source?
  1. AMake the field nullable, so silence has a place to go.
  2. BRetry each invented value until one passes validation.
  3. CKeep the field required and add a pattern that checks its form.
  4. DAsk for the field again with the exact error, so the model finds it.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. When the source may lack a fact, the honest answer has to fit the schema.
  • B The next value to pass validation is another invention that looks right.
  • C A pattern checks form. A made-up value of the right form passes.
  • D An error message cannot add a fact the document lacks.
8. Which two things can a schema not do? Select two.
  1. ATell whether a value in the right form is the true one.
  2. BReject a record whose total arrives as a string.
  3. CRequire that a due_date field is present in the record.
  4. DFill in a fact that the document never states.
Show the answer
Answer: A, D
  • A Correct. The schema checks the shape, so a wrong date in the right shape passes.
  • B A schema can do this. A type check is exactly what it enforces, so a string total fails.
  • C A schema can do this. A required field is part of the shape it checks.
  • D Correct. A schema describes what is allowed and adds no information.
9. A first fix for a date parser fails on 3 input shapes, and the description of the goal did not help. What do you add next?
  1. ARepeat the goal in capital letters at the top.
  2. BSend the same message again until a run passes.
  3. CAn input and expected output example for each shape.
  4. DA higher limit on attempts, from 2 to 6.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Capital letters add emphasis, not information about the three shapes.
  • B The same message leaves the same gap, so runs repeat the same fix.
  • C Correct. Examples show the model what each shape looks like and what it should become.
  • D More attempts on a request that lacks the examples repeat the miss.
10. A change has 4 requirements, each easy to check. How do you build it so that progress is visible?
  1. AWrite the code first and add tests at the end.
  2. BWrite the tests first, run them, and iterate on their failures.
  3. CDescribe the tests in prose and skip running them.
  4. DDelete any failing test that the first version cannot pass.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Tests written last check what the code happens to do, not what was wanted.
  • B Correct. Failing tests state the target, and each run shows what is left.
  • C A test that never runs says nothing about the code.
  • D A deleted test stops checking the requirement it stood for.
11. The requirement for a report is unclear, and the model has guessed wrong 3 times. What helps most?
  1. ASend the same request again until a guess is right.
  2. BPick the most likely guess and ship it.
  3. CWrite a longer request that lists every detail you can think of.
  4. DAsk the model to interview you with questions before it writes code.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Each guess comes from the same missing information.
  • B A guess shipped is a guess that the users find.
  • C A longer list of details still misses the ones you did not think of.
  • D Correct. Questions bring out the requirements that nobody had written down.
12. Which two things make a refinement request work better? Select two.
  1. AExamples of the output you want.
  2. BThe same request with more emphasis.
  3. CA failing test to iterate against.
  4. DLeaving out the error text, so the model is not anchored on it.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. An example shows the target in a way a description cannot.
  • B Emphasis raises the stakes without adding information.
  • C Correct. A failing test says what is wrong and tells you when it is fixed.
  • D The error text is what the model needs, and leaving it out removes the signal.

Validator
Code that checks a record against what the ledger accepts
Format error
A value that is there but written wrong, so a retry can fix it
Absent data
A value the document never states, so a retry cannot find it
Exact error
The validator's own message, sent back with the document and the failed record
Stop reason
Why a reply ended. max_tokens means it was cut off
Foundations, lesson 21
Confidence routing
Check confidence against labels before it routes anything
The refund desk auto-approves every field Claude rates as confident. Scanned forms carry misread digits, and Claude rates them as high as clean ones. Wrong refunds go out with nobody looking. This is the refund desk at Lumen Supply. You will watch confidence route wrong rows, then fix the router so it trusts a form type only after it is measured against labels.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
The router decides who reviews each row
Forms arrive typed and scanned. Claude reads each one and rates its own confidence. A router then decides which rows are approved and which go to a human.


The router sees a labelled set: rows where the right amount is known. That is the only way to learn which confidence to trust.


A proven form type runs on its own
The typed queue matches its labels on every row, so every row is approved. The router does not slow down a type that has proved itself. Open a card to see the row.

Measure each form type, then route on the measurement
A row is also held when it has no amount or a confidence below a floor of 0.5, even in a proven type. A missing read is never approved.


Three changes, made in this order in route.py. The report gives accuracy per form type from the labelled rows. A row is approved only when its type has met the target and the row has an amount and some confidence. An unmeasured type is held.


A stratified sample of the approved rows is also checked: a random draw from every type, so a type that drifts is noticed.


route.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""Build an accuracy report from labelled rows, then route each row."""23import random4from typing import Any56TARGET = 0.97FLOOR = 0.58910def by_segment(rows: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> dict[str, float]:11    """Accuracy per form type, measured against the labels."""12    report: dict[str, float] = {}1314    for segment in sorted({r["segment"] for r in rows}):15        pool = [r for r in rows if r["segment"] == segment]16        report[segment] = sum(1 for r in pool if r["correct"]) / len(pool)1718    return report192021def auto_approve(row: dict[str, Any], report: dict[str, float]) -> bool:22    """Approve a proven segment when the read was clear; hold the rest."""23    proven = report.get(row["segment"], 0.0) >= TARGET24    clear = row["amount"] is not None and row["confidence"] >= FLOOR2526    return bool(proven and clear)272829def sample(rows: list[dict[str, Any]], per: int, seed: int = 0) -> list[Any]:30    """`per` random rows from every segment, so a rare type is not missed."""31    rng = random.Random(seed)  # noqa: S311 - a sample, not security32    found: list[Any] = []3334    for segment in sorted({r["segment"] for r in rows}):35        pool = [r for r in rows if r["segment"] == segment]36        found += rng.sample(pool, min(per, len(pool)))3738    return found

The same queue now ends differently

What goes to a human
Switch between the two routers on the scanned queue. A weak type, an unmeasured type and a row with no amount all go to a human. A field whose source is unclear, such as a faded digit, goes to a human with the scan attached.


The router holds a row for a reason it can name, and never because Claude sounded unsure.


When two forms give different totals for one order, keep both values, each with the form it came from. Pass every value on with its source and the date it was read, so the next reader can check it.

Change one setting at a time. On the typed queue both routers approve everything. On the scanned queue only the measured router holds the rows.


Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch confidence-review.
