You do: route by segment
Copy the starting code and open work/confidence-review/route.py. It has three steps. Accuracy is one overall number, approval reads only the model's confidence, and the audit sample takes the first rows.


Terminal
./workshop start confidence-review
./workshop check confidence-review
./workshop watch confidence-review




The checks want accuracy per segment that matches the labels. A weak or unmeasured segment is held even when confident, and the audit sample covers every segment.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A refund router shows 97% accuracy over 900 forms a day, but scanned forms are right 61% of the time. What report would have shown this?
  1. AOne accuracy figure over the whole day, recomputed every hour.
  2. BThe average confidence Claude wrote on each form.
  3. CAccuracy for each form type, measured against human labels.
  4. DA count of how many forms a human reviewed.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A fresher average still blends the typed forms with the scans, so the weak type stays hidden.
  • B Confidence is what Claude wrote about its own reading. It is not a check against the paper.
  • C Correct. A per-type figure separates the 61% from the 97%.
  • D Review counts say how busy people were, not how often a type is wrong.
2. A router approves any form with a confidence of 0.9 or more. Nobody has compared that number with the true amounts. What should the team do first?
  1. AScore a labelled set and learn how often each confidence level is right.
  2. BAsk Claude to explain how it chooses its confidence numbers.
  3. CRaise the bar to 0.95, since a higher number is a safer number.
  4. DSend every form to a human until the model improves.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. Labels are the only way to learn what a confidence level is worth.
  • B Claude can describe its number, but the description is not a measurement of how often it is right.
  • C A higher bar on an unchecked number is still a guess, and scans may score high anyway.
  • D This works, but it gives up the speed of forms that have proved themselves.
3. The desk adds a new form type, handwritten notes, and there are 0 labelled examples. Claude rates them at 0.96. How should the router treat them?
  1. AApprove them, since the typed forms and the scans both passed review.
  2. BApprove them, since 0.96 is above the bar the router already uses.
  3. CApprove them while the overall accuracy stays above the target.
  4. DHold them until the type has been measured against labels.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Trust belongs to a measured type. A new type has not earned what another type earned.
  • B The number is a self-rating, and for this type nobody has checked it.
  • C The overall figure is dominated by the larger types and cannot vouch for a new one.
  • D Correct. An unmeasured segment is held, however confident Claude sounds.
4. Which two measurements should be in place before a form type skips review? Select two.
  1. AThe overall accuracy across every form type, as one figure.
  2. BAccuracy for that form type, against human labels.
  3. CAccuracy for each field, such as the amount, within that type.
  4. DThe average confidence Claude reports for that type.
Show the answer
Answer: B, C
  • A One blended figure can be high while a single type or field is poor.
  • B Correct. A type is trusted on its own measured accuracy.
  • C Correct. A type can be right on the name and wrong on the amount, so fields are measured too.
  • D This is Claude's opinion of its own work, not a measurement.
5. A scanned form reads 128.00 when the paper says 126.00. The value is a well-formed amount and Claude wrote 0.95. Which check catches it?
  1. AA check that the amount is a number.
  2. BA comparison with the labelled amount, reported for the scanned type.
  3. CA second question asking Claude whether it is sure.
  4. DHolding every form that has a decimal point in it.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A well-formed number can still be wrong, so this check passes it.
  • B Correct. Only the label knows the paper said 126.00, and the type's accuracy follows from it.
  • C Claude rates the same text it just read, so it tends to repeat the same answer.
  • D Most decimal amounts are right. This holds good rows and does not target the weak type.
6. A scanned form has no amount at all, and Claude returns a confidence of 0.97 with the amount empty. What should the router do?
  1. AApprove it, because the confidence clears the bar.
  2. BAsk Claude to lower its own confidence and route again.
  3. CHold every form in the queue until this one is resolved.
  4. DHold this row for a human, since there is no value to approve.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A high number beside an empty field is a mismatch, and approving it sends nothing to the ledger.
  • B Claude adjusting its own number does not add the missing amount.
  • C One empty row does not make the other rows wrong.
  • D Correct. A row with no value goes to a human even when the number beside it is high.
7. Approved rows are never looked at again, and a type that was 98% right last month has drifted. How does the team find out?
  1. ASample a few approved rows from each type at random and compare them with labels.
  2. BSample only the rows with the lowest confidence, since those are likeliest to be wrong.
  3. CRecompute the overall accuracy from the rows that were reviewed.
  4. DStop approving anything automatically until the month ends.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A random sample of the approved rows keeps measuring the error the router cannot see.
  • B Approved rows are the high scores. Drift hides in rows that looked fine.
  • C Reviewed rows were the ones already held, so they say nothing about approved rows.
  • D This stops the drift by stopping the automation, and it is not a measurement.
8. Which two things must a review sample of approved rows include? Select two.
  1. ARows from every form type that is approved.
  2. BOnly the rows Claude rated the lowest.
  3. CEvery approved row, so nothing is missed.
  4. DRows chosen at random inside each type.
Show the answer
Answer: A, D
  • A Correct. A type left out of the sample is a type nobody is measuring.
  • B Low scores were probably not approved, so this sample misses the rows that need checking.
  • C Checking every row removes the saving the router was built to give.
  • D Correct. Random picks stop the sample from repeating the rows that were easy to choose.
9. Two forms give different totals for the same order, 84.00 and 48.00. Both are read at high confidence. What should the record keep?
  1. AThe value with the higher confidence, and drop the other.
  2. BNeither value, and ask a human to retype the order from scratch.
  3. CBoth values, each with the form it came from.
  4. DThe value Claude says it trusts more, after asking it.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Two confidence numbers that are both high do not settle which form is right.
  • B Throwing away both loses what a human needs to resolve it.
  • C Correct. Keeping both with their sources lets a human decide with the evidence in front of them.
  • D Claude has no fresh information, so asking again repeats its guess.
10. A field in a faded scan cannot be told apart from a similar digit, and the source is unclear. What happens to that field?
  1. AIt is approved at the confidence Claude gave it.
  2. BIt goes to a human, with the scan attached.
  3. CClaude is asked to guess again until two readings match.
  4. DThe whole queue waits until every unclear field is settled.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A confident guess about an unclear source is still a guess.
  • B Correct. A human can look at the paper, which the model cannot do better than it did.
  • C Two matching guesses from the same unclear text are not evidence.
  • D The other rows are clear, so holding them costs time and buys nothing.
11. A report says a refund total was 96.50 and does not say which form it came from or when it was read. What is missing?
  1. AThe source and the date, kept next to the value.
  2. BAn average accuracy figure for the month.
  3. CA higher confidence score beside the total.
  4. DA sentence from Claude saying the total is reliable.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A value with no source or date cannot be checked or told apart from an older one.
  • B An average about the month says nothing about where this one total came from.
  • C Confidence is about the reading, and it does not say where the value came from.
  • D A claim of reliability is not provenance.
12. Which two items should survive with each extracted value when the record is passed on? Select two.
  1. AThe confidence number, used as proof that it is right.
  2. BThe source the value was read from.
  3. CThe overall accuracy of the whole pipeline.
  4. DThe date the value was read.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A The number is a self-rating and proves nothing on its own.
  • B Correct. The source lets the next reader check the value against the paper.
  • C The pipeline figure describes all rows, and it does not describe this one.
  • D Correct. The date shows whether a newer reading would replace it.
Play: predict the output
This audit draws 30 rows at random from 1,000 approved rows. 20 of them are handwritten forms.


python
def sample(rows: list[dict[str, Any]], n: int) -> list[Any]:
    return random.sample(rows, n)





Predict: How often does the sample hold no handwritten form at all?
  1. AAbout half the time.
  2. BAlmost never, since 30 rows is plenty.
Show the answer
A. Each draw misses a 2 percent segment 98 times in 100, so 30 draws miss it about 54 percent of the time. Draw a fixed number from every segment, so a rare type is always read.

  • Create strong empirical evaluations: how to build the labelled set your accuracy comes from.
    • 

  • Structured outputs: the form fields read back in a shape you can score.
    • 

  • Agent SDK custom tools: the routing rule served as a tool to an SDK agent.
    • 

  • Demystifying evals for AI agents: how teams grade agent output and keep the grades honest.
    • 



Conclusions
    

  • A confidence Claude reports is a self-rating. It routes nothing until it is checked against labels.
    • 

  • An overall accuracy hides a weak segment. Report accuracy by form type and by field.
    • 

  • A segment skips a human only after it meets its target. An unmeasured segment is held.
    • 



You can now route work on measured accuracy instead of a number Claude gives.


Calibration
Checking a confidence against known answers
Labelled set
Rows where the right answer is known
Segment
A slice of the data, such as a form type
Auto-approve
A row that skips a human
Stratified sample
A random sample drawn from every segment, to keep measuring approved rows
Foundations, lesson 22
Context editing and memory
Clear old tool results and keep the facts in memory
A refund case runs for many lookups, and every old result travels with every new request. The request grows past the budget, and the one fact the customer asked about sits in the oldest result. This is the refund desk at Lumen Supply. You will watch a long case overflow, then fix it by clearing old results and keeping the case facts in memory.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
Old results are the bulk of a long request
Three parts share the work. The API clears old tool results, your code saves the facts, and Claude answers. Compaction, a beta feature that swaps old turns for a summary, is the other server-side way to shrink a request.


The case is about 40 messages long at Lumen Supply. It holds the refund approval in its first tool result and 18 long shipment scans after it. Every lookup is sent again on every later call.


A subagent, a second agent started for one job, keeps noisy discovery out of the main context. The main agent coordinates and asks it a specific question, and only a short answer comes back.


A short case fits with no help
The short case has two lookups after the refund. Its largest request is 2,939 tokens, under the budget of 5,000, so nothing needs clearing and the answer is right.


Open a card to see the request size. This is the usage field of the API reply, which reports input_tokens.

The starting code sends everything and stores nothing
edits returns nothing, so no result is ever cleared. run_command stores nothing, so Claude has nowhere to keep a fact.


The cost is plain arithmetic. Each scan is about 400 tokens, and all 18 are sent again on every later call.

Clear old results, and note the facts first
Two changes. edits clears old tool results past 3,000 input tokens and keeps the last three. run_command runs the memory commands Claude sends. It refuses any path outside /memories. The memory tool has a sixth command, rename, which this lab leaves out, and its view is simplified to a directory listing or one file.


The case facts are written to memory first, and the prompt tells Claude to view memory before it answers. Count the input tokens before and after to see the fall. The context edit is a beta setting, sent with the header context-management-2025-06-27. If you want the memory tool's own results kept, exclude_tools lists tools the clear must skip.


A memory file also works as a scratchpad for a long investigation. Findings written outside the window can be read back exactly, after a clear, after a crash or in a new session. When a run crashes, it continues from the saved state, not from the start.

On the long case, editing alone fits and loses the amount. Memory alone keeps the amount and still goes over the budget at 9,565 tokens. Clearing keeps the conversation and the question. Only tool results go.


Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch memory-and-context-editing.
The Agent SDK serves memory as a tool
The memory tool is served by an in-process tool server, and your run_command handles each call. The context edit is an API setting that this SDK run does not use. This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run through the SDK. With the starting code the notes cannot be read, and Claude cannot answer.


Memory is not resume. A resumed session brings back the saved history, where cleared results are gone, while a memory file keeps what your code wrote. See A summary drops the facts unless code keeps them for resume and fork.


Do not confuse this memory tool with CLAUDE.md, the notes file Claude Code reads at the start of a session.

You do: clear old results and keep the facts
Copy the starting code and open work/memory-and-context-editing/memory.py. edits() clears nothing, and run_command() refuses every memory command.


Terminal
./workshop start memory-and-context-editing

./workshop watch memory-and-context-editing




The checks want old tool results cleared past a trigger, with recent ones kept. The memory tool must view, create, edit, insert into and delete files, and refuse any path outside /memories.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A 40-message refund case sends about 8,300 input tokens per request against a 5,000 budget. Eighteen old shipment scans are most of it, and only the last few matter. What is the cleanest fix?
  1. AClear old tool results past a trigger, keeping the latest few.
  2. BTell Claude in the system prompt to ignore the old shipment scans.
  3. CSwitch to a model with a larger window so the whole history fits.
  4. DSummarise the whole case by hand after every turn.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The edit drops stale results from the request, so tokens fall, while recent results stay.
  • B An ignored result is still sent and still billed on every call.
  • C A larger window still pays for the stale scans on every turn.
  • D A hand summary costs a call each time and can drop a fact, where clearing is one setting.
2. On turn 40 of a case each reply is slower and costs more, though the last question is one short line. What is the cause?
  1. AThe model reads older results more slowly than new ones.
  2. BClaude remembers earlier requests, and that stored work adds up on the server.
  3. CEvery request carries the whole history, so old results are paid again.
  4. DA larger window lowers the cost of each token, and the case has outgrown it.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Reading speed is not the cause. Input size is.
  • B The API keeps no memory of earlier requests. Everything the model sees is in the request.
  • C Correct. The history is sent again on each call, so its size is the cost.
  • D A larger window does not lower the cost of the tokens a request carries.
3. After old results are cleared, Claude cannot say what refund was approved. The 84.50 was only in the first result. What should the design have done?
  1. ATurn off clearing so that no result is ever removed from a case.
  2. BWrite the facts to memory first, then view memory to answer.
  3. CAsk the customer to repeat the amount whenever a result was cleared.
  4. DRaise the clearing trigger until the first result is never cleared.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Turning clearing off brings the token cost back.
  • B Correct. Memory sits outside the window, so a cleared result loses nothing that was noted.
  • C Making the customer repeat a fact the system already had is a poor answer.
  • D A higher trigger only delays the clearing, and the fact is lost later.
4. Select two effects of clearing old tool results past a trigger.
  1. AThe conversation and the customer's question stay in the request.
  2. BThe customer's question is cleared with the results, so Claude must ask again.
  3. CThe API saves each cleared result to a memory file for later.
  4. DInput tokens fall once the trigger fires, and cleared results are gone.
Show the answer
Answer: A, D
  • A Correct. Only tool results are cleared, so the conversation and the question stay.
  • B Clearing drops old tool results only. The messages and the question stay.
  • C The API does not save them. Your code writes memory files.
  • D Correct. A long case goes from about 8,300 tokens to about 4,100, and the old results do not come back.
5. An investigation resumes the next day. Old tool results in the saved history were cleared, and the agent has lost a file path it found on day one. What carries that path across?
  1. AResuming the session, which brings the cleared results back.
  2. BA larger context window, so nothing is ever cleared again.
  3. CA line in CLAUDE.md, which the memory tool writes for you.
  4. DA note saved to memory on day one, read at the start.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Resume brings back the saved history. The cleared results are not in it.
  • B A larger window does not bring back what was already cleared.
  • C The memory tool writes files your code stores. CLAUDE.md is a separate file that Claude Code loads.
  • D Correct. Memory is outside the window, so a saved note survives clearing and a new session.
6. A new session starts tomorrow on the same case, and the notes are in /memories. What should the prompt tell Claude to do first?
  1. ATrust its own recall of the case, which carries over between sessions.
  2. BAsk the customer to restate the case so the notes are not needed.
  3. CView the memory directory, and read the case notes before answering.
  4. DClear every tool result, so the new session starts empty.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A new session holds no recall of the old one. Only files your code stored remain.
  • B This repeats work the system already holds and puts the burden on the customer.
  • C Correct. Claude carries nothing over by itself, so the notes are its only record of the case.
  • D Clearing drops tool results and does not bring the case back.
7. A note in memory says the refund was 84.50. The order record has since changed to 94.50. What should the agent do when it sees the mismatch?
  1. AEdit the note to match the order record, then answer.
  2. BTrust the note, because memory is always right.
  3. CDelete the whole memory directory and start the case again.
  4. DRaise the clearing trigger so the old note is dropped.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The record is the source, and the note is edited to match it.
  • B A note is a copy. It goes stale when the record changes.
  • C This throws away every other fact that is still true.
  • D The trigger clears tool results, and a memory file is not one.
8. Select two rules that keep a memory tool handler safe.
  1. ALet Claude pick any absolute path, for flexibility.
  2. BRefuse any path outside /memories.
  3. CReturn an error string for a command it cannot run, so Claude can correct itself.
  4. DDelete the memory files after each answer, so storage stays small.
Show the answer
Answer: B, C
  • A An open path lets a bad command read or write files outside the case.
  • B Correct. Claude's paths are untrusted input, so the handler checks them.
  • C Correct. An error string goes back as the result, and Claude can retry or choose another command.
  • D Deleting the files loses the facts the next call needs.
9. Claude sends a memory tool command to create a file. What runs it?
  1. AThe API, which keeps the memory files on Anthropic servers.
  2. BClaude itself, which writes the file during the reply.
  3. CThe CLAUDE.md file, which Claude Code updates on each command.
  4. DYour application code, which applies the command to storage.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A The API does not store the files. Your code does.
  • B Claude only sends the command. It cannot write to your storage.
  • C CLAUDE.md is a file Claude Code loads. It is not the memory tool.
  • D Correct. The memory tool is client side. Claude asks, and your code decides what is stored and where.
10. A long investigation drifts into generic answers about typical patterns, and the specific findings from 25 turns ago are gone from the request. What should the agent do?
  1. ARaise the output token limit so replies can name more detail.
  2. BWrite key findings to a scratchpad file, and read them back.
  3. CSwitch to a model with a larger window.
  4. DTell the model in the system prompt to be specific.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A The output limit controls reply length, and the findings are missing from the input.
  • B Correct. A file outside the window holds the findings, so they can be read back exactly.
  • C A larger window holds more, but the findings are still buried or cleared.
  • D A prompt cannot bring back detail that is no longer in the request.
11. A long run crashes at turn 30 of 40. What lets it continue instead of starting over?
  1. AResume, which brings back every cleared result.
  2. BA longer prompt that explains what the run was doing.
  3. CSaved structured state that the run reads back on restart.
  4. DA larger window, so that the crash does not happen again.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Resume restores saved history, and results cleared earlier are not in it.
  • B A prompt from memory repeats what the agent thought, and misses what it found.
  • C Correct. State saved outside the window, such as the facts so far, lets the run pick up again.
  • D A larger window does not stop a crash, and saves nothing for the restart.
12. Select two good uses of a subagent in a long investigation.
  1. AGive it the whole history, so it can decide what matters.
  2. BAsk it one specific question, and take back a short answer.
  3. CHave it return every raw result, so the main agent sees everything.
  4. DKeep coordination in the main agent, discovery in the subagent.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A A subagent with the whole history brings the same bulk into a second window.
  • B Correct. A specific question with a short return keeps the noise out of the main context.
  • C Raw results return the bulk to the main agent, which defeats the point.
  • D Correct. The main agent coordinates, and the subagent's detail stays in its own context.

A. A prefix check reads the text, not where the path goes. Resolve the path first, then check it sits under /memories/, so a climb out is refused.

Conclusions
    

  • Old tool results are the bulk of a long request. Clear them past a trigger and keep the latest few.
    • 

  • A cleared result is gone. Any fact you need later goes to memory first.
    • 

  • The memory tool is client side. Claude sends a command and your code decides what is stored.
    • 



You can now keep a long case small without losing the facts it needs.


Context edit
A setting that clears old content from a request
Trigger
The input size at which clearing starts
Memory tool
A tool that views and edits files your code stores
Token budget
The input size a call must stay under
Professional, lesson 1
The discovery brief
Start from a measured outcome, not a capability
The Lumen Supply board has approved "use agents" for support. Ops, finance and support each want a different number to move, and nobody has said which. Six months in, each team reads a different chart. This is the brief writer at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch a brief pass a weak check, then fix the check so a team can test what it accepts.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
One board decision, three teams, three numbers
The board decision is a capability: use agents for support, at 10,000 tickets a day across three regions. Ops wants faster first replies. Finance wants a lower cost per ticket. Support wants fewer escalations to senior agents.


Claude reads one team's note and drafts a brief. A checker decides whether the draft can be tested. Three things go wrong: a named capability leaves a field weak, a target only restates the baseline, and scope waits for later.

This brief starts from the ops note. It names the metric, p95 first reply time, and the baseline, 38 minutes. The note gives no target or deadline, so Claude proposes 15 minutes by the end of Q2 and marks both for the team to confirm. It also lists the decisions that stay with people and the constraints.

A brief a team can test: Metric: p95 first reply time, measured in the helpdesk from ticket creation to the first human or automated reply, reported for each of the three regions separately. Baseline: 38 minutes (p95, last month, all regions). Slowest hours are the two after a product launch.. Target: 15 minutes p95 in every region, including during the two hours after a product launch. PROPOSED, not in the ops note: team to confirm.. Deadline: End of Q2. PROPOSED, not in the ops note: team to confirm..
The six fields, written as code
The starting checker asks for a title and nothing else. The fix checks six fields: the metric, the baseline, the target, the deadline, what stays with people, and the constraints.


A metric is a number with a unit and a way to measure it. A capability word with nothing measured, such as "agents deployed", is not one. A target with no baseline beside it means nothing. A target that only restates the baseline, such as "below 38 minutes", is a direction: any cut meets it.


A constraint changes the design, such as data that must stay in the EU or a spend cap. Each has an owner, and when two collide the brief ranks them and says which one gives. Scope is written down too, so a change to it becomes visible.

Can a team tell if "use agents" worked?
The board decision names a technology. It names no metric, no baseline and no decision that stays with people. Suppose a team builds exactly what the board approved.


Predict: Six months later, can the team tell whether "use agents for support" worked?

  2. BNo. The decision gives no metric and no baseline to compare against.
Show the answer
B. A capability is what you build. An outcome is what changes. Without a baseline, no target can be met or missed.

The checker names each weak field
The fixed checker returns the fields that are empty or too weak. On this draft it returns the target, and the refusal says to give a new number, not the baseline.


Claude revises and asks again: 15 minutes p95, 3.50 dollars a ticket, and escalations below 22 percent, each marked as proposed for the board to confirm. The check accepts it.


The check tests that a new figure is present, not that it is a good one. The escalation line still only restates its baseline, and a human has to read it. The refusal costs one more request: four instead of three.

restates today's number: a direction.24    """25    seen = set(NUMBER.findall(" ".join(str(k or "") for k in known)))26    found = NUMBER.findall(str(target or ""))2728    return has_figure(target) str(brief.get("metric") or "").strip()39    names_tech = CAPABILITY.search(metric) and not MEASURE.search(metric)40    if not metric or names_tech:41        weak.append("metric")4243    if not has_figure(brief.get("baseline")):44        weak.append("baseline")4546    known = (brief.get("baseline"), metric)47    if not new_figure(brief.get("target"), *known) or "baseline" in weak:48        weak.append("target")4950    for name in ("deadline", "stays_with_people"):51        if not str(brief.get(name) or "").strip():52            weak.append(name)5354    constraints = [c for c in brief.get("constraints") or [] if str(c).strip()]55    if len(constraints) < MIN_CONSTRAINTS:56        weak.append("constraints")5758    return weak
We doChange one setting at a time and predict.
The same note, two briefs
Switch between the two board asks. Both runs use the fixed checker on the ops note, and the card marked "This is where the runs split" is the draft.


The "Use agents" ask reads all three notes, and its targets restate each baseline, so the check refuses it once. The outcome ask reads one note and gives 15 minutes by the end of Q2 on the first draft.


Finance and support tell the same story. Their capability drafts set no new number, and the checker refuses the target until Claude names one. Finance was refused twice, because its revision dropped the constraints.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch discovery-brief.
Try it: checker, ask and note
Change one setting at a time. Turn the checker on or off, pick the board ask, then pick a note.


Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet. Some briefs with the checker off are accepted and still cannot be tested. The result line says which.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch discovery-brief.
The refusal tells Claude what to fix
The highlighted lines build the refusal. It names each weak field and how to fix it, so Claude revises instead of guessing. The checker decides. The prompt is only a request.


This support run proposed a target of 15% beside the 22% baseline, so the first check accepted it. A draft whose target only restates the baseline would come back with the refusal above.


Beyond this lab, three notes still need one brief. Reconcile them into one measured outcome with a named owner for the final call. Each audience then gets the view it decides with, drawn from the same numbers. The lab does not run that step, and the questions below ask about it.

Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A regional retailer with 10,000 support tickets a day tells you the board wants agents on the queue inside one 90-day quarter. The budget is fixed at 30,000 dollars a month. The request names the technology and a launch date but no result the business should see, and the three team leads each describe success differently. What do you ask first?
  1. AWhich agent framework and cloud platform the engineers already know best.
  2. BWhich tickets the support team finds most tedious to answer by hand today.
  3. CWhich result must move, by how much, and what that figure is today.
  4. DWhich executive will sign off the budget before the quarter begins.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A framework is a way to build. With 90 days on the clock, choosing it before the goal is agreed spends the time on the wrong question.
  • B Tedious tickets are a scope guess. They say where the work is boring, not what the business wants to change or how it would be measured.
  • C Correct. A measured result with today's figure is what the team can test at the end of the quarter.
  • D A name on a sign-off does not say what the project is for, so it settles who approves and nothing about success.
2. A brief sets the goal "cut handle time by 30 percent" for a pilot that starts in two weeks. Ops measures handle time from first reply to close and reports 14 minutes, while finance measures from creation to close and reports 26, and neither is written down. The readout is fixed for week 12. What comes before the target is set?
  1. AAgree one definition and one baseline figure, then take the 30 percent from it.
  2. BAverage the two figures to 20 minutes, a baseline both teams can accept.
  3. CUse the ops figure, since the ops team runs the queue and knows the work.
  4. DStart the pilot and read the baseline off the first month of live results.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A target is a change from a baseline, and two definitions give two different changes for the same pilot.
  • B An average of two definitions measures nothing real. Neither team can reproduce 20 minutes from its own data.
  • C Taking one team's number settles the argument by rank, and finance then reads a different result at the readout.
  • D A baseline taken after the change cannot show what the change did, and the pilot has no starting point.
3. The board asks what a testable outcome for the support agent pilot looks like. The pilot window is 12 weeks, finance closes the books monthly, and the helpdesk already stores a cost per ticket for every quarter before any change. Select two parts that the outcome needs so that someone outside the team can test it at the readout.
  1. AA count of tickets the agents touched by week 12.
  2. BA metric with a unit, such as cost per ticket in dollars.
  3. CA shortlist of vendors that could supply the agents.
  4. DA baseline figure taken before the change, such as 4.20 dollars.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A Tickets touched counts activity. It can rise while cost and wait times stay the same, so it does not test anything.
  • B Correct. A metric with a unit can be measured by someone other than the team that built the project.
  • C A vendor shortlist is part of how to build. It says nothing about what should get better.
  • D Correct. Without today's figure a target cannot be met or missed, and the readout has nothing to compare against.
4. A vendor demo shows an agent closing 8 test tickets in 4 minutes, and two directors ask to buy it at once. No metric has been agreed and the scope is unclear. The vendor's offer price lapses in 30 days, which is also when the current contract renews. What do you do before anything is signed?
  1. ATake a 90-day paid trial on the live queue and decide from what the team sees.
  2. BAsk for a reference customer with a similar ticket volume and compare notes.
  3. CHave the directors rank the features they liked so the brief follows the demo.
  4. DName the outcome the demo should move and today's figure, then test on it.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A trial with no agreed measure produces impressions. Nobody can say afterwards whether the result was good enough.
  • B A reference shows what worked for another queue. It does not say what this project must move.
  • C A feature ranking describes the product the directors saw, and the brief then follows the demo instead of the business need.
  • D Correct. The demo shows what is possible. The outcome and baseline say whether buying it is worth doing.
5. A support design must be fast, cheap and accurate. The budget caps spend at 30,000 dollars a month, the agreement caps p95 reply time at 2 seconds, and every accuracy gain adds calls that push both up. The three sponsors disagree about which goal matters most, and design starts on Monday. What should the brief record?
  1. AA weight for each goal, such as 40, 30 and 30 percent, folded into one score.
  2. BA ranking of the goals, with the one that wins a clash, agreed by sponsors.
  3. CEach goal as a listed risk with a mitigation note, reviewed once a month.
  4. DAccuracy as the single target, since a wrong answer costs more than a slow one.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A One blended score lets a miss on one limit hide behind a gain on another, and it names no decider for a clash.
  • B Correct. A written ranking tells the design which limit gives first, and the sponsors have agreed to it in advance.
  • C A risk list records that the goals collide. It does not say which one wins when they do.
  • D Accuracy alone ignores two limits that are written into a budget and a contract.
6. A design must hold a 2 second p95 reply time and a cost of 0.02 dollars a ticket, both written in the signed agreement and the budget. The accurate design costs 0.05 dollars a ticket, so the two limits cannot both hold. Launch is in six weeks. What do you do?
  1. AShip the cheap design and list the accuracy gap on the project risk register.
  2. BLet the engineering lead pick the trade, since the team built both designs.
  3. CName the limit that gives, say why, and have its owner sign the trade.
  4. DLaunch the accurate design and ask finance to raise the cap after go-live.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A line on a risk register is not a decision. Nobody agreed to the gap, so nobody owns it.
  • B The trade changes cost and service for other teams. The builder is not the owner of either limit.
  • C Correct. A limit that gives should be named, and the person who owns it should agree to the change.
  • D Asking after go-live commits the spend first. If finance refuses, the cap is already broken.
7. Half way through the build, legal says EU customer data cannot leave the EU, but the model endpoint the team chose is in the US. Five weeks remain on a fixed budget. The design review that passed two weeks ago had nobody from legal in the room. Which practice would have caught this at the cheapest point?
  1. ACollect constraints at discovery, each with an owner who approves the design.
  2. BAsk legal to review the finished design during the last sprint before release.
  3. CKeep a risk register that the whole team rereads at the start of every sprint.
  4. DLet the engineers decide which constraints matter, to keep the design moving.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A constraint written down at discovery changes the design while changing it is still cheap.
  • B A review at the end finds the problem when a rebuild is the only fix left.
  • C A register records a risk only when someone thinks to list it, and it does not make an owner approve the design.
  • D The engineers do not own data residency, so they cannot rule on it.
8. A support agent project handles EU tickets and has 30,000 dollars a month for model spend. The team is writing the constraints section of the brief, which goes to legal and finance for sign-off before design starts. Select two items that belong in that section because they limit what the design may do.
  1. ACustomer data for the EU region stays in the EU, owned by legal.
  2. BCustomers may be unhappy when a reply is slow, which is a risk to watch.
  3. CModel spend stays inside 30,000 dollars a month, owned by finance.
  4. DThe team hopes to reach 90 percent satisfaction by the end of the year.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. It changes where the system can run, and it has an owner who can approve a change.
  • B This is a risk to watch. It does not limit what the design may do.
  • C Correct. A spend cap changes which model and how many calls are allowed, and finance owns it.
  • D A hope is a goal, not a constraint. The brief holds it as a target, with a baseline.
9. Ops wants faster first replies, finance wants a lower cost per ticket, and support wants fewer escalations. Each sponsor has sent a note, all three share one budget, and the pilot has a single ten minute slot on the next board agenda. Nobody owns the final call yet. What goes into the brief?
  1. AThe metric from the sponsor with the largest budget share, and nothing else.
  2. BA general goal of better support that all three teams can put their name to.
  3. CThree briefs, one for each sponsor, each reported on its own chart.
  4. DOne measured outcome that reconciles the notes, with a named final owner.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A The other two teams then see a project that ignores their number, and they stop backing it.
  • B A goal everyone agrees with is one nobody can test, so it settles nothing.
  • C Three charts and three definitions of success are the problem the brief is meant to remove.
  • D Correct. One outcome with an owner turns three wishes into something a team can test.
10. The head of support fears the agent will replace her senior staff. The draft brief says nothing about which decisions stay with people, the holiday peak starts in 8 weeks, and escalations are 22 percent of tickets today. The team has no written scope yet. What should the brief do?
  1. ALeave scope for the first design meeting, when the team knows more.
  2. BState which decisions stay with people, such as refunds above 500 dollars.
  3. CLog her fear as a risk and have the sponsor address it in the launch message.
  4. DReview every ticket by hand until the holiday peak has passed.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Scope left for later becomes the first argument in the design meeting, with the fear unresolved.
  • B Correct. A stated boundary lets the team check the claim, and any change to it becomes visible.
  • C A logged risk and a message are not in the brief, so nobody can check them or see them change.
  • D Reviewing every ticket removes the saving the project exists to make.
11. The finance partner asks for a weekly update with ticket counts, and the sponsor wants one line a month on cost per ticket. The pilot team has three people and time for a single status report. Finance reads the log weekly, and the sponsor reads one page a month. How do you build the report?
  1. ASend the weekly counts to everyone, so there is one format for both readers.
  2. BSend only the sponsor's monthly line, and tell finance to ask if it needs more.
  3. CGive each audience the view its decision needs, drawn from the same numbers.
  4. DHold the report until the first monthly close, then send every figure at once.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Weekly counts bury the sponsor's one decision under detail that person did not ask for.
  • B Finance then has no view of its own number and will build a second one.
  • C Correct. Each audience decides something different, and both views come from the same data.
  • D A long silence lets each team form its own picture, and the pictures will not match.
12. A project brief for a support agent will be read by three teams and the board. Some reviewers want scope left out to keep the brief to one page. The pilot runs 12 weeks, and one stakeholder has already asked to widen it to billing tickets in week 3. Select two reasons to write the scope into the brief.
  1. AIt lets a stakeholder check a claim, such as which refunds stay with people.
  2. BIt keeps the brief short, because scope becomes obvious once the build starts.
  3. CIt gives the board a figure to quote in the first monthly report.
  4. DIt makes a later widening visible, so it is agreed rather than assumed.
Show the answer
Answer: A, D
  • A Correct. A stated boundary can be checked by the person it affects.
  • B Scope is not obvious. Each team reads it differently until it is written down.
  • C A figure to quote is a metric. Scope says what is in and out, not how it is measured.
  • D Correct. A written scope turns a quiet widening into a decision that someone has to approve.

Professional, lesson 2
Workflow or agent
Pick workflow, agent or augmented LLM by predictability
Lumen Supply gives a free agent every tool for refunds, a path that has been the same for two years. Nobody wrote down why an agent was chosen, so nobody can say when to stop using one. This is the refund desk at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will run one ticket two ways, then write the rule and the record that say which way to use.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
One refund path, two ways to run it
An agent chooses its own steps. A workflow has them fixed in code, and the model writes only the words. The code decides the order, and the model decides the language.


The refund path has three steps: read the order, check the policy, refund. Three things go wrong: a free agent takes a path the team already knows, no record says why, and a feedback loop is added as a prompt sentence.


A workflow answers a known ticket
The code reads the order, checks the policy and refunds $89. Then it asks Claude once, for the reply to the customer. The whole run is one request.


Open a card to see the result of each step. The refund and the policy check came from code, so the model cannot skip either one.

The choice rule, written as code
The starting choose sends every task to an agent. The fix sends a task to a workflow when its steps are known, and to an agent when they are not.


A third shape sits below both. An augmented LLM is one call with tools or retrieval, and it has no loop at all. Pick the lowest complexity that meets the need. Step up only when a simpler shape fails.


starter/pattern.py
1"""EDIT THIS FILE. choose() hands every task to an agent.2A refund path the team has run for two years is given a free agent,3and run_workflow() lists no steps. Run `./workshop check pattern-choice`4until it is green, then `./workshop watch pattern-choice`.5"""67from kit.api import Json8910def choose(task: Json) -> str:11    """Return "workflow" when the steps are known, "agent" when they are not.12    A task is a dict with a `kind`: refund, status, exception or none.13    """14    return "agent"151617def run_workflow(ticket: Json) -> list[str]:18    """Return the ordered step names of this ticket's known path.19    A path nobody can list ends with a person: get_order, then escalate.20    """21    return []
Should a known refund path be an agent?
The refund path has been the same for two years. Every ticket reads the order, checks the policy and refunds. An agent can do all of that, and it can handle a surprise too.


Predict: Should a refund path the team has run for two years be an agent?
  1. ANo. A known path is a workflow, and the code can own the order.
  2. BYes. An agent is more capable, so it is the safer choice.
Show the answer
A. Capability is not the goal. A known path in code cannot drift, and an agent adds cost and variance where nothing needs deciding.
An agent on a known path costs 22 times more
With the starting code, the refund ticket goes to an agent. This run took the right path: order, policy, refund. Nothing drifted, and this page does not pretend it did.


It took 3 requests and 3375 input tokens. The workflow took 1 request and 154. Each agent turn sends the tools and the history again. This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run, recorded once and replayed here.


Drift is a rate, not an event. One green run cannot show a repeated lookup or a skipped check. The tests catch the choice itself: a known path must not go to an agent.

Code decides the path, and the record says why
choose returns a workflow when the ticket has a listed path. run_workflow returns its steps in order, and ends with a person for a path nobody listed.


The record has four parts: the decision, the context, the alternative rejected, and the signal that would reverse it. A feedback loop is designed in the same way. The checker's verdict returns to the drafter as data, with its reasons, not as a sentence in the prompt.


pattern.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""Pick the pattern for a task, and list the steps of a known path."""23from kit.api import Json45PATHS = {6    "refund": ["get_order", "check_policy", "process_refund"],7    "status": ["get_order"],8}9UNKNOWN = ["get_order", "escalate"]101112def choose(task: Json) -> str:13    """A workflow when the steps are known, an agent when they are not."""14    return "workflow" if task.get("kind") in PATHS else "agent"151617def run_workflow(ticket: Json) -> list[str]:18    """The ordered steps of this ticket's path, or a person for a new one."""19    return list(PATHS.get(ticket.get("kind", ""), UNKNOWN))

The model writes only the customer reply.78## Context910The path has been the same for two years. A free agent can repeat a lookup11or skip the policy check, and every turn resends the tools and the history,12so it reads far more input tokens per ticket. Nothing on this path needs a13decision the code cannot make.1415## Alternative rejected1617A free agent with every tool. It is more capable, but a known path gains18nothing from that, and each drift costs a person time.19Tickets with no listed path still go to an agent or to a person.2021## Reverse if2223More than a fifth of refund tickets stop following the listed steps, or a24new refund rule needs judgement the code cannot express. The checker's25verdict returns to the drafter as data, so a rejected reply is revised26from the reasons, not from a prompt sentence.

The checks send a known path to a workflow and an open one to an agent. The refund path runs in a fixed order with the policy check first, and an unlisted path ends with a person. The record names the pattern and the alternative.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A support desk runs refunds through a free agent with every tool, on a path that has not changed in two years. The agent drifts on 1 ticket in 12 and costs 3 times a scripted run. The team needs the same policy check on every refund, and the budget is flat. What do you change?
  1. AGive the agent more tools so it can recover when it drifts.
  2. BRun the known path as a workflow that the code orders.
  3. CAdd a line to the prompt that says to always check the policy.
  4. DSwitch to a larger model so the agent drifts on fewer tickets.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A More tools give the agent more ways to wander. The path is already known, so nothing needs to be discovered.
  • B Correct. Code fixes the order and the policy check cannot be skipped. The model only writes the reply.
  • C A prompt sentence asks the model to behave. Code makes the step happen.
  • D A larger model costs more per ticket, and it still chooses its own steps on a path nobody needs to choose.
2. A product team proposes an agent to build a weekly report that always has the same four steps, in the same order. The latency budget is 8 seconds, and the cost per report is capped. The data sources do not change. Which pattern do you choose?
  1. AAn agent, because it is the most capable pattern on offer.
  2. BAn agent with a high turn limit, so it has room to explore.
  3. CAn agent, because a workflow cannot retry a step that failed.
  4. DA workflow, since the steps are known and can run in a fixed order.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Capability is not the goal. A known path gains nothing from it and pays for it in latency.
  • B Room to explore is cost on a path with nothing to explore. It threatens the 8 second budget.
  • C A workflow can loop and retry. The code owns the loop and bounds it.
  • D Correct. Known steps in a fixed order are what a workflow is for, and it is the cheapest shape that works.
3. A 40-ticket golden set scores the workflow at 94 percent and the agent at 91 percent. The agent costs 2.8 times as much per ticket. The team needs one pattern for the known refund path, and quality and cost both matter. Which do you choose?
  1. AThe workflow, since it is more accurate and costs less on this path.
  2. BThe agent, since a higher cost means it is doing more work.
  3. CThe agent, since the gap of 3 points is too small to matter.
  4. DThe workflow, but only after adding a loop so it can match the agent.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. It wins on quality and on cost, so nothing argues for the agent on this path.
  • B Cost is not a measure of value. The extra spend bought no accuracy.
  • C A small gap still points to the workflow, and the agent is 2.8 times dearer.
  • D A workflow may loop already, and it does not need a loop to win here.
4. A team is deciding whether a task suits a workflow. The steps have run the same way for two years, and each step returns a result a test can check. Select two signs that point to a workflow. The task has no judgement call inside it.
  1. AThe steps can be listed in advance, in a fixed order.
  2. BThe model should be free to pick any tool at any time.
  3. CEach step's output can be checked by the code.
  4. DThe task should use the newest and most capable model.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. A list of steps known in advance is the test for a workflow.
  • B Free choice of tools is what an agent offers. It is a cost, not a sign of fit.
  • C Correct. A checkable output lets the code decide what happens next, with no model.
  • D Model size does not choose a pattern. A known path can run on a small model.
5. A triage desk reads free-text messages and must pick from 14 tools, in no fixed order. About 4 in 10 tickets need a path nobody has written. Wrong routing costs a person 15 minutes. Which pattern fits best?
  1. AA workflow with 14 branches, one for each tool the desk has.
  2. BAn augmented LLM, with a single call that has all 14 tools.
  3. CAn agent, since the path cannot be listed in advance.
  4. DAn agent with no turn limit, so it can always finish the job.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Fourteen branches cannot cover paths nobody has written, and each exception needs a new branch.
  • B One call cannot work through an open task that needs several tools in an order it chooses.
  • C Correct. An open task with no fixed order is where an agent is worth its cost.
  • D Autonomy without a bound is a risk, not quality. An agent still needs a turn limit and a handoff.
6. One call with retrieval answers an FAQ correctly on 97 of 100 test questions. A team proposes a multi-step orchestration with a planner and three workers, and answers must stay under 2 seconds. The FAQ has a single source. What do you recommend?
  1. ABuild the orchestration, since more steps will lift 97 toward 100.
  2. BKeep the augmented LLM, the lowest complexity that works.
  3. CCall it a workflow, since retrieval and generation are two steps.
  4. DGive the model more autonomy so it can handle the 3 failures.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Each extra step adds latency and cost. The 2 second limit is at risk for a small gain.
  • B Correct. One call with retrieval meets the need, so nothing simpler or dearer is needed.
  • C An augmented LLM is one call with tools or retrieval. It has no fixed sequence of steps the code runs.
  • D Autonomy adds variance. The 3 failures need a look at the source, not a looser loop.
7. A checker rejects 1 draft in 5 from a reply writer, and the drafter never sees why. The team adds "be more careful" to the prompt, and the rate stays at 1 in 5. The checker already returns the failing rule for each draft. How should the loop be built?
  1. AAdd a second sentence to the prompt that says what careful means.
  2. BLet the drafter retry on its own until a draft passes.
  3. CReplace the drafter with an agent that picks its own checks.
  4. DReturn the checker's verdict to the drafter as data, in a bounded loop.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A longer sentence is still a request. The drafter never reads the reason for a single rejection.
  • B A blind retry repeats the same draft. It does not use what the checker knows.
  • C An agent does not fix a missing data path. It adds choices where the gap is a missing signal.
  • D Correct. The verdict, with its reason, is data the drafter can act on, and the bound stops a runaway loop.
8. An audit asks why an agent was chosen for a payment path, and nobody on the team can say. The path ships in 6 weeks. Select two things that make a pattern choice defensible. The audit wants a record, not a recollection.
  1. AA note that the team felt an agent was the modern choice.
  2. BThe alternative that was rejected, and why it lost.
  3. CA claim that the agent will need less supervision over time.
  4. DA signal that would reverse the choice, such as a rising drift rate.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A A feeling is not a reason. It cannot be checked, and it gives the audit nothing to test.
  • B Correct. Naming the rejected alternative shows the choice was weighed.
  • C Autonomy is not quality, and a forecast of less supervision is a promise that nobody has measured.
  • D Correct. A reversing signal lets the next team see when to revisit the choice.
9. An architect must justify a pattern to a sponsor who wants a one-page reason. The sponsor will read it once, before a 10,000 dollar monthly spend is approved. The team has two patterns in play. What goes on the page?
  1. AAn ADR with the context, the decision, the alternative and the consequence.
  2. BA slide deck of every framework the team looked at during the study.
  3. CA list of the agent's features, since the sponsor pays for capability.
  4. DA promise that the prompt will be tuned until the results look right.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. One page can hold the context, the decision, the alternative rejected and what follows from it.
  • B A deck of frameworks is a survey. It does not say what was chosen, or why.
  • C Features are capability, and capability is not a reason to spend.
  • D A promise about the prompt is not a decision. It gives the sponsor nothing to approve.
10. The pattern decision was made in a chat thread 6 months ago, and the thread has scrolled away. A new lead now questions it, and the planning review is in two weeks. The lead needs to see the reason and the alternative. What should have existed?
  1. AA longer thread, pinned to the channel where the choice was made.
  2. BA line in the prompt that says which pattern the team chose.
  3. CA versioned decision record, stored with the code it governs.
  4. DA reminder for the original author to explain the choice in person.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A pinned thread still scrolls, cannot be reviewed as a change, and does not sit beside the code.
  • B A prompt line says what was chosen. It does not say why, or what was rejected.
  • C Correct. A record in version control is found with the code and shows when the decision changed.
  • D A person leaves, forgets and is out of reach. The record has to outlive them.

Professional, lesson 3
Orchestration patterns
Match the pattern to the task, and write every seam down
Lumen Supply moved its support reports to a team of agents to go faster. The run cost more and was no quicker, and two workers returned shapes the next step could not read. This lesson picks the pattern by the shape of the task. This is the analytics desk at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will run four tasks, each with its own pattern, then write the rule that chooses one and the contract at every seam.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
One desk, four shapes of work
Orchestrator-workers, sectioning, voting and evaluator-optimizer each fit one shape. In orchestrator-workers the model splits the work. In the other three, the code splits it.


A seam is the point where one step hands its output to the next, such as a worker's answer going to the merge. The code owns each seam and checks what crosses it. The team owns the budget.


Three things go wrong. A linear task is split across workers. A seam has no contract, so workers return shapes nobody can read. A loop has no cap.


Independent sections run together
The weekly report has two parts that do not depend on each other: delivery times and refunds. Each goes to its own worker, and the code merges the two findings. It took 2 requests and 154 input tokens.


Open a card to see a worker's brief and what it returned. Each worker answered with the two keys its contract names, so the merge could read both.

The pattern rule, written as code
The starting plan sends every task to an orchestrator and never caps a loop. The fix reads the shape of the task. Independent parts are sectioned and one question is voted. An open split is orchestrated, and a draft is evaluated with a turn cap.


A fifth shape exists, where each step needs the one before. That is a chain, and it needs nothing more than order.


starter/orchestrate.py

Run `./workshop check orchestration-strategies` until it is4green, then `./workshop watch orchestration-strategies`.5"""67from kit.api import Json8910def plan(task: Json) -> Json:11    """Return {"pattern": ..., "turns": ...} for a task with a `shape`.12    Shapes: independent, one_question, open_split, draft and dependent.13    Patterns: sectioning, voting, orchestrator, evaluator and chain.14    A loop gets a turn cap; anything else has turns of None.15    """16    return {"pattern": "orchestrator", "turns": None}171819def contract(step: str) -> Json | None:20    """Return {"input": ..., "output": ...} for a seam, or None.21    The seams are worker, vote and draft. Each output is a dict of keys.22    The worker output has exactly the keys finding and evidence, and the23    draft input names the lab sheet under the key sheet.24    """25    return None
Does adding agents speed up a linear task?
The policy has three steps, and each reads the step before it: summarise the policy, write the reply from the summary, write the subject line from the reply. Splitting them across workers looks like a way to save time.


Predict: Does splitting a linear task across more workers make it faster?
  1. AYes. More workers finish sooner.
  2. BNo. Each step waits for the one before, and each seam adds cost.
Show the answer
B. Parallel workers help only where the parts are independent. A dependent task gains seams and tokens, and no speed.
A linear task split across workers gains nothing
With the starting code, the orchestrator spends one request planning the split, then runs the three steps one after another. It took 4 requests, 4 rounds and 504 input tokens. Each step still waited for the one before it, so the planner added a request and saved no time.


The fix step runs the same task as a chain, so the two costs can be set side by side. This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run, recorded once.

Pick by shape, and write what crosses each seam
plan returns the pattern for the shape, and a turn cap of 3 for a loop. contract returns the input and output of a seam. A worker returns a finding and evidence, a vote returns yes or no, and a draft returns text. The code refuses an output that does not fit, so nothing downstream reads free text.


Run as a chain, the same linear task skips the planner: 3 requests, 3 rounds and 394 input tokens, against 4, 4 and 504 for the orchestrator. Each step reads the one before it and returns the one key its seam names, draft.


A loop needs a cap and a contract. The starting plan has neither, so the worker never got the lab sheet and ran to the harness ceiling of 3 rounds, marked a runaway. The fixed plan's contract carries the sheet and the first draft passed. The cap is for the day a draft never passes.


orchestrate.pygreen lines are what the fix adds

The checks give each task shape its pattern and keep a linear task in one chain. Only a loop gets a turn cap. Every seam has a contract, and the draft seam carries the lab sheet.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A weekly report has four sections, and no section reads another. It must be ready in 20 seconds, with each worker call taking about 8, and one call can write only about 500 words against the 2,000 needed. The cost cap allows four calls and one merge. How should you build it?
  1. ARun one worker for the whole report, then a checker that reviews the finished text for quality.
  2. BPut all four sections in one prompt and ask for one long answer, then trim the result to fit.
  3. CRun the four sections as parallel workers, then merge their findings.
  4. DRun the four sections in order, each worker reading the finished text of the one before it.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A One worker takes the sections one by one, so it will not fit the 20 seconds, and it cannot write 2,000 words. A checker adds one more call.
  • B One prompt is one call, not a split. It hits the 500 word cap, gives no seam to check and no parallel speedup.
  • C Correct. Independent parts are sectioning. The four calls overlap, so the run takes about one call's time.
  • D Running in order makes the time four calls long, about 32 seconds. The sections do not need each other.
2. A compliance check asks one yes or no question about a message, such as whether it leaks a card number, and a wrong answer is costly. The budget allows three calls per message. A single call is right 9 times in 10, and the errors look random. How do you raise confidence in one decision?
  1. AAsk the same question three times and take the majority answer.
  2. BAsk three differently worded questions, each leaning toward a yes, and count the yes answers.
  3. CSplit the message into three parts and send one part to each call, then combine the three answers.
  4. DAdd three more workers that each write a longer explanation of why the message is safe or not.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. Voting repeats one check and takes the majority, which cuts the chance of a one-off error.
  • B Different wording changes the question, and a lean toward yes biases every vote. Votes are comparable only on the same prompt.
  • C A part of a message may miss the card number that sits in another part. This is sectioning, and it does not vote.
  • D Longer explanations are not votes. Nothing gets counted, and the answer is no more certain.
3. An analyst asks why ticket volume rose last month, and nobody knows how many causes there are. The subtopics only appear once the data is read, so two workers may be enough, or six. The budget is a flat 10 calls for the request. Which pattern fits it?
  1. AOne prompt that lists every cause the team has seen before and asks the model for each one.
  2. BSix fixed workers, one per cause the team thought of last year, each reading the same data.
  3. CWorkers that return free text, joined by the next step exactly as it arrives.
  4. DAn orchestrator that splits at run time, then workers on each part.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A fixed list in one prompt cannot name causes that the data has not shown yet.
  • B A fixed count of workers assumes the split is known. It wastes calls when there are two causes.
  • C Free text at the seam is the failure. Joining whatever comes back breaks on the first odd shape.
  • D Correct. The split is open, so the orchestrator decides it at run time and hands each part to a worker.
4. A team is choosing where an evaluator and drafter loop fits, with a hard spend limit and one more call for each pass. The draft is a product blurb that must meet a score the code can compute. Which conditions make a task fit this pattern? Select two.
  1. AThe draft can be scored by a clear rule that the code checks.
  2. BA good draft is worth any number of turns, so the loop needs no cap.
  3. CThe checker's reasons name what to change, so a second draft can fix it.
  4. DOne prompt can carry the draft, the rubric and the retries together.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. A checkable rubric gives the loop a test that does not depend on the drafter's opinion.
  • B A loop with no cap has no end if the rubric is never met, and the spend limit is hard.
  • C Correct. Reasons the drafter can act on make each turn better than the last, which is what pays for the loop.
  • D One prompt has no checker outside the model and no loop in code. It is not this pattern.
5. Two workers feed a merge step. On 1 run in 4 the merge fails, because one worker returns a sentence and the other returns a JSON object. The prompts were reviewed twice and are fine, and the model version is unchanged since the failures began. What is the fix?
  1. ARewrite the merge step so it tries to read whatever shape it receives from each worker.
  2. BWrite an input and output contract for the seam, and refuse output that does not fit.
  3. CMerge the two workers into one prompt so the two outputs can no longer differ in shape.
  4. DAdd a third worker to read both outputs, decide which is right and pass that one on.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A merge that accepts any shape hides the fault. It fails later, somewhere harder to see.
  • B Correct. The contract names the keys, and the code refuses a bad output at the seam where it is made.
  • C This drops the split and its speed. The seam still exists between the prompt and the next step.
  • D A third worker adds a seam with no contract, and a third place for the shape to differ.
6. A five-step pipeline passes each output straight to the next step. A bad output at step 2 surfaces as a wrong answer at step 4, two steps later. Engineers lose hours finding where it began, and the retry budget is one rerun per request. Where should the check go?
  1. AAt step 4, where the wrong answer first shows, because that is where it hurts the user.
  2. BAt the start, in a longer prompt that tells every step to be careful with its output.
  3. CAt every seam, so a bad output is refused at the step that made it.
  4. DAt the end, with a retry of the whole pipeline until the final answer passes.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Step 4 only sees the symptom. The fault is two steps upstream, and the error points at the wrong step.
  • B A prompt asks the model to be careful. Only code at the seam can refuse an output.
  • C Correct. A check at each seam stops the fault where it starts and names the step that owns it.
  • D Retrying the whole pipeline pays for five steps each time and does not say where it broke.
7. An evaluator and drafter loop has no stop rule. One night it ran 14 turns on a blurb whose rubric could not be met, and the cost rose each turn. The team wants the worst case bounded before the next nightly run, without losing the good drafts. What should be added?
  1. AA turn budget, and a stop rule on the score so the loop ends when it passes.
  2. BA turn count of 40 instead of 14, so the loop has more time to meet the rubric.
  3. CA second drafter, so two drafts are tried in each turn and the better one is kept.
  4. DA rule that the checker may skip its reasons on later turns to save tokens.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A cap ends the loop when the score is never met, and a stop rule ends it when it is.
  • B More turns raise the worst case. A rubric that cannot be met will still run out the budget.
  • C Two drafters double the cost of each turn, and the loop still has no end.
  • D Without reasons the drafter has nothing to fix, so the loop is less likely to converge.
8. A multi-agent design with three workers and one merge is under audit, and the reviewer asks what a decomposition must state at each seam. The audit is written down, and each answer must be something a test can check. What must each seam name? Select two.
  1. AThe model name that each worker runs on, so a run can be repeated.
  2. BThe input schema that the worker receives.
  3. CA note that the next step will work out the shape from the text it gets.
  4. DThe output schema that the next step reads.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A The model is a setting of the worker. It says nothing about what crosses the seam.
  • B Correct. The input schema says what the worker is given, so a wrong input is refused.
  • C A shape left to the next step is the missing contract, and it is where the merge fails.
  • D Correct. The output schema is what the next step reads, so a bad output is refused where it was made.
9. A team built a five-step task as a multi-agent system to go faster, and each step needs the output of the one before. The cost tripled and the time did not fall. The steps cannot change order, and each step still needs its own check. What should it have been?
  1. AFive workers run in parallel, with a longer timeout on each one so none is cut off.
  2. BFive workers run in parallel, merged by one more worker at the end of the run.
  3. COne prompt with the five steps numbered, run as a single long call with no seams.
  4. DA workflow that runs the steps in order, each reading the last output.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Parallel workers cannot start a step before its input exists. A longer timeout only waits longer.
  • B A merge after parallel workers still cannot run dependent steps together, and it adds a call.
  • C A numbered prompt drops the seams, so no step can be checked or retried alone.
  • D Correct. Dependent steps are a chain. Order is the only thing they need, so no split is worth its cost.
10. A support bot answers one question per message by reading one help article, and it needs no steps after that. A teammate proposes an orchestrator with three workers. Latency is 2 seconds now, the budget is flat, and answers are already correct. What is the right call?
  1. ABuild the orchestrator, because a team of workers is more reliable than a single call.
  2. BKeep the single call that reads the article, the lowest complexity that works.
  3. CBuild it, but run the three workers in parallel so the latency holds at 2 seconds.
  4. DSplit the article into three parts and have one worker read each part in order.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A More workers add seams and cost. Reliability comes from a check at the seam, not from headcount.
  • B Correct. One call with retrieval answers a single question. Step up only when that fails.
  • C Parallel workers still add calls and a merge to a job that one call already does.
  • D Reading parts in order adds steps with nothing to decide, and it slows a 2 second answer.
Play: predict the output
This vote asks four times whether a message leaks a card number.


python
def leaks(message: str) -> bool:
    votes = [ask(message) for _ in range(4)]
    return votes.count("yes") > votes.count("no")





Predict: Two voters say yes and two say no. What does the check decide?
  1. AFalse, so the message goes out as safe.
  2. BTrue, because half the voters saw a leak.
Show the answer
A. An even count can tie, and this tie falls on the unsafe side. Use an odd number of voters, and send a tie or a split vote to the cautious answer.

Professional, lesson 4
Service levels
A service level row turns a goal into a breach
Lumen Supply tells its board that support is faster and better, and the dashboard shows an average wait of 3 seconds in green. The contract promises 5 seconds, and some customers wait 40. This lesson writes the row that catches it. This is the support desk at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will measure 2000 tickets, see a green average hide a slow tail, then write the percentile and the row that says what happens on a breach.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
One table, five promises
A service level row has a threshold, a place where it is measured, and an action. The model answers tickets, the trace measures each one, and the code decides whether a row is breached.


Three things go wrong. The goal is "faster and better", with no number. Latency is reported as an average, which hides the slow tail. The row has no breach action and no spend cap, so a breach changes nothing.


A latency table with two numbers
The run measures 2000 tickets and reports the mean and the 95th percentile side by side. The mean is 3.17 seconds. The 95th percentile is 40.12, far over the 5 second promise, so the code flags the row and names its action and owner.


Open a card to see what each step found. The samples are a fixture of 110 slow tickets in 2000, built so the tail is easy to see.


Fifty real Haiku 5.5 calls were also timed. Their mean was 1.44 seconds and their 95th percentile 4.41, with the slowest at 10.7. Real traffic has a tail too.

  2. Codemeasure: 2000 samples

}

    Show the result
    {
  "mean": 3.167,
  "p95": 40.115
}
  4. Codeflag: latency, then page on-call (support lead)
    Show the result

  "row": "latency",
  "action": "page on-call",
  "owner": "support lead"

BREACH: p95 40.115 against latency. Mean 3.17, p95 40.12.
The service level row, written as code
A row holds the promise (sla), a tighter internal goal (slo), where it is measured, the action on a breach and the owner. The service level agreement is what the contract promises. The objective is what the team aims for, and it sits inside the promise so a miss is seen early.


The 95th percentile, p95, is the value that 95 of every 100 tickets meet or beat.


starter/sla.py
1"""EDIT THIS FILE. p95() returns the mean, so a slow tail never shows.2The table also has no breach action, no owner and no spend row. Run3`./workshop check value-and-sla` until it is green, then4`./workshop watch value-and-sla`.5"""67import statistics8from dataclasses import dataclass91011@dataclass(frozen=True)12class SlaRow:13    """One promise: how much is allowed, where it is read, and what follows."""1415    name: str16    unit: str17    sla: float18    slo: float1920    measured_at: str21    action: str22    owner: str232425ROWS = [26    SlaRow("latency", "seconds", 5, 5, "dashboard", "", ""),27    SlaRow("wrong answers", "per 100", 10, 10, "dashboard", "", ""),28    SlaRow("failed calls", "per 1000", 5, 5, "dashboard", "", ""),29    SlaRow("escalations", "per 100", 20, 20, "dashboard", "", ""),30]313233def p95(samples: list[float]) -> float:34    """Return the value that 95 percent of the samples are at or under."""35    return statistics.mean(samples)363738def breach(row: SlaRow, value: float) -> str | None:39    """Return the row's action when the value is over its SLA, else None."""40    return row.action if value > row.sla else None
Does a 3 second average meet a 5 second promise?
The dashboard shows a mean of 3 seconds. The contract says tickets are answered within 5. It looks as if the promise is met with 2 seconds to spare.


Predict: A 3 second average latency against a 5 second promise: is it met?
  1. ANot necessarily. The slow tail can still breach it.
  2. BYes. 3 is under 5.
Show the answer
A. An average hides the slow calls. The promise is met only if the agreed percentile is under the threshold.
The average looks fine while tickets wait 40 seconds
With the starting code, p95 returns the mean. On the long-history tickets, a slice of the same 2000, the run reports a mean of 3.19 seconds against a promise of 5, and the result is green.


No row names an action, so even a breach would change nothing. The fixture holds 110 tickets in 2000 that wait about 40 seconds, and the dashboard cannot see them.

  2. Codemeasure: 400 samples
