GREEN: mean 3.190 against latency. Mean 3.19, p95 3.19.
The percentile breaches, and the row says what to do
p95 sorts the samples. It returns the value that 95 of every 100 samples are at or under.


breach returns the row's action when the value is over the promise. Each row also gains an owner, a place it is measured, and an objective tighter than the promise.


The table gains a row for cost per ticket. At 10,000 tickets a day, this fixture's rate of 110 in 2000 is 550 slow tickets, each one a breach.

The same tickets, two metrics
Switch between the two metrics on the long-history tickets, a slice of the 2000. Its mean is 3.19, a little above the 3.17 of all 2000, and its 95th percentile is 40.11 against 40.12. With the mean, the run is green. The 95th percentile is 40.11, and the run is a breach that names an action.


Nothing about the tickets changed. The only difference is which number is read.

Try it: metric and slice
Change one setting at a time. Pick the metric, then the slice. Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet.


The all-traffic run and the long-history run give almost the same numbers, because the slow tickets are spread evenly. A real slice can breach while the total passes, so keep a row for each slice that matters. Watch the spend slice too: the 95th percentile is 5 cents against a cap of 2 cents.

Spend is a row, not a report
Cost per ticket breaches the same way latency does. The mean is 1 cent, under the cap, and the 95th percentile is 5 cents, over it. The row names its action, switching to the smaller model, and its owner.


The same breach function judges both rows. A spend cap that lives in a monthly report changes nothing. A row with an action does.

The checks want a slow tail to breach while the mean looks fine, and a value inside the SLA to pass. Every row needs an action, an owner, a named place it is read and an SLO tighter than its SLA. Cost per ticket must be a row.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A support agent must answer fast, cost little and be right. The contract caps p95 latency at 5 seconds, finance caps spend at 2 cents a ticket, and the quality lead wants 90 percent correct. Design cannot meet all three on the current model, and the launch is in 30 days. What do you do first?
  1. ASet one blended score across the three and aim to keep the total above an agreed line.
  2. BRank the three limits and name the one that decides a tie.
  3. CPick the fastest model on the list, since speed is the easiest of the three to demonstrate.
  4. DReport the average of each metric and call the design balanced once all three look close.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A blended score lets a miss on one limit hide behind a gain on another. Each limit is a separate row.
  • B Correct. A design with three competing limits needs a written ranking, so a tie has one decider.
  • C Speed is one of the three, and choosing it alone breaks the cost and quality limits without saying so.
  • D Averages hide the tail that the contract is written against, and they rank nothing.
2. A design meets a 2 second p95 only with a model that costs 5 cents a ticket, and finance caps spend at 2 cents. The product owner wants both limits kept, and nobody has said which one gives way. The design review is on Friday. What should the design record before it ships?
  1. AThat the faster model is used, because speed is the target that matters most to customers.
  2. BThat spend is a report for month end, so the cap can be looked at after launch.
  3. COne number that covers both limits, so that there is nothing left to trade between them.
  4. DWhich limit gives way, why, and who signed off the trade.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Faster is not a target by itself. The trade still breaks the spend cap without anyone agreeing to it.
  • B Spend is a row with a cap and an action. A report shows a breach only after the money is gone.
  • C One number for two limits hides which one broke, and each has its own owner and action.
  • D Correct. Two limits that cannot both hold need a named trade and a signature, or the breach is a surprise.
3. A dashboard shows a mean latency of 3 seconds over 2000 tickets, and the team calls it green. About 1 ticket in 18 waits 40 seconds. The contract names the 95th percentile and promises 5 seconds at that percentile. Which number should the team report against the contract?
  1. AThe 95th percentile, since the contract names it and it shows what the slow tail waits.
  2. BThe mean, since 3 is well under 5 and most of the tickets are answered quickly.
  3. CThe fastest ticket, since it shows what the system can do when everything goes right.
  4. DThe mean of one busy slice, on the view that every slice shares the same number.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The percentile the promise names is the number a breach is judged on.
  • B The mean averages 40 second waits away. It stays under 5 while customers break the promise.
  • C The fastest ticket says nothing about the promise. It ignores every customer who waits.
  • D Slices differ, and one slice's mean does not stand for the others.
4. A team is writing the rows of a service level table, and each row must be actionable when a number crosses it. The table is reviewed by finance and by the on-call lead, and the review is written down so that an auditor can read it later. Which parts must every row name? Select two.
  1. AA wish to be faster than last quarter, stated without a number.
  2. BA threshold, and the place where it is measured.
  3. CThe same value for the objective and the agreement, to keep the table short.
  4. DAn action to take on a breach, with an owner.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A A wish with no number cannot be missed, so it cannot be a row.
  • B Correct. A threshold without a measuring place cannot be checked, and two places give two numbers.
  • C An objective equal to the agreement gives no early warning. It sits tighter, inside the promise.
  • D Correct. A breach with no action and no owner is a chart, and nobody acts on it.
5. A sponsor is told the new support agent is faster and better, and the sponsor will judge the project at a review in 30 days. The team has no baseline yet, and the project plan currently holds only that one sentence about speed and quality. What should replace it?
  1. AA promise that the agent will be faster than a person on the desk.
  2. BAn average wait, measured once on a normal day and reported at the review.
  3. CA measured target with a percentile, a baseline and a date.
  4. DOne satisfaction score that is used for every kind of ticket.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Faster than a person is still a wish. It has no number, so nobody can miss it.
  • B One average measured once hides the tail and gives no baseline to compare with.
  • C Correct. A target with a percentile, a baseline and a date can be missed, so the sponsor can judge it.
  • D One score for every kind of ticket blends slices that differ, and it hides where it fails.
6. A business case must justify a build that costs 40,000 dollars. About 500 slow tickets a day each cost a customer 6 minutes of waiting. Finance will check every number in the case against the trace, and the case goes to the budget meeting on Monday. How should the saving be stated?
  1. AAs an average wait across the whole desk, in place of the slow tail.
  2. BAs 500 tickets times 6 minutes a day, from the trace.
  3. CAs a line in the month-end spend report, to be reviewed once the build is live.
  4. DAs one satisfaction score for the whole desk, with a note on what it covers.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A An average spreads the 500 slow tickets over the desk, and the saving disappears in it.
  • B Correct. The saving is 3,000 minutes a day, from numbers that the trace can confirm.
  • C A report after the fact is not a case. The saving is what the build changes, stated before it is built.
  • D A score for the whole desk has no source in the trace, so finance cannot check it.
7. Two stakeholders read different charts of one run. The product lead reads a 4 second line as the promise, and the platform lead reads a 5 second line as the promise. The contract says 5, and the customer review is next week. How do you stop the mix-up?
  1. AUse one line on both charts, so the two charts agree about the promise.
  2. BDraw the average on both charts, so that the lines look close to each other.
  3. CLeave both lines and name an owner for whichever line gets crossed first.
  4. DDefine both. The agreement is 5 seconds, and the objective is 4 and internal.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A One line loses the early warning. The objective sits tighter than the promise on purpose.
  • B An average draws neither line. The mix-up is about which line is the promise.
  • C An owner does not say which line is the customer's promise, so the two leads still disagree.
  • D Correct. The agreement is the promise to the customer. The objective is the internal goal inside it.
8. Finance reviews a value case for a support agent that cost 40,000 dollars to build and runs at a few cents a ticket on the main support desk. The review is in 30 days, and the sponsor wants numbers, not adjectives. What must the case hold to be credible? Select two.
  1. AA baseline and a measured target for the metric.
  2. BA claim that the agent will be faster at some point in the year.
  3. CAn objective that matches the promise exactly, so there is no margin to argue about.
  4. DThe spend against the saving, in the same period.
Show the answer
Answer: A, D
  • A Correct. A baseline and a measured target show how far the metric moved.
  • B Faster at some point has no number and no date, so finance has nothing to check.
  • C An objective equal to the promise gives no margin, and it says nothing about value.
  • D Correct. A saving means little without the cost of making it, in the same period.
9. A manager asks the team to make support faster, but no metric exists and no one has timed tickets. The team is about to choose a model and design the flow. The first release is due in 30 days, and the sponsor asks for a status every week. What comes before any design?
  1. AThe fastest model on the list, to get a head start on speed while the rest is agreed.
  2. BAn average wait, measured on a good day and used as the starting figure.
  3. CThe outcome, the baseline and the percentile that will measure it.
  4. DOne speed number for every kind of ticket, so the target is simple to state.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Choosing a model first builds for a goal nobody has written down.
  • B An average on a good day hides the tail and gives a baseline that is too kind.
  • C Correct. A design has no target until the outcome, the baseline and the percentile are named.
  • D Kinds of ticket differ in how long they take, so one number fits none of them well.
10. A support director wants fewer angry customers by next quarter. Tickets are logged with reply time and cost, but nothing records how a customer felt. Last quarter's 2,000 tickets are on file, and the plan is due in two weeks. What is the first step toward a target?
  1. APick a measurable stand-in, such as p95 reply time, and set its baseline from last quarter's tickets.
  2. BSet the target on the mean reply time, since an average is easy to explain.
  3. CMake replies as fast as possible, on the view that quicker means calmer.
  4. DStart building, and name an owner for any complaint spike once one appears.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. An outcome nobody measures needs a stand-in with a threshold and a baseline before design starts.
  • B A mean on reply time hides the slow tail where angry customers wait.
  • C Faster is not a target. Without a number there is no point at which the work is done.
  • D An owner named after the spike is late. The owner and the action belong on the row before launch.
11. A launch metric reports accuracy only, and accuracy rose 4 points after a prompt change. Cost per ticket doubled at the same time, and nobody noticed until month end. The team wants to stop this happening again before the next prompt change next week. What should they add?
  1. AA monthly spend report, read at the end of each month by the finance lead.
  2. BA paired metric, such as cost per ticket, reported beside accuracy.
  3. CAn average of accuracy, reported with more decimals so small moves show up.
  4. DOne score that blends accuracy and cost for every slice of the traffic.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A monthly report finds the change a month late. A row with a cap finds it on the day.
  • B Correct. A paired metric beside the main one catches a gain that is paid for somewhere else.
  • C More decimals on the same metric cannot show a cost that the metric never reads.
  • D A blend hides which side moved, and each metric needs its own threshold and action.
12. The latency row of a service level table has a threshold and a place where it is measured, but no owner. A breach was found in the month-end review, three weeks after it began. The team wants the next one found and acted on early, and the review cadence stays monthly. What changes?
  1. AThe objective is set equal to the agreement, so the table is simpler to read for the whole team.
  2. BA spend row is added with its own cap, and the latency row is left as it is.
  3. CThe target moves from 5 seconds to 3 so the desk has some margin.
  4. DThe row gets an owner and a breach action, so a breach is acted on.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A An objective equal to the agreement removes the early warning, so the customer sees the miss first.
  • B A spend row is useful, but the latency row still has no owner for its breach.
  • C A tighter number with no owner is still a number nobody acts on. Faster is not the fix here.
  • D Correct. An owner and an action turn a number crossing a line into a task with a name on it.
13. A weekly report for a support agent shows a mean reply time of 2.8 seconds over 1,500 tickets, against a promise of 5 seconds at the 95th percentile. A customer with a long order history complains of 30 second waits, and the ops lead wants the report changed before the next review in 7 days. Which change makes the report catch that customer's wait?
  1. AReport the mean for each day, so a bad day stands out from the rest of the week.
  2. BReport one 95th percentile across all tickets, since one number is easier to read.
  3. CReport the 95th percentile per slice, with long-history tickets on their own row.
  4. DMake the whole desk answer faster, so that every slice moves under the line together.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A daily mean still averages the slow tickets away, so the 30 second waits stay hidden.
  • B One percentile over every ticket can pass while one slice breaches, because fast slices pull it down.
  • C Correct. The promise names the 95th percentile, and a row of its own shows where the slow tail sits.
  • D Faster is not a measure. Without a per-slice number the report still cannot show which slice waits.
14. A launch review must decide whether a new support agent meets its latency goal before it goes to 3 more teams. A test run of 800 tickets gives a mean of 2.1 seconds, a median of 1.4 seconds and a 95th percentile of 9 seconds. The agreement promises 5 seconds at the 95th percentile, and the review has one hour. What should the review conclude?
  1. AIt passes, since both the mean and the median are well under 5 seconds.
  2. BIt fails, since the 95th percentile the agreement names is 9 seconds.
  3. CIt passes on latency, and the review turns to the spend report for the month.
  4. DIt is fine to launch, and the percentile can go in a report after go-live.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A The agreement names the 95th percentile, and the mean and median say nothing about it.
  • B Correct. The number the agreement names is 9 seconds against a promise of 5, so the launch fails.
  • C Spend is its own row. It cannot stand in for a latency row that is over its threshold.
  • D A breach known before launch needs an owner and an action now, not a report later.

Service level agreement
The promise made to the customer, with a threshold
Service level objective
The tighter internal goal, set inside the promise
Percentile
The value that a set share of calls meet or beat; p95 is the value 95% of calls meet or beat
Breach action
What happens, and who acts, when a value is over the promise
Professional, lesson 5
Model tiering
Choose the tier per step on a golden set
Lumen Supply runs its largest model on every step of its ticket pipeline, because one hard-coded id was copied everywhere. The bill is far above what the work needs, and a step that a small model does as well takes 5.9 seconds on the largest. This lesson measures each step on each tier and gives every step the lowest tier that passes. This is the ticket pipeline at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. It has three steps: classify labels a ticket, draft writes the return-window reply, and review finds the defect in a finished reply. You will sweep every step over three tiers, read quality, time and cost together, and write the registry that picks.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
One pipeline, three steps, three tiers
A tier is a model size: a small one, a middle one and the largest. A bigger tier costs more and takes longer. It does not always answer better, so the right tier depends on the step.


Each step has a golden set of thirty items with known answers, a quality bar and a latency budget. The sweep runs the step on each tier and scores it. The registry holds the bar and the budget, and pick chooses the tier.


Three things go wrong, in this order. One model id is hard-coded in every step, so cost and speed follow the biggest model. No step has a latency budget, so nothing says when a tier is too slow. And the sweep is read as one number for the whole set, so the trade-off inside a step is never seen.


A sweep table for one step
The classify step labels thirty tickets. All three tiers get all thirty right. The small tier takes 3.0 seconds and costs $1.19 for 10,000 tickets. The middle tier takes 2.9 seconds and costs $2.38, and the largest takes 5.9 seconds and costs $4.76.


Open a card to see the calls behind a cell: each keeps its tokens in and out, and its seconds. Cost is those tokens times the tier's price per million tokens, so the small tier's 1,118 in and 493 out come to $1.19 for 10,000 tickets. The prices are this lab's figures from recording day, so check the pricing page.


Each cell is one recorded run of the whole golden set. Its time stands in for the p95 you would read on live traffic, so treat a small gap as noise.

The pick rule, written as code
pick takes a step and the scores of each tier, and returns the lowest tier that meets the step's quality bar and fits its latency budget. If no tier passes, it returns nothing, so a failing step is seen and not hidden.


registry holds the bar and the budget for each step, and MODELS is the only place a tier becomes a model id. A tier is a cost and speed setting. It is not a guarantee of quality, so the bar decides what is good enough.

1"""EDIT THIS FILE. It has two planted defects.21. pick(): it returns the largest tier whatever the scores say.32. registry(): no step has a latency budget, so no tier is ever too slow.45Run `./workshop check model-tiering` until it is green, then6`./workshop watch model-tiering`.7"""89from kit.api import Json10from kit.models import TIERS1112MODELS = dict(TIERS)13ORDER = ["haiku", "sonnet", "opus"]141516def registry() -> Json:17    """The quality bar and latency budget of each step.18    `bar` is the share of the golden set a tier must get right, and19    `budget` the most seconds one run may take.20    """21    return {22        "classify": {"bar": 0.9, "budget": None},23        "draft": {"bar": 1.0, "budget": None},24        "review": {"bar": 0.95, "budget": None},25    }262728def pick(step: str, scores: Json) -> str | None:29    """Return the tier a step should run on.30    `scores` maps each tier to its `quality` and `seconds` on the golden set.31    """32    return ORDER[-1]

A registry and a pick per step
registry now gives every step a bar and a latency budget. Classify needs 90% inside 4 seconds. Draft needs every item right inside 12 seconds, because the customer reads it. Review needs 95% inside 10. pick walks the tiers from the smallest and stops at the first that passes both.


The same sweep now chooses the small tier for classify, the middle tier for draft and the middle tier for review. Across the three steps the bill is $15.48 for 10,000 tickets, against $32.00. The id lives in one file, so a new model is one line in MODELS and a new sweep.


Cost is tokens times price. The draft step writes the most, about 2,100 tokens for thirty replies on the middle tier, so it is the largest line in the bill. A saving on a step is worth most where the step writes the most.


tiers.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""The solution: a budget for every step, and the lowest passing tier."""23from kit.api import Json4from kit.models import TIERS56MODELS = dict(TIERS)7ORDER = ["haiku", "sonnet", "opus"]8910def registry() -> Json:11    """The quality bar and latency budget of each step.12    `bar` is the share of the golden set a tier must get right, and13    `budget` the most seconds one run may take.14    """15    return {16        "classify": {"bar": 0.9, "budget": 4.0},17        "draft": {"bar": 1.0, "budget": 12.0},18        "review": {"bar": 0.95, "budget": 10.0},19    }202122def pick(step: str, scores: Json) -> str | None:23    """Return the lowest tier that passes the bar within the budget.24    `scores` maps each tier to its `quality` and `seconds` on the golden set.25    Returns None when no tier passes, so a failing step is seen, not hidden.26    """27    rule = registry()[step]2829    for tier in ORDER:30        got = scores[tier]31        if got["quality"] >= rule["bar"] and got["seconds"] <= rule["budget"]:32            return tier3334    return None

The checks want a budget on every step and the lowest tier that meets both the bar and the budget. When no tier passes, pick() returns None.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. Lumen's ticket pipeline has three steps, classify, draft and review, and every one calls the same largest model id, copied from the first prototype. The monthly bill is far above plan, and the classify step takes 4 seconds against a 1 second budget. A golden set of 30 items exists for each step. What should the team change first?
  1. AMove all three steps to the smallest tier, because the bill is the loudest problem and one cheap model is simpler.
  2. BKeep the largest tier on every step and ask for a bigger budget, since it is the choice nobody can fault.
  3. CRun each step on each tier against its golden set, then give every step the lowest tier that passes.
  4. DScore the whole pipeline once on the combined sets and keep whichever single model has the best total.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A One small model may fail the draft or review step. The fix is a choice per step, and a smaller tier is right only where its score passes the bar.
  • B The largest tier is not the safest choice. It is the slowest and the dearest, and here it breaks the classify budget.
  • C Correct. A sweep of tier by step shows where a small tier passes and where it does not. Each step then gets the cheapest tier that is good enough and fast enough.
  • D One total hides the step where a tier fails. A tier that is excellent on classify can still be wrong on review.
2. On the classify golden set of 30 tickets, the smallest tier gets 96% right in 0.8 seconds. The middle tier gets 96% in 2, and the largest gets 97% in 4. The bar is 90% and the budget is 1 second. Which tier should the classify step use, and why?
  1. AThe smallest tier, because it passes the bar inside the budget at the lowest cost, and the extra point is not needed.
  2. BThe largest tier, because one more point of accuracy is worth paying for on every ticket that comes in.
  3. CThe middle tier, because it sits between the other two and so balances accuracy against cost and speed.
  4. DThe largest tier, with a cache added to bring its 4 seconds down to the 1 second budget for repeats.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The bar is 90%, and 96% clears it. The smallest tier also fits the budget, so it is the lowest tier that passes.
  • B The bar is 90%, so the extra point buys nothing the step needs, and the largest tier misses the 1 second budget.
  • C The middle tier scores the same 96% but takes 2 seconds, over the budget. Sitting between two tiers is not a reason.
  • D A cache changes what repeated calls cost, not how long a first call takes. The tier is the lever here.
3. The draft step writes the return-window reply a customer reads, so its bar is 100% on a golden set of 30 orders. The smallest tier gets 29 of 30 right in 7 seconds. The middle tier gets 30 of 30 in 10.8 and the largest gets 30 of 30 in 14.8, against a 12 second budget. Which tier should the draft step use?
  1. AThe largest tier, because the draft is customer facing and so the strongest model is the safe one.
  2. BThe smallest tier, after lowering the bar to 95% so that its 29 of 30 passes and the cost stays low.
  3. CThe smallest tier, with its thinking effort turned up until it reaches 30 of 30 on the golden set.
  4. DThe middle tier, the lowest tier that passes the bar and fits the budget.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A The largest tier also passes, but it takes 14.8 seconds against a 12 second budget. Safe does not mean over budget.
  • B A bar moved after the result is no bar. The reply is customer facing, so the 100% was set for a reason.
  • C Effort is a separate lever and it adds time. It does not turn a smaller tier into a larger one, and it was not measured.
  • D Correct. Move up one tier only as far as the bar needs. The largest is slower and dearer.
4. A review board asks what evidence supports the tier chosen for the review step before it goes live. The step must find the defect in a finished reply, with a stated bar and latency budget, and the board meets once. Which inputs should the team show it? Select two.
  1. AEach tier's score on the step's golden set, read against the bar.
  2. BThe order of the three tiers in the vendor's lineup, from the largest down, with each tier's list price.
  3. CThe time each tier took on the step, read against the latency budget.
  4. DOne accuracy average over classify, draft and review for each tier, shown in a single chart.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. A score on this step's own golden set is the evidence that the tier is good enough for the work.
  • B The lineup says which tier is larger, not whether it is needed. It is a reason to buy the most, not a measurement.
  • C Correct. A tier that passes the bar but misses the budget is still the wrong tier, so the time is half the evidence.
  • D An average over three steps hides the step where a tier fails, so it cannot support a choice for one step.
5. The draft step meets its accuracy bar on its golden set, but its p95 latency is 3.4 seconds and the SLA allows 2 seconds. Its mean latency is 1.6 seconds, and the SLA is a fixed term of the contract. The team owns the step's tier and its prompt, and the next review is in two weeks. What should the team do?
  1. AAccept it, because the mean is under 2 seconds and the accuracy bar is met, so the step is within the contract.
  2. BChange the tier or the step's design, such as a shorter output, then measure p95 again against the 2 seconds.
  3. CMove the step to the largest tier, since better answers will make the calls faster and bring the p95 down.
  4. DRetry every call that runs past 2 seconds, so that the slow calls are replaced by quick ones.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A The SLA is about the tail. A mean of 1.6 seconds can hold one call in twenty at 3.4, and those are the customers who wait.
  • B Correct. The tail is what is over, so change the lever that sets it, and then re-measure p95.
  • C A larger tier is usually slower, not faster, so this would widen the gap to the SLA.
  • D A retry waits out the slow call and then makes another, so a customer's wait grows. It does not fix what made the call slow.
6. A pipeline step runs on a middle tier with a mean latency of 2.1 seconds and a p95 of 3.0 seconds at normal traffic. When traffic doubles, the mean stays at 2.1 seconds but the p95 rises to 5.5 seconds. The SLA is a p95 of 4 seconds, and the cost per ticket has not changed. What does the team conclude?
  1. AThe step is healthy, because the mean did not move and the bill per ticket is the same as before.
  2. BThe tier is too small for the load, so move the step to the largest tier to absorb the traffic.
  3. CThe mean was the wrong number to watch, so set the budget on p95 and find what slows the slowest calls.
  4. DTreat the rise as a cost problem, since slower calls mean that the step is using more tokens.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A flat mean can sit beside a long tail. The p95 passed the 4 second SLA while the mean looked fine.
  • B A larger tier is slower per call, so it would not absorb the load and may push the p95 further past the SLA.
  • C Correct. Tune for the tail. Budget on p95, then look at what the slowest calls share, such as queueing.
  • D Latency and cost are different measures. A slow call is not a dear one, and the bill said nothing about the tail.
7. A review step runs on the middle tier and takes 11 seconds against a 10 second budget. Its golden set score is well above the bar, and the team may not move to a bigger tier because the bill is already at its cap. Which levers cut the latency without a bigger model? Select two.
  1. ATurn on extended thinking so that the model works out a shorter answer before it writes.
  2. BTry the smaller tier on the golden set, and use it if it still passes the bar.
  3. CCopy a faster model's id into this step's code and leave the other steps as they are.
  4. DAsk for less output, such as a one word label instead of an explanation.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A Extended thinking adds reasoning, so the call takes longer. It is a separate lever from the tier and it does not shorten the answer.
  • B Correct. A smaller tier is faster, and the sweep tells you whether it still clears the bar before you switch.
  • C A hard-coded id skips the sweep, so nobody knows if that model passes. The id belongs in the registry, chosen by the pick.
  • D Correct. Output tokens are generated one after another, so a shorter answer is a faster one at any tier.
8. On the draft step the larger tier gets 100% right in 14.8 seconds, and the smaller tier gets 97% right in 7 seconds. The sponsor asks for full accuracy and a 10 second answer, and no tier gives both on the golden set. The launch is in a week. How should the team respond?
  1. AChoose the largest tier and ship with a note that latency will be tuned after launch, since accuracy matters most.
  2. BState the trade-off with the numbers for each tier, and ask the owner to choose which to give up.
  3. CChoose the smaller tier and retry any answer it gets wrong, so that accuracy reaches 100% inside 10 seconds.
  4. DCombine accuracy and latency into one score and ship the tier with the higher number.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A The largest tier takes 14.8 seconds, so the 10 second goal is missed at launch. A note to tune it later is a promise the data does not support.
  • B Correct. When the goals conflict, put both numbers side by side and let the owner choose, so the trade is made in the open.
  • C A retry adds a second call to the wait, so the answer takes longer than 7 seconds. It also does not say which answers were wrong.
  • D A blended score hides which goal was given up, and the weights decide the answer. The owner should make that call openly.
Play: predict the output
This pick reads the tiers in the order the sweep file lists them.


python
def pick(step: str, scores: Json) -> str | None:
    rule = registry()[step]
    for tier, got in scores.items():
        if got["quality"] >= rule["bar"] and got["seconds"] <= rule["budget"]:
            return tier
    return None

A. A dict keeps the order its data arrived in, and that order is not cost. Walk a fixed list from cheapest to largest, so the file cannot change the pick.

Tier
A model size, which sets cost and speed but does not guarantee quality
Golden set
A fixed set of items with known answers, used to score a step
Quality bar
The share of the golden set a tier must get right for a step
Latency budget
The most seconds a step may take, set by the owner
Registry
The one place that holds each step's bar, budget and model ids
p95
The time that 95 of every 100 calls meet or beat
Professional, lesson 6
Prompt layers and caching
Stable layers first, then cache the prefix
A timestamp sits on the first line of the Lumen Supply system prompt, so the prefix changes on every call and the cache never hits. The 7,100-token prefix is billed in full on each call, and every team's tenant text is mixed into it. This lesson orders the layers so the second call reads the prefix from the cache. The prompt has three stable layers and one volatile turn. The policy layer is the shop's rules, shared by every team. The tenant layer is one team's tone, and the guardrail layer holds the limits on every reply. The turn is the question and the time it was sent.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
One prefix, many calls
The model reads all the layers, the API caches the stable ones, and your code decides their order. A cache hit needs the start of the prompt to be identical, byte for byte, up to a marker you place.


Three things go wrong, in this order. A timestamp at the top changes the prefix on every call. There is no cache marker, so nothing is reused even when the prefix is stable. And tenant text is mixed into the policy, so one edit changes the start of the prompt.


The second call reads from the cache
Two calls ask different questions with the same prefix. The first call writes 7,113 tokens to the cache and reads none. The second reads all 7,113 back and sends only 33 fresh tokens.


Cached tokens still fill the context window. A cache lowers the price of the prefix, not its size, so the prefix, the history and the reply must still fit together.


Open a card to see the usage fields behind each call. A cache write costs 1.25 times a fresh input token, and a read costs a tenth of one. Ten thousand calls like the second cost $9.89 on Haiku. The prices are this lab's figures.


  1. buildlayers: policy, tenant, guardrail, turn
    Show the result
    {
  "tenant": "Acme"
}
  2. Call 1wrote 9,779 tokens, read 0 tokens, fresh 39 tokens
    Show the result
    {
  "sent at": "2026-06-01 09:00:00",
  "ask": "Can I return a monitor after 20 days?",
  "cache written": 9779,
  "cache read": 0,
  "fresh input": 39,
  "output tokens": 120,
  "cost of 10,000 calls like this": "$12.86"
}
  3. Call 2wrote 0 tokens, read 9,779 tokens, fresh 37 tokens
    Show the result
    {
  "sent at": "2026-06-01 09:01:37",
  "ask": "How long is the warranty on the dock?",
  "cache written": 0,
  "cache read": 9779,
  "fresh input": 37,
  "output tokens": 120,
  "cost of 10,000 calls like this": "$1.61"
}
HIT: the second call read 9,779 tokens from the cache, and 10,000 calls like it cost $1.61.
The layer order, written as code
build takes the three layers and the turn, and returns the system prompt and the messages. Stable text goes first, the turn goes last, and one cache marker follows the guardrail.


The marker cannot sit inside text that changes. A conversation's earlier messages change on every turn, so they go in the messages after the marker, never in the system layers. The prefix must also reach a minimum size before the API will cache it, which is 4,096 tokens for this model. Below that, a marker is ignored without an error.


starter/layers.py
1"""EDIT THIS FILE. It has two planted defects.21. build(): the time is the first line of the system prompt, so the3   prefix changes on every call and the cache never hits.42. build(): the layers are one block with no cache marker, so nothing is5   cached even when the prefix does not change.63. SKILL.md, in this same folder, is graded by the checks too: give it a7   description that says when to use it, and keep its body to stable rules.89Run `./workshop check prompt-layers-caching` until it is green, then10`./workshop watch prompt-layers-caching`.11"""1213from kit.api import Json141516def build(policy: str, tenant: str, guard: str, turn: Json) -> Json:17    """Return the system prompt and the messages for one turn.18    `turn` holds the customer's `text` and the time it was sent, `at`.19    """20    system = f"Time now: {turn['at']}\n{tenant}\n{policy}\n{guard}"2122    return {23        "system": system,24        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": turn["text"]}],25    }
Does a changing timestamp at the top break the cache?
The time of each request is useful for audits. It seems harmless on the first line, because the rules that follow it never change.


Predict: Does a changing timestamp at the top of the prompt break the cache?
  1. ANo. Only the last lines matter.
  2. BYes. The cached prefix must match exactly.
Show the answer
B. A cache hit needs an identical prefix up to the marker. Anything that changes at the top invalidates all of it.
A timestamp at the top breaks the cache
This is a real Haiku 5.5 run, recorded once and replayed here. The starting build puts the time on the first line and sets no marker. Both calls send about 7,150 fresh tokens, and the cache writes and reads nothing.


At that rate, 10,000 calls cost $73.92. The prefix is the same rules every time, yet the API bills it in full on every call.

MISSED: the second call read 0 tokens from the cache, and 10,000 calls like it cost $10.42.
Policy, tenant, guardrail, then the turn
The time moves to the end, inside the turn. The three layers become separate blocks in order, and one marker follows the guardrail. Each tenant's text stays in its own layer, so an edit to it changes that layer and leaves the policy block unchanged.


With one marker, each team's cached prefix includes its own tenant text, so the teams do not share a cache.


The first call now pays a write of 7,113 tokens. Every later call reads them for a tenth of the price, so 10,000 calls cost $9.89 and not $73.92.


layers.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""The solution: stable layers first, one marker, the turn last."""23from kit.api import Json456def build(policy: str, tenant: str, guard: str, turn: Json) -> Json:7    """Return the system prompt and the messages for one turn.8    The layers run policy, tenant, guardrail. One cache marker follows the9    guardrail, so everything before it is the cached prefix. The time rides10    with the turn, after the marker, where a change cannot break the cache.11    """12    system = [13        {"type": "text", "text": policy},14        {"type": "text", "text": tenant},15        {16            "type": "text",17            "text": guard,18            "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},19        },20    ]21    asked = f"{turn['text']}\n\nSent at {turn['at']}."2223    return {24        "system": system,25        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": asked}],26    }

The stable layer as a Skill
A prompt that a whole team pastes drifts, because each copy is edited on its own. A Skill is one file the team loads, so the stable rules live in one place. Its body holds only text that does not change, which is the rule of the cached prefix: no time and no tenant name.


Its description says when to use it. A session loads the Skill by that description, so a vague one means the Skill is skipped.


The Messages API calls above do not load a Skill, so the Skill is a separate file. The checks grade SKILL.md in the same work folder, and Enforce in managed settings and hooks ships a skill to every team.


SKILL.mdgreen lines are what the fix adds

Holds the guardrails every team shares.4---56Answer in at most three sentences.7Never quote a price that is not in the rules, and never promise a delivery date.8Never ask for a card number or a password.9If the customer is angry, acknowledge it in one clause, then answer.10If the question is not about a Lumen order, say you can only help with Lumen orders.

Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A support agent sends a 7,000-token system prompt 10,000 times a day, and the usage field cache_read_input_tokens is zero on every call. The prompt has a cache marker after its last rule, the first line holds the current time, and the cost report shows the prefix billed in full. What should the team do first?
  1. ARaise max_tokens so the cache has room to store the prefix between the calls.
  2. BAdd a second cache marker at the top of the prompt, so the time line is cached as well.
  3. CMove the text that changes on every call to the end, then read the usage again.
  4. DWait a day, because a cache needs many calls before it starts to return reads.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A max_tokens limits the reply, not the cache. Raising it changes nothing about the prefix.
  • B A marker caches the text before it, and that text still changes on every call, so a second marker never matches.
  • C Correct. A hit needs an identical prefix. The time on the first line changes it every call, so it moves after the marker.
  • D A cache hit does not depend on call volume. A prefix that differs each call never hits, however long you wait.
2. The system prompt starts with the time of the request, and the compliance team wants it kept for audits. The prompt is 7,000 tokens long, 10,000 calls a day share the rest of it, and the cost report shows no cache reads. Both the audit record and the cost target must be met. What is the right change?
  1. ADelete the time, because audit records are not the prompt's job and cost comes first.
  2. BKeep the time, but send it after the marker with the turn, and log it from your code.
  3. CKeep the time on the first line and add a cache marker right after it, so it is cached.
  4. DRound the time to the nearest hour so the prefix changes less often than it does now.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A The audit need is real and can be met without the prompt. Deleting it drops a requirement.
  • B Correct. The time stays in the request, after the cached layers, so the prefix is identical while the audit still has the value.
  • C A marker after the time caches a prefix that starts with a changing line, so it still never matches.
  • D A prefix that changes every hour still misses on the first call of each hour, and it blurs the audit time.
3. Three teams share a 7,000-token policy and differ only in a short tone paragraph, and each team edits its tone about once a week. The tone paragraph now sits first in one block, above the policy. The layout must keep each edit inside that team's own text and leave the shared policy text untouched. How should the prompt be laid out?
  1. AGive each team its own full copy of the prompt, so one team's edit cannot reach another team.
  2. BKeep one block and cache each team's prompt for longer, so a weekly edit is covered by the cache lifetime.
  3. CKeep one block with the tone paragraph moved to the end and no marker, so the edit sits last.
  4. DPolicy, tenant and guardrail as separate layers, in that order, so an edit changes only the tenant layer.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Copies drift, and each copy is still one block with the tenant text mixed into the policy.
  • B An edit makes a new prefix whatever the cache lifetime is, and the policy is still mixed with the tone paragraph.
  • C Without a marker nothing is cached, and the policy and the tone paragraph still share one block.
  • D Correct. Each layer has one owner and one rate of change, so a tone edit changes the tenant layer and the policy block stays as it was.
4. A review of a cost report asks what must be true for a cached prompt to be read back. The system prompt is 7,000 tokens and the marker is placed after its last stable layer. The model has a minimum cacheable size. Select two facts that the team should rely on.
  1. AA longer prompt caches better, so padding the prefix raises the hit rate.
  2. BOnce a marker is set, every later call reads from the cache, whatever the prefix holds.
  3. CThe prefix up to the marker must match the earlier call exactly.
  4. DThe prefix must reach the model's minimum size, or the marker is ignored.
Show the answer
Answer: C, D
  • A Length helps only up to the point where the prefix is cacheable. Padding adds cost and does not change whether text matches.
  • B A read depends on a matching prefix and on the entry still being live. A marker alone guarantees nothing.
  • C Correct. One changed character before the marker is a different prefix and a miss.
  • D Correct. Below the minimum, the API ignores the marker and no error is raised.
5. Eight engineers each paste the same 20-line review prompt into their sessions, and the copies have drifted over a month. Reviews now vary by who ran them, and nobody knows which copy is current. The prompt must stay editable by the team and be versioned. What should the team do?
  1. APut it in one Skill the team loads, with a description that says when to use it.
  2. BAsk each engineer to re-paste the newest copy every Monday from the chat history.
  3. CCache the pasted prompt so every session sees the same text for the whole week.
  4. DMake the prompt longer so it covers every case and no engineer needs to edit it.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. One file is the home of the rule, the whole team loads it, and a change is made once.
  • B Re-pasting relies on memory and still leaves eight copies that can differ by Tuesday.
  • C A cache saves cost on a repeated prefix. It does not decide which text a session starts with.
  • D A longer prompt is a longer copy to drift, and it still needs edits.
6. A team keeps its 12 reply rules in a Skill and again in its agent's system prompt. Last week someone edited the Skill, and the agent still follows the old rules, which was found only after a customer complaint. The fix must stop a stale copy from existing and keep the Skill for the other teams that load it.
  1. AEdit both copies each time and add a reminder to the review checklist.
  2. BMove the rules into the system prompt only and delete the Skill, since that text is read first.
  3. CKeep one home for each rule and let the other place refer to it, so an edit is made once.
  4. DRaise the cache lifetime so the old rules are dropped sooner and the new ones load.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A checklist relies on memory, and two copies will drift again.
  • B That drops the reuse the Skill gave other teams, and it moves the problem without removing a copy.
  • C Correct. One home per rule means a change cannot leave a stale copy behind.
  • D Cached text is the prefix as it was sent. A lifetime does not decide which rules are current.
7. A reusable support prompt serves two teams, and each has its own house style. The shared rules are 90 percent of the text and change quarterly, while the style notes differ and change monthly. The design must keep one copy of the shared rules and let each team edit only its own style. Select two parts that the design should include.
  1. AA shared stable part that both teams load unchanged.
  2. BA small per-team layer for the house style, kept apart from the shared part.
  3. COne prompt for each team that repeats the shared rules in full.
  4. DThe current time at the top, so each team can see when it ran.
Show the answer
Answer: A, B
  • A Correct. The shared part has one owner and one rate of change.
  • B Correct. A team's edit touches only its own small layer.
  • C Repeating the rules makes two copies that drift, and each team edits its own.
  • D A changing time at the top would make the shared part differ on every run.
8. A platform team reviews a reusable prompt before it is published to 40 engineers. The prompt will be read thousands of times a day and edited about once a month, and the team wants every call to reuse the same cached prefix. Select two properties that a reviewer should require.
  1. AIt is versioned, so a change has an author and can be rolled back.
  2. BIt puts the per-request details first, so the model sees the task early.
  3. CIt is as short as possible, with every rule cut to a single word.
  4. DIts stable part comes first and its per-request part comes last.
Show the answer
Answer: A, D
  • A Correct. A version gives an owner and a way back when a change goes wrong.
  • B Per-request text first changes the start of the prompt on every call, so nothing is reused.
  • C Cutting rules to a word loses the detail the model needs. Size is not the property to require.
  • D Correct. Stable first and volatile last keeps the prefix identical, which is what makes reuse and caching work.
9. A team marks a 150,000-token document as a cached prefix on a 200,000-token window and expects the cache to free the space. Each call then adds 40,000 tokens of history and asks for a 20,000-token reply, and long cases fail with a length error. The cost target is already met. What explains the error?
  1. ACached tokens still fill the window, so 150,000 plus 40,000 plus 20,000 is over 200,000 and the input must shrink.
  2. BThe cache read is slower than a fresh read, so the call times out and reports a length error.
  3. CThe reply budget is too low, so raising max_tokens to 40,000 will leave room for the reply.
  4. DA second marker after the document would stop its tokens from counting against the window.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A cache lowers the price of the prefix and not its size. Input and reply share the window, and 210,000 does not fit in 200,000.
  • B A cache read is faster than a fresh read, and a slow call does not produce a length error.
  • C A larger max_tokens asks for a bigger reply, which leaves less room for the input and makes the error more likely.
  • D A marker changes how the prefix is billed. Every token of it is still in the window.
10. A support agent's history reaches 9,500 tokens after 20 turns, and the team appends each new exchange to the system prompt, between the guardrail and the cache marker. The 7,000-token prefix read from the cache on turn 1 and has read nothing since. The reply budget is 1,500 tokens. Where should the history go?
  1. ATrim the cached prefix to make room, since it is the biggest block in the prompt.
  2. BIn the messages after the marker, with the turn, so the prefix stays identical.
  3. CAt the top of the system prompt, so the model reads the history before the rules.
  4. DRaise max_tokens, so the cache can keep the longer history from one call to the next.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Trimming the prefix changes the text that matches, so the cache misses and the savings are lost.
  • B Correct. History changes on every turn, so it rides with the turn after the marker and the prefix stays the same.
  • C Text at the top that grows each turn changes the start of the prompt, so the prefix never matches.
  • D max_tokens limits the reply. It does not decide what the cache keeps.
11. A cost report shows a cache hit rate of 12 percent, and spend is four times the forecast. The prompt has a marker, and the team has already tried making the prefix longer without effect. The first line of the system prompt holds a session id that changes on every call. What is the right next step?
  1. AMake the prefix longer still, since a longer prompt caches better.
  2. BAdd a second marker at the top, so the session id line is cached as well.
  3. CRaise the forecast to match the spend and revisit it next quarter.
  4. DMove the session id after the marker, then measure the hit rate again.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Length does not help a prefix that changes at the top, and it makes each write dearer.
  • B A marker caches the text before it, and the session id still changes on every call, so it never matches.
  • C A forecast change hides the cost and fixes nothing.
  • D Correct. The cause is the changing line inside the prefix, so the fix is the order, and the hit rate proves it.
12. A team adds a cache marker to a prompt whose first line is the request time. The cost of 10,000 calls rises from $73.92 to $91.75, and cache_read_input_tokens is zero on every call. The cost target must still be met, and the time line cannot be dropped. What does the rise show, and what is the next step?
  1. AA cache read costs more than a fresh token, so the marker comes off and the prefix stays uncached.
  2. BEvery call paid the write price of 1.25 times a fresh token and nothing read it back, so fix the order.
  3. CThe marker doubled the input tokens, so the team halves the policy text to offset it.
  4. DThe extra $17.83 is output cost, so the team lowers max_tokens and measures again.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A read costs a tenth of a fresh token. This run never read, so the premium came from the writes.
  • B Correct. A write costs more than a fresh token, and a prefix that changes on every call is written and never read.
  • C A marker adds no tokens. It only marks where the cached prefix ends.
  • D The marker changes how the input is billed. The reply is the same, so max_tokens is not the lever.
13. A team's review Skill exists, but reviewers say it is rarely picked up, and each of the 14 reviewers still pastes a prompt of their own. The Skill's description reads "Lumen helper", and about 30 reviews a week should use it. The fix must make the Skill load when a review starts, without a reviewer naming it. What should change?
  1. ACache the Skill so every reviewer's session loads it faster than a pasted prompt.
  2. BMake the body longer so it covers more cases and matches more of the requests.
  3. CRewrite the description to say when to use it, such as when reviewing a Lumen pull request.
  4. DAsk each reviewer to paste the Skill text into their own prompt as a backup.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A cache lowers the cost of a repeated prefix. It does not change whether a session loads the Skill.
  • B A session decides by the description, so a longer body does not make the Skill load more often.
  • C Correct. The description says when the Skill applies, so a review that matches it loads the same rules for everyone.
  • D Pasting is the source of the drift, and it brings back 14 copies.
14. A team's reply Skill body opens with "Today is 3 March" and names the customer, Acme, on its second line. Both are edited by hand before each use, and nine copies of the file now exist with different values. The Skill must be one file with one owner. What should the body hold?
  1. AOnly text that does not change, with the date and customer supplied in the turn.
  2. BThe date and customer as placeholders in the body, which each developer fills in by hand.
  3. COne copy of the file per customer, each with its own date, so that the values stay correct.
  4. DA link to a wiki page that holds the rules, with the date and customer kept in the body.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The body is the stable layer, so the changing values ride with the turn and one file serves every team.
  • B Filling placeholders by hand is the edit that created nine copies.
  • C A copy per customer is more copies, and each date goes stale.
  • D The rules would live on a page that nobody versions with the Skill, and the values still change in the body.

Conclusions

You can now order a prompt into layers, place a cache marker, and read the usage fields to prove a hit.


Prefix
The start of the prompt, up to the cache marker, which must match exactly to hit
Cache marker
The cache_control field that ends the cached prefix
Cache write
The first call that stores the prefix, billed at 1.25 times a fresh input token
Cache read
A later call that reuses the prefix, billed at a tenth of a fresh token
Layer
One block of the system prompt with one owner and one rate of change
Skill
One file of reusable instructions that a team loads instead of pasting
Professional, lesson 7
Prompt techniques
Add a technique only for the failure it fixes
A Lumen Supply team adds chain-of-thought to a prompt whose real fault is its output format. The replies get longer and cost nearly five times as much, and none of them parses. This lesson matches each of four failures to the one technique that fixes it, and shows what the wrong ones cost. The Lumen support assistant makes four kinds of mistake. Its triage reply does not parse, its refund sums are wrong, its tone breaks the house rules, and it sends a ticket to the wrong queue. You will run four techniques on each, read the score and the cost, and write the table that picks.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
One prompt, four different failures
A technique is one block added to a prompt: a step-by-step instruction, worked examples, an output schema, or a rubric. The model follows the prompt, and your code scores the reply, so a fix is real only when the score moves.


Three things go wrong, in this order. Chain-of-thought is used for a format fault, so cost rises and the format still breaks. Examples are missing where the format is the issue. And no table maps a failure to its technique, so each fix is a guess.


A schema fixes a format fault
Three tickets are triaged with a schema in the prompt. All three replies parse, with the exact keys and allowed values, and the three replies use 135 tokens in all. Ten thousand tickets like these cost $3.22 on Haiku.


Open a card to see the prompt and the reply for one ticket, with its tokens in and out. The score is code and not opinion: the reply must parse as one JSON object with the right keys.

The failure-to-technique table, as code
pick takes a failure and returns the technique that fixes it. A schema fixes format, step-by-step reasoning fixes logic, a rubric fixes tone, and worked examples fix routing. build_prompt adds that one block to the task and nothing else.


Thinking before the answer is a lever for reasoning faults. It costs output tokens on every call, so it is not free, and it is the wrong tool for a fault that is not about reasoning.


starter/technique.py
1"""EDIT THIS FILE. It has two planted defects.21. pick(): chain-of-thought is returned for every failure, whatever fails.32. There is no table from a failure to its technique.45Run `./workshop check prompt-techniques` until it is green, then6`./workshop watch prompt-techniques`.7"""89from kit.api import Json1011STEP_BY_STEP = (12    "Work through the problem step by step first. Then give your final "13    "reply in the form asked above."14)151617def pick(failure: str) -> str:18    """Return the technique that fixes one failure.19    The failures are format, reasoning, tone and routing.20    """21    return "chain-of-thought"222324def build_prompt(technique: str, task: Json) -> Json:25    """Return the system prompt and messages with one technique added."""26    parts = {27        "chain-of-thought": STEP_BY_STEP,28        "schema": task["schema"],29        "examples": "Worked examples:\n"30        + "\n\n".join(f"Ticket: {a}\nReply: {b}" for a, b in task["examples"]),31        "rubric": task["rubric"],32    }3334    return {35        "system": f"{task['ask']}\n\n{parts[technique]}",36        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"Ticket: {task['ticket']}"}],37    }
Does chain-of-thought fix a broken output format?
Chain-of-thought is the best known technique. It seems safe to add whenever a reply is wrong.


Predict: Does chain-of-thought fix a broken output format?
  1. ANo. A schema or examples fix a format.
  2. BYes. Thinking first helps everything.
Show the answer
A. Reasoning helps logic faults. A format fault needs a specification the model can copy.
Chain-of-thought on a format fault
This is a real Haiku 5.5 run, recorded once and replayed here. The starting pick returns chain-of-thought for every failure. On the format fault, none of the three replies parses, because the model writes its working before the JSON.


The three replies use 902 tokens, against 135 for the schema. Ten thousand tickets cost $15.77, nearly five times the $3.22 a schema costs, and the format is still broken.

Match the technique to the failure
pick reads a table from each failure to one technique. It raises an error for a failure it does not know. build_prompt is the same in both files, so only the choice of technique changed.


A task with several steps is split into separate prompts, one technique each. A checked contract sits between them, so a failure belongs to one step. An order that must hold is enforced in code, and the prompt only asks for each step.


The cost of a wrong choice is paid on every call. Chain-of-thought adds about 250 output tokens per ticket for a fault it cannot fix, and 10,000 tickets a month make that $12.55 more than the schema.


technique.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""Pick the prompting technique that fixes a failure, and build its prompt."""23from kit.api import Json45TABLE = {6    "format": "schema",7    "reasoning": "chain-of-thought",8    "tone": "rubric",9    "routing": "examples",10}11STEP_BY_STEP = (12    "Work through the problem step by step first. Then give your final "13    "reply in the form asked above."14)151617def pick(failure: str) -> str:18    """Return the technique that fixes one failure.19    A technique fixes the failure it matches. Adding another one costs20    tokens and leaves the fault in place, so an unknown failure is an error.21    """22    if failure not in TABLE:23        raise ValueError(f"no technique for failure {failure!r}")2425    return TABLE[failure]262728def build_prompt(technique: str, task: Json) -> Json:29    """Return the system prompt and messages with one technique added."""30    parts = {31        "chain-of-thought": STEP_BY_STEP,32        "schema": task["schema"],33        "examples": "Worked examples:\n"34        + "\n\n".join(f"Ticket: {a}\nReply: {b}" for a, b in task["examples"]),35        "rubric": task["rubric"],36    }3738    return {39        "system": f"{task['ask']}\n\n{parts[technique]}",40        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"Ticket: {task['ticket']}"}],41    }

The checks want a schema for a format fault, chain-of-thought for reasoning, a rubric for tone and examples for routing. A failure with no technique raises an error.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A triage step must return JSON that a parser reads, and about 1 call in 6 returns text the parser rejects. The team added chain-of-thought last week, replies grew 40 percent in tokens, and the failure rate did not change. The cost cap is fixed, and the parser cannot change. What should the team do?
  1. AAsk for even more careful step-by-step reasoning, since the model is not thinking enough yet.
  2. BAdd three more sentences to the instruction that tell the model to be careful about the JSON.
  3. CRaise max_tokens so the long replies are no longer cut off before the JSON closes.
  4. DAdd a schema with the exact keys and values, and drop the chain-of-thought.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A More thinking adds tokens and cost, and the reply still has to be parsed. The fault is the form, not the logic.
  • B Longer instructions are still prose. They do not give the model a form to copy, so the rate stays near 1 in 6.
  • C A cut-off reply is one cause, but the replies grew because of the added reasoning, and the cap is fixed.
  • D Correct. A format fault needs a form the model can copy. Without the reasoning, the replies shrink and the cost falls.
2. A refund step returns the answer in the right form every time. But 1 call in 4 gets the arithmetic wrong on orders with a discount and a restocking fee. The cost cap is tight, and the other four steps of the pipeline already pass their scores. Which change fits?
  1. AAdd chain-of-thought to every step of the pipeline, so none of them can fail later on.
  2. BAdd stepwise reasoning to the refund step only, then re-score it on the same orders.
  3. CAdd a schema for the answer line, since a wrong number is a problem with the form.
  4. DAdd two worked examples of a refund that show the final amounts and no working.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A The other steps already pass. Reasoning tokens on them are cost with no score change.
  • B Correct. Logic faults need working before the answer, and only the failing step pays for it.
  • C The form is already right. A schema cannot make the arithmetic correct.
  • D Examples with bare amounts show the form, not how to get the number, so the sums still go wrong.
3. A prompt review finds that a team added a new technique to a support prompt last sprint. The review must decide whether the technique was chosen for a named failure or only because it is popular. It has the golden-set scores and the cost per call from before and after. Select two signs that it was added without a matching failure.
  1. AThe failing cases went from 4 of 6 to 6 of 6 after the change, on the failure it named.
  2. BCost per call rose and the score on the golden set did not change.
  3. CThe reply got longer, and the review reads that as the prompt being more thorough.
  4. DNobody wrote down which failure the technique was meant to fix.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A This is the opposite sign. A named failure and a score that moves are what a matching technique has.
  • B Correct. A technique that adds tokens and moves no score is paying for nothing.
  • C Length is not quality. Longer replies cost more and say nothing about whether the fault is fixed.
  • D Correct. Without a named failure there is nothing to match, so the choice is a guess.
4. A parser reads each reply as JSON and rejects about 1 in 6. One teammate wants chain-of-thought added and another wants a schema, and replies must parse on the first try while the token cost per call does not grow. Select two reasons that favor the schema over chain-of-thought.
  1. AThe schema gives the reply a form to copy, with named keys and allowed values.
  2. BA schema makes the model think harder before it answers, so the JSON comes out cleaner.
  3. CChain-of-thought puts working before the JSON, and that text costs output tokens on every call.
  4. DA schema works only when worked examples are added to it, so the two have to travel together.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. A schema is a form the reply can copy, and it adds few tokens.
  • B A schema adds no thinking. It fixes the form, which is a different fault from the logic.
  • C Correct. Reasoning before the reply puts prose ahead of the JSON, which breaks the parse and adds tokens.
  • D A schema is one block that works alone. In the recorded runs it scored 3 of 3 with no examples.
5. A team splits a refund task into steps by writing one prompt with a numbered list of six steps. The steps depend on each other, a late step fails about 1 call in 5, and nobody can tell which step produced the bad output. Each step needs its own check. What is the better design?
  1. AMake the list longer, with more detail for each of the six steps in the same prompt.
  2. BAsk the model to repeat each step number before it answers, so that the order is visible.
  3. CSeparate steps, each with its own prompt and a contract for its input and output.
  4. DRun the same prompt three times and take the most common reply as the answer.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A More detail in one prompt makes the single call harder to check, and a failure is still not tied to a step.
  • B Repeated numbers show an order but do not check any step's output.
  • C Correct. Each step gets the technique its failure needs, and its output is checked before the next step runs.
  • D Voting costs three times as much and hides which step is wrong.
6. A numbered list in a prompt says to check the order, then the refund limit, then send the reply. In production the model sometimes sends the reply before checking the limit, 1 call in 30. The order of the steps is a hard requirement, and a wrong send cannot be undone. What fixes this?
  1. ACode enforces the order, and the prompt only asks for each step.
  2. BWrite the list in capital letters so that the order is stressed to the model.
  3. CAdd chain-of-thought so the model thinks about the order of the steps first.
  4. DAdd two worked examples that follow the list in the right order every time.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A rule that must hold is enforced in code, so the send cannot run before the check passes.
  • B Emphasis is still a request. A prompt cannot guarantee that a step ran first.
  • C Thinking about the order makes the model more likely to follow it, but not certain, and it adds cost.
  • D Examples raise the odds and still leave 1 call in 30 that does not follow them.

References
    

  • Prompt engineering overview: test first, then pick the technique that fits the failure.
    • 

  • Prompting best practices: examples, formats, rubrics and thinking in one guide.
    • 

  • Extended thinking: reasoning in its own block, apart from the reply.
    • 

  • Structured outputs: a schema the reply must fit, so a format fault cannot ship.

Conclusions
    

  • Name the failure first, then add the one technique that fixes it.
    • 

  • A schema fixes a format, steps fix reasoning, a rubric fixes tone and worked examples fix routing.
    • 

  • Read the score and the cost together: a technique that adds tokens and moves no score is a bad bet.
    • 



You can now map a failure to its technique, build the prompt for it, and prove with a score that the fix worked.


Technique
One block added to a prompt, such as steps, examples, a schema or a rubric
Chain-of-thought
An instruction to work through the problem before the final answer
Schema
The exact form of the reply: its keys and allowed values
Worked examples
Sample inputs with the reply you want, shown in the prompt
Rubric
A checklist of house rules the reply must meet
Failure
The way a reply goes wrong, named before a fix is chosen
Professional, lesson 8
The context budget
Window minus output minus thinking is your room
A Lumen Supply agent fails with a context error on a 60-turn refund case, so a developer raises max_tokens. The error comes back with a larger overage, because output and thinking take their room from the same window as the history. This lesson budgets the room, trims on a rule, and keeps the case facts in a state object. The case is 60 turns long and holds 26,982 tokens of history. The window is fixed, and input, output and thinking all share it. You will count the tokens before the call, see what a raised output limit costs, and write the two functions that fix it.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
One 60-turn case and a fixed window
The model reads only what fits in its window. Your code decides what goes in, so your code does the budget: it counts the input, reserves the output and thinking, and trims the rest.


Three things go wrong, in this order. The output limit is raised to fix a context error, which leaves less room. The history is never trimmed, so long cases always overflow. And the case facts live only in the history, so a trim deletes them.


A case that fits
The medium window holds 40,000 tokens. The output limit is 1,024 and 2,000 are reserved for thinking, so the room for input is 36,976. The history and the state object come to 27,040 tokens, so all 60 turns are sent.


Open the count card to see the number the API returned before the call was made. The reply names the order and the refund, because both are in the history and in the state object.

}

The room formula, written as code
The room for input is the window minus the output limit minus the thinking budget. Thinking tokens count toward the window, so a thinking budget is not free. The API spends them from the output limit. This lab reserves them as a line of their own on top, which can only reserve more than a call uses.


compact then keeps the newest turns that fit in 80 percent of the room. The other 20 percent is margin, because a count is exact only for the request you counted.


A turn that states a case fact carries it in a facts key, such as the order number. compact merges those keys into the state object.

1"""EDIT THIS FILE. It has two planted defects.21. room(): the window is returned whole, so output and thinking are ignored3   and raising max_tokens looks free.42. compact(): nothing is trimmed and no state object keeps the facts, so a5   long case always overflows.67Run `./workshop check context-budget` until it is green, then8`./workshop watch context-budget`.9"""1011from collections.abc import Callable1213from kit.api import Json141516def room(window: int, out: int, thinking: int) -> int:17    """Return the tokens left for input.18    `out` is the output limit and `thinking` the thinking budget.19    """20    return window212223def compact(24    turns: list[Json], space: int, size: Callable[[Json], int]25) -> Json:26    """Return the turns to send and a state object of the case facts.27    `space` is the room for input, and `size` gives a turn's tokens.28    A turn that states a fact holds it in a `facts` dict, such as29    {"order": "LS-48213"}.30    """31    return {"turns": turns, "state": {}}

Raising max_tokens makes it worse
This is a real Haiku 5.5 count, recorded once and replayed here. The starting room returns the whole window, so it ignores the 16,000 output tokens that were added. The code sends all 60 turns and does not trim.


The request needs 44,982 tokens: 26,982 of input, 16,000 of output and 2,000 of thinking. The window is 24,000, a scaled-down stand-in, so the request is 20,982 over. A real window refuses a request that goes over. The raised limit took 14,976 tokens of room from the input.

Budget, compact and keep a state object
room subtracts the output limit and the thinking budget from the window. compact keeps the newest turns that fit in 80 percent of that room. It also collects the facts from every turn into a state object.


The state object is sent in the system prompt, outside the part that is trimmed. A trim can then drop any turn without losing a fact. Sending a 27,000-token history on each of 60 turns costs $1.62 of input on Haiku, and the compacted 16,237 tokens cost $0.97.


budget.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""Budget the window: the room for input, and a compaction that keeps facts."""23from collections.abc import Callable45from kit.api import Json67SHARE = 0.88910def room(window: int, out: int, thinking: int) -> int:11    """Return the tokens left for input.12    Input, output and thinking share one window, so a larger output limit13    or thinking budget takes room from the input.14    """15    return window - out - thinking161718def compact(19    turns: list[Json], space: int, size: Callable[[Json], int]20) -> Json:21    """Return the newest turns that fit 80 percent of `space`, and a state.22    The state object holds every fact the dropped turns stated, so a trim23    never deletes a fact the case still needs.24    """25    state: Json = {}26    for turn in turns:27        state.update(turn.get("facts", {}))2829    limit = int(SHARE * space)30    kept: list[Json] = []31    used = 032    for turn in reversed(turns):33        if used + size(turn) > limit:34            break3536        kept.append(turn)37        used += size(turn)3839    kept.reverse()40    while kept and kept[0]["role"] != "user":41        kept.pop(0)4243    return {"turns": kept, "state": state}

Trim and state keeps 36 of the 60 turns, counts 16,237 tokens, and the reply still names the order and the refund. The 24 oldest turns were trimmed, and they held all six facts. The state object carried them.

Count before you call
The token count is a real API call that returns the input size before you send. The lab counts the full history once and uses that number to size each turn. It then counts the request it plans to send, and sends it only if input, output and thinking fit the window.


The same budget covers what enters the history. Rank retrieved passages and send the top few, and cut a tool result to the fields the next step needs before it is stored. Cache the unchanging prefix. Each of these cuts input tokens, which are billed on every call.
