The log failed: the log holds the customer's email and name, and no span carries a run id.
Structured spans with a run id
span keeps the run id and only the fields in its allow-list. The prompt and the reply are not in it, so they are never written. redact hashes the six personal fields, emails and phone numbers in what remains.


If a log store that holds personal data leaks, that is a breach to report, and two years of prompts is two years of exposure. Hashing before the write keeps the readable value out of the store. The hash is stable, so the same customer keeps the same tag, and the log still counts as personal data.


trace.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""One record per call, tied to its run, with personal data hashed."""23import hashlib4import re56from kit.api import Json78ALLOWED = ("tool", "ms", "status", "error", "turns", "cost_usd", "result")9PERSONAL = "name|email|phone|address|card_last4|birth_date"10FIELD = re.compile(rf'"({PERSONAL})":\s*"([^"]*)"')11EMAIL = re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+")12PHONE = re.compile(r"\b\d{3}-\d{4}\b")131415def tag(kind: str, value: str) -> str:16    """A stable stand-in: the same value always gives the same tag."""17    digest = hashlib.sha256(value.encode()).hexdigest()[:8]1819    return f"{kind}#{digest}"202122def redact(text: str) -> str:23    """Hash the personal fields, emails and phone numbers in text."""24    text = FIELD.sub(lambda m: f'"{m[1]}": "{tag(m[1], m[2])}"', text)25    text = EMAIL.sub(lambda m: tag("email", m[0]), text)2627    return PHONE.sub(lambda m: tag("phone", m[0]), text)282930def span(run_id: str, name: str, data: Json) -> Json:31    """One record: the run id, the name and only the allowed fields."""32    kept = {k: data[k] for k in ALLOWED if k in data}33    clean = {34        k: redact(v) if isinstance(v, str) else v for k, v in kept.items()35    }3637    return {"run_id": run_id, "name": name, **clean}
We doChange one setting at a time and predict.
The same input now ends well
Use the switch to run the same case with raw prompts and then with structured spans. The card marked "This is where the runs split" shows what the log held.


The raw log found 0 spans for its run id and held the email. The structured log found 5 spans and held only hashed tags. The model's answer was the same kind in both runs, so the fix is in the log.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch tracing.
Try it: logging and case
Change one setting at a time. Pick a case, then switch between raw prompts and structured spans. Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet.


In the slow case, the hook measured the shipping tool at 4,213 ms. That is one of 2 timed spans, so p95 latency for the run is 4,213 ms against a limit of 2,000 ms, and the alert fires. A mean would hide a tail like that, which is why the alert reads p95 from the spans.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch tracing.
Triage from a trace
The runbook has three checks in order: find the run by its id, read the tool spans for errors or slow calls, then read the last model call. Each check has an owner.


Here the second check finds get_shipping with a carrier timeout, so the fix starts in that tool and not in the prompt. A fault in a tool span is not cured by rewording the prompt. The same spans show the path an agent took, which is the only record of a path that code did not fix in advance.


app/runbook.py
1"""The triage runbook: three checks in order, and who owns each one."""23from kit.api import Json45SLOW_MS = 20006CHECKS = (7    ("Find the run by its id", "on-call engineer"),8    ("Read the tool spans for an error or a slow call", "on-call engineer"),9    ("Read the last model call", "agent owner"),10)111213def first_bad(spans: list[Json]) -> str:14    """The first tool span with an error or a slow call, or none."""15    for s in spans:16        if s.get("status") == "error":17            return f"{s['name']}: {s.get('error', 'error')}"1819        if int(s.get("ms", 0)) > SLOW_MS and "tool" in s:20            return f"{s['name']}: {s['ms']} ms"2122    return "none"232425def triage(spans: list[Json], run_id: str) -> list[str]:26    """Run the three checks on a log and say what each one found."""27    mine = [s for s in spans if s.get("run_id") == run_id]28    tools = [s for s in mine if "tool" in s]29    last = next((s for s in reversed(mine) if s["name"] == "model"), None)3031    return [32        f"{len(mine)} spans found for {run_id}" if mine else "run not found",33        f"first bad tool span: {first_bad(tools)}" if mine else "no spans",34        f"last model call: {last['turns']} turns" if last else "no spans",35    ]

Keep the trace useful
Derived metrics come from the spans, and this slow run shows one. Alert on p95 latency and on the error rate over a window, not on every error. A cost per run that rises while traffic is flat points at a step that grew.


A trace belongs to its feature. Review the metrics on a schedule, so drift shows up in days. When a feature is retired, retire its span writing and delete the old spans with it.

The checks want no email or personal value in a span, a run id on every span and no prompt or reply. The same value always gets the same tag, other text is left alone, and a slow call still raises the alert.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A customer reports a wrong answer from the support agent and gives the time and the order number. The log holds 12,000 prompt lines from that hour, and none carries an id that ties a run's calls together. The on-call engineer has 20 minutes before the next escalation. What should the team add first?
  1. AA run id on every span, made once per run and passed to each call.
  2. BA longer retention period for the prompt lines, so nothing is lost.
  3. CSearch by order number for now, and add run ids when the log grows.
  4. DA second copy of each prompt line in another store.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. One id per run lets the engineer pull every span of that run in one query, whatever else is in the hour.
  • B Keeping the lines longer keeps the same 12,000 lines with no way to group them into one run.
  • C An order number can sit in many runs, and waiting means the same 20 minutes on the next report.
  • D A copy of a line with no run id is still a line with no run id.
2. An agent run writes one giant log line at the end, holding the prompt, every tool result and the reply. A slow run took 9 seconds, and finding which call was slow meant reading a 40 KB line by hand. The team wants the slow call to show up at once. What should it change?
  1. AWrite the line sooner in the run, so the log is fresher.
  2. BPrint the same 40 KB line with line breaks for readability.
  3. CWrite one span per model or tool call, each with its own timing.
  4. DAdd a flag to the line that says the run was slow.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A fresher line is still one line, so the slow call stays hidden inside it.
  • B Line breaks make a debug print easier to read. A trace is a set of records that can be queried by call.
  • C Correct. With one span and one timing per call, the slow call is the span with the largest number.
  • D A flag says that a run was slow and not which call was, so the search goes on by hand.
3. A log store keeps every prompt for two years. A privacy review finds customer emails and phone numbers in 3,400 of the lines. The team may keep the logs for debugging but must stop holding those values in clear text. What is the right change?
  1. ARestrict the log store to two engineers and keep writing the same lines.
  2. BDelete the logs older than one year and keep the newer ones as they are.
  3. CAdd a banner to the log viewer that warns readers about personal data.
  4. DRedact the personal fields before a span is written, with a stable hash.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Fewer readers still leaves the data in the store, and a breach of the store exposes it.
  • B The newer logs still hold the values, and the next year of lines will too.
  • C A warning is text for a person. It removes nothing from the store.
  • D Correct. Hashing before the write means the store never holds the value, and the same value keeps the same tag.
4. A design review lists the fields every span in the order status agent must carry. The team wants any span to be found in one query and read without opening the prompt. Select two fields that every span needs.
  1. AThe run id that ties it to its run.
  2. BThe full prompt, in case a reader needs it.
  3. CThe name of the call and its duration.
  4. DThe customer's email, to find their runs.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. Without the run id, a span cannot be grouped with the others from the same run.
  • B The prompt holds personal data and is large. A span keeps only the fields it needs.
  • C Correct. The name and the duration say which call it was and how long it took.
  • D An email in a span is personal data. The run id finds the run without it.
5. An alert pages the on-call engineer on every tool error, and the agent logs about 60 of them a day, mostly short carrier timeouts that retry and succeed. The team now ignores the pages. The goal is fewer pages that still catch a real outage. What fits?
  1. AMute the alert at night, when fewer customers are online.
  2. BSend each error to a chat channel as well as the page.
  3. CPage only when the error rate over a 10-minute window crosses a limit.
  4. DRaise the retry count so fewer errors are logged.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Muting at night removes the page when an outage starts at night, and the day noise stays.
  • B A second channel carries the same 60 messages, so it adds noise and fixes nothing.
  • C Correct. A rate over a window comes from the spans, and it fires when errors climb, not when one call retries.
  • D More retries hide the errors in the log while the outage goes on.
6. After a release, the mean latency of the agent is flat at 1.1 seconds, yet customers say some answers take 10 seconds. The spans show 5 percent of tool calls now take over 8 seconds. The team needs an alert that would have caught this. Which metric should it read from the spans?
  1. AThe p95 latency of the spans, with a limit.
  2. BThe count of runs per hour.
  3. CThe mean latency, with a tighter limit.
  4. DThe size of the log files.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. One call in twenty being slow moves p95 while the mean barely moves, and p95 comes from the span timings.
  • B A run count says how busy the agent is. It says nothing about how long a call took.
  • C The mean stays near 1.1 seconds whatever limit is set, because most calls are fast.
  • D Log size grows with traffic and says nothing about how long a call took.
7. Cost per run rose 40 percent this week, from 0.005 to 0.007 dollars, while traffic stayed flat at 2,000 runs a day. Nothing in the error alerts changed. The team wants to know which step got more expensive. What should it do?
  1. AAsk the model provider for last week's invoice.
  2. BCut the answer length in the prompt and watch the total.
  3. CSwitch to a cheaper model for every call.
  4. DDerive cost per run from the model spans and compare steps week on week.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A An invoice gives a total for the week. It cannot say which step of which run changed.
  • B A guess changes one thing and may miss the step that grew, such as a third model turn.
  • C A cheaper model may fail the task, and the cost of the step that grew would stay hidden.
  • D Correct. Each model span carries its own cost, so a sum per run and a comparison by step find the change.
8. An on-call setup for the agent needs alerts that read from the spans and say something about users, not only about servers. The team has room for two. Select two metrics that come from the spans.
  1. ACPU use of the host.
  2. Bp95 latency per step.
  3. CThe number of engineers on call.
  4. DCost per run.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A CPU use is read from the host, not from a span, and it can be high with every answer fast.
  • B Correct. Each span has a duration and a name, so p95 per step is a query over the spans.
  • C Staffing is a rota, not a measure of how the agent ran.
  • D Correct. The model spans carry cost, so a sum per run is a query over the spans.
9. An on-call engineer receives a report that the agent told a customer the wrong thing at 14:05. There is no runbook, and the engineer starts by reading raw log text for the whole hour. Twenty minutes pass with no cause found. What order of checks should the team write down?
  1. AEdit the prompt, then test, then read the log.
  2. BFind the run by its id, then read the tool spans, then the last model call.
  3. CRestart the agent, then read the log if the fault returns.
  4. DRead the whole hour of logs from the first line.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Editing first changes the prompt before anyone knows the fault is in it.
  • B Correct. The id finds the run, the tool spans show where a call failed, and the last model call shows what was said.
  • C A restart clears state and may remove the evidence, and the fault can return.
  • D A whole hour holds many runs, and the first line is unlikely to be the one that matters.
10. A wrong answer is reported, and the engineer on call starts to rewrite the system prompt. The run's spans show the get_shipping tool returned a carrier timeout, and the model then guessed a status from the order alone. The engineer has spent 30 minutes on the prompt. What should have come first?
  1. AAsk the customer for a screenshot of the answer.
  2. BSwitch the agent to a larger model before changing anything else.
  3. CFind the failing span and fix or handle that tool error.
  4. DAdd a line to the prompt that says to be accurate.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A screenshot shows the answer, and the spans already hold the cause.
  • B A larger model given no shipping data would still have to guess.
  • C Correct. The fault is in a tool span, so the fix starts there, and the prompt may need no change at all.
  • D A line about accuracy cannot supply data a failed tool did not return.
11. Two engineers debug the same incident on Monday and each finds half the cause. Their notes are in two chat threads, and on Tuesday a third engineer repeats both checks. The team wants the next incident to start from shared steps. What should it keep?
  1. AA runbook with a first check, the next checks and an owner for each step.
  2. BA longer chat history, pinned for everyone to read.
  3. CA rota that puts the most senior engineer on every incident.
  4. DA weekly meeting to go over last week's incidents.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The steps run in the same order each time, and an owner for each step stops two people doing the same check.
  • B A pinned thread holds the notes of one incident and gives no order of checks for the next one.
  • C One senior engineer is a single point of failure, and the steps stay in that person's head.
  • D A review helps the team learn, and it does not tell the engineer on call what to do at 02:00.
12. A platform review checks a triage runbook for the agent before it goes to the whole on-call rota. The runbook must work for an engineer who has never seen the agent. Select two parts the runbook must have.
  1. AThe first check to run, with what a good result looks like.
  2. BThe customer's email, so the engineer can call them.
  3. CA rule that hashing the customer's fields is optional when in a hurry.
  4. DThe owner of each step, so an engineer knows who to ask.
Show the answer
Answer: A, D
  • A Correct. A first check with a known good result tells the engineer at once whether to go on or stop.
  • B The runbook works from the run id. An email in it would be personal data in a document.
  • C Hashing is not optional, and a rush is when a leak is most likely.
  • D Correct. A named owner for each step means a stuck engineer knows who to ask.
13. A team chose a fixed workflow for an order status feature, then found that the next step depends on what each tool returns. The spans of 50 runs show the path branches in four different ways. The team wants to decide whether an agent fits better. What should it use?
  1. AA vote among the engineers on which design feels cleaner.
  2. BThe prompt length as a measure of how complex the task is.
  3. CThe number of tools the feature holds as a proxy for branching.
  4. DThe spans, to count how often and where the path branches.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A vote gives a preference. The spans hold 50 runs of evidence about the path.
  • B A long prompt can drive a fixed path, and a short one can drive a branching path.
  • C Two tools can branch many ways, and ten can run in a fixed order.
  • D Correct. The spans show each call in order, so the branch points can be counted where they happen.
14. An agent chooses its own tools, so the path it takes cannot be predicted from the code. A customer disputes an answer, and the team must show what the agent did step by step. Only a trace can answer that. What must be true of the trace?
  1. AIt was switched on after the dispute, for the next run.
  2. BIt holds only the final reply, to keep the log small.
  3. CEvery model and tool call is a span under the run id, so the path can be replayed.
  4. DIt holds the prompts in clear text, so the wording is exact.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A trace switched on after the dispute has nothing about the run in question.
  • B A final reply says what was answered and not how, so the path is lost.
  • C Correct. With one span per call under one id, the path can be read in order, however the agent chose it.
  • D Clear text adds personal data and is not needed to show the path.
15. The order status agent has run in production for six months, and its spans are stored and never read. Last week a slow tool went unnoticed for 9 days until a customer complained. The team wants to catch drift sooner. What should it schedule?
  1. AA regular review of the span metrics, such as p95 latency and cost per run.
  2. BA yearly rewrite of the system prompt from scratch.
  3. CA larger log store, so spans can be kept for longer.
  4. DA rule that any engineer may mute alerts they find noisy.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A review of the derived metrics on a schedule shows a slow tool in days, before a customer does.
  • B A rewrite changes the prompt and leaves a slow tool where it was.
  • C Keeping more spans that nobody reads adds cost and does not show drift.
  • D Muting alerts hides drift. It does not look for it.
16. A feature that used the agent was retired in March, yet its code still writes 15,000 spans a day. The log store grows by 2 GB a week, and nobody reads those spans. The team wants to stop paying for them. What is the right move?
  1. ACompress the old spans and leave the writer running.
  2. BRaise the alert limit so the feature stops showing up.
  3. CSample one span in ten and keep writing the rest.
  4. DRemove the span writing together with the feature, and delete its old spans.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A Compression shrinks the cost and leaves a writer for a feature nobody uses.
  • B An alert limit has nothing to do with storage, so the growth goes on.
  • C Sampling keeps writing spans for a retired feature, at a tenth of the cost.
  • D Correct. Logging belongs to the feature, and when the feature is retired the writer and its old spans go too.
Play: predict the output
This redact step hides phone numbers by their shape.


python
PHONE = re.compile(r"\b\d{3}-\d{4}\b")
redact("Call me on 020 7946 0958 after six.")





Predict: Does the phone number reach the log?
  1. AYes. The pattern wants three digits, a dash and four digits, so it misses this one.
  2. BNo. The pattern finds the digits and replaces them.
Show the answer
A. A pattern catches only the formats someone thought of. Keep spans to an allowlist of fields, so free text never reaches the log, and test redaction on real samples.

Conclusions
    

  • Give every span the run id, a name and only the fields it needs, so a run is found in one query.
    • 

  • Hash personal data before it is written, with a stable tag, and drop the prompt.
    • 

  • Alert on a metric derived from the spans, and triage from the run id to the failing span.
    • 



You can now make an agent's log find its run and keep personal data out of it.


Run id
One id shared by every span of one run
Span
One structured record for one model or tool call
Redaction
Hashing personal data before it is written
p95 latency
The time that 95 percent of calls beat
Runbook
The ordered checks for an incident, each with an owner
Professional, lesson 13
Eval datasets
A metric is a dataset plus a rule
The Lumen Supply team reports 94% accuracy on its support agent. The number comes from 150 tickets the prompt was tuned on, so it cannot show which kinds of ticket fail. You will watch one score hide a weak slice, then split the set and score each slice with a grader that fits it.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
94% on the set we tuned on
Lumen Supply is an online electronics shop. Its agent reads a ticket and picks one action: refund, deny, escalate or ask for the order number. The eval set has 270 labelled tickets: 240 in four slices and 30 sealed for the end.


Three things go wrong, in this order. The score is measured only on the tuned tickets. No slice holds edge cases, old failures or hostile tickets, so one average hides the weak ones. And one grader scores every field, even where a rule could.


A score per slice
Claude answers all 270 tickets, and each answer is graded. The report has one line for each slice, so the weak slice shows up by name. The edge slice is red at 70%: 28 of 40 passed.


Open the edge card to see the failing tickets. The agent denied a refund of exactly $500, and denied an item delivered on day 30. The slice with 5 German tickets belongs here too, because a language is a group you can score on its own.


  1. Eval set270 tickets answered by Claude, graded by a rule
  2. Representative134 of 150 passed, 89%

      "agent chose": "deny"
    },
    {

Reported per slice. The weakest is edge cases at 60%.
Slices and graders, written as code
Two functions hold the design. slices names the kinds of ticket: representative, edge, regression and adversarial. A regression ticket is a past failure kept so it cannot return. An adversarial ticket is hostile input.


score decides who grades a row. A code grader checks what a rule can check, such as the action. A model judge grades what a rule cannot, such as tone. The starting code does neither.


starter/evalset.py
1"""EDIT THIS FILE. It has two planted defects.21. slices(): it returns one list, the tickets the prompt was tuned on, so3   one number hides the weak slices and the held-out slice is never kept.42. score(): it sends every row to the same grader, even where a rule can5   check the answer.67Four of the six tests fail at the start. The fixture test and the tone8test already pass, because the starter sends every row to the grader.910Run `./workshop check eval-datasets` until it is green, then11`./workshop watch eval-datasets`.12"""1314from collections.abc import Callable1516from kit.api import Json1718type Row = Json192021def slices(rows: list[Row]) -> dict[str, list[Row]]:22    """Split the rows into named slices and seal the held-out rows.23    The slices are representative, edge, regression and adversarial, and24    `held_out`. Each row has `kind` and `sealed`.25    """26    tuned = [27        r for r in rows if r["kind"] == "representative" and not r["sealed"]28    ]2930    return {"representative": tuned}313233def score(row: Row, grader: Callable[[Row], bool]) -> bool:34    """Return whether the agent passed this row.35    A row with field "action" has a right answer in `row["expect"]`, and36    `row["answer"]["action"]` is what the agent chose.37    """38    return grader(row)

Slices, graders and a sealed set
slices splits the rows by kind. It keeps sealed rows in a held_out list of their own. score checks an action with code and sends only tone to the grader.


Cost decides the split. A judge reads 25 rows a request, so judging all 270 rows is 11 requests. Checking the 246 action rows with code is free, and the 24 tone rows take 1 request.


Repeatability decides it too. A code check gives the same answer on every run, while a judge is a model whose score can move between runs. A judge can drift, so compare a sample of its scores with labels a human wrote.


The judge is Claude Haiku 5.5, the same model as the agent it grades, so the labels a human wrote are what keep it honest. It returns an integer from 1 to 5 as JSON held to a schema, and a row passes at 4 or more.


evalset.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""Slices, graders and a sealed set: the solution.2slices() names four kinds of ticket and keeps the sealed rows apart.3score() checks an action with code and sends only tone to a grader.4"""56from collections.abc import Callable78from kit.api import Json910type Row = Json1112KINDS = ("representative", "edge", "regression", "adversarial")131415def slices(rows: list[Row]) -> dict[str, list[Row]]:16    """Split the rows into named slices and seal the held-out rows.17    The slices are representative, edge, regression and adversarial, and18    `held_out`. Each row has `kind` and `sealed`.19    """20    found: dict[str, list[Row]] = {kind: [] for kind in KINDS}21    found["held_out"] = []2223    for row in rows:24        found["held_out" if row["sealed"] else row["kind"]].append(row)2526    return found272829def score(row: Row, grader: Callable[[Row], bool]) -> bool:30    """Return whether the agent passed this row.31    An action has one right answer, so code checks it. Tone has none, so32    the grader decides.33    """34    if row["field"] == "action":35        return bool(row["answer"]["action"] == row["expect"])3637    return grader(row)

The sealed slice
The sealed rows are 30 tickets, drawn from every slice and used once, at the end. Here they score 97% (29 of 30). Nobody tunes on them, so that is the only honest final number.


Peek at them while you tune and they stop being sealed. A slice this small moves 3 points on one ticket, so read the number as a rough check. Pre-register the rule fixes the ship rule before you see the result.

The checks want every unsealed row in one named slice and the held-out rows sealed apart. A tuned set must show the weak slice, an action is checked by a rule and tone goes to the grader.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A support agent scores 94% on the 150 tickets its prompt was tuned on, and the team ships it. A week later one refund in four fails on split orders, where the delivery date differs from the order date. None of the 150 tickets was a split order. Which change to the eval would have shown the problem before launch?
  1. ARaise the pass mark from 94% to 98% on the same 150 tickets, and block the launch below it.
  2. BRun the same 150 tickets five times and average the five scores, to remove run-to-run noise.
  3. CAdd an edge slice of split orders and other boundary cases, and report it on its own.
  4. DTune the prompt on the 150 tickets until the score reaches 100%.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A higher bar on the same tickets still measures only what the prompt was tuned on. No split order is in the set, so the score cannot move for them.
  • B Averaging repeats steadies the number and adds no new kind of ticket. The failure is a missing kind, not noise.
  • C Correct. A slice of edge cases puts split orders in the set, and a score of its own stops the 94% from hiding them.
  • D Tuning to 100% on the same tickets measures the tuning. Tickets the prompt never met stay untested.
2. A team grows its eval set from 240 to 440 rows by adding 200 more tickets of the same kind as the existing representative slice. The score stays at 94%, and refunds of exactly $500 and orders that arrived in two parcels still fail in production. What should the team add to the set next?
  1. ASlices of a new kind, such as the $500 limit and split parcels.
  2. BAnother 200 representative tickets, so that the set reaches 640 rows and the score firms up.
  3. CA model judge that reads every ticket twice and reports where its two reads differ.
  4. DAn alert that fires when production refunds fail, with the failing tickets sent to the team.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. Coverage comes from new kinds of ticket. Slices for the $500 limit and split parcels put those failures in the set.
  • B More rows of the same kind repeat what is already covered. The set grows and the odd cases stay missing.
  • C A second read by a judge changes who grades a ticket and adds no ticket to grade.
  • D An alert reports a failure after a customer met it. It is not a test the team can run before a release.
3. A refund bug was fixed in March, when the agent denied a faulty item delivered on day 30. In May a prompt change brought it back, and the 240-row eval did not notice because that ticket was never kept. The team wants the same failure caught next time, at the cost of one ticket. What should it do?
  1. AWrite the fix and its cause in the changelog so that the next editor sees it before editing.
  2. BWatch the complaint queue for denied refunds after each release and report any it finds.
  3. CHave the judge re-grade the whole 240-row set each month and flag any score that moved.
  4. DAdd the failing ticket to a regression slice that runs on every change.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A changelog line is read by people when they remember to. Nothing runs it, so the May change passes without a check.
  • B A complaint arrives after a customer is hurt. The eval should fail before the release, not after.
  • C A judge re-grading the same set finds nothing new, because the failing ticket is still not in it.
  • D Correct. A regression slice keeps each fixed failure as a ticket, so a change that brings it back turns the slice red.
4. A reviewer reads an eval plan for the Lumen support agent. It has 150 tuning tickets and a model grader, and the agent will face 3,000 tickets a day from strangers. Which slices does every eval set for this agent need besides the representative one? Select two.
  1. AEdge cases, such as a refund of exactly $500 or a delivery on day 30.
  2. BA second copy of the tuning tickets, used as the test and scored with the same grader.
  3. CAdversarial inputs, such as a ticket that tells the agent to ignore the policy.
  4. DNothing more, because a hostile slice tests only the attacker and costs more than it finds.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. Boundary tickets sit where rules meet, and a representative slice rarely holds them.
  • B A copy of the tuning tickets measures the tuning, so it cannot tell the team what the prompt misses.
  • C Correct. Customers write the tickets, so a hostile slice shows whether the agent follows the policy or the customer.
  • D Hostile input arrives in production whether it is tested or not. A slice for it is part of the set.
5. An eval scores 250 tickets with one model grader. It checks that the action is one of four allowed words and that the reply is polite. Re-running the same set moves the score between 88% and 93%, and most of the movement is on the action check. What should change?
  1. ARun the grader three times on each ticket and average the three scores for the report.
  2. BCheck the action with a code rule and keep the judge for tone.
  3. CSwitch to a larger judge model for both checks, and keep the same rubric prompt.
  4. DAsk the judge in its prompt to be stricter and to answer with the allowed word only.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Averaging hides the spread and keeps paying for a model on an exact check. The noise has a cause that a rule removes.
  • B Correct. An action is one of four words, so a rule checks it exactly and for free. The judge keeps tone, which a rule cannot check.
  • C A larger model is still a model grading an exact field, so it still costs money and can still vary.
  • D A stricter prompt changes how the judge leans, not whether it gives the same answer twice.
6. A team judges all 270 rows with a model grader at 25 rows a request, which is 11 requests on every run. Of the 270 rows, 246 have one right action that exact comparison can check, and 24 are about tone. The team needs runs that are cheaper and exact. What should it do?
  1. AJudge only every second row, and double the passed count to estimate the full run.
  2. BShorten the judge's rubric so that it reads fewer tokens on every one of the 270 rows.
  3. CCompare the 246 actions with code and send only the 24 tone rows to the judge.
  4. DSwap the judge for a larger model on all 270 rows and keep the same batch size.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A Half the rows are then never graded, so the score covers less and is still judged where a rule would be exact.
  • B A shorter rubric trims tokens and leaves the judge on rows a rule checks exactly, so the answer stays noisy.
  • C Correct. Code is exact and free for the 246 actions, and the judge handles only the 24 rows a rule cannot check.
  • D A larger judge costs more per row and still grades fields that code checks exactly.
7. A model grader replies to each row in free text, such as "mostly fine but a bit curt". The team needs a pass rate for each slice across 240 rows. Reading the sentences by hand takes hours, and two reviewers sort the same sentence into different piles. Which change fixes this?
  1. AMake the judge return an integer score from 1 to 5 for each row, and pass at 4 or more.
  2. BAsk the judge for shorter sentences, no more than ten words for each row it grades.
  3. CAdd a second judge that reads the first judge's sentences and sorts them into piles.
  4. DHave a person label all 240 rows by hand on every run, and count the labels for the report.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A schema with a score gives each row a number, so a pass rate per slice is a count and two runs can be compared.
  • B A shorter sentence is still free text, and two reviewers still read it differently.
  • C A second reader of the same sentences adds a layer and no number, and it adds its own wording to sort.
  • D A person can label a sample to check the judge. Labelling 240 rows by hand every run does not scale.
8. A reliability review looks at the model grader that scores tone on the 24 rows a rule cannot check. The grader will gate a release, its scores feed a per-slice report, and the review has to decide this week. Which two properties make this grader trustworthy? Select two.
  1. AIt gives a verdict as a long paragraph for each row, so that no detail is lost.
  2. BIt returns a structured score on a fixed scale for each row.
  3. CIt is the same model with the same prompt as the agent, so the two always agree.
  4. DIts scores are compared with labels a person wrote for a sample of rows.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A A paragraph cannot be counted into a pass rate, and two reads of it can differ.
  • B Correct. A score on a fixed scale turns each verdict into a number, so slices can be counted and runs compared.
  • C A judge with the agent's own prompt shares its blind spots, and agreeing with it proves nothing about tone.
  • D Correct. A model grader is itself a measurement, so a sample checked against human labels shows whether to trust it.
9. A prompt technique lifts the pass rate from 94% to 96% on a 270-row set. On the 40-row edge slice the rate falls from 70% to 60%, and refunds at the limit are among the new failures. The team has to decide today whether to keep the change. What should it do?
  1. AKeep it, because the overall score rose from 94% to 96%, and that is the number the team reports.
  2. BRe-run the overall score until the two-point rise is stable, then keep the change if it holds.
  3. CDrop the edge slice from the report, since it is 40 rows of 270, and keep the change.
  4. DRead the change per slice, and treat the edge drop as a regression to explain first.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A The overall figure is mostly the large representative slice. A gain there can sit next to a drop in a small slice.
  • B A steadier overall number still hides the slice that fell.
  • C Removing the slice that shows the drop makes the report look better and the agent no safer.
  • D Correct. A score for each slice shows where the technique helped and where it hurt, so the edge drop is seen and weighed.
10. A prompt change is judged on three hand-picked tickets where it works. Across 5 runs the agent's answers on a ticket differ from run to run, and the owner wants to know whether the change really helps. The eval has a 150-row representative slice, a 40-row edge slice and a sealed 30-row held-out slice. How should the team judge the change?
  1. AKeep it if any one of the three hand-picked tickets passes on the next run, since it works.
  2. BScore it on the representative and edge slices and compare the rates.
  3. CTry variants against the held-out slice until one of them wins, and keep that variant.
  4. DRun the same three tickets 50 times, count the passes, and compare that to the old prompt.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Three chosen tickets where the change works show only that it can work. They say nothing about the rest.
  • B Correct. Run-to-run variation averages out over many tickets, so a difference in rates on a large set means something.
  • C Choosing variants by the held-out score tunes on it, and then it no longer gives an honest final number.
  • D Fifty runs of three tickets measure the variation on three tickets and still miss every other kind.
11. A fairness check on 270 support tickets in two languages reports 93% overall. German tickets are at 70% and English tickets at 95%, and the overall figure hides the gap. The team has to show whether the agent serves both groups. What should it do next?
  1. ASlice the eval by language, and report each group's rate.
  2. BTranslate every German ticket to English before scoring, so that one grader reads them all.
  3. CReport the overall 93%, because it clears a 90% bar and shows no failing group.
  4. DRemove the German tickets the agent fails, and report the rate on those that remain.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A slice for each group gives each its own rate, so a gap of 70% against 95% cannot hide in a 93% average.
  • B Translating first removes the thing being measured, how the agent handles German tickets.
  • C An overall figure above a bar says nothing about the group that is below it.
  • D Deleting failures lifts the German score and leaves the agent exactly as unfair.
12. One group has 12 rows in the set and scores 75%, and a group with 150 rows scores 95%. A manager says the agent is unfair to the small group and asks for a prompt change this week. One ticket moves the small group's rate by about 8 points. What is the right response?
  1. AChange the prompt now, because 75% is below 95% and the gap is already clear to the manager.
  2. BDrop the 12-row group from the report, since it is too small to count toward the score.
  3. CSay 12 rows is too small to conclude, and add rows to that slice before acting.
  4. DCopy the 12 rows until the group has 150, so that its rate is as firm as the other group's.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A With 12 rows, one ticket moves the rate about 8 points, so the gap may be chance.
  • B Dropping the group removes the one at risk. The fix is more rows in that slice.
  • C Correct. The sample is too small to show a gap, so the honest answer is that it is unproven until the slice has enough rows.
  • D Copies of 12 tickets are still 12 distinct cases. They add no information and make the rate look firmer than it is.

You can now split an eval set into slices, pick a grader for each field and seal a final set.


Slice
A named part of the eval set, scored on its own
Edge case
A ticket at a boundary, such as exactly $500 or day 30
Regression slice
Past failures kept as tickets so they cannot return
Adversarial slice
Hostile tickets that try to move the agent off policy
Held-out set
Sealed rows used once, never tuned on
Code grader
A rule that checks an answer with no model call
Model judge
A model that scores what a rule cannot, such as tone
Professional, lesson 14
A/B tests and guard metrics
Pre-register the rule; pair every lever with its own guard metric
A Lumen Supply change cuts what the support agent costs, and accuracy falls with it. The team decides afterwards that the loss is fine. You will watch a rule written after the result ship a change that should be held back. Then you will write the rule first and give every lever its own guard metric.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
A 22% saving and a 2 point loss
Lumen Supply is an online electronics shop. Its agent reads a ticket and picks one action: refund, deny, escalate or ask for the order number.


Two changes are proposed: a cheaper tier and a shorter prompt. Each runs on the same 100 recorded tickets next to the current setup, and the customer sees none of it.


Three things go wrong, in this order. The ship rule is written after the result, so it can always be met. A lever has no guard metric, so a gain in one place hides a loss in another. And the change goes straight to all traffic with no shadow run.


A lever with one guard metric
The cheaper tier sends the same prompt to Claude Haiku 5.5 instead of the larger tier. Both answer 100 of 100 tickets correctly. The cost for 10,000 tickets falls from $3.39 to $0.17.


The rule was saved before the run: cost down at least 10%, accuracy down at most 1 point. One point is one ticket, because a wrong refund costs more than the saving. The saving is 95% and accuracy held, so the lever ships. Open a card to see the two variants in detail.

    Show the result

  "threshold": 0.1,
  "guard": 0.01
}
  2. Current setupthe larger tier, long prompt: 100% correct, $3.39 for 10,000 tickets
    Show the result

  "typical tickets": "100%",
  "edge tickets": "100%",
  "input tokens a ticket": 123,
  "output tokens a ticket (estimated)": 9,
  "missed": []
}
  3. LeverHaiku 5.5, long prompt: 100% correct, $0.17 for 10,000 tickets
    Show the result

  "accuracy": "100 of 100",
  "typical tickets": "100%",
  "edge tickets": "100%",

}
  4. DecisionShipped: saves 95% and accuracy held within the guard
Shipped: the saving is real and accuracy held.
The ship rule, written as code
rule writes down the metric, the threshold and one guard metric before anyone sees a number. The threshold is the smallest saving that counts. Guard metrics are second metrics the lever must not hurt, here accuracy. decide reads both from the saved rule and returns a verdict with its reason.


Cost is tokens times price. The current setup uses about 123 input tokens and 9 output tokens a ticket on Haiku 5.5, at $0.10 and $0.50 per million tokens. Times 10,000 tickets that is about $0.17.


Three levers cut that cost: a cheaper tier, a shorter prompt, and a cached prefix. A cached prefix bills the long policy text at a lower rate when the same text opens every request. This lab runs the first two, and each lever gets its own guard metric.


The larger tier's prices are this lab's figures, so check the pricing page before you use them. Output tokens are estimated from the reply size.


starter/ab.py
1"""EDIT THIS FILE. It has two planted defects.21. decide(): it builds its own bar from the result, so any saving clears it.32. decide(): it never reads the guard, so a lever that loses accuracy ships.45Three of the seven tests fail at the start. The fixture, the saved rule,6the boundary and the shipped lever already pass.78Run `./workshop check ab-and-levers` until it is green, then9`./workshop watch ab-and-levers`.10"""1112from kit.api import Json131415def rule(metric: str, threshold: float, guard: float) -> Json:16    """Write the ship rule before the run.17    `metric` is what the lever improves, `threshold` the smallest saving18    that counts, and `guard` the most accuracy the lever may lose.19    """20    return {"metric": metric, "threshold": threshold, "guard": guard}212223def decide(result: Json) -> Json:24    """Return whether to ship the lever, and why.25    `result` has `rule`, `baseline` and `lever`; the last two hold `cost`26    per ticket and `accuracy` as a fraction.27    """28    saving = 1 - result["lever"]["cost"] / result["baseline"]["cost"]29    late = rule("cost", saving / 2, 1.0)30    shipped = saving >= late["threshold"]31    words = "clears" if shipped else "misses"3233    return {34        "ship": shipped,35        "reason": f"the saving of {saving:.0%} {words} the bar",36    }

A rule written after the result
This is a real run on Claude Haiku 5.5, recorded once and replayed here. With the full prompt it answers 100 of 100 tickets correctly. With the shorter prompt it answers 98, and the cost for 10,000 tickets falls from $0.17 to $0.13.


Both misses are tickets with no order number that got a refund instead of a request for one. The starting decide builds its bar from the result, so any saving clears it. It never reads accuracy, so the shorter prompt ships. Over 10,000 tickets that is about 200 refunds paid with no order number.

Pre-register, guard, then decide
rule is written and saved before the run. decide reads the saved threshold and guard, and returns not-ship with the reason when its guard metric is breached. The same run now reads "guard breached: accuracy fell 2.0 points, the limit is 1.0".


Every lever needs its own guard metric. A cheaper tier needs an accuracy limit. A change that lifts accuracy needs a latency limit and a cost limit, because it can double the wait.


Fix the sample size and the rule before the run, and read the result once. A team that checks the gap each morning and ships on the first good day is peeking. Every extra look is another chance to catch a lead that is only noise.


ab.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""Pre-register the rule, then decide with the guard: the solution.2rule() is written before the run and saved in the result.3decide() reads the threshold and the guard from it, never from the result.4"""56from kit.api import Json78POINTS = 10091011def rule(metric: str, threshold: float, guard: float) -> Json:12    """Write the ship rule before the run.13    `metric` is what the lever improves, `threshold` the smallest saving14    that counts, and `guard` the most accuracy the lever may lose.15    """16    return {"metric": metric, "threshold": threshold, "guard": guard}171819def decide(result: Json) -> Json:20    """Return whether to ship the lever, and why.21    `result` has `rule`, `baseline` and `lever`; the last two hold `cost`22    per ticket and `accuracy` as a fraction.23    """24    saved = result["rule"]25    base, lever = result["baseline"], result["lever"]2627    saving = round(1 - lever["cost"] / base["cost"], 4)28    drop = round(base["accuracy"] - lever["accuracy"], 4)29    points = round(POINTS * drop, 1)3031    if drop > saved["guard"]:32        limit = round(POINTS * saved["guard"], 1)33        reason = (34            f"guard breached: accuracy fell {points} points, "35            f"the limit is {limit}"36        )37        return {"ship": False, "reason": reason}3839    if saving < saved["threshold"]:40        reason = (41            f"the saving of {saving:.0%} is below {saved['threshold']:.0%}"42        )43        return {"ship": False, "reason": reason}4445    reason = f"saves {saving:.0%} and accuracy held within the guard"4647    return {"ship": True, "reason": reason}
We doChange one setting at a time and predict.
The same input now ends well
Switch between the two rules with the same shorter prompt. The two variants score the same in both runs: 100% and 98%. The card marked "This is where the runs split" is the decision, and only the pre-registered rule holds the change back.


The data did not change. The rule did. A saving of $0.04 for every 10,000 tickets is real, and so are the 200 refunds paid with no order number. The rule says which matters more before anyone is tempted.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch ab-and-levers.
Try it: rule and lever
Change one setting at a time, and only the shorter prompt splits the two rules. The cheaper tier ships under both, because Claude Haiku 5.5 matched the larger tier on all 100 tickets. The rule written after the result shipped it without reading accuracy, so a loss would have shipped too. Every combination is recorded and works offline.


Read a small difference with care. On 100 tickets one ticket is one point, so two variants that differ by less than a point differ by less than one ticket. That is inside the noise, so add data before you name a winner.


A test of significance tells you whether a gap is real. The rule tells you whether the gap is enough.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch ab-and-levers.
Run it in shadow first
In production, a shadow run answers live tickets with both variants and sends the customer only the current one. Guard metrics are then measured on real load. This lab uses a recorded replay of 100 tickets as its stand-in. Ask what changed first asks what changed when a case flips.


Read a change per step, not as one mean. A tier change can move the mean from 96% to 95% while the review step falls from 94% to 81%. That is a breach on review, and the smaller tier ships for classify only. Read p95 and failing slices too.


When the SLA lets either latency or cost win, state the trade-off and let the owner choose. A change 40% faster that doubles the bill passes both limits, and only the owner knows what a second is worth. Record the baseline first, then show value as money per ticket against the target.

The checks want the limits read from the saved rule. A lever that breaches its guard metric or saves too little is not shipped, and a drop equal to the limit still ships.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A change cuts the support agent's cost per ticket by 22% and accuracy falls 3 points. The team looks at both numbers after the run and decides that a 3 point drop is acceptable. Next quarter they ask why the decision process let a loss through. What should the team do differently before the next experiment?
  1. AAsk a second reviewer to approve the 3 point drop once the result arrives, and log the approval.
  2. BWrite the ship threshold and the accuracy guard down and save them before the run.
  3. CLower the saving needed to ship, so that more changes pass the review.
  4. DReport cost and accuracy on one chart, so the trade-off is easier to see for the whole team.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A second reviewer who sees the result still chooses the rule after it. Any result can be defended once it is known.
  • B Correct. A threshold and guard metrics saved before the run cannot be bent to fit the result. The same drop is held back or shipped by a rule nobody tuned.
  • C A lower bar makes it easier for a lever to ship. The problem was that the bar moved after the result, not its height.
  • D A chart shows both numbers and still leaves the decision to the room. The limit must exist before the chart does.
2. A team runs a shorter-prompt test on live traffic and checks the gap every morning. On day 6 the new prompt is ahead by 2 points, so they stop and ship it. The sample grew each day and nobody wrote down when the test would end. What would have made this decision sound?
  1. AChecking the gap twice a day, so a real lead is noticed sooner and the test can stop.
  2. BRunning the test for a fixed week and shipping on the first day that the gap exceeds 1 point.
  3. CKeeping the test running while the gap stays under 3 points, then shipping when it is wider.
  4. DFixing the sample size and the rule first, and reading the result once at the end.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A More looks give more chances to catch a lead that is pure noise. The team would stop even sooner on a false win.
  • B Shipping on the first good day is still stopping when it looks good. The gap on one day can be noise, and the rule must say when the decision is read.
  • C The team would keep choosing the stopping point from the running result, which is a rule chosen after the fact.
  • D Correct. A sample size and a rule fixed first mean the result is read once, so it cannot be stopped at a lucky moment.
3. Two prompt variants each answer the same 100 tickets. Variant A gets 91.0 tickets right on average and variant B gets 91.4. The sponsor wants to ship B today because it is ahead, and the pre-registered rule asks for a gain of at least 2 points. What should the team say?
  1. AThe 0.4 point gap is inside the noise and below the rule, so more data is needed.
  2. BShip B, because any gain counts when the sponsor has asked for one and B is ahead.
  3. CShip B and watch its accuracy for a month, since a test this small is too small to hurt.
  4. DRe-run the test on the first 50 tickets, where B looks stronger, and report that result.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. On 100 tickets one ticket is one point, so 0.4 points is less than one ticket. It is noise and it misses the 2 point rule.
  • B A gain that the sample cannot show is not a gain. The rule asked for 2 points and the gap is 0.4.
  • C Shipping first and watching later skips the check the rule exists for, and puts the change in front of customers.
  • D Choosing the half of the tickets where B looks best is choosing the data after the result.
4. A reviewer reads an experiment plan for a change to the support agent. The plan names the variants and the 100 tickets and says a meeting will decide after the result, and the reviewer wants it pre-registered. Which two parts must the plan add before the run? Select two.
  1. AThe threshold, such as a saving of at least 10%.
  2. BA list of reasons the team may use to explain a disappointing result after the run.
  3. CA second metric the lever must not hurt, with its limit, such as accuracy down at most 2 points.
  4. DThe name of the person who will make the final call on the day of the meeting.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. The threshold is the smallest gain that counts, and it is written before anyone sees a number.
  • B Reasons prepared in advance to explain a bad result are a way to write the rule afterwards.
  • C Correct. That guard metric is the loss the lever may not cause, with its limit, so a saving cannot hide a harm.
  • D A named decider still decides by judgement after the result. The rule has to decide, with no room to move.
5. A shorter prompt cuts the support agent's input by 18% of its tokens. The pre-registered rule asks for a saving of at least 10% with accuracy down at most 2 points. On the 100 recorded tickets, accuracy is flat at 95 of 100, and the customer sees none of the test. What should the team do?
  1. AHold it back, because a prompt change needs a larger saving than a tier change does.
  2. BHold it back until the prompt is tested again on a different set of tickets.
  3. CShip it, because the saving clears the threshold and the accuracy guard holds.
  4. DShip it only after the shorter prompt scores above the current one.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A The rule sets one threshold for every lever. Asking for more on a prompt change is a rule nobody wrote down.
  • B The shadow run on the recorded tickets is the test the rule asked for. A second set is a new condition added after the result.
  • C Correct. The saving is 18% against a threshold of 10%, and accuracy did not fall, so both parts of the rule are met.
  • D That guard metric asks that accuracy not fall by more than the limit. It is a limit on loss, and a gain is not a second goal.
6. A cheaper tier saves 30% of the monthly bill, and the threshold was 10%. Accuracy on refund tickets falls 4 points, and the pre-registered guard allows 1 point. The sponsor says the saving is large and the loss is small, and the change would reach all traffic next week. What does the rule say?
  1. AShip it, because the saving is three times the threshold.
  2. BDo not ship it, because that guard metric is breached.
  3. CShip it for half the traffic, so the loss is cut in half.
  4. DShip it and ask the sponsor to sign off on the 4 point loss.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A saving well over the threshold does not cancel a breached guard metric. Guard metrics are separate conditions.
  • B Correct. That guard metric allowed 1 point and the loss is 4, so the rule returns not-ship however large the saving.
  • C Splitting the traffic halves the harm and still ships a change the rule refuses. It is a compromise chosen after the result.
  • D A sign-off after the result moves the limit to fit the result, which is the failure its guard metric exists to stop.
7. A team plans a change that raises the agent's accuracy by 2 points by adding a second model call to review each answer. In a trial, p95 latency doubles and exceeds the support SLA, and the bill grows too. Which two guards should be paired with this lever in the ship rule? Select two.
  1. AA latency guard, such as p95 under the SLA.
  2. BA second accuracy target, set a little higher than the first.
  3. CA cost guard, such as cost per ticket under a set limit.
  4. DOne guard metric on the number of tickets in the test.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. A second call adds wait, and a latency guard is what catches a gain in accuracy bought with a slow reply.
  • B One guard metric protects what the lever may harm. A second accuracy target is another goal for the same metric.
  • C Correct. The review call also costs more per ticket, so a cost guard stops a gain that the bill cannot carry.
  • D The size of the test belongs in the plan. It does not protect latency or cost, which is where this lever can harm.
8. A cost review asks for ways to lower what the support agent costs per ticket without changing what it is asked to do. Each lever will get its own guard metric and a shadow run before it ships. Which two levers lower cost and belong on the list? Select two.
  1. AA cached prefix, so the long policy text is billed at a lower rate.
  2. BDropping the accuracy guard, so more changes clear the rule and the review goes faster.
  3. CA smaller tier on the steps where it passes that guard metric.
  4. DShipping each change to all traffic at once, with no shadow run, to get the saving sooner.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. A cached prefix cuts what a repeated policy costs, and it still needs its own guard metric and a shadow run.
  • B Removing that guard metric makes the rule easier to pass without lowering any cost. It hides a loss rather than a cost.
  • C Correct. A smaller tier saves the most where it holds, so it is tried step by step against that guard metric.
  • D Sending a change to all traffic first skips the shadow run. That is a risk, and it lowers no cost.
9. The agent has a classify step and a review step. A smaller tier is tried on the classify step only, where accuracy holds at 97% and cost falls 60%. The review step is left on the larger tier, because it was never tried on the smaller one and a wrong review costs the shop a refund. Where should the smaller tier go?
  1. AMove both steps to the smaller tier, since it is cheaper on one of them.
  2. BKeep both steps on the larger tier until the smaller tier wins on both.
  3. CMove the review step, where a mistake costs more, to the smaller tier first.
  4. DShip the smaller tier for the classify step only.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A The test showed the smaller tier holds on classify only. Nothing was measured for review, so moving it is a guess.
  • B A lever can ship for the step where it holds. Waiting for a win on both steps gives up a saving that is proven.
  • C The review step is the one where an error costs more, so it needs proof first and is not the place to start.
  • D Correct. The smaller tier held on classify and cut its cost 60%, so it ships there and the review step stays put.
10. A tier change is judged on the mean accuracy across all steps, which falls from 96% to 95%, inside the 2 point guard. A reviewer finds that the review step fell from 94% to 81% while the easy classify step rose. The release is due on Friday. How should the team read this result?
  1. AAccept the mean, since it is inside that guard metric and the easy step improved.
  2. BRaise the limit to 3 points so that the mean is comfortably inside it, and ship.
  3. CAverage the review step with the other steps twice as heavily, and read that number.
  4. DRead the change for each step, and treat the review step's drop as a breach.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A The mean is the one number that hides the loss. Any guard metric read on it only checks the average.
  • B Moving the limit after seeing the result is writing the rule afterwards, and the review step still loses 13 points.
  • C A different weighting of one mean is still one number. It does not show which step got worse.
  • D Correct. A mean hides a step that got worse. The 13 point drop on review is a breach when the change is read per step.
11. A change speeds up one step of the support agent by 30% on average. Accuracy on the long-ticket slice, the slowest 5% of requests, falls from 92% to 80%, and p95 latency is unchanged. The mean accuracy looks flat. How should the team read this result?
  1. AAs a pass, because the mean is flat and the average is 30% faster.
  2. BAs noise, because only 5% of requests are in the slice.
  3. CAs a breach on the slice, judged per slice and not on the mean.
  4. DAs a pass, once the average latency is checked again in a week.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A flat mean can hide a failing slice. The speed-up is an average, and the tail got worse where customers wait.
  • B A 12 point drop on a slice is not noise because the slice is small. Customers in that slice meet the failures.
  • C Correct. The tail and the slice carry the harm, so its guard metric is read there and the change is held back.
  • D Checking the same average again tells the team nothing new. The loss is in the slice, which the mean cannot show.
12. A change improves latency by 40% and doubles the cost per ticket. The SLA allows either a slower reply or a higher bill, and both options are within the pre-registered guards. The team cannot say which is better without knowing what the business values. What should they do?
  1. AShip whichever variant the engineers prefer, since both pass the limits.
  2. BState the trade-off in numbers and let the owner of the budget choose.
  3. CSplit the difference by shipping to half of the traffic.
  4. DAdd a third metric that combines latency and cost, and ship on its score.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Engineers choosing by preference is a decision made after the result. The owner sets what speed or cost is worth.
  • B Correct. When both pass, the choice is a business trade-off, so the team states it with numbers and the owner picks.
  • C Half the traffic gets half of each outcome and answers nothing. It avoids the choice rather than making it.
  • D A combined score hides the trade-off inside a weighting nobody agreed. The weights are the decision.
13. A sponsor asked the team for value, and a change saves cost on the support agent. The team has the tokens used per ticket and the prices of both tiers. The sponsor reads money, not tokens, and wants the saving compared with a target. How should the team report the result?
  1. AAs the percentage drop in tokens, which is the number the model reports.
  2. BAs money saved per ticket, set against the target the sponsor gave.
  3. CAs the accuracy of the new variant, which shows the agent still works.
  4. DAs the number of tickets in the test, which shows how strong the result is.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A token count leaves the sponsor to convert it. Two tiers with the same tokens cost very different amounts.
  • B Correct. Tokens times price gives money per ticket, and the target turns it into a yes or no for the sponsor.
  • C Accuracy is protected by its own guard metric and it matters, but it is not the value the sponsor asked for.
  • D The size of the test says how much to trust the number. It is not the value of the change.
14. A project reports that a change raised accuracy by 4 points and claims it as value. The baseline was never recorded, because the old version was replaced before it was measured. A sponsor asks how anyone can know the gain is real. What should the team do on the next project?
  1. AReport the gain with a larger font and a clear chart, since the number is clear.
  2. BEstimate the old accuracy from memory and show it as the baseline in the report.
  3. CRun the new version for longer, to make the 4 points more certain for the sponsor.
  4. DRecord the baseline before any change, then report the gain against it.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A How the number is shown does not make it checkable. Without a baseline there is nothing to compare it with.
  • B A baseline written after the change is a number chosen after the result, and nobody can test it.
  • C A longer run makes the new number steadier and still has no old number to compare with.
  • D Correct. A gain is a difference, so the old figure is measured before the change, and only then is the claim checkable.

Conclusions

You can now write a ship rule, set guard metrics for each lever and read a shadow run.


Pre-registered rule
A threshold and guard metrics saved before the result is seen
Guard metric
A second metric a lever must not hurt
Lever
A change that moves cost or speed, such as a cheaper tier or a shorter prompt
Shadow run
A variant answers real tickets without reaching the customer
Baseline
The measured current setup, recorded before any claim of gain
Noise
A difference too small for the sample to show as real
Professional, lesson 15
Diagnosing a regression
Ask what changed first, then check the layers in order
Lumen Supply answers get worse after a Friday release. A developer adds rules to the prompt and the wrong answers stay. You will run 40 cases before and after a change, name the cases that flipped, and write the ladder that points at the layer to check first.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
Worse after Friday, and a prompt that grew
Lumen Supply is an online electronics shop. Its agent answers a policy question from the passage that the help centre returns for it.


The Friday release touched the layers that can break an answer: the index, the lookup tool, the model setting and the prompt. On Monday the answers are worse. A developer adds "do not make things up" to the prompt, and it grows by twelve lines of rules. The wrong answers continue.


Three things go wrong, in this order. A prompt rule is added for a fault that sits in retrieval. No baseline run exists, so nobody can say which cases flipped. And the fix is not kept as a regression case, so the fault can come back.


A baseline and a flip list
The team runs the same 40 cases before the change and after it. Before, all 40 are right. After the new index, 30 are right, and the flip list names the 10 that changed.


Open the flip list to see one case. The question is the same and the agent is the same. The passage is different, because the new index returned the retired page with the old value. The answer follows the passage.


  1. Releasea new index, built on Thursday, that also holds retired pages

  3. Run after the change30 of 40 right, 10 cases got worse
  4. Flip list10 cases named

Diagnosed: the ladder named the index, and the fix cleared 10 of 10 cases that got worse.
The ladder, written as code
A release can change several layers at once, so ladder takes the list of layers that changed. It returns the one to check first: the index, then the tool, then the model, and the prompt last.


The order follows the path of the data. A wrong passage ruins every layer after it, so the index comes first. The prompt is the easiest layer to edit, and that is why teams reach for it first.


Change one layer per run. Then a flip has one cause, and the ladder's answer can be tested.

1"""EDIT THIS FILE. It has three planted defects.21. ladder(): it names the prompt for every change, the easiest layer to edit.3   The order to check is index, tool, model, prompt: the path of the data.42. flips(): it compares nothing, so no flipped case is ever named.53. regression_cases(): it keeps nothing, so a fixed fault can return unseen.67Six of the ten tests fail at the start. The fixture, the stale index, the8empty-flips and the prompt ladder tests already pass.910Run `./workshop check diagnose` until it is green, then11`./workshop watch diagnose`.12"""131415def ladder(change: list[str]) -> str:16    """Return the layer to check first for a release that changed `change`.17    `change` lists the layers that changed: index, tool, model or prompt.18    """19    return "prompt"202122def flips(before: dict[str, bool], after: dict[str, bool]) -> list[str]:23    """Return the ids of the cases whose result changed, in sorted order.24    `before` and `after` map a case id to whether it was answered right.25    """26    return []272829def regression_cases(30    flipped: list[str], rows: list[dict[str, str]]31) -> list[dict[str, str]]:32    """Return one regression case for each flipped id, in the order given.33    A case is a dict with the row's `id`, `question` and `expect`.34    """35    return []
Where should the team look first?
Answers worsen after a release, and nobody has compared the failing cases with the last good run. The prompt is the layer a developer can edit in a minute.

A prompt rule for a retrieval fault
This is a real run on Claude Haiku 5.5, recorded once and replayed here. The starting ladder names the prompt for every change, so the team adds twelve lines of rules. The run after them is still at 30 of 40, and the same 10 cases are wrong.

  2. Baseline run40 of 40 right before the change
  3. Run after the change30 of 40 right, 10 cases got worse

Misdiagnosed: the prompt was blamed for a fault in the index, and 10 of 10 cases that got worse still fail.
Find the layer, then keep the case
ladder names the index, so the team checks the passages the agent was shown. The 10 flipped cases all got the retired page, which the new index also holds and which matches "standard" best. The lab repairs the named layer and gets 40 of 40, while naming the prompt would leave 30. A chunking change is an index change, so fix it and measure recall at 3, the share of questions with the right passage in the top 3.


flips lists the ids whose result changed. A flip can go either way. Judge flipped cases against a limit set before the run. regression_cases keeps each flipped id as its own case, so the same fault cannot return unseen.


The cost is easy to count. If a prompt try takes an hour, a day of them is eight tries that all leave the same 10 cases wrong. One run against the baseline points at the index the first time.


diagnose.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""Ask what changed first, then name the flipped cases: the solution.2ladder() checks the layers from the retrieval side down to the prompt.3flips() lists the cases whose result changed, and regression_cases()4keeps each of them as a case, so the same fault cannot return unseen.5"""67LADDER = ["index", "tool", "model", "prompt"]8910def ladder(change: list[str]) -> str:11    """Return the layer to check first for a release that changed `change`.12    `change` lists the layers that changed: index, tool, model or prompt.13    """14    found = [layer for layer in LADDER if layer in change]15    if not found:16        raise ValueError("nothing changed, so there is no layer to check")1718    return found[0]192021def flips(before: dict[str, bool], after: dict[str, bool]) -> list[str]:22    """Return the ids of the cases whose result changed, in sorted order.23    `before` and `after` map a case id to whether it was answered right.24    """25    return sorted(i for i in before if before[i] != after.get(i))262728def regression_cases(29    flipped: list[str], rows: list[dict[str, str]]30) -> list[dict[str, str]]:31    """Return one regression case for each flipped id, in the order given.32    A case is a dict with the row's `id`, `question` and `expect`.33    """34    by_id = {r["id"]: r for r in rows}3536    return [37        {k: by_id[i][k] for k in ("id", "question", "expect")} for i in flipped38    ]
We doChange one setting at a time and predict.
The same input now ends well
Switch between the two checks with the same index change. The baseline and the changed run score the same in both: 40 and 30. The card marked "This is where the runs split" is the ladder, and only the ladder points at the index.


The data did not change and neither did the agent. The habit did. A team that asks what changed reaches the fault in one run, and a team that starts with the prompt never reaches it.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch diagnose.
Try it: change and check
Change one setting at a time. The index change breaks 10 cases, the trimmed tool 12, and the pasted prompt 8. Every combination is a recorded run, so it works offline.


The model setting flipped no case here: moving the effort from medium to low left all 40 right. A model change is rarely the cause of a fault that follows a release.


To tell the layers apart, compare the passages shown. An index fault shows the wrong page, the retired "14 days" one. A tool fault shows the page cut short, so the reply is "Not specified in passage". A prompt fault shows the right page and a wrong answer, "14 days" instead of "30 days".


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch diagnose.
Keep it as a regression case
The run lists the flips, names the layer, and then keeps every flipped case with its question and expected value. After the fix it checks that each kept case is right again.


A guardrail is a check with an address puts a check at each layer, so a fault like this one fails a test on the day it appears. Until then, the flip list and the regression slice are the record of what changed.
