The checks want the ladder to check the index before the tool, the model and the prompt. Every case whose result changed is named, and each one is kept as a regression case.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. Answers from the support agent got worse after a Friday release. Accuracy fell from 40 of 40 to 30 of 40 cases, and the release also rebuilt the retrieval index on Thursday and added four lines to the prompt. The team has one afternoon and a saved baseline run. What should they do first?
  1. ARewrite the four new prompt lines, since the prompt is the layer the team can edit fastest and test today.
  2. BAdd a rule telling the agent never to answer when it is unsure, and run the 40 cases again.
  3. CRe-run the 40 cases with the old index, then compare the passages in the failing cases.
  4. DSwitch to a larger model for the afternoon and see whether accuracy returns to 40 of 40.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A The prompt is the last layer on the ladder. Editing it first can hide an index fault for a day and leave the cause in place.
  • B A rule about unsure answers does not reach a fault where the agent was given the wrong page. It answers correctly for that page.
  • C Correct. The index is the first layer that changed, so the team checks it against the baseline and reads the passages that the failing cases were shown.
  • D A larger model reads the same wrong page and gives the same wrong value. The model is rarely the cause of a fault that follows a release.
2. A developer added "do not make things up" and eleven other lines to the support prompt after answers got worse. The next run still gets 30 of 40 cases right, and the same 10 cases are wrong. Every wrong answer matches the passage the agent was given. What does this result show about the fault?
  1. AThe fault is upstream of the prompt, so check what was retrieved for those 10 cases.
  2. BThe prompt needs more rules, because 10 cases is a small number and the rules so far were too general to help.
  3. CThe agent ignores the prompt, so the next step is a model that follows instructions better.
  4. DThe 40 cases are at fault, so the 10 cases should be removed from the set and the run repeated.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The answers follow the passages, so the prompt did its job. The fault is upstream, and the passages for those 10 cases show whether retrieval found the right page.
  • B More rules add lines and leave the wrong passage where it was. The same 10 cases stay wrong because the prompt never changed what the agent was shown.
  • C The agent followed the prompt and answered from the passage. Every answer matches its passage, so it did not ignore anything.
  • D Removing failing cases raises the score and keeps the fault. The 10 cases are the evidence that points at the layer.
3. One Friday release changed the lookup tool, the prompt and the model setting together. Answers are worse, with 28 of 40 cases right against 40 of 40 on the last good run. The team wants to know which change caused it and has the same 40 cases and the old version of each layer. How should they find out?
  1. ARead the diff of all three changes, pick the one that looks riskiest and revert it.
  2. BRevert all three changes, ship the old version and leave the question of the cause open.
  3. CAdd a rule to the prompt for each symptom in the failing cases and run the 40 again.
  4. DApply the changes one at a time to the old version and run the 40 cases after each.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A guess from a diff is not a measurement. The riskiest-looking change is often not the one that flipped the cases.
  • B Reverting everything restores the old answers and teaches nothing. The same mix of changes will be shipped again later.
  • C Rules for symptoms grow the prompt and leave the cause alone. The team would not know which change was at fault.
  • D Correct. One change per run gives each flip one cause, and each run is compared with the baseline on the same 40 cases.
4. In a postmortem after a Friday incident, the index change flipped 10 of 40 cases and a fix restored all 40 after two days. The team wants the postmortem to stop the same fault from returning unseen. Which two things should the team keep from the diagnosis? Select two.
  1. AThe list of flipped cases, with each question and its expected value.
  2. BA list of the prompt rules that were tried and did not help, with the date of each try.
  3. CA regression case for each flipped case, run with every later release.
  4. DThe name of the developer who built the new index, so the team knows who to ask.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. The flipped cases are the exact evidence of what broke, and each has a question and a value that can be checked again.
  • B Rules that did not help are a record of what was tried, and they keep no fault from returning. They also add lines to the prompt.
  • C Correct. A fixed fault kept as a test fails on the day it returns, so the fix does not depend on anyone remembering it.
  • D A name may help a follow-up conversation, and it checks nothing in the next release.
5. A bad run of 40 cases shows 12 wrong answers that all say the value is not stated. The team has the run, the passage shown for each case and the raw result of the lookup tool, and only an hour before the next release. Which two things should the team read first in this bad run? Select two.
  1. AThe prompt text, line by line, for a rule that might suppress answers.
  2. BThe passage the agent was shown for each of the 12 cases.
  3. CThe accuracy of the same agent on another dataset of questions.
  4. DThe raw result of the lookup tool for one failing case.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A The prompt is the last layer to check. A rule that suppresses answers is possible, and it is the most likely reading of the symptom only after the earlier layers are cleared.
  • B Correct. The passage is the input the agent answered from. A passage without the value explains an answer that says the value is not stated.
  • C Another dataset shows how the agent does elsewhere and says nothing about these 12 cases. The evidence is in this run.
  • D Correct. The tool result shows whether the tool handed over the full passage or a cut one, which is a tool fault and not a prompt fault.
6. A trace of a failing case shows the lookup tool returned an empty result for a refund limit question. The agent then answered with a plausible dollar figure that is wrong, and 4 of the 40 cases fail in the same way. The prompt has not changed since the last good run. Where is the fault?
  1. AThe prompt, because it should forbid a guess when the tool returns nothing.
  2. BThe tool, because it handed over nothing and the agent had nothing to read.
  3. CThe model, because it should refuse instead of inventing a number.
  4. DThe dataset, because 4 of 40 is too few failures to draw a conclusion.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A rule may make the symptom rarer and leaves the empty result where it is. The tool still fails on the next question.
  • B Correct. The first wrong thing in the trace is the empty result. The agent answered without a passage, and fixing the tool removes the cause.
  • C A guess after an empty result is the symptom. The earlier layer, the tool, is the first place to check.
  • D Four failures that share a cause on the same kind of question are a pattern. Comparing with the baseline shows them as flips.
7. After the index was rebuilt, 10 of 40 answers cite a policy page that was retired in March, and each of them gives the old value. The prompt and the model setting did not change. The retired pages were added to the new index by mistake. What should the team check first?
  1. AWhether the prompt tells the agent to prefer the newest page when two pages differ.
  2. BWhether a larger model reads the two pages and picks the right value by itself.
  3. CWhether the new index still filters out retired pages when it ranks the passages.
  4. DWhether the 10 questions are phrased more loosely than the other 30.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A The agent is shown one passage, so it has no second page to prefer. The wrong page is chosen before the prompt is read.
  • B The agent never sees both pages, so a stronger model cannot choose between them. The fault happens at retrieval.
  • C Correct. The rebuilt index is the layer that changed. Without a version filter the retired page competes with the current page and can win.
  • D Wording decides which page wins only because the index has no filter. Checking the filter addresses the cause.
8. A chunking change on the index lowers recall at 3 from 95% to 80% on the 40 questions. The right passage is now missing from the top 3 results for 6 more questions. The prompt is unchanged, and answers for those 6 questions are wrong. What should the team do?
  1. AAdd a prompt rule that says to answer only when the value is in the passage, and run the 40 again.
  2. BRaise the number of passages in the prompt until the answers look right again on the 6 questions.
  3. CMove the six questions to a separate dataset and report recall on the rest of the set.
  4. DFix or revert the chunking, then measure recall at 3 on the same 40 questions.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A The rule would make the agent refuse when the value is missing, and the value is missing because retrieval lost it. The wrong answers become no answers.
  • B More passages can hide the loss on a few questions and raise cost and noise everywhere. Without a measurement the team cannot tell whether the loss was fixed.
  • C Moving the six questions away removes the evidence and keeps the fault. The recall figure would rise without any fix.
  • D Correct. The chunking is the change, so the team fixes it and measures recall again on the same 40 questions to show the loss is gone.
9. A team ships a new index and reads the score a week later. The average looks steady at 38 of 40, and nobody listed which cases changed. Support then reports 5 wrong refund answers that were right before the release. What should the team have done before shipping?
  1. AWaited a week more, so the average would settle into a clearer number.
  2. BList the flipped cases against the baseline run, and keep each fixed one as a case.
  3. CRead the average again with a second reviewer, so a drop would be seen by two people.
  4. DAdded a prompt rule for refund answers, since refunds are where the errors appeared.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Waiting gives more time for wrong answers and no better view of which cases changed. The average hides cases that flip in both directions.
  • B Correct. A list of flips against the baseline run names the 5 wrong refund answers before shipping, and each becomes a regression case.
  • C A second reviewer of the same average sees the same average. The 5 cases are visible only when the two runs are compared case by case.
  • D A rule aimed at refunds treats one symptom and leaves the index that caused it. The list of flips would have pointed at the cause.
10. A change to the lookup tool raises the average from 34 to 36 of 40 cases. The team wants to keep it. The comparison with the baseline shows that 4 cases that were right before are now wrong, and 6 cases that were wrong are now right. How should the team decide?
  1. AName the 4 flipped cases and decide against the limit written before the run.
  2. BKeep the change, because 6 cases improved and 4 got worse, and the net result is better.
  3. CReject the change, because any case that gets worse is a reason to revert.
  4. DRun the 40 cases three more times and keep the change if the average stays above 34.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The 4 flipped cases are a list a person can read, and the limit written before the run says whether they are acceptable.
  • B A net gain can hide 4 cases that matter more than the 6 that improved. The decision needs the names of the flipped cases.
  • C A rule that allows no flip would block most useful changes. The limit must be written first, so the decision is not made by reflex.
  • D More runs of the same average show that it is stable and say nothing about the 4 flipped cases.

Conclusions

You can now run a baseline, name the flipped cases and write the ladder that points at the layer to check first.


Baseline
A run of the same cases before the change, kept to compare with
Flip
A case whose result changed between two runs
Ladder
The order in which layers are checked: index, tool, model, prompt
Regression case
A fixed fault kept as a test so it cannot return unseen
Retrieved passage
The text the index hands the agent for a question
Professional, lesson 16
The safety stack
A guardrail is a check with an address
Lumen Supply gives its support agent one paragraph of rules and calls that a guardrail. A courier page asks for a customer's phone and address, and the agent sends both. This lesson wraps the agent in six checks, each with an owner, and writes down every risk and who catches it. This is the support desk at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will run three attacks against a prompt-only agent, then against six layers, and then review the risk register that names who owns each risk.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
A hostile page and a paragraph of rules
The model reads, and the layers check. A guardrail is a check somewhere in the system that can fail loudly and has a named owner. A register row names a risk, its owner and at least two independent catchers.


Three things go wrong. The guardrail is a sentence in the prompt, so it has no place to fail. The register names risks with no owner or one catcher. Only the input is checked, so an unsafe reply still reaches the customer.


Six layers around one call
The agent reads a courier page that asks for the recipient's phone and address. It writes both into its reply, ready to email to the courier. The second call, a separate Haiku 5.5 check, judges the reply unsafe. The output screen stops the reply before it is sent.


Open a card to see what each step found. The blocking layer has a name and an owner, here the security lead, so a failure has somewhere to go.

output_screen stopped it. Its owner is security lead.
The stack, written as code
A layer is a name, an owner, a reason and a test. Here is the starting file, with one layer; the six arrive in the fix. They are the input screen, the tool allow-list, the action approval, the output screen, the rate limit and the audit. Each one answers a question about one message.


A check by the model that wrote the output is not independent. A register row needs an owner and two catchers that are not the system prompt or the model.


Keep the guardrail text in the fixed part of the prompt, before the turn that changes on each call, so it can be cached. Its place does not stop an edit, so keep it in a fixed, reviewed template that tenants cannot change.


starter/stack.py
1"""EDIT THIS FILE. The only guardrail is a paragraph in the system prompt.21. layers(): returns the prompt as the only layer, and it never blocks.32. gap(): returns nothing, so a risk with no owner or one catcher passes.45Run `./workshop check safety-stack` until it is green, then6`./workshop watch safety-stack`.7"""89from collections.abc import Callable10from dataclasses import dataclass1112from kit.api import Json131415@dataclass(frozen=True)16class Layer:17    """One check: its name, who owns it, why it blocks, and its test."""1819    name: str20    owner: str21    reason: str22    test: Callable[[Json], object]2324    def check(self, ctx: Json) -> str:25        """Return the reason to block this message, or an empty string."""26        return self.reason if self.test(ctx) else ""272829def layers() -> list[Layer]:30    """Return the checks that run around the agent, in order."""31    return [Layer("system prompt", "", "", lambda ctx: False)]323334def gap(register: list[Json]) -> list[str]:35    """Return each risk with no owner or under two independent catchers."""36    return []
A rule the model has been told
The prompt says not to leak customer data and not to follow hostile instructions. The model has been told the rule, so it may seem the rule is in place.


Predict: Is a paragraph in the system prompt a guardrail?
  1. AYes. The model is told the rule.
  2. BNo. It has no address and no second catcher.
Show the answer
B. A guardrail is a check somewhere in the system that can fail loudly and be owned. A sentence the model may or may not follow is neither.
A prompt is the only guardrail
With the starting code the only layer is the prompt, and it never blocks. The agent writes the customer's phone and address into its reply for the courier, and the run ends as FOLLOWED. The second call even flags the reply as personal data.


The flag changes nothing, because no layer reads it. The same happens for the staff message and the handover note: both go out as written.


The handover note shows why. The agent is not told the note goes to a shared channel, so it keeps the address and phone for the next shift. Only the system knows where the words go.

Layers with an owner
layers returns six checks, each with an owner. gap returns every risk with no owner or fewer than two independent catchers. The output screen reads the second call's verdict, so the flag now stops the reply.


Each recorded call used about 700 to 1,000 input tokens. Six cheap checks cost far less than one customer's details sent to the wrong address, which also has to be reported.

The register as data
Each row has a risk, an owner and the layers that catch it. gap reads the table and returns four risks. Two have no owner: runaway usage and provider outage. Two have one independent catcher: abusive reply and staff code in a reply.


The gap list is what a review reads. The revised register gives every risk an owner and two catchers, and gap returns nothing.

The checks want six layers, each with an owner, and the right layer to stop each of twelve messages. The register names every risk with no owner or fewer than two catchers, and the model does not count as one.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A risk register at an online shop lists prompt injection, and its only control is one paragraph in the support agent's system prompt. In a test of 3 hostile messages, the agent followed 1 and emailed a customer's phone number to an outside address. An auditor asks for a control that can fail loudly and has an owner. What do you add?
  1. AA second paragraph in the prompt that repeats the rule in capital letters.
  2. BA line in the register that says the model has been told the rule.
  3. CA check outside the model, such as a tool allow-list, with a named owner.
  4. DA lower temperature setting so the agent follows the paragraph each time.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A More emphasis is still a sentence the model may not follow. It has no place to fail loudly and no owner.
  • B Writing that the model was told changes nothing in the run. The register needs a check that someone owns.
  • C Correct. A check outside the model can fail loudly, and its owner knows to act when it does.
  • D A lower temperature makes the output steadier, not safer. The paragraph is still the only control.
2. A support agent reads a courier web page that says to reply by email with the recipient's phone number and address. The agent has a send_email tool that can reach any address, and in a test of 3 attacks the page-driven one went out as written. The team wants the harm stopped, not only noticed. Which layer limits the tool that could send it?
  1. AAn allow-list that blocks any recipient outside the company domain.
  2. BAn audit log that records the email after it is sent.
  3. CA second model call that writes a summary of the page first.
  4. DA banner in the dashboard that tells staff to watch for hostile pages.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The allow-list is code with an owner. It refuses the outside address, whatever the page says.
  • B A log is a detective check. It shows the leak after the email has gone and does not stop it.
  • C A summary of the page is still read by a model that can be talked into acting. Nothing in code limits the tool.
  • D A banner asks people to watch, and the tool still reaches any address. It is not a check with an owner.
3. A team asks the same model that wrote a customer reply to check the reply for leaked data before it is sent. In 20 test replies, the check missed 4 that held a phone number, and the writing step had missed the same 4. The team wants a second catcher for this risk that does not share the fault. What should it be?
  1. ARun the same check twice, and send the reply when either run passes.
  2. BAsk the model to explain why it thinks the reply is safe.
  3. CAdd a sentence to the prompt that says to check carefully.
  4. DA pattern check in code for phone numbers, with its own owner.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A The same model makes the same miss, and a rule that sends on either pass is looser than a single check.
  • B An explanation comes from the model that made the miss. It is not an independent view.
  • C A sentence asks for care and adds no catcher. The 4 misses show the model does not see the fault.
  • D Correct. Code with its own owner does not share the model's blind spot, so it is an independent catcher.
4. A review board compares two controls for an agent that can email customers. One is a sentence in the prompt, and the other is a check in code that refuses outside recipients. The board wants the properties that make a guardrail count in a register. Select two properties of a good guardrail.
  1. AIt is written in the system prompt where the model reads it.
  2. BIt runs outside the model, so no reply can talk past it.
  3. CIt is long and detailed so the model has no room to misread it.
  4. DIt has a named owner who acts when it blocks something.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A A sentence in the prompt is a request. It has no place to fail loudly, so it is not a guardrail on its own.
  • B Correct. A check outside the model holds whatever the page or the user says to the model.
  • C A longer rule is still a request. Detail does not give it an address or an owner.
  • D Correct. An owner means a failure has someone to act, which is what the register records.
5. An audit of a support agent finds six controls in place, an input screen, an allow-list, an approval, an output screen, a rate limit and a log. None has a named owner. When the output screen blocked 3 replies last week, nobody looked at them. The auditor asks what to change before the next review.
  1. AAdd a seventh control, so the risk has one more check on it.
  2. BName an owner for each control, who acts on its blocks.
  3. CMove all six controls into the system prompt as rules.
  4. DReplace the controls with one stronger output screen.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A More checks with no owner add more blocks nobody reads. The 3 blocked replies show the gap is action.
  • B Correct. A guardrail is a check with an address. The owner is who acts when it fires.
  • C Rules in the prompt have no place to fail, so the six checks would become requests.
  • D One layer is one place to fail. Defence in depth keeps several, each with an owner.
6. A shop screens every incoming message for phrases such as ignore previous instructions, and it blocked 12 last month. A staff-style message with no such phrase asked the agent for a customer's phone number, and the agent replied with it. The team wants a second layer that would have stopped this reply. What is it?
  1. AAn output screen that reads each reply for phone numbers.
  2. BA longer list of hostile phrases in the input screen, updated weekly.
  3. CA weekly report of the replies that went out.
  4. DA note in the prompt that staff messages may be fake.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The message had no hostile phrase, so only a check on the reply sees the phone number.
  • B The message had no phrase to find. A longer list still checks only the input.
  • C A report is read after the reply has gone. It does not stop this one.
  • D A note in the prompt is a request the model may not follow, with no owner and no place to fail.
7. A register row says staff code in a reply has one catcher, the output screen, and it has an owner. Last month a pattern change made the screen miss a code in 2 of 30 replies, and nothing else noticed. The reviewer wants the row to meet the rule for a risk. What does the row need?
  1. AA second line in the prompt that tells the model to hide codes.
  2. BA note that the owner will watch the screen more closely.
  3. CA rule that the screen is checked by the model that wrote the reply.
  4. DA second independent catcher, such as a log search for codes.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A prompt line is a request, so it is not a second catcher. It cannot fail loudly.
  • B The row already has an owner. Watching more closely is not a second check that works while the owner sleeps.
  • C The model that wrote the reply shares its blind spot, so it is not independent.
  • D Correct. Two independent catchers mean one failing silently, as the screen did in 2 of 30, does not leave the risk open.
8. A design review asks which two of the proposed layers belong in the stack for an agent that can send email. The team has room for a tool allow-list, an output screen, a longer system prompt and a note that the model should be careful. Select two layers of a safety stack.
  1. AA tool allow-list that refuses outside recipients.
  2. BA longer system prompt with more rules.
  3. CAn output screen that reads each reply before it is sent.
  4. DA note in the handbook that the model should be careful.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. It is a check in code with an owner, and it limits what the tool can do.
  • B More rules in the prompt are still requests. They have no address and no second catcher.
  • C Correct. It reads what would reach the customer, so it catches what the input screen cannot see.
  • D A handbook note asks people to be careful. It does not run, so it cannot block anything.
9. A moderation call flags 3 of 3 attack replies as personal data, but the agent sends all 3 because no layer reads the flag. The desk sends 2,000 emails a day, about 1 in 200 is flagged, and a flagged reply may wait up to 4 hours. The team wants each flagged message decided before the send. Which design does that?
  1. ALog the flag so a weekly report counts it.
  2. BAsk the moderation model to try again until it says safe.
  3. CHold each flagged reply for a named reviewer before it goes.
  4. DLower the number of flags by loosening the moderation prompt.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A report counts the leaks after they went out. It is a detective control and stops nothing.
  • B Retrying until the answer is safe removes the warning and lets the send through.
  • C Correct. The flag now has an address. A named reviewer decides within the 4 hours, before the email goes, and 10 a day is a load one person can carry.
  • D Fewer flags do not make fewer leaks. They hide the signal the stack needs.
10. A stack has an approval step before any email leaves, and 40 emails waited last week. No one is named as the approver, so 9 of them sat for two days and a few were released by whoever was free. The reviewer wants the layer to count in the register. What should the team do?
  1. ALet the approval lapse after 4 hours, so a stuck email sends itself.
  2. BName the approver, and keep an independent check beside it.
  3. CLet the model approve its own emails when it is confident.
  4. DApprove every email in bulk at the end of the week.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A timeout that releases the email turns the layer off whenever it is slow. The fix is an owner, not a way around the layer.
  • B Correct. A layer needs an owner who acts, and a second independent check covers the day the owner misses.
  • C The model that wrote the email shares its blind spot, so its approval is not independent.
  • D A weekly bulk approval has no owner who reads each one, so the risk stays open.
11. A shared agent keeps its guardrail text in the cached start of the prompt, so every tenant reads it and the cache saves cost. One tenant edits its copy to remove a rule, and 2 of 5 tenants now run a different guardrail. The security lead wants the guardrail to stay the same and reviewed. What do you do?
  1. ARepeat the guardrail in each user turn, so an edit to one copy is outvoted.
  2. BTurn off the cache so each call reads a fresh prompt.
  3. CAdd a second copy of the guardrail at the end of the prompt.
  4. DKeep it in a fixed, reviewed template that tenants cannot change.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A tenant can edit the turn as easily as the prefix, and a repeated request is still a request with no owner.
  • B The cache is not the fault. A fresh prompt still carries whatever text a tenant edited.
  • C A second copy of text the tenant can edit is still editable, and still a request.
  • D Correct. A fixed template with a reviewer means a tenant's edit cannot change the guardrail.
12. A team puts the guardrail text after the user turn, which changes on every call, so the cached start is rebuilt each time and costs more. In 50 calls, the guardrail was read last and 3 replies ignored it. The team wants the guardrail stable and cheap. Where should it sit?
  1. AIn the fixed start of the prompt, before the changing turn.
  2. BAfter the user turn, repeated three times.
  3. CIn a separate system message sent after the user turn, marked as high priority.
  4. DIn the user turn, so it changes with each request.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A fixed guardrail before the changing turn can be cached and reviewed, and it does not move.
  • B Repeating it after the turn still changes the end of the prompt on every call and adds a request, not a check.
  • C A message after the user turn still moves on every call, so the cached start is rebuilt, and a priority label is a request.
  • D Putting it in the turn means it changes with each call, which breaks the cache and the review.
Play: predict the output
The input screen looks for the usual override phrases.

  2. BYes. The message asks the agent to ignore its rules.

A. A phrase list stops only the phrasing someone wrote down. That is why it is one layer of six: the allowlist and the output screen still stop the email.

Conclusions

  • A flag from a classifier does nothing until a layer acts on it.

You can now wrap an agent in layers that each have an owner, and review a register for gaps.


Guardrail
A check outside the model that can fail loudly and has an owner
Layer
One check in the stack, such as an input screen or an allow-list
Independent catcher
A second check that does not share the first one's failure
Risk register
A table of risks, each with an owner and its catchers
Professional, lesson 17
Human approval
A yes for $640 that paid $6,400
A Lumen manager approves a $640 refund, and the agent then refunds $6,400 on a different order without asking again. The agent rated itself 0.9 sure, so the gate never looked at the approval, and that approval covered the whole session anyway. This lesson binds a yes to one exact call, gives it an expiry, and reads the agent's confidence through labelled outcomes. This is the support desk at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch a self-rated score and an approval for a session pay the wrong refund, then fix the gate in code the model cannot talk past.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
One yes, three ways to misuse it
The model proposes a refund. A callback pauses the call before it runs. A human says yes, and the gate checks that the yes fits this exact call.


Three things go wrong, in this order. An approval covers the session, so a different action rides on it. An approval never expires, so a stale yes is used days later. And the agent's own confidence score routes decisions, though nobody has checked it against labels.


An approval that fits one call
The manager approved the $640 refund on order O-1004, and asks the agent to process it. The agent reads the order, then proposes the refund with a confidence of 0.9. The labels do not back that score, so the gate hashes the call, finds that it matches the approval, and lets it run.


Open the gate card to see the two hashes side by side. They are equal, so the refund is paid. The agent held only the read tool in its list, so the refund tool reached the gate through the callback.


  1. ManagerThe manager approved the $640 refund on order O-1004 this morning. Please process it.
  2. Agentcalls: get_order, process_refund
  3. Gateapproval for 0c37f726882…, call is 0c37f726882…
    Show the result
    {

    "hash": "0c37f726882c8796",
    "by": "Maya Chen",
    "expires_at": "2026-10-01T10:30",
    "session": "S-1"
  },
  "call": "0c37f726882c8796"
}
  4. AgentThe $640 refund on order O-1004 (4K monitor) is processed. The order amount matched your approved figure.
Refund paid: refund O-1004 for $640.
The binding, written as code
Two functions hold the binding. action_hash names a call, and valid checks an approval against it. The starting action_hash names only the session, and valid says yes to any call in that session.


The fix hashes the tool name and every argument, and leaves the model's confidence out. valid then needs a matching hash and a call made before the expiry. A mismatch is refused with a reason the agent can read.


starter/approve.py
1"""EDIT THIS FILE. An approval covers a whole session, and trusts a score.21. valid(): any call in the same session passes, whatever it asks for.32. needs_approval(): skips the gate at a confidence of 0.9 or more.45Run `./workshop check human-approval` until it is green, then6`./workshop watch human-approval`.7"""89from kit.api import Json1011SURE = 0.9121314def action_hash(call: Json) -> str:15    """Return a name for the call. The start names the session instead."""16    return str(call["session"])171819def valid(approval: Json, call: Json) -> bool:20    """Return True when this approval covers this call right now."""21    return bool(approval["session"] == call["session"])222324def needs_approval(call: Json, table: list[Json]) -> bool:25    """Return True when a person must say yes before the call runs."""26    return float(call["confidence"]) < SURE
Does a yes for one refund cover a second, larger refund?
The manager has approved one $640 refund and is watching the desk. The agent now proposes a $6,400 refund on another order.


Predict: Does a yes for one refund cover a second, larger refund?
  1. AYes, the manager is already engaged.
  2. BNo, approval binds to the exact action.
Show the answer
B. An approval is for one call. A hash of the call turns that into a check in code instead of a hope that the manager is still looking.
An approval for the whole session
This is a real Claude Haiku 5.5 run, recorded once and replayed here. The agent read order O-1008, a $6,400 server rack, and proposed a full refund with a confidence of 0.9.


The starting gate skips a human at 0.9 or more, so it never checked the approval. Open the gate card: the approval covers the session, so it would have matched too. Either defect alone pays this refund.


The agent said the refund was done. The result card is red, because $6,400 left the shop on a $640 yes.


  1. ManagerThe manager approved a refund this morning. Please refund order O-1008 in full.
  2. Agentcalls: get_order, process_refund
  3. Gateskipped: a score of 0.9 let the call through, so the approval was never checked. The session approval would have matched too.
    Show the result
    {
  "approval": {
    "hash": "S-1",
    "by": "Maya Chen",
    "expires_at": "2026-10-01T10:30",
    "session": "S-1"
  },
  "call": "S-1"
}
  4. AgentOrder O-1008 (server rack) has been refunded in full: $6,400.00.
Refund paid: refund O-1008 for $6,400.
Hash the call, expire the approval
action_hash hashes the tool and its arguments. valid compares that hash with the one on the approval and checks the time against the expiry. The solution run proposes the same $6,400 refund at 0.9. The labels do not back that score, so the gate checks the approval and refuses it with "approval does not match".


A wrong refund of $6,400 on a $640 yes costs $5,760 in error. One extra minute of review costs far less.


approve.pygreen lines are what the fix adds

The model's own score is not one."""14    args = {15        k: float(v) if isinstance(v, int | float) else v16        for k, v in call["args"].items()17    }18    raw = json.dumps([call["tool"], args], sort_keys=True)1920    return hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]212223def valid(approval: Json, call: Json) -> bool:24    """True when the hash matches and the approval has not ended."""25    same = approval["hash"] == action_hash(call)2627    return bool(same and call["at"] <= approval["expires_at"])282930def needs_approval(call: Json, table: list[Json]) -> bool:31    """A person must approve, unless a small call has a proven confidence."""32    bucket = [33        r["right"]34        for r in table35        if r["confidence"] == round(call["confidence"], 1)36    ]37    proven = bool(bucket) and sum(bucket) / len(bucket) >= MIN_ACCURACY38    small = call["args"].get("amount", 0) <= SMALL3940    return not (proven and small)

With the bound approval, the score is read through labels, the two hashes differ, and the refund is refused. The ask, the agent and the order are the same in both runs. Only the gate changed.

Change one setting at a time. Pick the approval, then the call. Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet.


With the approval for the session, every call was paid, because the agent rated each one 0.9 and the score skipped the gate. With the bound approval, the Monday call has the right hash but is refused as expired, and the agent asks for a fresh yes.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch human-approval.
Read confidence through labels
The starting needs_approval skips the gate at a confidence of 0.9 or more. On the labelled set, 10 answers were reported at 0.9, and 6 were right. That is 60 percent, so the score is not accuracy.


The fix reads the labelled accuracy for the reported confidence. It skips the gate only where that accuracy is at least 0.95, and only for a small refund of $100 or less. A score with no labels never skips. The same habit applies to an eval: a score over everyone can hide a group where it fails.


A reported 0.9 lands in the 0.9 group. The 1.0 group is right 6 of 6, few labels to trust, so the skip is capped at $100. Once a score skips the human, label a sample of skipped calls from each group, so a drifting group shows early.

The start names the session instead."""16    return str(call["session"])171819def valid(approval: Json, call: Json) -> bool:20    """Return True when this approval covers this call right now."""21    return bool(approval["session"] == call["session"])222324def needs_approval(call: Json, table: list[Json]) -> bool:25    """Return True when a person must say yes before the call runs."""26    return float(call["confidence"]) < SURE

The checks want an approval to fit only the call it was given for, and to end at its expiry. A confidence skips the gate only when labels prove it, and only on a small call.


Check your understanding
Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. A support manager at an online shop approves a $640 refund on one order. Minutes later the agent refunds $6,400 on a different order and the gate lets it through, because the approval was stored as a yes for the whole session. The team must fix this cause, not add a review of the result. What should the approval be bound to?
  1. AThe manager's name, so only that manager can approve a refund.
  2. BThe session id, with a shorter session so the yes ends sooner.
  3. CA hash of the tool name and every argument of the one approved call.
  4. DA daily limit on total refunds, so a large one is caught by the total.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A named approver says who said yes, not what they said yes to. A $6,400 call still rides on the $640 yes.
  • B A shorter session still covers every call inside it. The approval needs to name the call, not the window.
  • C Correct. The hash changes when the amount or the order changes, so the second refund no longer matches.
  • D A daily limit is a compensating control. It reacts after the money moves and does not bind the yes to a call.
2. An agent at an online shop is about to refund a $640 order. The approval on file was given on Monday for the same call, and today is Thursday. The hash still matches the call, but the gate must not use a yes from three days ago. Which property of the approval stops this?
  1. AAn expiry time the gate compares with the time of the call.
  2. BA longer hash, so a changed order is more likely to be noticed.
  3. CA note in the prompt that asks the agent to check the date.
  4. DA weekly report that lists the approvals older than one day.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The gate refuses when the call is later than the expiry, however well the hash matches.
  • B The hash already matches. A longer hash cannot tell that the yes is old.
  • C The model may not follow the note, and the stale yes still passes in code. The check must be in the gate.
  • D A report finds old approvals after the refund has run. It does not stop the call.
3. An auditor reviews the approval gate of a refund agent. The agent proposes calls, a human says yes, and the gate runs the call. The auditor lists what makes an approval safe to rely on for a $640 refund, with 300 approvals a week shared by 4 managers. Select two properties that an approval that binds must have.
  1. AIt is stored in the session, so it follows the manager across calls.
  2. BIt covers one exact call, named by a hash of the tool and arguments.
  3. CIt is confirmed by a second yes in the same chat window.
  4. DIt expires, so a later call cannot use it.
Show the answer
Answer: B, D
  • A A session-wide approval lets a different call ride on it. That is the failure the binding removes.
  • B Correct. A hash of the tool and every argument means a changed amount or order no longer matches.
  • C A second click is more of the same checkbox. It still does not say which call was approved.
  • D Correct. An expiry means a Monday yes cannot be used on Thursday.
4. A refund agent skips human approval whenever it rates its own answer 0.9 sure. A labelled set of 10 answers reported at 0.9 shows 6 were right, which is 60 percent. The team wants to keep some automatic approvals so reviews stay affordable. What should it do before any score skips approval?
  1. ARaise the cutoff to 0.95 without checking labels, since higher is surer.
  2. BKeep the 0.9 cutoff, and send a refund to a human when a customer complains.
  3. CAsk the model to explain its confidence in each reply.
  4. DCheck each score against labelled outcomes before it may skip.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A higher number is still a self-rating. Without labels there is no evidence it means 95 percent.
  • B A complaint arrives after the money moves, and 4 in 10 calls at 0.9 are wrong and still skip the gate.
  • C An explanation is more words from the same model. It is not a measurement against labelled answers.
  • D Correct. The table says what each score really means, and only a bucket that is right often enough may skip.
5. A refund gate skips approval for small calls where the measured accuracy at the reported confidence is high. An auditor wants controls that keep this safe over time, because the labelled set was drawn last quarter and today's calls may differ. Select two things the approval control needs.
  1. AA named approver for every call that does go to a human.
  2. BA bigger prompt that lists the refunds the agent may skip.
  3. CA reviewed sample of skipped calls from each confidence group.
  4. DA monthly review of the calls the agent itself marked as wrong.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. A named approver means the yes has an owner who can be asked why.
  • B A list in the prompt is a request the model may not follow. It also does not check the skipped calls.
  • C Correct. A sample drawn by stratum catches a bad calibration early, including in buckets with few calls.
  • D Sampling only what the agent flags misses the confident errors, which are the ones that skip the gate.
6. A refund agent calls a tool that pays $640. The team adds a gate that logs the call and asks a manager to confirm, but the gate runs after the payment is made. Last week 2 of 10 calls reached the wrong order and the manager could only report them. Where should the gate sit to prevent the loss?
  1. AAfter the write, with a faster alert to the manager.
  2. BBefore the write, so a refused call never runs.
  3. CAfter the write, with a second tool that reverses the refund.
  4. DBefore the write, but only for calls the model rates under 0.9 sure.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A faster alert is a detective control. The money has already moved when the manager reads it.
  • B Correct. A gate before the write is preventive, and a refused call leaves the order untouched.
  • C A reversal is a compensating control. It costs a second action and may fail after the customer has the money.
  • D The score is not calibrated, so skipping on it lets the wrong calls run with no one asked.
7. A manager approves a refund of $640 on order O-1004, and the hash matches the call. The agent runs the tool with its own broad rights, and the order belongs to a customer the signed-in manager's team does not serve. A reviewer asks why the approval did not catch this. What is the missing control?
  1. AA longer approval window, so the manager can look at the order first.
  2. BA second approval from the same manager on the same call.
  3. CAn owner check in the tool that refuses the wrong caller.
  4. DA prompt line that tells the agent to read the owner before it refunds.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A longer window makes the yes live longer. It does not check whose order it is.
  • B The same manager saying yes twice adds a click, not a different check.
  • C Correct. The tool checks the owner in code, so a yes for the call does not widen what the caller may touch.
  • D A prompt line is a request. A model can skip it, and nothing in code refuses the call.
8. A team stores each approval as a line in the conversation so the agent can read it. In a test of 5 turns, a later message told the agent to treat an expired approval as current, and the refund of $640 ran. The team needs an approval store the model cannot change. Where should approvals live?
  1. AIn a store the model cannot write, read by the gate on each call.
  2. BIn the system prompt, with a warning that approvals cannot be edited.
  3. CIn the tool result, so the model reads it after every call.
  4. DIn a signed message in the chat, so a later message cannot forge it.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The gate reads the record from code, so a message in the chat cannot change what was approved.
  • B A warning is a sentence the model may not follow, and a later message can still talk past it.
  • C Text the model reads can be paraphrased or misread. The gate must read the record, not the model.
  • D A signature proves who wrote the line, but the model still reads and reports it. The gate must read the record itself.

Conclusions

    • 

  • Give every approval an expiry, and check it in the gate.
    • 

  • Read a self-rated confidence through labelled outcomes before it skips a human.

You can now bind an approval to one action, expire it, and calibrate a score before it routes a decision.


Human in the loop
A human says yes to a specific action before it runs
Action hash
A name for the tool and every argument of one call
Expiry
The time after which an approval no longer counts
Calibrated confidence
A score checked against labelled outcomes at each level
Professional, lesson 18
Compliance and fairness
A policy that says data stays home
Lumen sells in three regions, and the legal team asks whether personal data leaves the region. Nobody has drawn where a ticket goes, and the agent scores 92% overall, which hides a group at 78%. This lesson turns regulation into a data-flow map and fairness into an eval sliced by group. This is the compliance desk at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will watch an analyst answer from a map that lists only the shop's own services, then fix the map and the eval.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
Where does a ticket go, and who does it fail?
The model is one hop among many. A ticket passes through the form, the gateway, a queue, the agent, a database, and vendors that nobody drew. Each hop has a region and a class of data.


Three things go wrong, in this order. Nobody has drawn the flow, so a hop that leaves the region is invisible. Fairness is claimed from one overall score. And the claim that data stays home lives in a policy line, with no check in the system behind it.


A data-flow map
The analyst asks one question: does personal data leave the home region? It loads the system description, then calls hops. The map lists all eleven hops, each with its kind, region and data class.


Open the hops card. One row is flagged: the model provider, which holds personal data in the US while the home region is the EU. The flag is computed from the data, not typed in by hand.

Hops and gaps, written as code
Two functions hold the work. hops walks the system description, and gap_by_group scores the labelled rows by group. The starting hops keeps the services and drops the vendors and the provider.


The fix lists every hop with its region, and flags a hop that carries personal data out of the home region. A gap on a small group is reported with its sample size, never waved off as noise.

The start lists services only."""14    return [15        {**h, "flagged": False}16        for h in system["hops"]17        if h["kind"] == "service"18    ]192021def gap_by_group(rows: list[Json]) -> Json:22    """Return the accuracy per group and the largest gap between groups."""23    right = sum(r["answer"] == r["label"] for r in rows)2425    return {"overall": round(right / len(rows), 3)}

Map every hop, slice by group
hops now lists all eleven hops and flags personal data outside the home region. The same question gets a different answer, because the provider is on the map with its region.


A flagged hop is a decision: move it, or accept it. Under GDPR, accepting a US hop needs two things. One is a data processing agreement, the contract that lets a vendor handle personal data for you. The other is a transfer basis, the legal reason the data may leave the region, such as standard contractual clauses.


Health data under HIPAA needs a business associate agreement, and US federal work needs a FedRAMP authorised provider.


The eval gets the same treatment. Tamil is 36 of 180 rows, 20% of the tickets, at 78% accuracy. English is 97%, a gap of 19 points, and 14 points below the overall 92%. A 14 point gap on 20% of tickets is a real cost, and one targeted fix is cheaper than a failure found by a regulator.


flow.pygreen lines are what the fix adds
1"""A map of every hop, and an eval sliced by group with its sample sizes."""23from kit.api import Json45PERSONAL = "personal"678def hops(system: Json) -> list[Json]:9    """List every hop, and flag personal data that leaves the home region."""10    home = system["home"]1112    return [13        {**h, "flagged": h["data"] == PERSONAL and h["region"] != home}14        for h in system["hops"]15    ]161718def gap_by_group(rows: list[Json]) -> Json:19    """Score each group, and name the largest gap with the sample sizes."""20    seen: dict[str, list[int]] = {}2122    for r in rows:23        count = seen.setdefault(r["group"], [0, 0])24        count[0] += r["answer"] == r["label"]25        count[1] += 12627    scores = {g: right / n for g, (right, n) in seen.items()}28    worst = min(scores, key=lambda g: scores[g])29    best = max(scores, key=lambda g: scores[g])30    overall = sum(c[0] for c in seen.values()) / len(rows)3132    return {33        "overall": round(overall, 3),34        "groups": {35            g: {"accuracy": round(scores[g], 3), "n": seen[g][1]} for g in seen36        },37        "worst": worst,38        "best": best,39        "gap": round(scores[best] - scores[worst], 3),40    }

With own services only, both concerns are missed, since the eval returns one number too. With the full map and the slices, both are named. A control in a document is a claim, and a control in the flow is a fact.

Slice the eval by group
The starting gap_by_group returns one number. The fixed version returns the accuracy and the row count for each group, then the worst group, the best group and the gap. The tool returns Tamil at 78% on 36 rows and English at 97% on 72. The recorded reply names both groups and a gap of 0.194, but not the row counts.


The sample size sits beside every number. With 36 rows, a gap of 19 points is far more than chance, so it is a finding, not noise. If a model judge or grader scores the rows, check it against human labels for each group first, or its own bias shows up as a gap.

Answer each question, then read why every option is right or wrong. The wrong options are the mistakes engineers make on the job.


1. The legal team at an online shop asks whether personal data from EU customers leaves the EU. Support tickets pass through a form, a gateway, a queue, an agent, a database and two vendors, and nobody has drawn the path. The team has 3 days to answer. What should it produce first?
  1. AA list of every hop a ticket takes, with the region and the data class of each.
  2. BA paragraph that says all data stays in the EU, signed by the head of support.
  3. CA log alert that fires when a request leaves the EU, after the request has already been sent.
  4. DA shorter retention period, so less data is held in any region.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. The map shows each hop and its region, so a hop that leaves the EU can be seen and flagged.
  • B A signed statement is a claim. It does not show where any hop sits, so it cannot be checked.
  • C An alert after the request has left is a detective control. The legal question is where data goes, which needs a map.
  • D Less retention reduces exposure but does not say whether data leaves the region at all.
2. A policy document at an online shop says personal data stays in the EU. An engineer reads the system and finds the model provider runs in the US, and no one listed it as a hop. Legal wants the policy to be true by Friday, and the audit is next week. What closes the gap?
  1. AAdd the provider to the map with its region, flag the hop, then move it or accept it.
  2. BAdd a line to the policy that says the provider is trusted and has signed a contract that covers privacy.
  3. CMove the policy into the system prompt, so the agent refuses to send data abroad.
  4. DAsk the provider to send a monthly email that confirms where the data is held for the shop.
Show the answer
Answer: A
  • A Correct. A flagged hop makes the gap visible. Accepting it then needs a data processing agreement and a transfer basis, recorded as a decision.
  • B A line in a policy changes the document, not the flow. The US hop still holds personal data.
  • C The agent does not choose where the provider runs. A prompt line cannot move a hop, and the US hop still holds the data.
  • D An email after the fact is detective. The map is where the hop is listed and flagged in the first place.
3. A regulator asks an online shop for evidence that EU personal data does not leave the EU. The team has a 10 page policy and no diagram, and eleven systems touch a ticket. The regulator wants something it can check line by line. What should the team hand over?
  1. AThe 10 page policy, with the sections about data highlighted and a cover note from the head of legal.
  2. BA data-flow map with one row per system, giving its region and the class of data it holds.
  3. CThe model provider's ISO 27001 certificate and its security report.
  4. DA count of how many tickets were handled in the EU last month.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A A policy says what should happen. The regulator asks for evidence of what does happen.
  • B Correct. One row per system with a region and a data class can be checked line by line, and a gap shows.
  • C A certificate says the provider runs a security programme. It does not say which region holds the EU data or list the other hops.
  • D A count of tickets says how many were handled, not where each hop ran.
4. An auditor reads the data-flow map of an online shop that has eleven hops in three regions. The map should let her find any hop that moves personal data out of the home region without reading the code. Select two facts the map must list for each hop.
  1. AThe region where the hop runs, so a hop outside home can be found.
  2. BThe name of the engineer who wrote the hop.
  3. CThe class of data the hop holds, such as personal data or metrics.
  4. DThe number of tickets the hop handled last week.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. The region says where the data sits, and a region other than home is the thing to find.
  • B An author says who to ask, not where data goes.
  • C Correct. Metrics may leave a region where personal data may not, so the class decides the flag.
  • D Volume is useful for cost, but it does not say whether the hop breaks residency.
5. A support agent at an online shop scores 92% on 180 labelled tickets, and the board wants to say it serves every customer well. The rows cover three languages, the smallest group has 36 rows, and the board meets in a week with no budget for a new labelling round. Which step shows a problem the overall score could hide?
  1. ARaise the overall target to 95% and run the eval again, so the board sees a higher number.
  2. BAdd 100 more English rows, so the average is more stable.
  3. CSlice the eval by group, and report the accuracy and the row count of each.
  4. DAsk the model whether it treats every language equally.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A A higher target on the same number still averages the groups together.
  • B More rows for the largest group move the average toward it and hide the smallest group further.
  • C Correct. The slice shows each group's accuracy beside its row count, so a weak group the 92% averaged away can be seen.
  • D The model does not know its own accuracy by group. The eval measures it.
6. A sliced eval of an online shop's agent finds a group with 12 rows at 67% accuracy, against 95% for the largest group. A product manager says 12 rows is too few and the gap is noise, so no action is needed. The report goes to the board on Friday, and labelling more rows takes a week. What is the right response?
  1. ADrop the group from the report until it has more rows, because a small group is not worth a finding.
  2. BReport the gap with its sample size of 12, and add rows for that group before concluding.
  3. CMerge the group into the next largest group, so every slice has at least 30 rows.
  4. DTreat the gap as proven and retrain the model on that group.
Show the answer
Answer: B
  • A Dropping a group hides it, and a group with few rows is the one most likely to be served badly.
  • B Correct. The sample size is shown beside the gap, and more rows turn a signal into a finding.
  • C Merging hides the small group inside a bigger one, and the gap is averaged away again.
  • D 12 rows is a signal, not proof, and a retrain without more data may fix nothing.
7. The vendor of an online shop's support agent says the model is neutral across languages, and the team plans to repeat that to its customers. No eval by group exists, and the 180 labelled rows are on hand. The launch is in 2 weeks. What should the team do before it makes the claim?
  1. AQuote the vendor's statement and name the vendor as the source.
  2. BSet a flag in the model settings that turns on equal treatment.
  3. CAdd a line to the prompt that tells the agent to treat every language alike.
  4. DBuild a sliced eval on the labelled rows, and publish the accuracy by language.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A quoted statement is the vendor's claim. The team's own system still has to be measured.
  • B No setting makes a system fair. Fairness is a measured property of the whole system.
  • C A prompt line is a request. The eval shows whether the agent follows it for each language.
  • D Correct. Neutrality is a claim to test, and the sliced eval on the rows already held tests it.
8. A fairness review at an online shop finds that the agent scores 97% for English and 78% for Tamil. The reviewer must write the finding so the board can act on it and a later reviewer can check it, and the report must fit on one page. Select two things to report with the gap.
  1. AThe accuracy of each group, so the size of the gap and who it hurts is clear.
  2. BThe overall score alone, since it summarises everything.
  3. CThe sample size of each group, so the strength of the evidence is clear.
  4. DA note that the gap is probably noise, to avoid alarm.
Show the answer
Answer: A, C
  • A Correct. The two accuracies show who is served worse and by how much.
  • B The overall score is what hid the gap in the first place.
  • C Correct. The row count behind each score shows how strong the evidence for the 19 point gap is.
  • D Calling it noise without a sample size is a guess, and it is what small-group-is-noise gets wrong.
9. An online shop scores its agent's answers with a model judge, and the fairness report says every language group is within 2 points. Nobody has compared the judge's scores with human labels, and the judge reads English best. The report goes to the board next week. What should the team check first?
  1. AWhether the judge is a larger model than the agent.
  2. BWhether the judge prompt is shorter than 200 words and lists the scoring steps in order.
  3. CWhether the overall score has risen since last month.
  4. DWhether the judge agrees with human labels.
Show the answer
Answer: D
  • A A larger model may still score one language worse. Only labels per group show that.
  • B Prompt length does not say whether the judge treats a language differently.
  • C A rising overall score can still hide a falling group.
  • D Correct. A judge that is stricter or looser in one language skews the gap, so it is checked against labels per group.
10. An automatic grader at an online shop gives Tamil answers 71% and English answers 90% on rows that humans rated about the same. The team wants to use the grader to track fairness each week. It has 40 human-rated rows per language and one week before the first report. What should it do?
  1. AUse the grader as it is, and note the Tamil gap as a finding about how the agent serves that language.
  2. BAverage the two languages into one score, so the grader's bias cancels and the board sees one clear number.
  3. CTest the grader on each group against the human ratings, and fix it before using it to measure the agent.
  4. DSwitch the grader off and rely on the overall score.
Show the answer
Answer: C
  • A The humans rated the answers the same, so the gap is the grader's, not the agent's.
  • B Averaging hides the gap, and the grader is still wrong for one language.
  • C Correct. The human ratings show the grader is stricter on Tamil, and fixing it first makes the measure fair.
  • D The overall score is the number that hid the gap, so it is not a safer fallback.

Professional, lesson 19
Decision records
One decision, two documents: an ADR and a memo
Lumen Supply picked a model tier and a retrieval design in a chat thread, and six months later nobody can say why. A new team lead asks for the reasons, the alternatives and the way back, and the answer is a search through messages. This lesson writes the decision down twice, once for the engineers and once for the sponsor. This is the support desk at Lumen Supply, an online electronics shop. You will read a decision thread and see a checker accept a memo with no cost figure and no time to undo the change. Then you write the ADR and a checker that scores each section.
I doWatch the failure and its fix.
A decision nobody can explain
A decision record is read by someone who was not in the room. An architecture decision record, an ADR, holds the context, the options, the decision, the consequences and the rollback in one place.


A memo is the one page a sponsor reads before approving the spend. The model drafts the memo, the checker scores it, and the team owns the decision.


Three things go wrong. The decision lives in chat, so its reasons and alternatives are lost. One document serves the sponsor and the engineers, so it suits neither. And no implementation guide or rollback plan sits beside the decision.


An ADR and the memo drawn from it
The model reads the ADR, drafts a memo for the sponsor, and asks the checker to accept it. The ADR holds three options and the one chosen: the small tier with hybrid retrieval, the top 5 passages. It cuts the cost from 6 cents to under 1 cent a ticket, about 500 dollars a day at 10,000 tickets.


Open a card to see the draft. The memo opens with the outcome, the cost and the ask. It then gives the risk and the rollback: one config change, about 10 minutes, with a trigger of wrong answers above 12 in 100.


  1. ReaderWrite the memo the sponsor approves the spend from.
  2. RecordRead the ADR

The memo can be acted on: it has every section.
The memo checks, written as code
A memo is for a decision maker, and an ADR is for the next engineer. The memo needs five sections: the outcome, the cost, the ask, the risk and the rollback. A check on each one is a rule the model cannot talk past.


The starting check_memo accepts any text with a title. A memo that gives no cost figure, or no time to undo the change, passes.


starter/memo.py
1"""EDIT THIS FILE. check_memo() accepts any memo that has a title.2A memo with no cost and no rollback passes. Run3`./workshop check decisions-and-handoff` until it is green, then4`./workshop watch decisions-and-handoff`.5"""678def check_memo(text: str) -> list[str]:9    """Return the sections that are missing or too weak to act on.10    An empty list accepts the memo. The sections are outcome, cost, ask,11    risk and rollback.12    """13    return [] if text.lstrip().startswith("# ") else ["title"]
Is a chat thread a decision record?
The thread has forty messages. Priya, Marcus and Dana weigh the options, quote the numbers and agree on the small tier. Every reason is in there somewhere.


Predict: Is a chat thread a decision record?
  1. ANo. Nobody can find or trust it later.
  2. BYes. It holds every reason.
Show the answer
A. A record names the context, the options, the decision and the rollback in one place. A thread holds the reasons in no order, with the cost and the rollback missing.
The decision lives in chat
The model reads the thread and writes a memo for a new team lead. The checker accepts it, because it has a title. Judged by the real checker, the cost and the rollback are too weak to act on.


The memo says the small tier "is cheaper than the big tier", with no figure. Its How to Undo section says the time and the steps "are not recorded", and its trigger has no number. Nobody wrote either down in the thread. The new lead reads a confident page with the answer missing.


  1. ReaderWrite the memo a new lead needs: why, and how to undo it.
  2. RecordRead the thread

Accepted, but it cannot be acted on: cost, rollback.
Two documents, one checker
check_memo returns the sections that are missing or too weak: the outcome, the cost, the ask, the risk and the rollback. Each part is found by the words in its heading, so "How to Undo" and "Rollback" get the same verdict. A refused draft goes back to the model with the sections to fix.


A section is weak when it is a few words or says nothing was recorded. The cost needs a money figure, and the rollback needs a time and a trigger. The ADR carries both, so the model has something to say.


The arithmetic is plain. Rebuilding a lost reason takes a week of asking around, and writing it down takes an hour.


memo.pygreen lines are what the fix adds. file: 64 lines
1"""Score a memo: name each section that is missing or too weak to act on."""23import re45# A section is found by any of the headings a writer might give it, so a6# rename from "How to Undo" to "Rollback" does not change the verdict.7NAMES = {8    "outcome": ("outcome", "decision", "summary", "what changed"),9    "cost": ("cost", "spend", "saving"),10    "ask": ("ask", "approv", "request", "next step"),11    "risk": ("risk", "could go wrong", "downside"),12    "rollback": ("rollback", "roll back", "undo", "revert", "way back"),13}14SECTIONS = tuple(NAMES)15HEADING = re.compile(r"^#{2,3}\s*(.+?)\s*$", re.M)16EMPTY = re.compile(17    r"^\W*(none|tbd|n/a|unknown)\b|\bnot (stated|recorded|discussed|decided"18    r"|mentioned)\b|\bno [\w ]{0,20}(plan|recorded|mentioned)\b",19    re.I,20)21MONEY = re.compile(r"\$\s?\d|\b\d[\d,.]*\s*(cents?|dollars?)\b", re.I)22TIME = re.compile(r"\b\d+\s*(minutes?|hours?|days?)\b", re.I)23TRIGGER = re.compile(r"\b(if|when|once|trigger\w*)\b", re.I)24MIN_WORDS = 6252627def sections(text: str) -> dict[str, str]:28    """Split a memo into its sections: heading to body."""29    marks = list(HEADING.finditer(text))30    ends = [m.start() for m in marks[1:]] + [len(text)] * bool(marks)3132    return {33        m.group(1).lower(): text[m.end() : end].strip()34        for m, end in zip(marks, ends, strict=True)35    }363738def body_of(found: dict[str, str], name: str) -> str:39    """Every section whose heading names this part, joined."""40    hits = [b for h, b in found.items() if any(w in h for w in NAMES[name])]4142    return "\n\n".join(hits)···4 lines not shown47    A section is weak when it is a few words or says nothing was recorded.48    The cost needs a money figure; the rollback needs a time and a trigger.···1 line not shown50    found = sections(text)51    weak = []5253    for name in SECTIONS:54        body = body_of(found, name)55        thin = len(body.split()) < MIN_WORDS or EMPTY.search(body)56        no_figure = name == "cost" and not MONEY.search(body)57        no_when = name == "rollback" and not (58            TIME.search(body) and TRIGGER.search(body)59        )6061        if thin or no_figure or no_when:62            weak.append(name)6364    return weak
We doChange one setting at a time and predict.
The same input now ends well
Switch the record for the new team lead. With the chat thread, the memo is accepted and cannot be acted on. With the ADR, the checker refuses a draft with no size for the outcome, then one with no cost figure. The third is accepted: its rollback takes about 10 minutes, triggered by wrong answers above 12 in 100.


The decision did not change. Only the record did: the ADR holds the figures and the chat thread does not. The checker scores sections, not facts. This draft works out about 14 wrong answers in 100 from the ADR figures, and nothing checks that sum, so a human still reads the memo.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch decisions-and-handoff.
Try it: record and reader
Change one setting at a time. Pick the record, then the reader. Every combination is a recorded run, so this works with no internet.


An implementation guide sits beside the ADR, with steps and an owner. With the ADR, the sponsor's memo is accepted at once. The engineer's first draft has no risk section and is refused; the second adds one and is accepted. The new lead's memo is refused twice, for the outcome and then the cost, and the third draft is accepted.


This part is interactive in the lab: run ./workshop watch decisions-and-handoff.
The implementation guide
The ADR has a guide that lists the steps in order. Each step names an owner, and a check says whether the change did what the ADR promised. A guide with no owner has nobody to call when a step fails. Enforce in managed settings and hooks ships it to the team.


The ADR also has a life after launch. It names a review date, 12 March, and an owner, Priya, who compares the measured outcome with the promise. A record that is never reviewed cannot be corrected when the numbers drift.


A reversed decision is never deleted. The new ADR marks the old one superseded and links back, so a later reader sees what was tried. The lifecycle plan also covers the end: retiring the agent names an owner, a date and what happens to the stored tickets.


app/records.py
1"""The decision record the lab grades: the sections of an ADR.23An ADR has five sections and an implementation guide. The guide lists the4steps, an owner for each step, and a check that the change did what the5ADR said.6"""78import re910SECTIONS = ("context", "options", "decision", "consequences", "rollback")11HEADING = re.compile(r"^#{2,3}\s*(.+?)\s*$", re.M)12OWNER = re.compile(r"\(owner:\s*\w+", re.I)13MIN_WORDS = 614MIN_STEPS = 3151617def sections(text: str) -> dict[str, str]:18    """Split a markdown record into its sections: heading to body."""19    marks = list(HEADING.finditer(text))20    ends = [m.start() for m in marks[1:]] + [len(text)] * bool(marks)2122    return {23        m.group(1).lower(): text[m.end() : end].strip()24        for m, end in zip(marks, ends, strict=True)25    }262728def guide_problems(body: str) -> list[str]:29    """Name what an implementation guide lacks: steps, owners, a check."""30    steps = [x for x in body.splitlines() if re.match(r"\d+\.", x.strip())]31    found = []3233    if len(steps) < MIN_STEPS:34        found.append("steps")35    if len(OWNER.findall(body)) < len(steps) or not steps:36        found.append("owner")37    if not re.search(r"^check:", body, re.I | re.M):38        found.append("check")3940    return found414243def check_adr(text: str) -> list[str]:44    """Return the ADR sections that are missing or too thin to use."""45    found = sections(text)46    weak = []4748    for name in SECTIONS:49        body = next((b for h, b in found.items() if name in h), "")50        if len(body.split()) < MIN_WORDS:51            weak.append(name)5253    guide = next((b for h, b in found.items() if "guide" in h), "")5455    return weak + guide_problems(guide)
